```bash
  --form "description=Token used by deploy jobs"

# Group variables use /groups/:id/variables, instance variables /admin/ci/variables
curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups/678/variables" | jq '.[].key'
```

Settings variables are not visible to developers in the repository. They can still be **read by any job** that receives them, which means by anyone who can change `.gitlab-ci.yml` on a branch that receives them. Protection (section 5.2) restricts which branches receive them.

**Key takeaways**

- Project, group and instance variables are stored in settings, not in the repository, and are inherited down the hierarchy.
- Define a value once at the highest scope that genuinely shares it, and no higher.
- Project variables need Maintainer, group variables need Owner, instance variables need an administrator.
- Anyone who can edit the pipeline on a branch can read every variable that branch receives.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a group variable `COMPANY_NAME` and a project variable `TEAM_NAME` in one of the group's projects. Print both from a job.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a script that reads a local `vars.json` file (key, value, protected, masked, scope) and creates or updates project variables through the API. Make it idempotent: running it twice must not fail.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Forty projects need the same deploy credential. Where do you define it, and how do you limit the blast radius if one project's pipeline is compromised?" *Hint:* compare one group variable with per-project credentials, protected variables and environment scopes.

#### Variable Precedence

**Why it matters.** The same name is often defined in several places: a global default in the YAML, an override in project settings, a value typed into the Run pipeline form. When jobs behave differently than the YAML suggests, the reason is almost always precedence. Knowing the order lets you predict the value instead of guessing.

**What it is.** When several sources define the same variable, GitLab uses the value from the source with the highest precedence. From highest to lowest:

| Rank | Source |
|---|---|
| 1 | Variables from pipeline execution policies and scan execution policies (only for jobs the policy adds) |
| 2 | Manual job variables, entered when running a manual job |
| 3 | Pipeline variables: Run pipeline form, schedules, Pipelines and Triggers APIs, the `ci.variable` push option, variables passed from an upstream pipeline |
| 4 | Project variables |
| 5 | Group variables (the closest subgroup wins among nested groups) |
| 6 | Instance variables |
| 7 | Variables from `dotenv` reports of jobs in `needs` or `dependencies` |
| 8 | `.gitlab-ci.yml` variables: `rules:variables`, then job `variables`, then `workflow:rules:variables`, then top-level `variables` |
| 9 | Deployment variables |
| 10 | Predefined variables |

Inputs (section 5.3) are not variables and are not part of this order.

An analogy: the YAML is the printed schedule, project settings are the notice pinned on the board, and pipeline variables are the announcement made over the loudspeaker today. The most immediate source wins.

```yaml
variables:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"                    # rank 8 (top-level)

test:
  variables:
    LOG_LEVEL: "debug"                 # rank 8 (job), beats top-level
  script:
    - echo "LOG_LEVEL=$LOG_LEVEL"
```

```text
Defined:                                     test prints:
YAML only                                    LOG_LEVEL=debug
+ project variable LOG_LEVEL=warn            LOG_LEVEL=warn    (settings beat YAML)
+ Run pipeline with LOG_LEVEL=trace          LOG_LEVEL=trace   (pipeline variable beats settings)
```

Two consequences cause most surprises:

- A **project variable overrides YAML**, even job-level YAML. A forgotten project variable can override a carefully reviewed YAML change.
- **Pipeline variables override almost everything**, including project variables that hold configuration. That is why the **Minimum role to use pipeline variables** setting (**Settings > CI/CD > Variables**) exists. Its options are `no_one_allowed`, `owner`, `maintainer` and `developer`. `no_one_allowed` is the default for new projects in new namespaces on GitLab.com, and `maintainer` on self-managed. Users below the minimum get "Insufficient permissions to set pipeline variables".

**Key takeaways**

- Policies and manual job variables rank highest, followed by pipeline variables and then settings variables (project, group, instance).
- Settings variables override every YAML variable. `dotenv` variables override YAML variables but not settings.
- Within the YAML: `rules:variables` > job `variables` > `workflow:rules:variables` > top-level `variables`.
- Restrict pipeline variables with the minimum role setting, and prefer typed inputs for user-supplied values.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Define `COLOR` at top level, at job level and as a project variable. Predict the printed value, run the job, then delete the project variable and run again.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a `dotenv` report that sets `COLOR` in a build job and have a test job `needs` it. Determine experimentally where `dotenv` sits relative to job-level YAML and project variables.
> 3. **Interview question:** "After a merge, a job uses `TIMEOUT=30` even though the reviewed YAML says `TIMEOUT: \"300\"`. Nobody ran the pipeline manually. Where would you look?" *Hint:* list every source above the YAML in the precedence order and check each one, including groups higher up.

#### Variable Expansion

**Why it matters.** Variables often reference other variables: `IMAGE_TAG: "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA"`. Such a reference can be expanded at three different points, by three different programs with different rules. Knowing which one handles a keyword explains why `${VAR}` works in one place, `%VAR%` in another, and why some references stay unexpanded.

**What it is.** "Expansion" means replacing `$NAME` with its value. There are three mechanisms:

| Mechanism | When | Syntax supported | Keywords |
|---|---|---|---|
| GitLab | Pipeline creation, before the runner gets the job | `$VAR`, `${VAR}`, `%VAR%`, on every OS. Nested references expanded recursively | `environment:name`, `environment:url`, `include`, `tags`, `rules:changes`, `rules:exists`, `variables` (first pass) |
| Runner | When the runner prepares the job | `$VAR`, `${VAR}`. One pass only | `image`, `services:name`, `cache:key`, `artifacts:paths`, `variables` (second pass for what GitLab could not expand) |
| Shell | While `script` runs | Whatever the shell supports: `$VAR` in bash/sh, `$env:VAR` in PowerShell, `%VAR%` in cmd | `before_script`, `script`, `after_script` |

`rules:if` is special: it compares variables in its own expression language and must use the `$VAR` form.

```text
.gitlab-ci.yml                     GitLab                       Runner                      Shell
environment: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG ──> review/feature-x
image: node:$NODE_VERSION          (left for runner) ─────────> node:20.15
script: echo "$CI_JOB_ID"          (passed through) ──────────> (passed through) ─────────> echo 554433
```

```yaml
variables:
  BASE_URL: "https://api.example.com"
  HEALTH_URL: "${BASE_URL}/health"            # expanded by GitLab: refers to another YAML variable
  PRICE: "costs $$5"                          # $$ escapes: the value is "costs $5"

deploy-review:
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG          # GitLab expansion
    url: https://$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG.review.example.com
  image: alpine:$ALPINE_VERSION               # runner expansion (project variable ALPINE_VERSION)
  script:
    - curl -fsS "$HEALTH_URL"                 # shell sees the already expanded value
    - BUILD_STAMP=$(date +%s)                 # shell variable, exists only in this script
    - echo "built at $BUILD_STAMP"
  artifacts:
    paths: ["out/$BUILD_STAMP/"]              # does NOT work: script-defined variables never reach keywords
```

Some job-level predefined variables, such as `CI_JOB_ID`, `CI_JOB_TOKEN` and `CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD`, are **persisted variables**. They are known only when the job starts. They expand in runner- and shell-expanded places, but not in GitLab-expanded keywords or in `rules`. In `environment:name`, for example, `$CI_JOB_ID` would not be expanded.

To use a value computed in `script` in a keyword such as `artifacts:paths` or `cache:key`, write it to the file named by `$GITLAB_ENV` (supported by recent runners for these keywords), or to a `dotenv` report for later jobs (section 5.3).

**Key takeaways**

- GitLab, the runner and the shell expand variables at different times with different syntax.
- GitLab-expanded keywords (`environment`, `include`, `tags`) cannot use job-only (persisted) variables.
- Runner expansion runs a single pass, so deeply nested references can stay unexpanded.
- Variables created in `script` do not reach keywords. Use `$GITLAB_ENV` or `dotenv` reports for that.
- Write `$$` for a literal dollar sign in YAML values.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Define `A: "one"`, `B: "$A-two"` and `C: "$B-three"` as YAML variables and print `C`. Then define `B` as a project variable instead and compare the output.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build an `image` reference from two project variables (`REGISTRY_HOST` and `BUILDER_TAG`) and an `environment:name` from `CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG`. Then try `$CI_JOB_ID` in `environment:name` and explain the result using the mechanism table.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A Windows job uses `%BUILD_DIR%` successfully in `environment:url`, but the same syntax fails in `image`. Why?" *Hint:* compare the syntaxes supported by GitLab's expansion and the runner's expansion.

<a id="52-variable-types-and-protection"></a>
### 5.2 Variable Types and Protection

Settings variables carry attributes that change how they are delivered and who can see them. This subchapter covers file-type variables, the three visibility levels (visible, masked, hidden), protected and environment-scoped variables, and the raw versus expanded behavior.

#### File-Type Variables

**Why it matters.** Many tools do not read credentials from an environment variable. They expect a **path to a file**: `kubectl --kubeconfig`, `gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file`, `curl --cacert`, SSH with `-i`. Writing a multi-line secret to disk by hand with `echo` is clumsy and error-prone, because quoting and newlines get mangled. File-type variables do this for you.

**What it is.** A file-type variable has a key, a value and a file. When the job starts, the runner writes the value to a temporary file inside the job's build directory, and the environment variable named by the key contains the **path** to that file, not its content. The file is removed when the job finishes.

```text
Settings: KUBECONFIG_PROD (type File) = "apiVersion: v1\nclusters: ..."

In the job:
  $KUBECONFIG_PROD  ->  /builds/acme/shop.tmp/KUBECONFIG_PROD     (a path)
  cat "$KUBECONFIG_PROD"  ->  apiVersion: v1 ...                   (the content)
```

```yaml
deploy:
  image: bitnami/kubectl:1.30
  script:
    # kubectl expects a path, and the file variable already is one
    - kubectl --kubeconfig "$KUBECONFIG_PROD" get nodes
    # Many tools read KUBECONFIG directly: point it at the file
    - export KUBECONFIG="$KUBECONFIG_PROD"
    - kubectl apply -f k8s/

call-internal-api:
  script:
    # INTERNAL_CA_CERT is a File variable containing a PEM certificate
    - curl --cacert "$INTERNAL_CA_CERT" https://internal.example.com/health
```

Rules and caveats:

| Topic | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Where they can be defined | Project, group and instance settings, or the API (`variable_type=file`). Not in `.gitlab-ci.yml` |
| Assigning to another variable | `KUBECONFIG: $KUBECONFIG_PROD` in YAML passes the path, which is usually what you want |
| Need the content, not the path? | Read it: `TOKEN="$(cat "$MY_FILE_VAR")"` |
| YAML-only workaround | Write the content to a file in a script step, for example `printf '%s' "$CERT" > ca.pem` |
| Docker services | The path exists only in the job container, not inside service containers |

```bash
# Create a file-type variable from a local kubeconfig through the API
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/variables" \
  --form "key=KUBECONFIG_PROD" \
  --form "variable_type=file" \
  --form "value=<~/.kube/prod-config" \
  --form "protected=true"                       # the < prefix makes curl send the file's content as the value
```

**Key takeaways**

- A file-type variable delivers a **path** to a temporary file holding the value.
- Use them for tools that take a file: kubeconfigs, certificates, service account keys, SSH keys.
- They can be defined only in settings or the API, not in the YAML.
- Use `cat` when you need the content, and never print the file in the log.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a file-type variable `SAMPLE_CONFIG` with three lines of text. In a job, print the variable, then print `wc -l "$SAMPLE_CONFIG"`, and explain the difference.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Store an SSH private key as a file-type variable and use it to `ssh` into a test host with strict host key checking enabled. Pay attention to the file permissions SSH requires.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is a file-type variable usually safer and more reliable than `echo \"$KEY\" > key.pem` with an ordinary variable?" *Hint:* think about quoting, trailing newlines, shell history and accidental `set -x` output.

#### Masked Variables

**Why it matters.** Job logs are widely visible: every project member with access to pipelines can read them, and in public projects possibly anyone. One debugging `echo $TOKEN` or a verbose tool printing its configuration can leak a credential to all of them. Masking is a safety net that replaces known secret values in the log.

**What it is.** When a variable is **masked**, the runner scans the job log and replaces every occurrence of the value with `[MASKED]`. The value still reaches the job unchanged. Only the log output is filtered.

A value can be masked only if it meets these requirements:

- A single line, with no spaces.
- At least 8 characters.
- It does not match the name of an existing predefined or custom variable.
- If "Expand variable reference" is enabled, the only allowed non-alphanumeric characters are `_ : @ - + . ~ = /`. With expansion disabled, any character can be used.

GitLab rejects the masked setting if the value does not qualify.

```yaml
debug-oops:
  script:
    - echo "Token is $API_TOKEN"               # log shows: Token is [MASKED]
    - echo "$API_TOKEN" | base64               # log shows the base64 text: NOT masked
    - echo "${API_TOKEN:0:4}"                  # first 4 characters: NOT masked
    - curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" https://api.example.com   # header masked, but avoid -v anyway
```

Masking is a filter on **exact matches in the log**. It is not encryption:

| Masking protects against | Masking does not protect against |
|---|---|
| Accidentally echoing the value | Transformed values (base64, URL-encoded, split, reversed, escaped) |
| Tools printing the value verbatim | Writing the value into artifacts, caches or images |
| | Sending the value to an external server from a malicious script |
| | Anyone who can edit the pipeline and exfiltrate it deliberately |

```text
Analogy: masking is a censor reading the transcript after the fact and blacking out
one exact phrase. Say the phrase in another language (base64) and the censor misses it.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Masking replaces exact occurrences of a value with `[MASKED]` in job logs only.
- Masked values must be single-line, at least 8 characters and use a restricted character set when expansion is enabled.
- Transformed values, artifacts and deliberate exfiltration are not covered.
- Mask every secret, and still treat masking as a last line of defense, not access control.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a masked variable and try to print it with `echo`, `printenv`, `base64` and `rev`. Record which outputs are masked.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* A secret contains a space and cannot be masked. Propose two ways to store it so that it can be masked anyway, and implement one.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A security review says: 'All our secrets are masked, so they cannot leak from CI.' What is wrong with this statement?" *Hint:* list who can modify `.gitlab-ci.yml` and what a job can do with a value besides printing it.

#### Hidden Variables

**Why it matters.** Masking protects logs, but project Maintainers can still open **Settings > CI/CD > Variables** and reveal a masked value in the UI. For high-value credentials, you may want a value that nobody can read back once saved: it can be used by pipelines and replaced, but never viewed.

**What it is.** The visibility option **Masked and hidden** (GitLab 17.4, generally available in 17.6) masks the value in job logs **and** prevents it from ever being shown in the settings UI or returned by the API after saving.

| Visibility | Shown in UI after saving | Masked in job logs |
|---|---|---|
| Visible | Yes | No |
| Masked | Yes, to users who can manage variables | Yes |
| Masked and hidden | Never | Yes |

Rules:

- A variable can only be made hidden **when it is created**. An existing variable cannot be switched to hidden. Delete and recreate it instead.
- The value must meet the masking requirements.
- Hidden variables cannot use variable expansion.
- To change the value, you overwrite it. You never see the old one.
- Instance-level variables gained the "Masked and hidden" option in GitLab 19.0.

```bash
# Create a hidden variable through the API
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/variables" \
  --form "key=SIGNING_KEY" \
  --form "value=$SIGNING_KEY_VALUE" \
  --form "masked_and_hidden=true" \
  --form "protected=true"
```

Hiding protects against reading the value **in GitLab's settings**. A job that receives the variable can still use it, and therefore still misuse it. Combine hiding with protection and environment scopes.

**Key takeaways**

- "Masked and hidden" values cannot be viewed in the UI or API after saving, only replaced.
- Hiding is chosen at creation time and cannot be added to an existing variable.
- Hidden values must satisfy the masking rules and cannot use expansion.
- Hidden does not stop pipelines from using the value, so combine it with protection.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a hidden variable and confirm that the UI no longer offers to reveal the value. Then use it in a job and confirm the log shows `[MASKED]`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Convert an existing masked variable to a hidden one without breaking running pipelines. Write down the exact steps and the order in which you perform them.
> 3. **Interview question:** "If hidden variables cannot be read in the UI, why do you still need protected branches for them?" *Hint:* consider who can write a job that runs `curl` with the variable's value.

#### Protected Variables

**Why it matters.** Every developer can push a branch and change `.gitlab-ci.yml` on it. If production credentials reached every branch, any developer, or any compromised developer account, could write a job that sends them elsewhere. Protected variables tie secrets to the branches that already require review before anything lands there.

**What it is.** A variable with **Protect variable** set is passed only to pipelines running on a **protected branch** or **protected tag**. On any other ref the variable simply does not exist. The job does not fail. It sees an empty value.

```text
Protected branches: main, release/*          Protected tags: v*

Pipeline on main            -> PROD_DEPLOY_TOKEN available
Pipeline on release/2.4     -> available (wildcard protected branch)
Pipeline on tag v2.4.0      -> available (protected tag)
Pipeline on feature/login   -> not available (empty)
MR pipeline from a fork     -> not available, never
```

```yaml
deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    # Fail fast with a clear message instead of a confusing auth error later
    - '[ -n "$PROD_DEPLOY_TOKEN" ] || { echo "PROD_DEPLOY_TOKEN missing: is this ref protected?"; exit 1; }'
    - ./deploy.sh --token-file <(printf '%s' "$PROD_DEPLOY_TOKEN")
  environment: production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

**Merge request pipelines.** By default, MR pipelines run for the source branch, which is usually unprotected, so they get no protected variables. Since GitLab 18.1, the project setting **Allow merge request pipelines to access protected variables and runners** (**Settings > CI/CD > Variables**) allows it only when:

- both source and target branches are protected,
- the user who starts the pipeline can push or merge to the target branch, and
- both branches are in the same project (forks never get access).

Protection is only as strong as the protection of the branches:

| Weakness | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Developers allowed to push to `main` | Any developer can change the pipeline on `main` and read protected variables |
| Wildcard such as `*` protected | Every branch counts as protected |
| Developers allowed to create protected tags `v*` | A tag can be pushed from any commit, including unreviewed ones |

**Key takeaways**

- Protected variables are passed only to pipelines on protected branches and protected tags.
- On unprotected refs the variable is empty and the job is not stopped, so check for it explicitly.
- MR pipelines get protected variables only through an opt-in setting with strict conditions, and fork MRs never do.
- The security of protected variables equals the security of your branch and tag protection rules.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a protected variable and print its length (`echo ${#VAR}`) in a job. Run the job on `main` and on a feature branch and compare.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Protect tags matching `v*` so that only Maintainers can create them. Verify that a Developer's tag pipeline cannot read the release signing key.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your production secret is protected, yet an engineer extracted it from CI without Maintainer rights. Name three ways this could have happened." *Hint:* look at branch protection settings, tag protection and the MR pipeline access setting.

#### Environment-Scoped Variables

**Why it matters.** Staging and production usually need the same variable names with different values: `DATABASE_URL`, `API_KEY`, `REPLICAS`. Different names (`STAGING_DATABASE_URL`, `PROD_DATABASE_URL`) lead to duplicated scripts and to mistakes such as a staging job reading a production credential. Environment scopes let one name carry different values per environment, and keep each value away from jobs deploying elsewhere.

**What it is.** Each settings variable has an **environment scope**. A job receives the variable only if the job declares an `environment:name` that matches the scope.

| Scope | Matches environment names |
|---|---|
| `*` (default) | All, including jobs without an environment |
| `production` | Exactly `production` |
| `review/*` | `review/feature-x`, `review/fix-123`, ... |
| `staging-*` | `staging-eu`, `staging-us` |

When the same key exists with several matching scopes, the most specific scope wins: an exact name beats a wildcard pattern, which beats `*`. Project-level scopes are available in all tiers. Group-level scopes require Premium or Ultimate.

```text
Settings:
  DATABASE_URL   scope *            -> postgres://dev-db/app
  DATABASE_URL   scope staging      -> postgres://staging-db/app
  DATABASE_URL   scope production   -> postgres://prod-db/app     (protected, masked)
```

```yaml
.deploy:
  script:
    - ./migrate.sh "$DATABASE_URL"            # same name, value depends on the environment
    - ./deploy.sh

deploy-staging:
  extends: .deploy
  environment: staging                        # receives the staging value
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

deploy-production:
  extends: .deploy
  environment: production                     # receives the production value
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
      when: manual

unit-tests:
  script: [./test.sh]                         # no environment: only the "*" value, never production's
```

Environment scopes combine well with protection and with **protected environments** (chapter 12): the variable is available only to jobs that deploy to `production`, on protected refs, and the deployment itself can require approval.

**Key takeaways**

- An environment scope restricts a variable to jobs whose `environment:name` matches.
- One variable name can carry different values per environment, which keeps scripts identical.
- The most specific matching scope wins. Jobs without an environment receive only `*`-scoped values.
- Combine scope, protection and protected environments for production credentials.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create `GREETING` with scopes `*`, `staging` and `production`. Write three jobs (no environment, staging, production) that print it.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure review apps with environment `review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` and a variable scoped to `review/*`. Confirm that a production-scoped secret is unavailable in review jobs.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is an environment-scoped production variable safer than a variable named `PROD_DB_PASSWORD` with scope `*`, even if both are protected?" *Hint:* count the jobs on `main` that can read each one.

#### Raw vs Expanded Values

**Why it matters.** Generated passwords often contain `$`. If GitLab treats `pa$sW0rd!` as "`pa` followed by the variable `$sW0rd`", the job receives `pa!` and authentication fails with no obvious reason. Some values must be passed exactly as written.

**What it is.** A variable is either **expanded** (`$NAME` inside the value is replaced by that variable's value) or **raw** (the value is used literally).

| Where defined | How to make it raw | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Settings UI | Clear **Expand variable reference** | Not expanded in current versions (cleared by default since GitLab 18.6) |
| API | `raw=true` | `raw` defaults to `false` (expanded) when omitted |
| `.gitlab-ci.yml` | `expand: false` in the long form | Expanded |
| `.gitlab-ci.yml`, single `$` | Escape with `$$` | |

```yaml
variables:
  GREETING_TEMPLATE:
    value: "Hello $USER, your build is $STATUS"
    expand: false                       # GitLab and the runner leave $USER and $STATUS untouched
  LITERAL_PRICE: "costs $$10"           # escaping alternative: value becomes "costs $10"

render:
  script:
    - echo "$GREETING_TEMPLATE"          # prints: Hello $USER, your build is $STATUS
    - USER=ana STATUS=green envsubst <<< "$GREETING_TEMPLATE"   # expand later, on purpose
```

```text
Value stored: pa$sW0rd!

Expand variable reference ON  -> job receives "pa!"           ($sW0rd is undefined, so it becomes empty)
Expand variable reference OFF -> job receives "pa$sW0rd!"
```

The shell does not re-expand the contents of an environment variable. `echo "$PASSWORD"` prints the raw value, unless you pass it through `eval` or a template tool.

Raw values also matter for masking. With expansion off, any character can be masked, and masked or hidden variables cannot use expansion anyway. Keep secrets raw.

**Key takeaways**

- Expanded values replace `$NAME` references. Raw values are used exactly as written.
- Clear "Expand variable reference" (UI), use `raw=true` (API) or `expand: false` (YAML) for literal values.
- Secrets containing `$` must be raw, or they are silently corrupted.
- `$$` escapes a single dollar sign in YAML values.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create two project variables with the value `abc$HOME`, one expanded and one raw. Print both and explain the output.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Audit a project's variables through the API (`GET /projects/:id/variables`) and list every variable whose value contains `$` and has `raw: false`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A deploy started failing with 'invalid credentials' right after a password rotation, though the new password works locally. What would you check first?" *Hint:* look at the characters in the new password and at how the variable is configured.

<a id="53-dynamic-variables"></a>
### 5.3 Dynamic Variables

The variables so far are fixed before the pipeline starts. Real pipelines also produce values while they run (a computed version number, a deployed URL) or accept values from the person starting them. This subchapter covers `dotenv` reports, the options for passing data between jobs, prefilled variables in the Run pipeline form, and typed pipeline inputs.

#### dotenv Report Artifacts

**Why it matters.** Each job runs in its own shell, often on a different machine. A variable exported in one job's `script` is gone when that job ends. Yet later jobs often need values that only exist at runtime: the version computed from git tags, the ID of a created resource, the URL of a freshly deployed review app. `dotenv` reports carry such values forward as real CI/CD variables.

**What it is.** A job writes `KEY=VALUE` lines to a file and declares that file under `artifacts:reports:dotenv`. GitLab parses it after the job finishes, and the variables become available to later jobs that download the job's artifacts.

```yaml
stages: [build, test, deploy]

version:
  stage: build
  script:
    - VERSION="$(git describe --tags --always)"        # computed at runtime
    - echo "APP_VERSION=$VERSION" >> build.env          # one KEY=VALUE per line
    - echo "BUILD_TIME=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)" >> build.env
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dotenv: build.env                                 # turns the lines into variables

test:
  stage: test
  script:
    - echo "Testing $APP_VERSION built at $BUILD_TIME"  # available automatically (later stage)
```

The file format is strict:

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| One `KEY=VALUE` per line | `APP_VERSION=1.4.2` |
| Names: ASCII letters, digits, underscores | `IMAGE_DIGEST` |
| No empty lines, no `#` comments | |
| No quoting. Quotes are kept as literal characters | `A="x"` gives the value `"x"`, with quotes |
| No multi-line values, no values that need escaping | Put JSON in a regular artifact instead |
| Leading and trailing whitespace is stripped | |
| UTF-8 only, at most 5 KB | |

There is also a limit on the number of inherited variables (20 by default on self-managed, configurable by administrators, with plan-based limits on GitLab.com).

Who receives the variables:

```text
version (build) ──dotenv──> every job in later stages             (default)
                         └─> jobs with needs: [version]           (needs with artifacts: true, the default)
                         └─> NOT jobs with dependencies: []       (no artifacts downloaded)
                         └─> NOT jobs in the same stage, unless they use needs
                         └─> NOT rules:if anywhere                 (rules run before any job)
```

`dotenv` variables rank above YAML variables but below settings and pipeline variables (section 5.1). If a name appears twice in a file, the last value is used.

A special case: a deployment job can set its own environment URL from a `dotenv` report, which is how review apps on platforms that generate random URLs get a working link.

```yaml
deploy-review:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - URL="$(./deploy-review.sh)"                       # platform returns a generated URL
    - echo "DYNAMIC_ENVIRONMENT_URL=$URL" >> deploy.env
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dotenv: deploy.env
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: $DYNAMIC_ENVIRONMENT_URL                       # filled in after the job finishes
```

**Key takeaways**

- A `dotenv` report turns `KEY=VALUE` lines into CI/CD variables for later jobs.
- The format is strict: no comments, no blank lines, no quoting, no multi-line values, at most 5 KB.
- Artifact download rules (`stages`, `needs`, `dependencies`) decide which jobs receive the variables.
- `dotenv` variables are never available in `rules`, because rules are evaluated before any job runs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Compute `SHORT_DATE=$(date +%F)` in a build job, pass it through a `dotenv` report and print it in a test job.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a `dotenv` file containing a blank line, a comment and a quoted value. Run the job, observe the result, then fix the file. Separately, show that `dependencies: []` prevents a job from receiving the variables.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A job in the `deploy` stage has `rules: - if: $APP_VERSION =~ /-rc/` where `APP_VERSION` comes from a `dotenv` report, and the job never runs. Why, and how would you restructure it?" *Hint:* compare pipeline creation time with job run time. Consider making the decision in a script or in a child pipeline.

#### Passing Variables Between Jobs

**Why it matters.** "How do I get this value from job A to job B?" is one of the most common CI questions, and the right answer depends on the shape of the data and on where B runs: same pipeline, child pipeline or another project. Picking the wrong mechanism leads to fragile workarounds such as committing files back to the repository.

**What it is.** Jobs share nothing by default (section 2.2). Data moves only through mechanisms GitLab provides:

| Scenario | Mechanism | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Small key/value pairs to later jobs, same pipeline | `artifacts:reports:dotenv` | Values become CI/CD variables |
| Files or structured data (JSON, binaries), same pipeline | `artifacts:paths` + `needs`/`dependencies` | Parse the file in the receiving job |
| Static values into a child pipeline | Trigger job `variables`, or `include:inputs` | Section 3.3 |
| Runtime values into a child pipeline | `dotenv` in the parent + `needs:pipeline:job` in the child | Section 3.3 |
| Values into another project's pipeline | Trigger job `variables` or `trigger:inputs` | Subject to the downstream pipeline-variable restriction |
| Runtime values from another project | `needs:project` with a `dotenv` artifact | Premium, section 3.4 |
| Values within one job | Plain shell variables, `before_script` to `script` | Not into `after_script` |

```yaml
stages: [build, test, deploy]

build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - make build
    - echo "IMAGE_DIGEST=$(cat out/digest.txt)" >> vars.env       # small value -> dotenv
    - ./generate-manifest.sh > out/manifest.json                    # structured data -> file
  artifacts:
    paths: [out/manifest.json]
    reports:
      dotenv: vars.env

scan:
  stage: test
  needs: [build]                                                    # gets IMAGE_DIGEST and manifest.json
  script:
    - trivy image "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE@$IMAGE_DIGEST"
    - jq -r '.services[].name' out/manifest.json                    # read structured data from the file

notify:
  stage: deploy
  needs:
    - job: build
      artifacts: false                                              # blocks ALL artifacts, including dotenv
  script:
    - echo "digest is '${IMAGE_DIGEST:-unset}'"                     # prints: digest is 'unset'
```

```text
Same pipeline                 Parent ─> child                  Project A ─> project B
build ──dotenv/artifacts──>   parent job ──trigger vars──>    trigger job ──vars/inputs──> B pipeline
          test                child job <──needs:pipeline:job  B job <──needs:project── A job (Premium)
```

Avoid the anti-patterns: writing values to the cache (not guaranteed to exist), committing files back to the repository (triggers new pipelines and pollutes history), or calling the variables API to store runtime state (needs a powerful token and races between pipelines).

**Key takeaways**

- Small values go through `dotenv` reports, files and structured data through regular artifacts.
- `needs` and `dependencies` decide which jobs receive both kinds, and `artifacts: false` blocks both.
- Child and downstream pipelines receive static values through trigger variables or inputs, and runtime values through `needs:pipeline:job` or `needs:project`.
- Do not use caches, commits or the variables API as a message bus.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Pass a build number and a JSON file listing built binaries from a `build` job to a `package` job. Use the appropriate mechanism for each.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* In a parent-child setup, compute `RELEASE_ID` in the parent at runtime and use it in a child job without hard-coding the parent pipeline ID.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A teammate stores the deployed version in a project variable by calling the API from the deploy job, so that the next pipeline can read it. What risks does this introduce, and what would you use instead?" *Hint:* think about token scope, concurrent pipelines, precedence of project variables and the environments and deployments API.

#### Prefilled Variables for Manual Pipelines

**Why it matters.** Pipelines started by hand from **Build > Pipelines > Run pipeline** often need parameters: which environment, which log level, whether to run slow tests. Without guidance, users have to know the variable names by heart and type them without typos. Prefilled variables turn the form into a documented, partly constrained input screen.

**What it is.** Top-level `variables` written in the long form with a `description` appear pre-populated in the Run pipeline form. `value` sets the default, and `options` turns the field into a drop-down list (the `value` must be one of the options).

```yaml
variables:
  DEPLOY_ENV:
    description: "Target environment. Only used by manual runs."
    value: "staging"                      # default shown in the form
    options: ["staging", "production"]    # drop-down; value must be in the list
  LOG_LEVEL:
    description: "Verbosity of deployment scripts."
    value: "info"                         # free text with a default
  RUN_E2E:
    description: "Set to true to run the slow end-to-end suite."
    value: "false"                        # strings, not booleans

e2e:
  script: [./run-e2e.sh]
  rules:
    - if: $RUN_E2E == "true"
```

```text
Run pipeline
  Branch: [ main         v]
  DEPLOY_ENV  [ staging  v]   Target environment. Only used by manual runs.
  LOG_LEVEL   [ info       ]  Verbosity of deployment scripts.
  RUN_E2E     [ false      ]  Set to true to run the slow end-to-end suite.
  [ + Add variable ]                                      [ Run pipeline ]
```

How it behaves:

- On push, schedule and MR pipelines, the YAML `value` is used as a normal top-level variable.
- When a user changes a value in the form, it is submitted as a **pipeline variable** (high precedence, section 5.1). The minimum-role setting for pipeline variables applies.
- `options` is enforced only in the form. The API and trigger tokens can send any value.
- Everything is a string, so there is no type checking.

These limitations are why GitLab recommends **pipeline inputs** (next topic) for new parameterized pipelines.

**Key takeaways**

- Top-level variables with `description` (and optionally `value` and `options`) prefill the Run pipeline form.
- `options` creates a drop-down list, but other entry points can still send any value.
- Changed values become pipeline variables, subject to the pipeline-variable role restriction.
- Values are untyped strings. Prefer inputs for new parameterized pipelines.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a prefilled `REGION` variable with options `eu-west-1` and `us-east-1` and a description. Run the pipeline manually with each value.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Trigger the same pipeline through the API with `REGION=ap-south-1`. Observe that the value is accepted, then add a validation job in the `.pre` stage that fails for values outside the allowed list.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why are prefilled variables with `options` not a security control?" *Hint:* list every way a pipeline variable can be set besides the Run pipeline form.

#### Pipeline Inputs

**Why it matters.** Variables are untyped, can be overridden from many places and leak into every job as environment variables. For parameters that callers pass in ("deploy to which environment, with how many replicas?"), you want something stricter: declared up front, typed, validated and immutable once the pipeline starts. That is what inputs provide. Chapter 9 covers inputs for reusable components; this topic covers inputs for whole pipelines.

**What it is.** Since GitLab 17.11, the main `.gitlab-ci.yml` can declare inputs in a `spec:inputs` header, separated from the rest of the file by `---`. Inputs are interpolated with `$[[ inputs.name ]]` while GitLab **builds the configuration**, before rules are evaluated and before any job runs. They are not CI/CD variables and do not appear in the precedence order.

```yaml
spec:
  inputs:
    environment:
      type: string                         # string (default), number, boolean or array
      default: staging                     # no default = required input
      options: [staging, production]       # validated on every entry point, not just the form
      description: Target environment
    replicas:
      type: number
      default: 2
    run_e2e:
      type: boolean
      default: false
    version:
      default: latest
      regex: ^(latest|v\d+\.\d+\.\d+)$      # value must match
---
deploy:
  stage: deploy
  environment: $[[ inputs.environment ]]                   # interpolated at configuration time
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh --version "$[[ inputs.version ]]" --replicas $[[ inputs.replicas ]]

e2e:
  stage: test
  variables:
    RUN_E2E: "$[[ inputs.run_e2e ]]"                       # bridge an input into a variable for rules
  rules:
    - if: $RUN_E2E == "true"
  script: [./run-e2e.sh]
```

Ways to pass inputs:

| Entry point | How |
|---|---|
| Run pipeline form | Each input is shown with its type, default, description and options |
| Pipelines API | `inputs` object in the request body |
| Pipeline triggers API | Inputs alongside the trigger token |
| Pipeline schedules | Inputs stored on the schedule |
| Git push options | Inputs on push |
| Downstream pipelines | `trigger:inputs`, or `include:inputs` for child pipelines |

```bash
# Start a pipeline on main with typed inputs (numbers and booleans stay typed)
curl --request POST \
  --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"ref": "main", "inputs": {"environment": "production", "replicas": 4, "run_e2e": true}}' \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/pipeline"
```

```yaml
# Upstream project: start the deployment project's pipeline with inputs
deploy-shop:
  trigger:
    project: ops/deploy
    inputs:
      environment: production
      replicas: 6
```

Interpolation can be modified with functions (up to three per block): `expand_vars` expands CI/CD variables inside the input value, `truncate(offset,length)` shortens it, and `posix_escape` escapes shell metacharacters (not a security control for untrusted values). Example: `$[[ inputs.name | expand_vars | truncate(0,20) ]]`.

| | Variables (prefilled) | Inputs |
|---|---|---|
| Types | Strings only | string, number, boolean, array |
| Validation | `options` in the form only | `options` and `regex` on every entry point |
| Required values | Not possible | Omit `default` |
| Override after start | Higher-precedence sources can override | Fixed at configuration time |
| Scope | Environment variable in every job | Only where interpolated |
| Usable in `rules:if` directly | Yes | Through interpolation or a bridging variable |

Limits: up to 20 inputs per pipeline. Give every input a `default` if the pipeline also runs automatically, because a missing required input makes automatic pipelines fail.

**Key takeaways**

- Pipeline inputs are declared in `spec:inputs` above `---` in the main `.gitlab-ci.yml` and used with `$[[ inputs.name ]]`.
- They are typed, validated with `options` and `regex`, and fixed when the configuration is built.
- They can be passed from the UI, API, triggers, schedules, push options and upstream pipelines.
- Prefer inputs over pipeline variables for user-supplied parameters, and give them defaults when pipelines also run on push.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Convert the prefilled `DEPLOY_ENV` variable from the previous topic into a string input with options. Run the pipeline manually and through the API with an invalid value, and compare the errors.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `services` array input with default `["api", "web"]` and use it with `parallel:matrix` to create one deploy job per service. Pass a different array through the API.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why are pipeline inputs considered safer than pipeline variables for a deployment pipeline that other teams trigger?" *Hint:* compare typing, validation, precedence and how far each value spreads into jobs.

<a id="54-secrets-management"></a>
### 5.4 Secrets Management

CI/CD variables store secrets inside GitLab as long-lived values copied into settings. Dedicated secret stores add rotation, fine-grained policies, audit logs and short-lived credentials. This subchapter shows how jobs prove their identity with ID tokens, and how they use that identity to fetch secrets from HashiCorp Vault, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and GitLab's own secrets manager.

#### ID Tokens and OIDC Authentication

**Why it matters.** The classic approach puts a cloud access key into a masked, protected variable. That key never expires, works from anywhere, is often over-privileged and has to be rotated by hand. If it leaks, the attacker keeps access until someone notices. A better model is that the job proves **who it is** (this project, this branch, this environment), and the cloud provider issues a short-lived credential based on that proof. No long-lived secret is stored in GitLab at all.

**What it is.** The `id_tokens` keyword makes GitLab issue one or more **JSON Web Tokens** (JWTs) for a job, signed by GitLab and exposed as variables. The token follows OpenID Connect (OIDC) conventions. A cloud provider or Vault that trusts your GitLab instance as an identity provider verifies the signature using GitLab's public keys, checks the claims against its policy, and returns temporary credentials.

Think of a hotel key card issued at reception: it is printed for one guest, one room and one stay, and it stops working on checkout. A long-lived access key is a master key someone copied.

```text
1. Job starts       GitLab ── issues signed JWT (aud, sub, project_path, ref, environment...) ──> job
2. Job presents     job ── JWT ──> AWS STS / Vault / Azure AD / GCP STS
3. Provider checks  signature (keys from https://gitlab.example.com/oauth/discovery/keys)
                    + issuer + audience + claims match the trust policy
4. Provider grants  short-lived credentials ──> job            (expire minutes to an hour later)
```

```yaml
deploy:
  image:
    name: amazon/aws-cli:2.17.0
    entrypoint: [""]                          # the image's default entrypoint is the aws binary
  id_tokens:
    AWS_OIDC_TOKEN:                           # variable name chosen by you
      aud: https://gitlab.example.com         # audience: must match the provider's configuration
  variables:
    AWS_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-deploy-shop
    AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE: /tmp/web-identity-token
  script:
    - printf '%s' "$AWS_OIDC_TOKEN" > "$AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE"   # AWS SDKs and CLI read the token file
    - aws sts get-caller-identity                                       # temporary credentials, no access keys stored
    - aws s3 sync dist/ s3://shop-prod-assets/
  environment: production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

Important claims in the token, which trust policies match on:

| Claim | Example | Use in policies |
|---|---|---|
| `iss` | `https://gitlab.example.com` | Which GitLab issued it |
| `aud` | `https://gitlab.example.com` | Who the token is meant for |
| `sub` | `project_path:acme/shop:ref_type:branch:ref:main` | The main identity string |
| `project_id`, `project_path`, `namespace_path` | `42`, `acme/shop`, `acme` | Restrict to projects or groups |
| `ref`, `ref_type`, `ref_protected` | `main`, `branch`, `true` | Restrict to protected refs |
| `environment`, `environment_protected` | `production`, `true` | Restrict to protected environments |
| `pipeline_source`, `user_login`, `job_id` | `push`, `jdoe`, `554433` | Auditing and finer rules |

The trust policy on the provider side is where security is decided. An AWS IAM role trust policy for the job above:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/gitlab.example.com" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {
        "gitlab.example.com:aud": "https://gitlab.example.com",
        "gitlab.example.com:sub": "project_path:acme/shop:ref_type:branch:ref:main"
      }
    }
  }]
}
```

Notes:

- Tokens are short-lived and valid only around the job's run. Never log them: they are bearer credentials until they expire.
- `id_tokens` can be set in `default` to apply to every job, but issue tokens only to the jobs that need them.
- The older `CI_JOB_JWT` and `CI_JOB_JWT_V2` variables were removed in GitLab 17.0. `id_tokens` replaces them.
- A trust policy that matches only on `project_path` lets **every branch** of the project assume the role. Always include the ref, or `ref_protected`/`environment_protected` claims where the provider supports them.

**Key takeaways**

- `id_tokens` issues signed, short-lived OIDC JWTs whose claims describe the project, ref, environment and pipeline.
- Cloud providers and Vault exchange them for temporary credentials, so no long-lived secret is stored in GitLab.
- `aud` must match the provider's configuration. The provider's trust policy decides who gets access.
- Bind trust policies to specific projects **and** protected refs or environments, never to the project alone.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add an `id_tokens` entry to a job and print the decoded payload only (not the signature): `echo "$TOKEN" | cut -d. -f2 | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d 2>/dev/null`. Identify `sub`, `ref` and `ref_protected`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure an AWS IAM OIDC provider and a role that `main` can assume but feature branches cannot. Prove both outcomes with `aws sts get-caller-identity`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your trust policy uses `StringLike` on `sub` with `project_path:acme/*`. What could go wrong?" *Hint:* consider who can create projects under `acme` and which refs are matched.

#### HashiCorp Vault Integration

**Why it matters.** Many organizations centralize secrets in HashiCorp Vault (or its open-source fork OpenBao) to get one place for policies, rotation, dynamic database credentials and audit logs. Pipelines should read from that source of truth instead of keeping copies in GitLab settings.

**What it is.** The `secrets` keyword (Premium and Ultimate) lets the runner fetch secrets from Vault before the job's script runs. Authentication uses an ID token and Vault's JWT auth method. By default each secret is exposed as a **file-type variable** (the variable holds a path). `file: false` exposes the value directly.

```text
Runner ── VAULT_ID_TOKEN ──> Vault auth/jwt/login (role myproject-production)
       <── Vault token (TTL 60s) ──
       ── read ops/data/production/db ──> field "password" ──> $DATABASE_PASSWORD
```

**Vault side (one-time setup):**

```bash
# 1. Trust GitLab as a JWT issuer
vault auth enable jwt
vault write auth/jwt/config \
  oidc_discovery_url="https://gitlab.example.com" \
  bound_issuer="https://gitlab.example.com"

# 2. A policy allowing read access to the production database secret (KV v2 adds /data/)
vault policy write myproject-production - <<'EOF'
path "ops/data/production/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
EOF

# 3. A role that only protected main-branch jobs of project 42 can use
vault write auth/jwt/role/myproject-production - <<'EOF'
{
  "role_type": "jwt",
  "policies": ["myproject-production"],
  "token_explicit_max_ttl": 60,
  "user_claim": "user_email",
  "bound_audiences": "https://vault.example.com",
  "bound_claims_type": "glob",
  "bound_claims": {
    "project_id": "42",
    "ref_protected": "true",
    "ref_type": "branch",
    "ref": "main"
  }
}
EOF
```

**GitLab side:**

```yaml
variables:
  VAULT_SERVER_URL: https://vault.example.com:8200   # required (often a group variable)
  VAULT_AUTH_ROLE: myproject-production              # optional: role to log in with
  VAULT_AUTH_PATH: jwt                               # optional: mount path of the JWT method (default jwt)
  # VAULT_NAMESPACE: admin/payments                  # optional: Vault Enterprise namespace

deploy:
  id_tokens:
    VAULT_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://vault.example.com                 # must match bound_audiences
  secrets:
    DATABASE_PASSWORD:
      vault: production/db/password@ops              # <path>/<field>@<engine mount>: reads ops/data/production/db, field password
      token: $VAULT_ID_TOKEN
      file: false                                    # value in the variable instead of a file path
    TLS_CERT:
      vault:                                         # long form, for non-KV-v2 engines or clarity
        engine:
          name: kv-v2                                # kv-v2 is the default engine
          path: ops                                  # where the engine is mounted
        path: production/tls
        field: certificate
      token: $VAULT_ID_TOKEN                         # file-type by default: $TLS_CERT is a path
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh --db-password "$DATABASE_PASSWORD" --cert-file "$TLS_CERT"
  environment: production
```

On the Free tier, or when you need Vault features the `secrets` keyword does not cover (dynamic database credentials, PKI), log in with the CLI yourself using the same ID token:

```yaml
read-secret-manually:
  image: hashicorp/vault:1.17
  id_tokens:
    VAULT_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://vault.example.com
  script:
    - export VAULT_ADDR="$VAULT_SERVER_URL"
    - export VAULT_TOKEN="$(vault write -field=token auth/jwt/login role=myproject-production jwt="$VAULT_ID_TOKEN")"
    - export DB_CREDS="$(vault read -format=json database/creds/shop-readonly)"   # dynamic, auto-expiring credentials
```

**Key takeaways**

- Vault trusts GitLab through the JWT auth method. Roles bind access to token claims such as `project_id`, `ref` and `ref_protected`.
- `secrets:vault` (Premium) fetches values before the script runs. Short form: `path/field@mount`, with `kv-v2` as the default engine.
- Secrets are file-type variables by default. Use `file: false` for plain values.
- `VAULT_SERVER_URL` is required. `VAULT_AUTH_ROLE`, `VAULT_AUTH_PATH` and `VAULT_NAMESPACE` are optional.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run a Vault dev server, store `secret/ci/demo` with field `greeting`, configure JWT auth for your project and print the length of the fetched value in a job.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create two Vault roles, `staging` and `production`. Bind the production role to `environment: production` with `environment_protected: true`, and show that a staging job cannot read production secrets even on `main`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is `token_explicit_max_ttl: 60` a reasonable setting for a CI role, and what problem would a 24-hour TTL create?" *Hint:* consider what a job could do with a leaked Vault token after the job ends.

#### AWS Secrets Manager Integration

**Why it matters.** Teams running on AWS often already keep database passwords and API keys in AWS Secrets Manager, with rotation handled by Lambda functions. Reading them directly from pipelines avoids a second copy in GitLab that would go stale after each rotation.

**What it is.** Since GitLab 18.3 (Premium and Ultimate), `secrets` supports `aws_secrets_manager`. The runner authenticates to AWS, either with OIDC through an ID token and `AWS_ROLE_ARN`, or with the IAM role attached to the runner itself (GitLab Runner 18.3 or later), and fetches the secret before the script runs.

```yaml
variables:
  AWS_REGION: eu-west-1                                          # region of the secrets
  AWS_ROLE_ARN: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gitlab-secrets-shop  # role to assume via OIDC

deploy:
  id_tokens:
    AWS_ID_TOKEN:                                                # default name the runner looks for
      aud: sts.amazonaws.com
  secrets:
    DB_PASSWORD:
      aws_secrets_manager:
        secret_id: shop/production/database                      # name or ARN
        field: password                                          # key inside a JSON secret
      file: false
    API_KEY:
      aws_secrets_manager: 'shop/production/api#api_key'         # short form: <secret_id>#<field>
    LEGACY_TOKEN:
      aws_secrets_manager:
        secret_id: arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789012:secret:legacy-token-AbCdEf
        version_stage: AWSPREVIOUS                               # or version_id (not both)
        region: us-east-1                                        # per-secret override
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh
  environment: production
```

| Option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `secret_id` | Secret name or ARN |
| `field` | Key to extract from a JSON secret. Omit it to get the whole value |
| `version_id` / `version_stage` | Pin a version or stage (`AWSCURRENT`, `AWSPREVIOUS`) |
| `region`, `role_arn`, `role_session_name` | Per-secret overrides of `AWS_REGION`, `AWS_ROLE_ARN`, `AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME` |
| `token` | Use an ID token not named `AWS_ID_TOKEN` |

On the AWS side, the role needs a trust policy for GitLab's OIDC provider (previous topic, with `aud` set to `sts.amazonaws.com`) and a permissions policy that allows `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on exactly the secrets the project needs. If the secrets use a customer-managed KMS key, it also needs `kms:Decrypt` on that key.

**Key takeaways**

- `secrets:aws_secrets_manager` (Premium, GitLab 18.3+) fetches secrets by name or ARN, optionally a JSON `field` and a version.
- Authentication is OIDC (`AWS_ID_TOKEN` + `AWS_ROLE_ARN`) or the runner's own IAM role.
- Scope the IAM role to specific secret ARNs and bind its trust policy to protected refs.
- Rotation in AWS is picked up automatically, because pipelines always read the current version.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a JSON secret with `username` and `password` keys and fetch only `password` in a job, using the short form.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure two roles: one for `main` that can read `shop/production/*` and one for any branch that can read only `shop/dev/*`. Use per-secret `role_arn` overrides and prove the separation.
> 3. **Interview question:** "When would you prefer the runner's IAM role over OIDC for fetching AWS secrets, and what is the security trade-off?" *Hint:* consider who shares the runner and whether the role can distinguish between projects and branches.

#### Azure Key Vault Integration

**Why it matters.** On Azure, Key Vault is the standard store for secrets, keys and certificates, with access governed by Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) and RBAC. Pipelines deploying to Azure should read from it with federated identity rather than storing a client secret in GitLab.

**What it is.** `secrets:azure_key_vault` (Premium and Ultimate) fetches a secret from Key Vault. The job's ID token is exchanged for an Entra ID token through a **federated identity credential** on an app registration (or user-assigned managed identity).

```yaml
variables:
  AZURE_KEY_VAULT_SERVER_URL: https://shop-prod-kv.vault.azure.net   # the vault
  AZURE_CLIENT_ID: 00000000-1111-2222-3333-444444444444              # app registration / identity
  AZURE_TENANT_ID: 55555555-6666-7777-8888-999999999999

deploy:
  id_tokens:
    AZURE_JWT:
      aud: https://gitlab.com                     # must match the federated credential's audience
  secrets:
    DATABASE_PASSWORD:
      token: $AZURE_JWT
      azure_key_vault:
        name: DATABASE-PASSWORD                    # secret name in Key Vault
        version: 00000000000000000000000000000000  # optional: pin a specific version
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh
  environment: production
```

Azure side, in summary:

```text
App registration "gitlab-shop-deploy"
  └── Federated credential
        Issuer:   https://gitlab.com                                   (your GitLab URL)
        Subject:  project_path:acme/shop:ref_type:branch:ref:main      (exact match)
        Audience: https://gitlab.com
Key Vault "shop-prod-kv" (RBAC)
  └── Role assignment: "Key Vault Secrets User" -> gitlab-shop-deploy
```

The federated credential matches the `sub` claim exactly, so each branch or tag that needs access requires its own credential. This is restrictive by design. Grant only **Key Vault Secrets User** (read secret values) to the pipeline's identity, not administrative roles.

**Key takeaways**

- `secrets:azure_key_vault` (Premium) needs `AZURE_KEY_VAULT_SERVER_URL`, `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` and `AZURE_TENANT_ID`, plus an ID token.
- Trust is a federated identity credential whose issuer, subject and audience must match the token.
- Subjects are matched exactly, so a credential for `main` does not work for other branches.
- The identity needs the "Key Vault Secrets User" role (with RBAC) and nothing more.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a Key Vault secret and an app registration with a federated credential for your project's `main` branch. Fetch the secret in a job on `main`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Run the same job on a feature branch and capture the error. Then decide whether to add a second federated credential or a separate identity for non-production branches, and implement it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A colleague created an Azure client secret for the pipeline and stored it as a masked GitLab variable. How would you migrate to federated credentials, and what do you gain?" *Hint:* compare credential lifetime, rotation effort and what a leaked value lets an attacker do.

#### Google Cloud Secret Manager Integration

**Why it matters.** On Google Cloud, service account JSON keys are the traditional way for CI to authenticate, and they are a well-known source of leaks: they never expire unless rotated and are trivially reusable. **Workload Identity Federation** (WIF) removes them. GitLab can use WIF to read from Secret Manager directly.

**What it is.** `secrets:gcp_secret_manager` (Premium and Ultimate) exchanges the job's ID token at Google's Security Token Service through a workload identity pool and provider. It then reads the secret with the permissions granted to that federated identity.

```yaml
variables:
  GCP_PROJECT_NUMBER: "123456789012"
  GCP_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_FEDERATION_POOL_ID: gitlab-pool
  GCP_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_FEDERATION_PROVIDER_ID: gitlab-provider

deploy:
  id_tokens:
    GCP_ID_TOKEN:
      # Audience must identify the WIF provider
      aud: https://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${GCP_PROJECT_NUMBER}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${GCP_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_FEDERATION_POOL_ID}/providers/${GCP_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_FEDERATION_PROVIDER_ID}
  secrets:
    DATABASE_PASSWORD:
      gcp_secret_manager:
        name: shop-db-password      # secret name in Secret Manager
        version: 1                  # version number, or omit for the latest
      token: $GCP_ID_TOKEN
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh
  environment: production
```

Google Cloud side:

```bash
# 1. Pool and OIDC provider trusting GitLab, mapping token claims to attributes
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create gitlab-pool --location=global
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc gitlab-provider \
  --location=global --workload-identity-pool=gitlab-pool \
  --issuer-uri="https://gitlab.example.com" \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub,attribute.gitlab_project_id=assertion.project_id,attribute.ref_protected=assertion.ref_protected" \
  --attribute-condition="assertion.ref_protected == 'true'"      # only protected refs may federate

# 2. Allow identities from GitLab project 42 to read one secret
gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding shop-db-password \
  --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor" \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/123456789012/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/gitlab-pool/attribute.gitlab_project_id/42"
```

The attribute mapping decides which claims you can use in `principalSet` members and in the attribute condition. Mapping `project_id` and `ref_protected` lets you grant access per project and refuse unprotected refs at the pool level.

**Key takeaways**

- `secrets:gcp_secret_manager` (Premium) uses Workload Identity Federation instead of service account keys.
- Three variables identify the pool and provider, and the ID token's `aud` must point at that provider.
- Map GitLab claims to attributes, then grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` per secret to a `principalSet` for the project.
- Use an attribute condition such as `ref_protected == 'true'` to refuse untrusted refs before any IAM check.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a pool, provider and secret, and read the secret from a job on a protected branch.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add `attribute.environment=assertion.environment` to the mapping and restrict a production secret to jobs with `environment: production`. Verify that a staging job on the same branch is denied.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is an attribute condition on the provider more robust than relying only on IAM bindings to block feature branches?" *Hint:* think about defense in depth and about bindings that other teams may add later.

#### GitLab Secrets Manager

**Why it matters.** External secret stores are powerful, but they need infrastructure, trust configuration and someone to run them. Small and medium teams often fall back to CI/CD variables, which were never designed as a secrets manager: they have no fine-grained permissions on who can read which secret, no rotation reminders and limited auditing. GitLab Secrets Manager is a native store with secret-manager semantics, built into GitLab.

**What it is.** GitLab Secrets Manager (Premium and Ultimate, generally available since GitLab 19.5) stores secrets in an OpenBao backend managed by GitLab. It is enabled per top-level group on GitLab.com (**Secure > Secrets manager**, billed through GitLab Credits) or by an administrator on self-managed instances, where OpenBao must be installed first. Jobs need GitLab Runner 19.0 or later. GitLab handles authentication itself, so no `id_tokens` or trust configuration is required in the YAML.

Secrets are created in **Secure > Secrets manager > New secret**:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| Name | Letters, digits and underscores. Unique, cannot be changed later |
| Value | Up to 10 KB |
| Environments | All (`*`), a specific environment, or a wildcard |
| Branches (project secrets) | A specific branch or a wildcard such as `release/*` |
| Protected branches (group secrets) | Restrict to pipelines on protected branches |
| Rotation reminder | Optional, at least 7 days. Owners get an email when rotation is due |

By default a project can store 100 secrets and a group 500.

```yaml
deploy:
  environment: production                     # must match the secret's environment scope
  secrets:
    KUBE_CA_PEM:
      gitlab_secrets_manager:
        name: kube_cert                        # project secret
    REGISTRY_TOKEN:
      gitlab_secrets_manager:
        name: registry_token
        source: group/acme/platform            # group secret: group/<full group path>
      file: false                              # plain value instead of a file path
  script:
    - kubectl config set-cluster prod --server="$KUBE_SERVER" --certificate-authority="$KUBE_CA_PEM"
    - ./deploy.sh
```

Permissions are managed separately from repository roles. In GitLab 19.4 and later, project Owners manage secrets permissions, Maintainers can read metadata, create and update by default, and Developers can read metadata and create but not update. For group secrets, permissions must be granted explicitly to users or roles. Reading and using secrets is audited.

| | CI/CD variables | GitLab Secrets Manager | External store (Vault, cloud) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Setup effort | None | Enable per group or instance | Run or buy a store, configure OIDC trust |
| Scoping | Protected refs, environment | Environment, branch, protected branches | Anything the store's policies express |
| Read access in the UI | Maintainers can reveal (unless hidden) | Values never shown, separate permissions | Store's own access control |
| Rotation | Manual | Reminders | Automated, dynamic credentials possible |
| Cost | Included | Premium + GitLab Credits | Infrastructure or cloud fees |
| Best for | Non-secret configuration, simple secrets | Teams wanting a native store with little setup | Organizations with existing central secret management |

**Key takeaways**

- GitLab Secrets Manager is a native, OpenBao-backed secret store (Premium, GA in 19.5) that needs no external infrastructure on GitLab.com.
- Secrets are scoped by environment and by branch (project) or protected branches (group), with optional rotation reminders.
- Jobs use `secrets:<VAR>:gitlab_secrets_manager:name`, with `source: group/<path>` for group secrets. Runner 19.0+ is required.
- Its permissions are separate from repository roles, which fixes the "every Maintainer can read every secret" problem of CI/CD variables.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Enable the secrets manager, create a project secret scoped to `production`, and use it in a job with `environment: production`. Run a job without an environment and observe the result.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Move three masked CI/CD variables of a project into GitLab Secrets Manager, scoping them by environment and branch. Plan the cut-over so that no pipeline runs without credentials, and delete the old variables at the end.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your company already runs Vault. A team asks to use GitLab Secrets Manager instead for its new service. What questions would you ask before agreeing?" *Hint:* think about a single source of truth, audit requirements, dynamic credentials, cost and who operates each system.

---

<a id="6-gitlab-runners"></a>
## 6. GitLab Runners

Every job in the previous chapters ran "somewhere": that somewhere is a GitLab Runner, a separate agent that asks GitLab for work, prepares an environment, runs the script and reports the result back. This chapter covers how runners connect to and authenticate with GitLab, how executors decide where and how a job runs, how `config.toml` shapes a runner's behavior, and how fleets of runners are autoscaled, monitored and upgraded. Understanding runners explains why jobs sit in `pending`, why the same job behaves differently on two machines, and where most of the CI/CD infrastructure bill comes from.

<a id="61-runner-architecture"></a>
### 6.1 Runner Architecture

A runner is the bridge between GitLab, which decides *what* must run, and the machines that actually run it. This subchapter covers the polling protocol, the three runner scopes, the runners GitLab operates for you, how runners authenticate, and how one runner can be served by many processes.

#### How Runners Pick Up Jobs

**Why it matters.** GitLab itself never executes a job. Keeping execution out of the GitLab server protects it from untrusted build code, lets builds run on any operating system or network, and lets build capacity scale independently of GitLab. The price is a protocol between the two, and most "my job is stuck" problems are really questions about that protocol.

**What it is.** GitLab Runner is a single Go binary, `gitlab-runner`, that runs on Linux, Windows, macOS and FreeBSD, in a container, or inside Kubernetes. It works on a **pull model**: the runner always starts the conversation. Think of delivery couriers who periodically ask the dispatch office "anything for me?", rather than a dispatcher who has to know where every courier is and phone them.

```text
GitLab (Rails + Workhorse)                                   Runner (gitlab-runner)
───────────────────────────                                  ──────────────────────
                     <── POST /api/v4/jobs/request ───────── "Any job for token glrt-...?
                                                              I use the docker executor, v19.4"
Workhorse holds the request open (long polling, ~50 s)
── 204 No Content ─────────────────────────────────────────> nothing yet: wait check_interval, ask again
...
Job 554433 becomes pending and matches this runner
── 201 Created + job payload ──────────────────────────────> script, image, services, variables,
                                                              CI_JOB_TOKEN, git ref and SHA
                     <── PATCH /api/v4/jobs/554433/trace ─── stream log chunks while running
                     <── PUT   /api/v4/jobs/554433 ───────── update state: running, success, failed
```

Because the runner opens every connection, it only needs **outbound HTTPS** to GitLab. A runner can sit behind NAT, in a private subnet or on a laptop, and GitLab never needs credentials for the build machine. The only inbound connection is optional: the session server used by interactive web terminals (section 6.3).

**How GitLab chooses a job for a runner.** When a runner asks for work, GitLab looks for a pending job that this runner is allowed to take:

| Check | The runner can take the job only if... |
|---|---|
| Scope | The runner is available to the job's project (instance, group or project runner, see the next topic) |
| Tags | The runner has every tag the job lists (section 2.2) |
| Untagged jobs | The job has no tags and the runner has "Run untagged jobs" enabled |
| Protection | The runner is not protected, or the pipeline runs for a protected branch or tag |
| State | The runner is not paused |

If several jobs qualify, project and group runners take them roughly in queue order. Instance runners use a **fair usage queue**: jobs from projects that currently have the fewest jobs running on instance runners go first, so one project with 200 parallel jobs cannot starve everyone else.

**What happens after pickup.** Once the runner accepts a job, it hands it to an **executor** (section 6.2), which runs a fixed sequence of stages. These stages are exactly the collapsible sections in the job log (section 1.3):

```text
prepare executor  ─> get sources ─> restore cache ─> download artifacts
   (pull image,       (git fetch,     (from local      (from earlier jobs
    start services)    checkout)       or S3 cache)     via needs/dependencies)
        ─> step_script (before_script + script) ─> after_script
        ─> archive cache ─> upload artifacts ─> cleanup ─> report final status
```

The runner exposes information about itself to the job through predefined `CI_RUNNER_*` variables, which are job-only (section 5.1):

```yaml
whoami:
  script:
    - echo "Runner ID:        $CI_RUNNER_ID"
    - echo "Description:      $CI_RUNNER_DESCRIPTION"
    - echo "Tags:             $CI_RUNNER_TAGS"            # JSON-like list, for example ["docker", "linux"]
    - echo "Version:          $CI_RUNNER_VERSION"
    - echo "Architecture:     $CI_RUNNER_EXECUTABLE_ARCH" # for example linux/amd64
    - echo "Short token:      $CI_RUNNER_SHORT_TOKEN"     # identifies the runner in logs, safe to print
```

The job page shows two durations worth separating: **queued** time (pending until a runner took the job) and **duration** (running). Long queue times are a capacity or matching problem, never a code problem.

**Key takeaways**

- Runners pull jobs from GitLab over outbound HTTPS. GitLab never connects to a runner to start a job.
- Long polling makes pickup almost immediate without hammering the API.
- A job matches a runner only if scope, tags, untagged setting, protection and paused state all allow it.
- Instance runners use a fair usage queue across projects.
- A job's lifecycle on the runner (prepare, sources, cache, script, artifacts) maps one-to-one to the sections of the job log.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add the `whoami` job above to a project and run it twice. Compare the runner ID, tags and version, and find the same runner in **Settings > CI/CD > Runners**.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Run a self-managed runner in the foreground with `gitlab-runner --debug run` and trigger a pipeline. In the output, identify the job request that returned no job, the request that returned a job, and the trace updates. Measure the delay between the pipeline starting and the job being picked up.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why does GitLab Runner pull jobs instead of GitLab pushing jobs to runners?" *Hint:* think about firewalls and NAT, which side needs credentials for the other, and how capacity is added or removed.

#### Instance, Group and Project Runners

**Why it matters.** Not every runner should serve every project. A company-wide pool of Linux runners is useful to everyone, a GPU machine bought by the data team is not, and a runner holding production credentials must serve only one deployment project. Runner **scope** decides who can use a runner and who can manage it.

**What it is.** Every runner belongs to exactly one of three types, which mirror the hierarchy from section 1.2:

| Type | Available to | Created and managed by | Where in the UI | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Instance runner (formerly "shared runner") | Every project on the instance (unless disabled) | Administrators | **Admin > CI/CD > Runners** | General-purpose pool. GitLab-hosted runners on GitLab.com are instance runners |
| Group runner | All projects in the group and its subgroups | Group Owners | Group **Build > Runners** | A team's or business unit's own capacity |
| Project runner | The projects it is assigned to | Project Maintainers | Project **Settings > CI/CD > Runners** | Special hardware, deployment runners, isolated workloads |

A project runner can be assigned to several projects, unless it is **locked** to its current projects. A Maintainer of another project can then enable the unlocked runner for their project too.

```text
Instance runners:  [linux-pool-1] [linux-pool-2]          available to every project (if allowed)
  └── Group acme:  [acme-docker]                          available to all acme projects
        └── Subgroup acme/payments: [payments-arm64]      available to payments projects only
              └── Project shop: [shop-deploy] (locked)    only shop

Runners the "shop" project can use: linux-pool-1, linux-pool-2, acme-docker, payments-arm64, shop-deploy
```

Each level can switch off what it inherits:

| Setting | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Enable instance runners for this project | Project **Settings > CI/CD > Runners** | Turn off to keep jobs off the shared pool (or off paid GitLab-hosted minutes) |
| Enable instance runners for this group | Group **Settings > CI/CD > Runners** | Disables them for every project in the group. Projects can be allowed to re-enable them |
| Enable group runners | Project **Settings > CI/CD > Runners** | Ignore runners inherited from groups |

The same information is available through the API, which helps when auditing many projects:

```bash
# List every runner the project can use (project, inherited group, and allowed instance runners)
```
