```bash
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/runners?per_page=100" \
  | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .runner_type, .status, .description] | @tsv'

# Assign an existing, unlocked project runner (ID 77) to another project
curl --silent --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/67890/runners" --data "runner_id=77"

# Turn off instance runners for one project
curl --silent --request PUT --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345" --data "shared_runners_enabled=false"
```

Choosing a scope is a trade-off between sharing (fewer idle machines) and isolation (fewer people and projects that can run code on a machine):

| Concern | Prefer broader scope (instance, group) | Prefer narrower scope (project) |
|---|---|---|
| Utilization | Many projects share idle capacity | Capacity reserved even when idle |
| Maintenance | One fleet to upgrade and monitor | Many small fleets |
| Trust | Workloads of similar trust level | Runners with credentials, network access to production, or special hardware |
| Cost attribution | Harder to charge back per team | Clear ownership |

**Key takeaways**

- Instance runners serve the whole instance, group runners serve a group subtree, project runners serve the projects they are assigned to.
- Runner types follow the group hierarchy: a project sees its own runners plus those of every ancestor group plus allowed instance runners.
- Lock project runners that must never be reused by other projects.
- Projects and groups can disable inherited instance and group runners.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For one of your projects, list all available runners in the UI and classify each as instance, group or project runner.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Design runner scopes for a company with a shared Linux pool, a data team with two GPU machines and a payments team whose deploy runner can reach production. State which runners are locked and which inherited runners each team's projects disable.
> 3. **Interview question:** "An auditor asks which projects can run code on the runner that holds production database credentials. How do you answer, and how would you make the answer short?" *Hint:* consider runner type, locking, assignment lists, and the protected flag from section 6.3.

#### GitLab-Hosted Runners

**Why it matters.** Running your own build machines means patching, scaling and paying for them even when idle. On GitLab.com, GitLab operates a fleet of runners for you, so a new project can run pipelines with zero infrastructure. Knowing what they offer, and where they stop, tells you when to bring your own.

**What it is.** GitLab-hosted runners are instance runners operated by GitLab. They are available on GitLab.com and, as an add-on, on GitLab Dedicated. Self-managed instances have none. Key properties:

- **One fresh VM per job.** Each job gets a new, ephemeral virtual machine that is deleted after the job, so nothing leaks between jobs or projects.
- **Linux runners use the Docker executor in privileged mode**, so Docker-in-Docker builds (chapter 7) work out of the box.
- **Billing in compute minutes.** Job duration is multiplied by a **cost factor** that grows with machine size, and the result counts against the namespace's quota (section 1.2).
- **Selection by tags.** Each machine type has a predefined tag. Untagged jobs run on the small Linux amd64 machine.

| Platform | Tags | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Linux amd64 | `saas-linux-small-amd64`, `-medium-`, `-large-`, `-xlarge-`, `-2xlarge-amd64` | Small is the default for untagged jobs |
| Linux arm64 | `saas-linux-small-arm64`, `saas-linux-medium-arm64`, `saas-linux-large-arm64` | Native ARM builds without emulation |
| Linux GPU | `saas-linux-medium-amd64-gpu-standard` | For ML training and GPU tests |
| macOS | `saas-macos-medium-m1`, `saas-macos-large-m2pro` | Apple silicon, Xcode images. Premium and Ultimate only |
| Windows | `saas-windows-medium-amd64` | Windows Server with common build tools |

The Linux amd64 sizes scale linearly in resources and cost. The values below are a guide; check the current documentation, because machine specs and cost factors change over time.

| Size | vCPUs | Memory | Cost factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| small | 2 | 8 GB | 1 |
| medium | 4 | 16 GB | 2 |
| large | 8 | 32 GB | 3 |
| xlarge | 16 | 64 GB | 6 |
| 2xlarge | 32 | 128 GB | 12 |

```yaml
lint:
  image: node:20-alpine
  script: [npm ci, npm run lint]                 # untagged: small Linux amd64, cost factor 1

build-arm-image:
  tags: [saas-linux-medium-arm64]                # native arm64: no QEMU emulation needed
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]                     # works because hosted Linux runners are privileged
  script:
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:arm64-$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA" .

ios-build:
  tags: [saas-macos-medium-m1]
  image: macos-15-xcode-16                       # on macOS runners, image selects the VM image
  script:
    - xcodebuild -scheme App -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' build
```

A bigger machine is not automatically more expensive per pipeline: a test suite that takes 20 minutes on `small` (20 x 1 = 20 compute minutes) and 6 minutes on `large` (6 x 3 = 18) is both faster and cheaper on `large`. Measure before choosing (section 13.2 covers sizing).

**When to bring your own runners**

| Need | Why hosted runners do not fit |
|---|---|
| Access to private networks (internal registries, databases, on-premises clusters) | Hosted runners run on the public internet |
| Fixed egress IPs for allowlisting | Hosted runner IP ranges are not guaranteed to stay fixed |
| Custom hardware, OS versions, or kernel settings | Machine types and images are fixed by GitLab |
| Very high, steady load | Your own autoscaled fleet can be cheaper than compute minutes |
| Self-managed GitLab | No hosted runners exist |

Both can coexist: a project can use hosted runners for ordinary jobs and route deployment jobs to its own runner with a tag.

**Key takeaways**

- GitLab-hosted runners are instance runners on GitLab.com (and Dedicated) that give each job a fresh, ephemeral VM.
- Jobs pick a machine type with predefined `saas-*` tags. Untagged jobs use small Linux amd64.
- Usage is billed as job duration times the machine's cost factor.
- Bring your own runners for private network access, fixed IPs, special hardware, steady heavy load or self-managed GitLab.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the same CPU-heavy job (for example a large test suite or a compression benchmark) on `small`, `medium` and `large` Linux runners. Record duration and compute minutes consumed for each.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Your pipeline builds a multi-architecture image using QEMU emulation on amd64 and takes 25 minutes. Redesign it to build each architecture natively on hosted runners and combine the results into one manifest. Estimate the change in compute minutes.
> 3. **Interview question:** "When would you recommend that a team on GitLab.com stops using hosted runners for some of its jobs?" *Hint:* network reachability, IP allowlists, hardware, and the cost curve at high volume.

#### Runner Authentication Tokens and Registration

**Why it matters.** A runner receives every job it picks up, including the job's CI/CD variables, secrets and `CI_JOB_TOKEN`. Whoever holds a runner's token can therefore receive jobs and their secrets. How runners are created and how their tokens are protected is a core security question, not an installation detail.

**What it is.** **Registration** links a `gitlab-runner` process to a runner record in GitLab. The current workflow separates the two steps cleanly:

1. **Create the runner in GitLab** (UI or API). Here you set the scope, description, tags, "Run untagged jobs", protected, paused, locked and maximum job timeout. GitLab returns a **runner authentication token** with the prefix `glrt-`, shown only once.
2. **Register on the machine** with `gitlab-runner register --token glrt-...`. The command verifies the token, asks for the executor, and writes a `[[runners]]` entry to `config.toml`.
3. The runner starts polling. In the runner list, its status changes from "Never contacted" to "Online".

```text
Maintainer / Owner / Admin                     Build machine
──────────────────────────                     ─────────────
New runner: tags, scope, protected...
GitLab creates runner #42, token glrt-AbC...
            ── token handed over securely ──>  gitlab-runner register --url ... --token glrt-AbC...
                                               config.toml: [[runners]] token = "glrt-AbC..."
                                               gitlab-runner run  ─── polls with the token ──> GitLab
```

Creating a runner through the API needs a personal, group or project access token with the `create_runner` scope:

```bash
# Create a group runner; the response contains the authentication token exactly once
RUNNER_TOKEN=$(curl --silent --request POST \
  --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/user/runners" \
  --data "runner_type=group_type" \
  --data "group_id=42" \
  --data "description=docker-linux-amd64" \
  --data "tag_list=docker,linux,amd64" \
  --data "run_untagged=false" \
  | jq -r '.token')                       # glrt-...: store it in a secret manager, never in git
```

Then register it on the target machine. Non-interactive registration is what provisioning scripts and images use:

```bash
sudo gitlab-runner register \
  --non-interactive \
  --url "https://gitlab.example.com" \
  --token "$RUNNER_TOKEN" \
  --executor "docker" \
  --docker-image "alpine:3.20" \
  --name "docker-linux-01"                # local name of this entry in config.toml
```

With an authentication token, settings that belong to the runner record (tags, untagged, locked, protected, paused, maximum timeout) cannot be passed to `register`. They live in GitLab and are changed in the UI or with `PUT /runners/:id`. Only local settings, such as the executor and its options, are set on the machine.

**Tokens around runners.** Several tokens are easy to confuse:

| Token | Prefix | Held by | Purpose | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Runner authentication token | `glrt-` | `config.toml` of each runner manager | Authenticates the runner when requesting jobs | Until reset, or until the configured expiration (rotated automatically) |
| Runner registration token (legacy) | `GR1348941` | Admins, group Owners, project Maintainers | Created runner records implicitly at registration time | Until reset |
| Job token (`CI_JOB_TOKEN`) | `glcbt-` | One running job | Lets the job call selected GitLab APIs (section 5.1) | Expires when the job finishes |

The **legacy registration token** workflow (`gitlab-runner register --registration-token ...`) is deprecated. Anyone with the shared registration token could create runners and set their own tags, which made it impossible to track who created which runner. It has been disabled by default since GitLab 17.0 and is scheduled for removal. New setups should use authentication tokens only.

**Protecting and rotating tokens.**

- `config.toml` contains the token in plain text. Keep it readable only by root (or the service account) and never bake it into a shared VM or container image.
- Administrators can enforce a maximum lifetime for authentication tokens (**Admin > Settings > CI/CD > Runners**). The runner rotates its token automatically before it expires and records `token_obtained_at` and `token_expires_at` in `config.toml`.
- If a token leaks, reset it immediately. The old token stops working at once, and every runner manager using it must be updated:

```bash
# Reset the authentication token of runner 42 and print the new one
curl --silent --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/runners/42/reset_authentication_token" \
  | jq -r '.token'
```

To remove a runner from a machine cleanly, use `gitlab-runner unregister --name docker-linux-01`. To prune `config.toml` entries whose runner no longer exists in GitLab, run `gitlab-runner verify --delete`.

**Key takeaways**

- Create the runner in GitLab first (scope, tags, protection), then register the machine with the `glrt-` token it returns.
- Tags, protection, locking and timeouts are server-side settings and cannot be set by `register` when using an authentication token.
- A runner token grants access to every job the runner picks up, including secrets: protect `config.toml` and reset leaked tokens.
- Legacy registration tokens are deprecated and disabled by default. Do not build new automation on them.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a project runner in the UI with the tag `local-docker`, register it on your machine with the Docker executor, and run a job that targets it with that tag.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a provisioning script that creates a group runner through the API, stores the token in your secret manager (or a file with mode `0600`) and registers the runner non-interactively. Then reset the token through the API and update the runner without re-creating it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why did GitLab replace registration tokens with runner authentication tokens created in the UI?" *Hint:* think about who could create runners, who controlled their tags and protection, and traceability.

#### Runner Managers

**Why it matters.** One build machine is a single point of failure. Teams run the same runner configuration on several hosts for redundancy, in autoscaling groups, or as several Kubernetes replicas. Without a way to group them, each host would appear as a separate runner with duplicated settings, and runner lists would fill up with entries for machines that no longer exist.

**What it is.** GitLab separates two concepts:

- A **runner** is the configuration record in GitLab: its token, scope, tags, protection and description.
- A **runner manager** is a `gitlab-runner` process that uses that runner's token to request jobs.

Several managers can share one runner. Each manager is identified by a **system ID**, which it creates on first start and stores in a `.runner_system_id` file next to `config.toml`. IDs starting with `s_` are stable. IDs starting with `r_` were generated randomly because the file could not be persisted, which is typical for containers without a persistent volume, and they create a new manager on every restart.

```text
Runner #42 "docker-linux-amd64"   tags: docker, linux, amd64   token: glrt-AbC...
  ├── manager s_1a2b3c4d5e6f   host build-01   v19.4.0   last contact: 4 s ago
  ├── manager s_7a8b9c0d1e2f   host build-02   v19.4.0   last contact: 2 s ago
  └── manager s_3f4e5d6c7b8a   host build-03   v19.3.1   last contact: 9 days ago (stale)
```

The runner's detail page lists every manager with its system ID, version, platform, IP address and last contact. The job log names both the runner and the manager that ran the job:

```text
Running with gitlab-runner 19.4.0 (abcdef12)
  on docker-linux-amd64 AbC1234x, system ID: s_1a2b3c4d5e6f
```

Adding a manager is simply registering (or copying the same `[[runners]]` entry) with the same token on another host:

```bash
# On build-02: same token as build-01, so it becomes another manager of runner #42
sudo gitlab-runner register --non-interactive \
  --url "https://gitlab.example.com" \
  --token "$RUNNER_TOKEN" \
  --executor "docker" --docker-image "alpine:3.20" \
  --name "docker-linux-01"

cat /etc/gitlab-runner/.runner_system_id    # s_7a8b9c0d1e2f: keep this file on a persistent volume
```

| Aspect | Shared by all managers (set in GitLab) | Per manager (set in each `config.toml`) |
|---|---|---|
| Tags, scope, protected, locked, paused | Yes | |
| Executor, images, volumes, resources | | Yes |
| `concurrent`, `limit` | | Yes |
| Version | | Yes (can differ during upgrades) |

Because local settings are per manager, two managers of the same runner can behave differently if their `config.toml` files drift. Generate the file from one template (configuration management, Helm values or a VM image) so all managers stay identical. Pausing a runner in GitLab pauses **all** of its managers. To drain a single manager, stop that process gracefully instead (section 6.4).

**Key takeaways**

- A runner is the GitLab-side record. A runner manager is a process using its token. One runner can have many managers.
- Managers are identified by a system ID stored in `.runner_system_id`. Persist that file to avoid creating a new manager on every restart.
- Tags and protection are shared by all managers. Executor settings, concurrency and version are per manager.
- Keep managers' `config.toml` identical through automation, and drain individual managers by stopping them gracefully.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Register the same runner token on two machines (or two containers with separate config volumes). Run ten short parallel jobs and check in the job logs which system ID ran each job.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Start a runner in a container without a persistent volume for `/etc/gitlab-runner`, restart it three times, and look at the runner's manager list. Fix the setup so the manager list stays stable.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your runner list shows hundreds of managers with `r_` system IDs that were last seen weeks ago. What is the likely cause, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* where the system ID is stored, and what happens when that location is ephemeral.

<a id="62-executors"></a>
### 6.2 Executors

The runner process does not run job scripts by itself. It delegates each job to an **executor**, which decides where the script runs (host, container, pod, virtual machine) and how isolated it is. Each `[[runners]]` entry in `config.toml` uses exactly one executor. The table below gives an overview, and the topics that follow explain each executor in detail.

| Executor | Where the job runs | Isolation between jobs | `image:` honored | Elastic capacity | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shell | Directly on the runner host | None | No | No | Native toolchains, special hardware |
| Docker | A container on one Docker host | Container | Yes | No (one host) | Default choice for Linux builds |
| Kubernetes | A pod in a cluster | Pod | Yes | Through cluster autoscaling | Organizations that already run Kubernetes |
| Docker Autoscaler | A container on autoscaled cloud VMs | Container, optionally one VM per job | Yes | Yes | Elastic Docker capacity on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure |
| Instance | Directly on autoscaled cloud VMs | One VM per job (if configured) | Only with nested VM isolation | Yes | Jobs that need a whole machine |
| VirtualBox, Parallels | A clone of a VM on one host | VM | No | No | Windows or macOS builds on your own hardware |
| SSH | A remote host over SSH | None | No | No | Legacy targets |
| Custom | Whatever your scripts provision | Your choice | Your choice | Your choice | Platforms with no built-in executor |

#### Shell Executor

**Why it matters.** Some jobs cannot run in a container: an iOS build needs Xcode on macOS, a firmware job must flash a board attached by USB, a Windows build needs a licensed toolchain installed on the machine. The shell executor is the simplest way to run such jobs, and also the easiest way to create an unsafe runner.

**What it is.** The shell executor runs the job script directly on the runner host, as the user the runner service runs as (on Linux packages, the `gitlab-runner` user). It uses whatever tools are installed on the machine. The `image` and `services` keywords are ignored. Supported shells are `bash` and `sh` on Unix, and `pwsh` and `powershell` on Windows.

```text
Runner host (macOS, user gitlab-runner)
 ├── gitlab-runner service
 └── ~/builds/<short-token>/<concurrency-id>/acme/ios-app   ← working directory, persists between jobs
       job 1: git fetch, xcodebuild ...                       same user, same file system, same keychain
       job 2: git fetch, xcodebuild ...                       sees everything job 1 left behind
```

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "macos-xcode-01"
  url = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  token = "glrt-..."                      # written by gitlab-runner register
  executor = "shell"
  shell = "bash"
  builds_dir = "/Users/gitlab-runner/builds"
  environment = ["LANG=en_US.UTF-8", "DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode-16.app/Contents/Developer"]
```

```yaml
ios-build:
  tags: [macos, xcode16]                  # route to the shell runner with the toolchain
  variables:
    GIT_STRATEGY: fetch                   # reuse the existing checkout: fast on persistent hosts
    GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS: -ffdx                # but remove untracked files from earlier jobs (the default)
  script:
    - xcodebuild -scheme App -configuration Release build
```

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| No container runtime needed. Works on any OS the runner supports | No isolation: jobs share the user, files, installed tools and credentials |
| Direct access to hardware, GUI sessions, keychains and licenses | Tool versions drift with manual updates. "Works on runner A only" bugs |
| Fast: no image pull, persistent working directories | State left by one job affects the next |

**Security.** Any job on a shell runner can read the working directories of other projects that run there, install software for later jobs, read files the `gitlab-runner` user can read, and in some setups escalate privileges. Use shell runners only as project runners (or narrowly scoped group runners) for **trusted** code, never as instance runners. If a job needs Docker, do not add the `gitlab-runner` user to the `docker` group on a shared host: that is equivalent to giving every job root on the machine.

**Key takeaways**

- The shell executor runs scripts directly on the host as the runner's user and ignores `image` and `services`.
- It is the right choice for native toolchains and attached hardware, typically on macOS, Windows or embedded test benches.
- It provides no isolation between jobs: restrict it to trusted projects and keep it off shared pools.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Register a shell runner on your machine and run a job that prints `whoami`, `pwd` and the installed versions of `git` and your language runtime.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Run two jobs on the same shell runner: the first writes a file outside the project directory (for example in `$HOME`), the second reads it. Then describe two configuration changes that limit this kind of leakage.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A team wants a shell runner as an instance runner because 'Docker is too slow'. What do you advise?" *Hint:* compare isolation between projects with the actual sources of slowness, and consider caching and image choice.

#### Docker Executor

**Why it matters.** Most build problems come from environment differences. The Docker executor gives every job a fresh container from the image it asks for, so the toolchain is declared in `.gitlab-ci.yml`, identical on every runner, and thrown away afterwards. It is the default choice for Linux runners.

**What it is.** The runner talks to a Docker Engine (local socket or remote TCP) and, for each job, creates several containers on a per-job network:

```text
Docker host
 ├── gitlab-runner                     (service or container; talks to the Docker socket)
 └── per-job network
       ├── helper container      image: gitlab-runner-helper:<arch>-<version>
       │     git fetch, restore cache, download artifacts, upload artifacts
       ├── build container       image: from the job's "image:" (or the runner default)
       │     before_script + script + after_script
       └── service containers    images: from "services:" (postgres, docker:dind, ...)
       shared volumes: /builds (the checkout), /cache (local cache)
```

The **helper image** contains `git`, the artifact and cache tools, and is pulled automatically in the version matching the runner. This is why job images do not need `git` (section 2.2). The build container runs the script, and service containers are reachable by their hostname or `alias` (chapter 7).

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "docker-linux-01"
  url = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  token = "glrt-..."
  executor = "docker"
  [runners.docker]
    image = "alpine:3.20"                                    # default when a job has no image:
    pull_policy = ["always", "if-not-present"]               # try always, fall back to local copy if the registry is down
    allowed_pull_policies = ["always", "if-not-present"]     # what jobs may request with image:pull_policy
    allowed_images = ["registry.example.com/*", "docker.io/library/*"]   # restrict job images
    privileged = false                                       # true only for Docker-in-Docker, and only on trusted runners
    volumes = ["/cache"]                                     # persistent local cache volume
    memory = "4g"                                            # per-container limits avoid noisy neighbors
    cpus = "2"
    shm_size = 268435456                                     # 256 MiB /dev/shm (browsers in e2e tests need more than the default)
```

| Option | Effect | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `image` | Image for jobs without `image:` | Required at registration |
| `pull_policy` | `always`, `if-not-present`, `never`, or a list tried in order | `always` |
| `allowed_images`, `allowed_services` | Patterns of images that jobs may use | Any |
| `privileged` | Runs containers with full host capabilities | `false` |
| `volumes` | Extra volumes or bind mounts for every job container | `["/cache"]` (written at registration) |
| `memory`, `cpus` | Resource limits per job container | Unlimited |
| `disable_cache` | Disables the local `/cache` volume (distributed cache still works) | `false` |
| `network_mode` | Network for job containers | Per-job network |

**Privileged mode and the Docker socket.** Building images with Docker inside a job needs either `privileged = true` (Docker-in-Docker) or mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` into the job. Both effectively give the job root on the host. Prefer rootless builders such as BuildKit in rootless mode or Buildah, covered in section 7.3, and keep privileged runners for trusted projects only.

**Windows.** The `docker-windows` executor runs Windows containers on a Windows host. The job image's Windows version must match the host's (for example `servercore:ltsc2022` on Windows Server 2022), and the Linux-only options of `[runners.docker]` do not apply.

**Key takeaways**

- The Docker executor runs each job in a fresh container from `image:`, with a helper container for git, cache and artifacts.
- Services run as sibling containers on a per-job network.
- `allowed_images`, `allowed_pull_policies`, `memory` and `cpus` let administrators constrain what jobs can do.
- `privileged = true` or a mounted Docker socket gives jobs root on the host: avoid both on shared runners.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Register a Docker executor runner with `alpine:3.20` as the default image. Run one job without `image:` and one with `image: python:3.12-slim`, and compare `cat /etc/os-release` in both.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* While a job with a `postgres` service runs, run `docker ps` and `docker network ls` on the host. Identify the helper, build and service containers and the per-job network. Then restrict the runner with `allowed_images` and show that a job using a disallowed image fails.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is enabling `privileged = true` on an instance-wide Docker runner dangerous, even if all users are employees?" *Hint:* consider what a privileged container can do to the host and to other jobs' containers and secrets.

#### Kubernetes Executor

**Why it matters.** Organizations that already run Kubernetes have a scheduler, autoscaling, monitoring and access control in place. The Kubernetes executor turns that cluster into CI capacity: every job becomes a pod, scheduled and scaled like any other workload, with no separate VM fleet to operate.

**What it is.** The runner manager usually runs inside the cluster, installed with the official Helm chart (or the GitLab Runner Operator on OpenShift). For each job, it creates a pod through the Kubernetes API:

```text
Namespace gitlab-runner
 ├── Deployment gitlab-runner (runner manager pod)   ── polls GitLab, creates and deletes job pods
 └── Pod runner-abc123-project-12345-concurrent-0     (one per job)
       ├── init container  init-permissions          prepares shared volumes
       ├── container       build                     job image: before_script, script, after_script
       ├── container       helper                    git fetch, cache, artifacts
       └── containers      svc-0, svc-1, ...         services: share the pod network, reachable on localhost
```

Install the runner with Helm and keep its token in a Kubernetes Secret:

```bash
helm repo add gitlab https://charts.gitlab.io
kubectl create namespace gitlab-runner
kubectl --namespace gitlab-runner create secret generic gitlab-runner-token \
  --from-literal=runner-registration-token="" \
  --from-literal=runner-token="$RUNNER_TOKEN"        # the glrt- token of a runner created in GitLab
helm install gitlab-runner gitlab/gitlab-runner \
  --namespace gitlab-runner --values values.yaml
```

```yaml
# values.yaml
gitlabUrl: https://gitlab.example.com/
concurrent: 20                       # max job pods this runner manager runs at once
rbac:
  create: true                       # lets the manager create pods, secrets and services in its namespace
runners:
  secret: gitlab-runner-token        # Secret created above
  config: |
    [[runners]]
      [runners.kubernetes]
        namespace = "{{.Release.Namespace}}"
        image = "alpine:3.20"                       # default job image
        cpu_request = "500m"                        # requests drive scheduling and node autoscaling
        memory_request = "1Gi"
        memory_limit = "2Gi"
        helper_cpu_request = "100m"
        helper_memory_request = "128Mi"
        cpu_limit_overwrite_max_allowed = "4"       # jobs may raise their CPU limit up to 4 cores
        memory_limit_overwrite_max_allowed = "8Gi"  # and their memory limit up to 8 GiB
        memory_request_overwrite_max_allowed = "8Gi"
        poll_timeout = 600                          # seconds to wait for a pod to start (node scale-up, image pull)
        service_account = "ci-jobs"                 # identity of job pods inside the cluster
```

Jobs request resources through variables, capped by the `*_overwrite_max_allowed` settings:

```yaml
integration-tests:
  image: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21
  variables:
    KUBERNETES_CPU_REQUEST: "2"
    KUBERNETES_MEMORY_REQUEST: "6Gi"
    KUBERNETES_MEMORY_LIMIT: "8Gi"       # above 8Gi would be rejected by the runner
  services:
    - name: postgres:16
      alias: db                          # services are also reachable on localhost in the pod
  script:
    - mvn verify
```

| Option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `namespace` | Namespace for job pods |
| `cpu_request`, `cpu_limit`, `memory_request`, `memory_limit` | Defaults for the build container (`helper_*` and `service_*` variants exist) |
| `*_overwrite_max_allowed` | Upper bound for job-level `KUBERNETES_*` overrides. Overrides are refused if unset |
| `node_selector`, `node_tolerations`, `affinity` | Place job pods on dedicated CI nodes |
| `service_account` | Kubernetes identity of job pods (for example for cloud workload identity) |
| `privileged` | Privileged build containers. Avoid on shared clusters |
| `poll_timeout` | How long to wait for the pod to become ready before failing the job |

**Differences from Docker.** Services share the pod's network namespace, so two services cannot listen on the same port. There is no Docker daemon, so building images needs a rootless builder or a privileged Docker-in-Docker service. Pods that stay `Pending` longer than `poll_timeout` (no node with enough resources, image pull problems) fail the job with a system failure.

**Key takeaways**

- The Kubernetes executor creates one pod per job, with build, helper and service containers.
- Install the runner with the Helm chart and keep the `glrt-` token in a Secret.
- Default requests and limits come from `config.toml`. Jobs can override them with `KUBERNETES_*` variables up to the configured maximums.
- Services share the pod network and are reachable on `localhost`. Pod scheduling delays count against `poll_timeout`.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Install the runner in a local cluster (kind, minikube or k3d) with the Helm chart and run a job. While it runs, inspect the job pod with `kubectl describe pod` and identify its containers.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure `memory_limit_overwrite_max_allowed` and run three jobs requesting 1Gi, 4Gi and a value above the maximum. Explain each outcome, then trigger an out-of-memory kill and find the evidence in the job log and in `kubectl get events`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your Kubernetes jobs often fail with a pod timeout during business hours only. What would you investigate?" *Hint:* node autoscaling speed, resource requests versus node sizes, image pull time, and `poll_timeout`.

#### Docker Autoscaler Executor

**Why it matters.** CI load is spiky: quiet at night, overloaded before a release. A fixed Docker host is either idle (wasting money) or saturated (making developers wait). The Docker Autoscaler executor adds and removes cloud VMs to match the job queue while keeping the familiar Docker executor behavior.

**What it is.** The runner manager drives a cloud **instance group** (an AWS Auto Scaling group, a Google Cloud managed instance group or an Azure virtual machine scale set) through a **fleeting plugin**. It connects to each instance over SSH (or WinRM) and runs jobs as Docker containers on that instance, just like the Docker executor does on a single host.

```text
Runner manager (small, always on)
  ├── taskscaler: how many job slots are needed now?
  └── fleeting plugin (aws | googlecloud | azure) ── resize ──> Instance group
                                                                 ├── VM 1: Docker ── job A, job B
                                                                 ├── VM 2: Docker ── job C
                                                                 └── VM 3: idle, ready for the next job
```

It replaces the **Docker Machine executor** (`docker+machine`), which depended on the abandoned Docker Machine project and is deprecated. New autoscaling setups should use Docker Autoscaler.

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "docker-autoscaler-aws"
  url = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  token = "glrt-..."
  executor = "docker-autoscaler"
  [runners.docker]
    image = "alpine:3.20"                 # same [runners.docker] options as the Docker executor
  [runners.autoscaler]
    plugin = "aws"                        # installed with: gitlab-runner fleeting install
    capacity_per_instance = 2             # jobs that may run at once on one VM
    max_use_count = 20                    # replace a VM after 20 jobs (limits state build-up)
    max_instances = 30                    # hard cap on the group size
    [runners.autoscaler.plugin_config]
      name = "ci-runner-asg"              # name of the Auto Scaling group to control
    [runners.autoscaler.connector_config]
      username = "ubuntu"                 # SSH user on the instances
    [[runners.autoscaler.policy]]
      idle_count = 4                      # keep 4 idle job slots ready
      idle_time = "20m0s"                 # remove idle capacity after 20 minutes
```

| Setting | Effect | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| `capacity_per_instance` | Jobs per VM | Higher is cheaper, but jobs share CPU, disk and the Docker daemon |
| `max_use_count` | Jobs per VM lifetime | `1` gives one fresh VM per job (strong isolation, slower). Higher reuses warm caches and images |
| `max_instances` | Upper bound on VMs | Caps cost and protects quotas |
| `idle_count`, `idle_time` | Warm capacity | More idle slots mean faster pickup and higher cost |

Setting up the instance group, the plugin and scaling policies is covered in section 6.4.

**Key takeaways**

- Docker Autoscaler runs jobs in Docker containers on cloud VMs that are created and removed on demand.
- It uses fleeting plugins for AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, and replaces the deprecated Docker Machine executor.
- `capacity_per_instance` and `max_use_count` set the balance between cost, speed and isolation.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Explain in your own words what happens, step by step, when 10 jobs arrive at a Docker Autoscaler runner with `idle_count = 2`, `capacity_per_instance = 2` and no running VMs.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Compare two configurations for a fleet running 500 short jobs a day: (a) `capacity_per_instance = 4`, `max_use_count = 50`; (b) `capacity_per_instance = 1`, `max_use_count = 1`. Discuss isolation, pickup latency, cache warmth and cost.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why did GitLab replace the Docker Machine executor rather than continue maintaining it?" *Hint:* upstream project status, cloud-provider coupling, and how the new design uses native instance groups.

#### Instance Executor

**Why it matters.** Some jobs need a whole machine rather than a container: system tests that load kernel modules, builds that run Docker without a privileged container, tools that expect a full OS, or workloads that must not share a kernel with anyone. The Instance executor gives such jobs autoscaled VMs with the same elasticity as Docker Autoscaler.

**What it is.** The Instance executor uses the same fleeting and taskscaler machinery, but runs the job script **directly on the VM** through a shell, like the shell executor, instead of inside a container. With `max_use_count = 1`, every job gets a fresh VM that is destroyed afterwards. This gives shell-like freedom without shell-executor leakage.

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "instance-aws"
  url = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  token = "glrt-..."
  executor = "instance"
  shell = "bash"                          # the VM image must have bash, git and the tools jobs need
  [runners.autoscaler]
    plugin = "aws"
    capacity_per_instance = 1             # one job per VM
    max_use_count = 1                     # fresh VM for every job, deleted afterwards
    max_instances = 20
    [runners.autoscaler.plugin_config]
      name = "ci-instance-asg"
    [runners.autoscaler.connector_config]
      username = "ec2-user"
    [[runners.autoscaler.policy]]
      idle_count = 2
      idle_time = "15m0s"
```

```yaml
kernel-module-test:
  tags: [full-vm]                         # tag of the instance runner
  script:
    - sudo modprobe ./build/mydriver.ko   # possible because the job owns the whole VM
    - ./tests/run-driver-tests.sh
```

The Instance executor can also run **nested virtualization** (`[runners.autoscaler.vm_isolation]`), where each job runs in its own VM inside the instance. Here `image:` selects the nested VM image. This is useful, for example, for macOS jobs on Apple hardware, where each job gets its own macOS VM.

| | Docker Autoscaler | Instance |
|---|---|---|
| Job runs in | Container on the VM | Shell directly on the VM |
| `image:` | Container image | Ignored (or nested VM image with VM isolation) |
| Tools come from | Job image | VM image (AMI, machine image) |
| Typical isolation | Container, optional VM per job | VM per job |
| Best for | Ordinary builds and tests | Jobs needing root, kernel access, or a full OS |

**Key takeaways**

- The Instance executor runs jobs directly on autoscaled VMs, without a container.
- With `max_use_count = 1`, each job gets a clean, disposable VM.
- Tools must be baked into the VM image, because `image:` does not apply (except with nested VM isolation).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* List three kinds of jobs from your own projects that would benefit from the Instance executor rather than Docker, and explain why.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a VM image (for example with Packer) containing `git`, `bash` and Docker Engine, configure an Instance executor that uses it with `max_use_count = 1`, and run a job that builds a Docker image without a privileged container.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Shell executor and Instance executor both run scripts directly on a machine. Why is one considered safe for untrusted code and the other not?" *Hint:* lifetime of the machine and what the next job inherits.

#### VirtualBox and Parallels Executors

**Why it matters.** Teams that build for Windows or macOS on their own hardware need full OS isolation, but may not have a cloud or a Kubernetes cluster. The VirtualBox and Parallels executors give each job a clean VM on a single physical host.

**What it is.** You prepare a **base VM** with the OS, build tools, an SSH server, `git` and `gitlab-runner` (the runner binary inside the VM handles artifacts and caches). For each job, the executor creates a linked clone of the base VM from a snapshot, starts it, connects over SSH, runs the job, and deletes the clone.

```text
Physical host (Linux or Windows with VirtualBox, or macOS with Parallels)
 ├── gitlab-runner
 ├── base VM "win2022-build" + snapshot "tools-2026-09"     never modified by jobs
 └── per job: linked clone  ── SSH ──> run script  ──> delete clone
```

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "windows-vbox-01"
  url = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  token = "glrt-..."
  executor = "virtualbox"
  shell = "pwsh"                                      # shell inside the guest
  [runners.ssh]
    user = "builder"
    identity_file = "/home/gitlab-runner/.ssh/id_ed25519"
  [runners.virtualbox]
    base_name = "win2022-build"                       # VM to clone
    base_snapshot = "tools-2026-09"                   # clone from this snapshot (linked clone)
    disable_snapshots = false                         # false: fast linked clones; true: full copy per job
```

Parallels is configured the same way with a `[runners.parallels]` section (`base_name`, `template_name`, `disable_snapshots`) and is mainly used for macOS guests on Mac hardware.

| Strength | Limitation |
|---|---|
| Full OS isolation on your own hardware | Capacity bounded by one host's CPU and memory |
| Clean VM per job from a known snapshot | Slower start than containers (clone and boot) |
| Works for Windows and macOS builds | No autoscaling. Base images must be maintained by hand |
| | Licensing: macOS guests require Apple hardware |

To update tools, update the base VM, take a new snapshot and change `base_snapshot`. Jobs never see half-updated images.

**Key takeaways**

- VirtualBox and Parallels executors clone a base VM per job and run the script over SSH.
- The base VM needs an SSH server, a shell, `git` and `gitlab-runner`.
- They provide strong isolation on a single host but no elastic capacity. For cloud capacity, prefer the Instance executor.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Describe the steps to prepare a base VM for the VirtualBox executor and explain why each component (SSH server, `git`, `gitlab-runner`) is needed.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Design a process for updating the toolchain in a Parallels base VM used by 15 iOS projects without breaking running jobs, including how to roll back.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your company has three Mac minis for iOS builds. Would you use the shell executor or the Parallels executor, and why?" *Hint:* isolation between projects, signing keys in keychains, boot time and capacity.

#### SSH and Custom Executors

**Why it matters.** Not every environment fits a built-in executor. Some legacy systems can only be reached over SSH, and some organizations run jobs on platforms GitLab has no native support for, such as LXD, Podman on a hardened host, a mainframe partition or an in-house VM orchestrator. These two executors cover the edge cases.

**SSH executor.** The runner connects to a fixed remote host over SSH and runs the job script there. It is the least featured executor: it supports only Bash scripts, does not support caching, needs `gitlab-runner` on the remote host to upload artifacts, and provides no isolation, because every job runs on the same remote host and user. Use it only when nothing else can reach a target, and prefer installing a runner on that host instead.

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "legacy-aix-ssh"
  executor = "ssh"
  [runners.ssh]
    host = "aix-build.internal.example.com"
    port = "22"
    user = "builder"
    identity_file = "/home/gitlab-runner/.ssh/id_ed25519"
```

**Custom executor.** The Custom executor lets you write the executor yourself as four executables that the runner calls at fixed points:

```text
config_exec   (optional) print JSON to adjust builds_dir, cache_dir, driver name
prepare_exec  create the environment (VM, container, chroot...)
run_exec      called once per stage: run_exec <script-path> <stage-name>
                 stages: prepare_script, get_sources, restore_cache, download_artifacts,
                         step_script, after_script, archive_cache, upload_artifacts_on_success,
                         upload_artifacts_on_failure, cleanup_file_variables
cleanup_exec  destroy the environment, always called, even after failures
```

Your scripts receive the job's variables with a `CUSTOM_ENV_` prefix (for example `CUSTOM_ENV_CI_JOB_ID`, `CUSTOM_ENV_CI_JOB_IMAGE`). They report failures with two exit codes provided by the runner: `$BUILD_FAILURE_EXIT_CODE` means the job's script failed, `$SYSTEM_FAILURE_EXIT_CODE` means the infrastructure failed (which `retry:when: runner_system_failure` can target, section 4.3).

A minimal driver that runs each job in its own Podman container:

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "podman-custom"
  url = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  token = "glrt-..."
  executor = "custom"
  builds_dir = "/builds"                          # path inside the job environment
  cache_dir = "/cache"
  [runners.custom]
    prepare_exec = "/opt/ci-driver/prepare.sh"
    run_exec = "/opt/ci-driver/run.sh"
    cleanup_exec = "/opt/ci-driver/cleanup.sh"
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /opt/ci-driver/prepare.sh: create one container per job
set -eo pipefail
trap 'exit "$SYSTEM_FAILURE_EXIT_CODE"' ERR             # any failure here is an infrastructure failure

CONTAINER="ci-job-$CUSTOM_ENV_CI_JOB_ID"
IMAGE="${CUSTOM_ENV_CI_JOB_IMAGE:-debian:bookworm}"     # honor the job's image: keyword
podman run --detach --name "$CONTAINER" "$IMAGE" sleep infinity
# get_sources needs git; artifacts and cache need the gitlab-runner binary in the environment
podman exec "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'command -v git >/dev/null || (apt-get update && apt-get install -y git curl)'
podman cp /usr/bin/gitlab-runner "$CONTAINER":/usr/bin/gitlab-runner
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /opt/ci-driver/run.sh: $1 = generated script for this stage, $2 = stage name
CONTAINER="ci-job-$CUSTOM_ENV_CI_JOB_ID"
if ! podman exec --interactive "$CONTAINER" /bin/bash < "$1"; then
  exit "$BUILD_FAILURE_EXIT_CODE"                        # the job failed, not the infrastructure
fi
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /opt/ci-driver/cleanup.sh: always runs; never leave containers behind
podman rm --force "ci-job-$CUSTOM_ENV_CI_JOB_ID" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
```

| | SSH | Custom |
|---|---|---|
| Effort | Configuration only | You write and maintain the driver |
| Isolation | None | Whatever your driver provides |
| Cache and artifacts | No cache. Artifacts only if `gitlab-runner` is installed on the remote host | Supported if `gitlab-runner` is available in the environment |
| Use when | A remote host cannot run a runner itself | No built-in executor fits your platform |

**Key takeaways**

- The SSH executor runs Bash scripts on one remote host. It has no isolation or caching and is a last resort.
- The Custom executor delegates prepare, run (per stage) and cleanup to your own executables.
- Custom drivers read job variables with the `CUSTOM_ENV_` prefix and signal build versus system failures with the provided exit codes.
- Cleanup must be idempotent and must never fail the job.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Implement the Podman driver above (or the same idea with Docker) and run a job with `image: python:3.12-slim`. Print `$2` in `run.sh` to see each stage name in the job log.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend the driver with `config_exec` that reports a driver name and version, and make `prepare.sh` fail on purpose. Check that the job fails as a system failure and is retried by `retry: { max: 1, when: [runner_system_failure] }`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "When would you write a Custom executor instead of using the Kubernetes or Instance executor?" *Hint:* think about platforms without built-in support, compliance-mandated sandboxes, and the maintenance cost you take on.

<a id="63-runner-configuration"></a>
### 6.3 Runner Configuration

A runner's behavior is split between settings stored in GitLab and the local `config.toml` file on each runner manager. This subchapter covers the structure of `config.toml`, how concurrency is controlled, how tags and protection decide which jobs a runner accepts, and how administrators inject commands into every job.

#### config.toml Structure

**Why it matters.** Almost every runner problem, from "only one job runs at a time" to "the job cannot reach the cache", is fixed in `config.toml`. Knowing its layout, and which settings live there rather than in GitLab, saves hours of guessing.

**What it is.** `config.toml` is a [TOML](https://toml.io) file read by the runner process. Its location depends on how the runner runs:

| Installation | Location |
|---|---|
| Linux package, running as root (the usual service) | `/etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml` |
| Running as a non-root user | `~/.gitlab-runner/config.toml` |
| Windows | Next to `gitlab-runner.exe`, for example `C:\GitLab-Runner\config.toml` |
| Docker container | `/etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml` inside the container (mount a volume) |
| Helm chart | Generated from `values.yaml` (`runners.config`) |

The file has three levels: **global settings** for the whole process, an optional `[session_server]`, and one or more `[[runners]]` entries (double brackets mean "array of tables": each entry is one runner the process serves). Each entry has executor- and feature-specific subsections.

```toml
# ---------- Global: the whole gitlab-runner process ----------
concurrent = 8                     # max jobs running at once across all [[runners]] entries
check_interval = 3                 # seconds between job requests per entry (long polling makes this rarely visible)
log_level = "info"                 # debug | info | warn | error
log_format = "json"                # runner (default) | text | json; json suits log shipping
shutdown_timeout = 7200            # seconds to wait for running jobs on graceful shutdown
listen_address = ":9252"           # Prometheus metrics endpoint (section 6.4)

[session_server]                   # needed only for interactive web terminals
  listen_address = "[::]:8093"
  advertise_address = "runner-01.example.com:8093"
  session_timeout = 1800

# ---------- One runner entry ----------
[[runners]]
  name = "docker-linux-01"         # local label
  url = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  id = 42                          # runner ID in GitLab
  token = "glrt-..."               # authentication token (keep this file 0600)
  token_obtained_at = 2026-09-01T08:00:00Z
  token_expires_at = 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z   # zero value: no expiration configured
  executor = "docker"
  limit = 6                        # max jobs for this entry (0 = no per-entry limit)
  request_concurrency = 2          # parallel job requests this entry may have open
  output_limit = 16384             # max job log size in KB (default 4096)
  environment = ["HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.internal:3128", "NO_PROXY=.internal,localhost"]
  pre_get_sources_script = "git config --global http.sslCAInfo /etc/ssl/certs/internal-ca.pem"

  [runners.feature_flags]
    FF_USE_FASTZIP = true          # faster artifact and cache compression

  [runners.cache]                  # distributed cache shared by all managers (chapter 8)
    Type = "s3"
    Shared = true                  # share cache between runners, not only between jobs of one runner
    [runners.cache.s3]
      ServerAddress = "s3.amazonaws.com"
      BucketName = "acme-runner-cache"
      BucketLocation = "eu-central-1"

  [runners.docker]                 # executor-specific options (section 6.2)
    image = "alpine:3.20"
    privileged = false
    volumes = ["/cache"]
```

**Server-side versus local settings.** Some settings live in GitLab and are shared by all runner managers, others live only in `config.toml`:

| Set in GitLab (UI or `PUT /runners/:id`) | Set in `config.toml` |
|---|---|
| Description, tags, run untagged jobs | Executor and its options (`[runners.docker]`, `[runners.kubernetes]`...) |
| Protected, locked, paused | `concurrent`, `limit`, `request_concurrency` |
| Maximum job timeout | Cache backend, proxy and environment variables |
| Scope (instance, group, project) and project assignments | Hooks, feature flags, log size, metrics endpoint |

**Changing the file.** The runner watches `config.toml` and reloads most changes automatically within a few seconds, without interrupting running jobs. A few global settings, such as `listen_address`, need a restart. Useful commands:

```bash
sudo gitlab-runner list                  # entries in config.toml with their URL and executor
sudo gitlab-runner verify                # check each entry's token against GitLab
sudo gitlab-runner verify --delete       # remove entries whose runner no longer exists
sudo gitlab-runner restart               # restart the service (running jobs are interrupted unless drained)
```

Keep `config.toml` under configuration management (Ansible, Chef, a Helm chart, a VM image build) with the token injected from a secret store. Hand-edited files on many machines drift apart, and managers of the same runner start behaving differently (section 6.1).

**Key takeaways**

- `config.toml` has global settings, an optional `[session_server]` and one `[[runners]]` entry per runner served by the process.
- Executor, cache, concurrency, hooks and environment live in `config.toml`. Tags, protection, locking and timeouts live in GitLab.
- Most edits are reloaded automatically. Manage the file as code and keep it readable only by the runner's service account.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open the `config.toml` of a runner you registered, label each line as global, entry-level or executor-level, and look up two settings you have not seen before in the runner documentation.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure an S3-compatible distributed cache (for example MinIO) for two runner managers of the same runner. Prove that a cache written by a job on one manager is restored by a job on the other.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A developer asks you to add the tag `gpu` to a runner by editing its `config.toml`. Why does that not work with the current registration workflow, and where do you change it?" *Hint:* which side owns tags when using runner authentication tokens.

#### Concurrency Settings

**Why it matters.** A newly registered runner has `concurrent = 1`, so it runs **one job at a time** no matter how powerful the machine is. Conversely, a runner allowed to run too many jobs overloads its host and makes every job slow. Three settings control parallelism, and they interact in ways that surprise many teams.

**What it is.**

| Setting | Scope | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `concurrent` | Global | Maximum jobs running at once across **all** `[[runners]]` entries of the process | `1` |
| `limit` | Per `[[runners]]` entry | Maximum jobs for this entry. For autoscaling executors, also see `max_instances` | `0` (no per-entry limit) |
| `request_concurrency` | Per `[[runners]]` entry | How many job requests this entry may have open at once | `1` |

The effective limit is the smaller of the two caps. Think of `concurrent` as the number of seats in a restaurant, and `limit` as the number of seats reserved for each party.

```toml
concurrent = 10                  # the whole process: at most 10 jobs

[[runners]]
  name = "docker-general"
  executor = "docker"
  limit = 8                      # at most 8 of the 10 slots
  request_concurrency = 2        # ask for up to 2 jobs at once: fills free slots faster under load

[[runners]]
  name = "docker-heavy"          # second runner record, e.g. with the tag "heavy"
  executor = "docker"
  limit = 2                      # heavy jobs never take more than 2 slots
```

```text
Queue: 12 general jobs, 3 heavy jobs
  docker-general  runs 8  (its limit)
  docker-heavy    runs 2  (its limit)
  total           10      (concurrent): the remaining 5 jobs stay pending

If concurrent were 6:  general and heavy compete for 6 slots, limits never reached
```

**Sizing concurrency.** Choose `concurrent` from the host's resources and the typical job, not from the queue length:

```text
Host: 16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM, fast SSD
Typical job: ~2 vCPU, ~6 GB RAM peak
  CPU bound:    16 / 2  = 8
  Memory bound: 64 / 6 ≈ 10  (leave headroom for Docker, page cache, the runner)
  => concurrent = 8, and set [runners.docker] cpus = "2", memory = "6g" so one job cannot starve the others
```

On autoscaling executors, capacity is mostly controlled by the autoscaler (`max_instances` times `capacity_per_instance`, section 6.4), while `concurrent` and `limit` must be at least that large or they become the real bottleneck. On Kubernetes, `concurrent` caps the number of job pods per runner manager, and cluster resources cap the rest.

`request_concurrency` matters when many jobs are queued: with the default of `1`, an entry fills free slots one request at a time. Raising it to a small number (2 to 4) fills slots faster. Very high values only add load on GitLab. Increase it if the metric `gitlab_runner_request_concurrency_exceeded_total` (section 6.4) keeps growing.

**Key takeaways**

- `concurrent` (global) and `limit` (per entry) both cap running jobs. The smaller one wins.
- The default `concurrent = 1` is the most common reason a powerful runner runs jobs one by one.
- Size concurrency from CPU and memory per job, and set per-job resource limits to avoid noisy neighbors.
- On autoscaling executors, make sure `concurrent` and `limit` do not cap below the autoscaler's maximum capacity.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* On a runner with `concurrent = 1`, start a pipeline with five parallel jobs and observe them run one by one. Raise `concurrent` to 5 without restarting the runner and observe the next pipeline.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure two `[[runners]]` entries on one host (one for general jobs, one for jobs tagged `heavy`) so heavy jobs never use more than 2 slots and the host never runs more than 6 jobs in total. Prove it with a pipeline of 10 general and 5 heavy jobs.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Jobs wait in `pending` for minutes although your runner host's CPU is at 20%. Walk through what you check." *Hint:* `concurrent` versus `limit`, `request_concurrency`, tag matching, and whether the runner is actually online.

#### Runner Tags and Untagged Jobs

**Why it matters.** Section 2.2 showed tags from the job's side: a job lists the capabilities it needs. This topic covers the runner's side: which tags to give runners, whether they should accept untagged jobs, and how bad choices send jobs to the wrong machine, or nowhere.

**What it is.** A runner's tags and its "Run untagged jobs" flag are set on the runner record in GitLab (at creation, in the runner's **Edit** page, or with the API). The matching rule from section 2.2 still applies: a runner can take a job only if it has **all** of the job's tags.

| Runner configuration | Takes tagged jobs | Takes untagged jobs |
|---|---|---|
| Tags `[docker, linux]`, run untagged: on | Jobs whose tags are a subset of `[docker, linux]` | Yes |
| Tags `[docker, linux]`, run untagged: off | Jobs whose tags are a subset of `[docker, linux]` | No |
| No tags, run untagged: on | None (any job with a tag needs a runner having it) | Yes |

A runner created without tags runs untagged jobs. A runner created with tags must have "Run untagged jobs" turned on explicitly if it should also take them.

```bash
# Change tags and untagged behavior of runner 42 (server-side settings)
curl --silent --request PUT --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/runners/42" \
  --data "tag_list=docker,linux,amd64" \
  --data "run_untagged=true"
```

**Designing tags.** Tags work best when they describe **capabilities**, not machines. A job asking for `build-server-07` breaks when that server is replaced. A job asking for `[linux, arm64, docker]` keeps working on any runner that offers those capabilities.

| Tag style | Examples | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| Platform and architecture | `linux`, `windows`, `macos`, `amd64`, `arm64` | Choosing an OS and CPU |
| Executor or tooling | `docker`, `kubernetes`, `xcode16`, `gpu` | Choosing an environment |
| Size class | `small`, `large`, `high-mem` | Cost and performance (section 13.2) |
| Purpose or trust zone | `prod-deploy`, `pci` | Restricted runners, combined with protection (next topic) |
| Machine identity | `build-server-07` | Avoid: couples jobs to one machine |

**Untagged jobs as a policy decision.** Untagged jobs go to any runner that accepts them. Decide deliberately which runners those are:

- A general-purpose pool should usually accept untagged jobs, so simple projects work without knowing any tags.
- Specialized runners (GPU, macOS, deployment, large machines) should **not** accept untagged jobs, or every ordinary lint job may land on your most expensive machine.
- On GitLab.com, if your project has its own runners **and** hosted instance runners enabled, untagged jobs may run on either. Disable instance runners for the project, or tag your jobs, if consumption of compute minutes matters.

```yaml
default:
  tags: [docker, linux]           # every job targets the general pool unless it says otherwise

unit-tests:
  script: [make test]

train-model:
  tags: [linux, gpu]              # replaces the default list: only GPU runners
  script: [python train.py]

deploy-prod:
  tags: [prod-deploy]             # restricted runner, see "Protected Runners"
  script: [./deploy.sh production]
```

**Key takeaways**

- Runner tags and "Run untagged jobs" are server-side settings on the runner record.
- Name tags after capabilities (OS, architecture, tooling, size, trust zone), not after machines.
- Only general-purpose runners should accept untagged jobs. Specialized and expensive runners should not.
- Mixed fleets of own and hosted runners can route untagged jobs to either. Tag jobs or disable instance runners when that matters.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create two runners: one with tags `[docker, linux]` that accepts untagged jobs, one with `[docker, linux, large]` that does not. Predict and then verify where an untagged job, a `[docker]` job and a `[large]` job run.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Audit all runners available to a group using the API (`GET /groups/:id/runners`, then `GET /runners/:id` for `tag_list` and `run_untagged`). Produce a table of which runners accept untagged jobs and flag any specialized runner that does.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your cloud bill doubled after a team added a 32-core runner. Pipelines did not change. What is a likely cause?" *Hint:* which jobs the new runner is allowed to take, and what it means for an untagged job.

#### Protected Runners

**Why it matters.** Deployment runners often hold the most sensitive things in CI: cloud credentials in their IAM role, network access to production, signing keys. If any branch could send a job to them, any developer (or any merge request from a fork) could run arbitrary code with those privileges. Protected runners close that gap.

**What it is.** A runner marked **Protected** (API: `access_level=ref_protected`) only takes jobs from pipelines that run for **protected branches or protected tags**. Jobs from other refs never reach it: if no other runner matches, they stay pending.

```text
Pipeline for                       Job tags         Protected runner "prod-deploy"
───────────────────────────────    ─────────────    ───────────────────────────────
main (protected)                   [prod-deploy]    takes the job
v2.4.0 (protected tag)             [prod-deploy]    takes the job
feature/login (unprotected)        [prod-deploy]    refuses: job stays pending (stuck)
MR pipeline from a fork            [prod-deploy]    never sees it: runs in the fork's project
```

```bash
# Make runner 77 protected, untagged-proof and locked to its project
curl --silent --request PUT --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/runners/77" \
  --data "access_level=ref_protected" \
  --data "run_untagged=false" \
  --data "locked=true" \
  --data "tag_list=prod-deploy"
```

Protection is one layer. Combine it with the others from earlier chapters so that each covers a different gap:

| Control | What it prevents |
|---|---|
| Protected branches and tags (section 11.4) | Unreviewed code becoming a protected ref |
| Protected runner | Code from unprotected refs running on the privileged machine |
| Dedicated tag, untagged jobs off | Ordinary jobs from protected branches landing on the deploy runner by accident |
| Locked project runner | Other projects enabling the runner for themselves |
| Protected variables and environments (chapter 5, chapter 12) | Secrets and deployment approvals leaking to unprotected pipelines |

Protection controls **which refs** can use the runner, not **what the code does**. Anyone who can push or merge to a protected branch can still run arbitrary code on the runner, so the protected branch rules (who can push, who can merge, required approvals) are part of the runner's security. Section 11.4 builds a complete least-privilege runner design on these pieces.

**Key takeaways**

- Protected runners take jobs only from pipelines for protected branches and tags.
- Use them for every runner with deployment credentials or privileged network access.
- Combine protection with a dedicated tag, untagged jobs off and locking.
- Protection is only as strong as the rules on who can push and merge to protected refs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Mark a project runner as protected and give it a unique tag. Run a job with that tag from `main` (protected) and from a feature branch, and compare the outcomes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Design the full set of controls for a runner that deploys to production through an IAM role, including branch protection rules, runner settings, tags, and environment protection. For each control, describe the attack it prevents.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A runner is protected, so only `main` can use it. A developer opens a merge request that changes `.gitlab-ci.yml` to print the runner's cloud credentials. Under what conditions does this succeed?" *Hint:* consider who can merge to `main`, approval rules, and code owners for CI configuration.

#### Pre- and Post-Build Hooks

**Why it matters.** Platform teams often need something to happen in every job on their runners: trust the company's internal certificate authority, configure a proxy or a package mirror, rewrite git URLs, record audit information. Asking every project to add these lines to `before_script` does not scale and is easy to forget. Runner hooks inject commands centrally.

**What it is.** Four `config.toml` settings in a `[[runners]]` entry add commands at fixed points of every job. They run in the job's own environment with the job's privileges, and a failing hook fails the job.

| Setting | Runs | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `pre_get_sources_script` | Before the repository is fetched | Git configuration, CA certificates for git, cleaning the workspace |
| `post_get_sources_script` | After fetch and checkout | Checking out large files, verifying the commit |
| `pre_build_script` | Before `before_script` | Installing CA certificates, configuring mirrors and proxies, logging |
| `post_build_script` | After `script`, before `after_script` | Collecting metrics, cleanup |

Together with the job-level `hooks:pre_get_sources_script` keyword (section 2.4), the order inside a job is:

```text
get sources step     (helper container for Docker and Kubernetes executors)
  1. pre_get_sources_script               config.toml (administrator)
  2. hooks:pre_get_sources_script         .gitlab-ci.yml (developer)
  3. git fetch + checkout
  4. post_get_sources_script              config.toml
restore cache, download artifacts
step script          (build container)
  5. pre_build_script                     config.toml
  6. before_script + script               .gitlab-ci.yml
  7. post_build_script                    config.toml
after_script                              .gitlab-ci.yml
```

For the Docker and Kubernetes executors, note **where** each hook runs: the get-sources hooks run in the helper container, the build hooks in the job's image. A hook that installs a certificate with `update-ca-certificates` works only if the job image has that tool, so write build hooks defensively.

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "docker-internal"
  executor = "docker"
  # Trust the internal CA for git operations (runs in the helper image, which has git)
  pre_get_sources_script = '''
    git config --global http.sslCAInfo /certs/internal-ca.pem
    git config --global url."https://mirror.internal/github/".insteadOf "https://github.com/"
  '''
  # Add the internal CA to the job image if it is Debian- or Alpine-based; never fail other images
  pre_build_script = '''
    if command -v update-ca-certificates >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      cp /certs/internal-ca.pem /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/internal-ca.crt
      update-ca-certificates >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    fi
    echo "Runner $CI_RUNNER_SHORT_TOKEN, job $CI_JOB_ID, project $CI_PROJECT_PATH, ref $CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME"
  '''
  environment = ["PIP_INDEX_URL=https://pypi.mirror.internal/simple", "npm_config_registry=https://npm.mirror.internal/"]
  [runners.docker]
    image = "alpine:3.20"
    volumes = ["/cache", "/etc/gitlab-runner/certs:/certs:ro"]   # mount the CA into every container
```

**Hooks are not a security control.** They run with the job's privileges, so job code can undo whatever a hook did, and a hook cannot stop a malicious script. Use them for convenience and consistency. Enforce policy with runner settings, protection, network controls and pipeline execution policies (chapter 11).

| | Runner hooks (`config.toml`) | `default: before_script` / `hooks` (YAML) |
|---|---|---|
| Who controls it | Runner administrators | Project developers |
| Applies to | Every job on that runner, all projects | Jobs of that project (or that include the template) |
| Visible to developers | Only in job logs | In `.gitlab-ci.yml` |
| Best for | Environment-specific setup (CA, proxy, mirrors) | Project-specific setup |

**Key takeaways**

- `pre_get_sources_script`, `post_get_sources_script`, `pre_build_script` and `post_build_script` inject commands into every job on a runner.
- Get-sources hooks run in the helper container, build hooks in the job image. Write them so they work, or skip safely, in any image.
- Use `environment` in `config.toml` for simple variables such as proxies and mirrors.
- Hooks run with the job's privileges and are not a security boundary.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a `pre_build_script` that prints the runner, job and project in a single line, and verify it appears in the logs of jobs from two different projects.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Your runners sit behind a TLS-intercepting proxy with an internal CA. Configure hooks, `environment` and volumes so that `git fetch`, `pip install` and `npm ci` work in jobs using `python:3.12-slim` and `node:20-alpine` images, without changing any project's `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Security asks you to block `curl` uploads to the internet from CI jobs by adding a check to `pre_build_script`. Is that a good control?" *Hint:* who controls the rest of the job's commands, and which layer can enforce egress rules.

<a id="64-autoscaling-and-fleet-management"></a>
### 6.4 Autoscaling and Fleet Management

One runner on one machine is easy to run. Dozens of runner managers serving hundreds of projects need elastic capacity, visibility and a maintenance routine. This subchapter covers cloud autoscaling with fleeting, scaling on Kubernetes, the fleet dashboard, Prometheus monitoring and keeping runners up to date.

#### Fleeting Plugins and Cloud Autoscaling

**Why it matters.** Paying for peak capacity around the clock is expensive, and sizing for the average makes developers wait at peak times. Autoscaling adds VMs when jobs queue up and removes them when they are idle. Done well, it gives short queue times at a fraction of the cost of a static fleet.

**What it is.** Autoscaling for the Docker Autoscaler and Instance executors (section 6.2) is built from three parts:

```text
GitLab ── jobs ──> runner manager
                    ├── taskscaler      decides how many job slots are needed:
                    │                   running jobs + idle target from the active policy
                    ├── fleeting plugin  translates "N instances" into cloud API calls
                    │     aws ─────────> EC2 Auto Scaling group      (SetDesiredCapacity, terminate)
                    │     googlecloud ─> Compute Engine instance group
                    │     azure ───────> Virtual machine scale set
                    └── connector        SSH or WinRM into each instance to run Docker or the job shell
```

- The **cloud provider** only hosts an instance group. Its own scaling rules must be off: the runner sets the desired size itself.
- The **fleeting plugin** is a small separate binary, distributed as an OCI image and installed with `gitlab-runner fleeting install`, which downloads every plugin referenced in `config.toml`.
- **Taskscaler** keeps track of slots: each instance offers `capacity_per_instance` job slots and is retired after `max_use_count` jobs.

**Preparing AWS (example).**

1. Build an AMI with Docker Engine (for Docker Autoscaler) or your toolchain (for Instance), for example with Packer.
2. Create a launch template from it, and an Auto Scaling group with minimum and desired capacity `0`, a maximum such as `30`, and **instance scale-in protection** enabled so AWS never terminates instances that are running jobs.
3. Give the runner manager an IAM role that can describe and resize the group, terminate its instances, and connect to them (for example `autoscaling:SetDesiredCapacity`, `autoscaling:TerminateInstanceInAutoScalingGroup`, `autoscaling:DescribeAutoScalingGroups`, `ec2:DescribeInstances`, `ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey`).
4. Configure the runner and install the plugin.

```toml
concurrent = 60                            # must not cap below max_instances x capacity_per_instance

[[runners]]
  name = "docker-autoscaler-aws"
  url = "https://gitlab.example.com"
  token = "glrt-..."
  executor = "docker-autoscaler"
  limit = 60
  [runners.docker]
    image = "alpine:3.20"
  [runners.cache]                          # instances are short-lived: use a distributed cache
    Type = "s3"
    Shared = true
    [runners.cache.s3]
      BucketName = "acme-runner-cache"
      BucketLocation = "eu-central-1"
  [runners.autoscaler]
    plugin = "aws"                         # short for the official AWS fleeting plugin image
    capacity_per_instance = 2
    max_use_count = 40
    max_instances = 30
    [runners.autoscaler.plugin_config]
      name = "ci-docker-asg"               # Auto Scaling group name
    [runners.autoscaler.connector_config]
      username = "ubuntu"
      use_external_addr = false            # connect over private IPs inside the VPC

    # Policies: when several match, the last matching one applies
    [[runners.autoscaler.policy]]          # baseline: nights and weekends
      idle_count = 0
      idle_time = "10m0s"

    [[runners.autoscaler.policy]]          # business hours: keep warm capacity
      periods = ["* 8-18 * * mon-fri"]     # cron syntax
      timezone = "Europe/Rome"
      idle_count = 6                       # idle job slots, not instances: 6 slots = 3 VMs here
      idle_time = "30m0s"
      scale_factor = 0.5                   # also keep idle slots equal to 50% of slots in use...
      scale_factor_limit = 10              # ...but at most 10 extra
```

```bash
sudo gitlab-runner fleeting install        # downloads the plugins referenced in config.toml
sudo gitlab-runner restart
```

**Cost and speed levers.**

| Lever | Lower cost | Faster pickup |
|---|---|---|
| `idle_count` | `0` outside working hours | Higher during peaks |
| `idle_time` | Short | Long (fewer cold starts) |
| `capacity_per_instance` | Higher (better packing) | Not directly |
| `max_use_count` | Higher (fewer boots, warm image cache) | Higher (no boot between jobs) |
| Instance type and purchasing | Spot or preemptible capacity through the instance group's mixed instances policy | Faster instance families, pre-pulled images in the AMI |
| `max_instances` | Lower (hard spend cap) | Higher (no queueing at peak) |

Spot instances can be reclaimed mid-job. Combine them with `retry: { when: [runner_system_failure] }` (section 4.3) for jobs that tolerate restarts, and keep deployment jobs on on-demand capacity.

**Key takeaways**

- Autoscaling uses taskscaler (how many slots) plus a fleeting plugin (how to resize the cloud instance group) plus a connector (how to reach instances).
- The instance group is created by you with desired capacity `0` and scale-in protection. The runner, not the cloud, decides its size.
- Scaling policies set idle capacity per time window. `idle_count` counts job slots, and the last matching policy wins.
- Use a distributed cache, because autoscaled instances are short-lived.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Given `capacity_per_instance = 4`, `idle_count = 8`, `max_instances = 10` and 30 running jobs, compute how many instances the runner wants and how many it actually gets.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Set up a Docker Autoscaler runner on a cloud account with an instance group of maximum size 3. Run a pipeline of 10 parallel jobs and record when instances start and stop. Then add an office-hours policy and verify that idle instances disappear outside it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Finance wants the CI bill cut by 40% without slowing developers down. Which autoscaling settings and infrastructure changes would you consider first?" *Hint:* idle capacity by time of day, packing, spot capacity, image pull time and `max_use_count`.

#### Kubernetes Runner Scaling

**Why it matters.** With the Kubernetes executor, "add capacity" means something different: job pods are scheduled by Kubernetes, and the cluster itself must grow when pods do not fit. Three independent layers have to scale together, and a bottleneck in any one of them shows up to developers as jobs stuck in `pending` or failing with pod timeouts.

**What it is.**

```text
Layer 1: runner managers    Deployment replicas x concurrent  = max job pods
            │                (2 replicas x concurrent 40 = up to 80 job pods)
            ▼
Layer 2: job pods           created per job with resource requests (cpu_request, memory_request)
            │                Pending if no node has room
            ▼
```
