#### include:template

**Why it matters.** GitLab ships ready-made CI configuration inside the product: security scanners, workflow presets, Auto DevOps jobs and starter pipelines for many languages. `include:template` adds one of them to your pipeline with a single line, without copying anything.

**What it is.** The value is the template's path inside GitLab's template directory (`lib/gitlab/ci/templates/` in the GitLab source code). The template content comes from **your GitLab instance**, so its version is the version of GitLab you run.

```yaml
include:
  - template: Jobs/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml                         # static application security testing
  - template: Jobs/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml             # leaked credentials in the repository
  - template: Workflows/MergeRequest-Pipelines.gitlab-ci.yml  # workflow:rules for MR-based pipelines
```

**Versioning.** Because templates follow the instance version:

- Upgrading GitLab can change the jobs you include. Read the release notes for template changes before upgrading.
- Some templates have a `.latest` variant (for example `Jobs/SAST.latest.gitlab-ci.yml`). It contains changes planned for the next major release, so you can test them early. Switch back to the stable name for production use.
- To freeze a template, copy it into your repository (losing updates), or move to the equivalent CI/CD component, which supports pinned versions (9.3).

**Reading a template.** To see the exact content your instance uses, read it in the GitLab source code for your version, or check the Full configuration tab after including it. The templates API lists the starter pipeline templates (the root-level ones described in 9.4):

```bash
# List starter pipeline templates available on this instance
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/templates/gitlab_ci_ymls?per_page=100" | jq -r '.[].key'

# Print the content of one of them
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/templates/gitlab_ci_ymls/Python" | jq -r '.content'
```

**Templates and components.** GitLab is moving reusable CI functionality from templates to CI/CD components, which have typed inputs and explicit versions. Many templates, including the main security scanners, already have component equivalents. Section 9.4 covers how to use and customize templates.

**Key takeaways**

- `include:template` adds a GitLab-bundled template by its path, such as `Jobs/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml`.
- The template version is the GitLab version: upgrades can change your pipeline.
- `.latest` variants preview upcoming breaking changes. Do not leave them in production.
- Inspect the merged result in the Full configuration tab before relying on a template.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Include `Jobs/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml` in a project, run a pipeline, and find the job it adds and the report artifact it uploads.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Include `Workflows/MergeRequest-Pipelines.gitlab-ci.yml` and use the Full configuration tab to read the `workflow:rules` it adds. Push to a feature branch with and without an open merge request and explain which pipelines are created.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your SAST jobs suddenly behave differently after a GitLab upgrade, although nobody changed `.gitlab-ci.yml`. How is that possible and how would you prevent surprises?" *Hint:* where `include:template` content comes from, release notes, `.latest` variants, and versioned components.

#### Conditional Includes with rules

**Why it matters.** Not every file is needed in every pipeline. Node.js jobs are useless in a repository without `package.json`, deployment configuration only matters on the default branch, and a team may want to opt in to an expensive scanner. `include:rules` decides whether a file is included at all, which keeps the configuration and the pipeline view smaller than disabling each job individually.

**What it is.** `include` entries accept `rules` with `if`, `exists` and `changes`, and `when: never` or `when: always`. If a rule matches (and is not `when: never`), the file is included. If no rule matches, it is skipped. The rules are evaluated **once, while the configuration is built**, before `workflow:rules` and before any job rules.

```yaml
include:
  - local: ci/node.yml
    rules:
      - exists:                           # the file exists in the repository at this commit
          - package.json

  - local: ci/python.yml
    rules:
      - exists:
          - pyproject.toml
          - requirements*.txt             # glob patterns are allowed

  - local: ci/deploy.yml
    rules:
      - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

  - local: ci/docs.yml
    rules:
      - changes:                          # files changed by this push or merge request
          - docs/**/*

  - project: platform/ci-templates
    ref: v3.2.0
    file: /templates/dast.yml
    rules:
      - if: $ENABLE_DAST == "true"        # project or group variable: an opt-in switch
```

**Which variables are available.** Only variables that exist before the configuration is read: predefined variables, project, group and instance variables, and variables passed by triggers, schedules, the API or the Run pipeline form. Variables defined in the YAML `variables:` section are **not** available, and a condition that uses them never matches:

```yaml
# Broken: ENABLE_E2E is defined in the YAML itself, so the include is always skipped
variables:
  ENABLE_E2E: "true"

include:
  - local: ci/e2e.yml
    rules:
      - if: $ENABLE_E2E == "true"
```

Two fixes: keep the `include:rules` and define `ENABLE_E2E` as a project or group variable (**Settings > CI/CD > Variables**) instead of in the YAML, or include the file unconditionally and move the decision into job rules, which do see YAML variables:

```yaml
# Fixed (job-level variant): the file is always included, each job decides for itself
variables:
  ENABLE_E2E: "true"

include:
  - local: ci/e2e.yml
```

```yaml
# ci/e2e.yml
e2e-tests:
  rules:
    - if: $ENABLE_E2E == "true"       # job rules are evaluated after the YAML variables are known
  script: [npm run test:e2e]
```

**include:rules compared with job rules.**

| | `include:rules` | Job `rules` |
|---|---|---|
| Decides | Whether a whole file is part of the configuration | Whether one job is added to the pipeline |
| Evaluated | Once, while the configuration is built | For each job, after the configuration is merged |
| YAML `variables:` usable | No | Yes |
| Supported clauses | `if`, `exists`, `changes`, `when: never/always` | All `rules` keywords, including `variables`, `needs`, `allow_failure` |

**Dependency pitfall.** If a job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` uses `extends: .deploy-template` and `.deploy-template` lives in a conditionally included file, every pipeline that skips the file fails with an error about an unknown `extends` key. Keep templates and the jobs that use them in the same conditional file, or keep templates in an unconditional file.

**Key takeaways**

- `include:rules` supports `if`, `exists` and `changes`, and is evaluated once while the configuration is built.
- Use it to include whole files by repository content (`exists`), branch (`if`) or opt-in variables.
- YAML-defined `variables:` are not available in `include:rules`. Use project or group variables, or job rules.
- Jobs must not depend on templates from a file that might be skipped.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Include `ci/node.yml` only when `package.json` exists. Delete `package.json` on a branch and confirm that the Node jobs disappear.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build a monorepo configuration where `ci/frontend.yml` is included only if files under `frontend/` changed, and `ci/release.yml` only for tag pipelines. Then reproduce the "unknown `extends`" error by moving a template into the conditional file, and fix it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why can `include:rules` not see a variable defined in the `variables:` section of the same file?" *Hint:* think about the order in which GitLab reads, merges and evaluates the configuration.

#### Include Merge Behavior

**Why it matters.** When a pipeline uses five included files and two of them define a job with the same name, which values win? When a job "mysteriously" has a variable you never set, where did it come from? Answering these questions requires knowing the exact merge order GitLab follows.

**What it is.** GitLab builds the final configuration in a fixed sequence:

```text
1. Read .gitlab-ci.yml
2. Fetch every include entry (evaluating include:rules), and recursively their own includes
3. Merge the included files in the order they are listed: later files override earlier ones
4. Merge .gitlab-ci.yml on top: the main file overrides all included files
5. Resolve extends and !reference on the merged result (section 9.2)
6. Evaluate workflow:rules, then each job's rules, and create the pipeline
```

The merge in steps 3 and 4 is a **deep merge**: mappings (such as a job, `variables` or `artifacts`) are combined key by key, while lists and scalars are replaced. Section 9.2 describes the algorithm in detail.

```yaml
# ci/test.yml (included)
pytest:
  stage: test
  image: python:3.12-slim
  variables:
    PYTEST_ADDOPTS: "-q"
    DB_HOST: postgres
  script:
    - pytest
```

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
include:
  - local: ci/test.yml

pytest:                          # same job name: merged into the included job
  variables:
    DB_HOST: db.internal         # overrides one variable
  tags: [docker, large]          # adds a keyword
```

```yaml
# Merged result
pytest:
  stage: test                    # from ci/test.yml
  image: python:3.12-slim        # from ci/test.yml
  variables:
    PYTEST_ADDOPTS: "-q"         # from ci/test.yml
    DB_HOST: db.internal         # from .gitlab-ci.yml (main file wins)
  script:
    - pytest                     # from ci/test.yml
  tags: [docker, large]          # from .gitlab-ci.yml
```

This is how you customize included jobs without editing the included file: redefine the job in your own file with only the keys you want to change.

**How specific keys combine.**

| Key | Behavior across files |
|---|---|
| Jobs with the same name | Deep-merged. The main file, or the later include, wins per key |
| `stages` | A list: replaced as a whole. The last definition wins, usually the main file |
| Top-level `variables` | Merged by variable name |
| `default` | Deep-merged like a job |
| `workflow:rules` | A list: replaced as a whole by a later definition |
| YAML anchors | Never shared between files |

**Limits.**

| Limit | Default |
|---|---|
| Includes per pipeline, nested ones included | 150 (administrators can change it on self-managed instances) |
| Nesting depth | 100 levels |
| Time to resolve all includes | 30 seconds |
| Same file included more than once | Included once, but each occurrence counts toward the limit |

**Debugging.** The Full configuration tab of the pipeline editor shows the merged result, and the CI Lint API returns it too:

```bash
# Validate the stored configuration of project 12345 and print the merged YAML
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/ci/lint?include_merged_yaml=true" \
  | jq -r '.merged_yaml'
```

**Key takeaways**

- Includes are merged in listed order, then the main file is merged on top and wins.
- The merge is deep for mappings and replaces lists and scalars.
- Redefining an included job with only some keys is the standard way to customize it.
- `stages` and `workflow:rules` are lists: the last definition replaces earlier ones entirely.
- Use the Full configuration tab or the Lint API's merged YAML when the result surprises you.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Include a file that defines a `lint` job with `image`, `script` and two variables. In `.gitlab-ci.yml`, override one variable and add `allow_failure: true`. Predict the merged job, then check it in the Full configuration tab.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Include two files that both define `stages` and a `build` job with different `image` and `script` values. Swap their order in the `include` list and document how the result changes. Then fetch the merged YAML with the Lint API.
> 3. **Interview question:** "An included file defines `before_script` with three setup commands. A project redefines `before_script` with one extra command and the job breaks. Explain why." *Hint:* how lists behave in a deep merge compared with mappings.

<a id="92-configuration-reuse-patterns"></a>
### 9.2 Configuration Reuse Patterns

Once configuration is spread across files, jobs need a way to share it. This subchapter covers `extends` for job inheritance, `!reference` for reusing individual values, how to design libraries of hidden job templates, and the deep-merge algorithm that all of these mechanisms (and `include`) rely on.

#### extends Keyword

**Why it matters.** Ten deployment jobs that each repeat the same image, tags, `before_script` and rules drift apart over time: one gets a fix, the other nine do not. YAML anchors (section 2.1) help within a single file, but they cannot cross file boundaries and their merge is shallow. `extends` is GitLab's own inheritance mechanism, and it works across every included file.

**What it is.** `extends` names one or more jobs (usually hidden jobs, starting with a dot) whose configuration the current job inherits. It works like class inheritance in object-oriented languages: the child gets everything from the parent and overrides what it defines itself.

- It is resolved **after** all includes are merged, so the template can live in any included file.
- The merge is deep: mappings are merged key by key, and lists and scalars from the child replace the parent's (see Deep Merge Semantics below).
- A template can itself use `extends`. GitLab allows up to 11 levels of inheritance, but more than three levels are hard to follow.
- Any job can be extended, not only hidden ones.

```yaml
.base:
  image: alpine:3.20
  tags: [docker]
  retry: 1
  variables:
    LOG_LEVEL: info

.deploy:
  extends: .base                       # a template that extends another template
  stage: deploy
  image: bitnami/kubectl:1.31          # overrides .base's image
  variables:
    KUBE_NAMESPACE: default
  script:
    - kubectl apply -n "$KUBE_NAMESPACE" -f k8s/

deploy-staging:
  extends: .deploy
  environment: staging
  variables:
    KUBE_NAMESPACE: staging            # overrides one variable, keeps the others
```

The resolved job:

```yaml
deploy-staging:
  image: bitnami/kubectl:1.31          # .deploy beats .base
  tags: [docker]                       # from .base
  retry: 1                             # from .base
  stage: deploy                        # from .deploy
  variables:                           # merged across all three levels
    LOG_LEVEL: info                    #   from .base
    KUBE_NAMESPACE: staging            #   from the job
  script:
    - kubectl apply -n "$KUBE_NAMESPACE" -f k8s/   # from .deploy
  environment: staging                 # from the job
```

**Multiple parents.** `extends` accepts a list. Parents are applied from left to right, so for the same key **the last parent wins**, and the job itself beats all parents. This makes small, single-purpose templates ("mixins") easy to combine:

```yaml
.node:
  image: node:22-slim
  before_script: [npm ci]

.mr-and-main:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

.large-runner:
  tags: [docker, large]

lint:
  extends: [.node, .mr-and-main]
  script: [npm run lint]

e2e:
  extends: [.node, .mr-and-main, .large-runner]
  script: [npm run test:e2e]
```

```text
Resolution order for e2e (later layers override earlier ones):

  .node  ->  .mr-and-main  ->  .large-runner  ->  e2e (job keys)
  first                           last parent      highest priority
```

**Interaction with other layers.** `extends` sits between `default` and the job in the precedence order from section 2.4: job keys beat `extends` templates, which beat `default`. `inherit` controls only `default` and global variables, not what comes through `extends`.

**Common errors.**

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Validation error naming an unknown key in `extends` | Typo in the template name, or the template is in a file that was not included (for example, skipped by `include:rules`) |
| Error about a circular dependency in `extends` | Two templates extend each other, directly or through a chain |
| Job ignores the template's `rules` | The job defines its own `rules`, a list that replaces the template's |

**Key takeaways**

- `extends` inherits configuration from one or more jobs, usually hidden templates, and works across included files.
- Mappings are merged deeply, and lists and scalars are replaced by the child.
- With several parents, the last one wins, and the job's own keys always win.
- Prefer flat compositions of small templates over deep inheritance chains (three levels at most).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Refactor three jobs that share `image`, `tags` and `before_script` into a `.python-base` template used through `extends`. Confirm with the Full configuration tab that the jobs are unchanged.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create `.a` with `image: alpine`, `variables: {X: "1", Y: "1"}` and `.b` with `image: ubuntu`, `variables: {Y: "2"}`. Predict the resolved job for `extends: [.a, .b]` and for `extends: [.b, .a]`, each with its own `variables: {Z: "3"}`, then verify.
> 3. **Interview question:** "When would you use `extends` rather than YAML anchors with merge keys?" *Hint:* compare file scope, deep and shallow merges, the order in which multiple parents win, and readability.

#### !reference Tags

**Why it matters.** `extends` works per keyword: if a template and a job both define `script` or `rules`, the job's list replaces the template's. Real pipelines often need to *combine* lists: the shared registry login commands plus one extra step, or a shared set of rules plus one exception. `!reference` lets you pull a single value out of another job and place it exactly where you need it.

**What it is.** `!reference [job, keyword, subkey, ...]` is a custom YAML tag that GitLab replaces with the value found at that path in another job. The path starts with a job name (usually a hidden job), followed by a keyword and optionally deeper keys. It works across included files.

When a `!reference` that returns a list is placed **inside** another list (in `script`, `before_script`, `after_script` or `rules`), GitLab flattens it into the surrounding list. References can be nested up to 10 levels deep.

```yaml
.registry-login:
  script:
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY"

.vault-login:
  script:
    - export VAULT_TOKEN="$(vault write -field=token auth/jwt/login role=ci jwt=$VAULT_ID_TOKEN)"

build-image:
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]
  script:
    - !reference [.registry-login, script]        # flattened into this list
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" .
    - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"

deploy:
  image: registry.example.com/tools/deployer:2.4
  script:
    - !reference [.vault-login, script]
    - !reference [.registry-login, script]        # combine several snippets
    - ./deploy.sh
```

**Reusing rules.** Combining rule sets is the most valuable use, because rules are evaluated in order and the first match wins. You control that order explicitly:

```yaml
.skip-docs-only-rules:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TITLE =~ /^docs:/
      when: never

.mr-and-main-rules:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

unit-tests:
  rules:
    - !reference [.skip-docs-only-rules, rules]   # checked first
    - !reference [.mr-and-main-rules, rules]
  script: [make test]

nightly-benchmarks:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"       # a job-specific rule first
    - !reference [.mr-and-main-rules, rules]
      # flattened, this list is: schedule, merge_request_event, default branch
  script: [make bench]
```

**Reusing variables.** A reference can return a whole mapping or a single value inside it:

```yaml
.shared-vars:
  variables:
    API_URL: https://api.internal.example.com
    TIMEOUT_SECONDS: "30"

integration-tests:
  variables: !reference [.shared-vars, variables]               # the whole mapping

smoke-tests:
  variables:
    BASE_URL: !reference [.shared-vars, variables, API_URL]     # one value, under a new name
  script: [./smoke.sh "$BASE_URL"]
```

**Comparing the three reuse mechanisms.**

| | YAML anchors (`&`, `*`, `<<`) | `extends` | `!reference` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resolved by | The YAML parser | GitLab | GitLab |
| Works across included files | No | Yes | Yes |
| Granularity | Whole node | Whole job | Any single value |
| Merge | Shallow (`<<`) | Deep | None: inserts the value as is |
| Combining lists | Not possible | Not possible (replaced) | Yes, by flattening |
| Standard YAML tools | Understand it | Understand it (plain key) | Reject the custom tag |

Because `!reference` is a custom tag, generic YAML linters and parsers such as Python's `yaml.safe_load` fail on it (section 2.1). Validate files that use it with CI Lint or the pipeline editor.

**Key takeaways**

- `!reference [job, keyword, ...]` inserts one value from another job, including jobs from included files.
- Inside `script`, `before_script`, `after_script` and `rules`, referenced lists are flattened, which is how you append to shared lists.
- Rule sets composed with `!reference` keep an explicit, readable order.
- Use `extends` for "this job is a kind of that job" and `!reference` for "this job also needs that piece".

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a `.setup` hidden job with two `before_script` commands, and a job whose `before_script` runs both of them followed by a third command, using `!reference`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Put `.mr-and-main-rules` and `.skip-docs-only-rules` in an included `ci/rules.yml`. Use them in three jobs in different orders, and verify with commits titled `docs: update README` and `feat: add endpoint` which jobs run.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A job extends a template that defines `rules`, and you need to add one `when: never` rule in front of them without copying the template's rules. How?" *Hint:* the job's `rules` replaces the template's list, but nothing stops that new list from referencing the template's.

#### Hidden Job Templates

**Why it matters.** Section 2.2 introduced hidden jobs as places to store templates. When a team or a whole organization shares dozens of templates, the questions change: how to name them so that they do not collide, how to layer them, and how to make their requirements obvious to the people who use them. A template library is an API, and it deserves the same care.

**Design principles.**

1. **Namespace your templates.** Hidden jobs with the same name from two included files are silently **deep-merged**, not reported as a conflict. A prefix such as `.acme-` prevents accidental merges with templates from other sources.
2. **Compose small templates instead of deep chains.** Prefer `extends: [.acme-python, .acme-mr-rules, .acme-large-runner]` over a five-level inheritance chain. Each template does one thing.
3. **Make the contract explicit.** Document which variables a template requires, and fail fast if they are missing.
4. **Keep templates incomplete on purpose.** A template provides what is shared and leaves job-specific parts, such as `script`, to the job.

```text
Layered template library (platform/ci-templates)

  .acme-base                 tags, retry, interruptible
     │
     ├── .acme-python        image, pip cache, before_script
     ├── .acme-node          image, npm cache, before_script
     └── .acme-docker        docker image, dind service, registry login

  Mixins (combined with extends lists):
     .acme-mr-and-main-rules   .acme-large-runner   .acme-manual-on-main
```

```yaml
# templates/docker.yml in platform/ci-templates
.acme-base:
  tags: [docker]
  retry:
    max: 2
    when: [runner_system_failure, stuck_or_timeout_failure]
  interruptible: true

.acme-docker:
  extends: .acme-base
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]
  variables:
    DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: /certs
  before_script:
    # Contract check: the job must set IMAGE_NAME, otherwise fail with a clear message
    - ': "${IMAGE_NAME:?IMAGE_NAME must be set by the job using .acme-docker}"'
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY"

.acme-large-runner:
  tags: [docker, large]          # a list: replaces .acme-base's tags when listed later
```

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml in an application project
include:
  - project: platform/ci-templates
    ref: v3.2.0
    file: /templates/docker.yml

build-api-image:
  extends: [.acme-docker, .acme-large-runner]
  stage: build
  variables:
    IMAGE_NAME: api                       # fulfills the template's contract
  script:
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE/$IMAGE_NAME:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" services/api
    - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE/$IMAGE_NAME:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
```

**Removing something a template provides.** Setting a key to `null` in the child removes it from the inherited configuration, while an empty value (`[]` or `{}`) behaves according to the merge rules:

```yaml
build-docs:
  extends: .acme-docker
  services: null              # removes the dind service completely
  before_script: []           # replaces the template's list with an empty one: no setup commands
  script: [make docs]
```

**Choosing a reuse mechanism.**

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Several jobs share most of their configuration | Hidden template with `extends` |
| Several jobs share one script snippet or rule set, combined with their own | `!reference` |
| Quick reuse inside a single file, with no cross-file needs | YAML anchors |
| Reuse across many projects, with parameters and versions | CI/CD components (9.3) |

**Key takeaways**

- Treat a template library as an API: namespaced names, documented contracts and stable versions.
- Same-named hidden jobs from different files merge silently. Prefixes prevent collisions.
- Compose small single-purpose templates with `extends` lists instead of deep chains.
- Fail fast with a clear message when a required variable is missing (`${VAR:?message}`).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write `.acme-node` and `.acme-mr-and-main-rules` templates and use them together in `lint` and `test` jobs.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Include two files that both define `.base` with different `image` and `variables`. Observe the silent merge in the Full configuration tab, then rename both with distinct prefixes and fix the jobs that use them.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you design a CI template library for 50 teams so that template changes are safe to roll out?" *Hint:* naming, small composable templates, explicit contracts, versioned refs, and a test pipeline in the template project.

#### Deep Merge Semantics

**Why it matters.** `include`, `extends` and job overrides of included jobs all combine configuration with the same algorithm. Most "my job lost its setup commands" or "where did this artifact setting come from" problems come from not knowing exactly how it works. Learn the algorithm once and you can predict every resolved job.

**The algorithm.** Merging a child (the overriding side) into a parent:

1. If both values are **mappings**, merge them key by key, recursively applying these rules.
2. Otherwise (lists, strings, numbers, booleans), the **child's value replaces** the parent's.
3. A key set to `null` in the child is **removed** from the result.
4. With several parents, merge them from left to right, then merge the job on top.

The same logic in Python:

```python
def deep_merge(parent, child):
    """Return the result of merging child (higher priority) into parent."""
    if not (isinstance(parent, dict) and isinstance(child, dict)):
        return child                          # lists and scalars: the child replaces the parent
    result = dict(parent)
    for key, value in child.items():
        if value is None:
            result.pop(key, None)             # null removes the key
        elif key in result:
            result[key] = deep_merge(result[key], value)   # recurse into nested values
        else:
            result[key] = value
    return result
```

**A worked example.**

```yaml
.template:
  image:
    name: registry.example.com/tools/terraform:1.9
    entrypoint: [""]
  variables:
    TF_ROOT: infra
    TF_IN_AUTOMATION: "true"
  artifacts:
    paths: [infra/plan.cache]
    expire_in: 1 week
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  script: [terraform plan -out=plan.cache]

plan-prod:
  extends: .template
  image: registry.example.com/tools/terraform:1.10   # string replaces the mapping
  variables:
    TF_ROOT: infra/prod
  artifacts:
    paths: [infra/prod/plan.cache]                    # list replaced, expire_in kept
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG                              # list replaced: the branch rule is gone
```

```yaml
# Resolved
plan-prod:
  image: registry.example.com/tools/terraform:1.10   # entrypoint [""] is lost with the mapping
  variables:
    TF_ROOT: infra/prod                               # child value
    TF_IN_AUTOMATION: "true"                          # kept from the parent
  artifacts:
    paths: [infra/prod/plan.cache]                    # child list
    expire_in: 1 week                                 # kept from the parent mapping
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG                              # only the child's rule
  script: [terraform plan -out=plan.cache]
```

The `image` line is a classic surprise. Writing `image: {name: registry.example.com/tools/terraform:1.10}` instead would merge with the parent's mapping and keep `entrypoint`.

**Empty values compared with null.**

| Child value | Parent `variables: {A: "1"}` becomes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `variables: {B: "2"}` | `{A: "1", B: "2"}` | Mappings merge |
| `variables: {}` | `{A: "1"}` | Merging an empty mapping adds nothing |
| `variables: null` | No `variables` key | `null` removes the key |
| `script: []` (parent has a script) | Empty list | Lists are replaced |

**Who merges how.** Not every layer uses the deep merge:

| Combination | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Included files and the main file | Deep merge, later file wins |
| `extends` templates and the job | Deep merge, job wins |
| YAML merge key `<<: *anchor` | Shallow: a key in the job replaces the anchor's whole value |
| `default` and the job | No merge: a job keyword replaces the default keyword entirely (section 2.4) |
| Global `variables` and job `variables` | Merged by name at runtime, the job wins |

The difference between shallow and deep merges, side by side:

```yaml
.vars: &vars
  variables: {A: "1", B: "1"}

anchored:
  <<: *vars
  variables: {B: "2"}         # result: {B: "2"} only, A is lost (shallow)

.vars-template:
  variables: {A: "1", B: "1"}

extended:
  extends: .vars-template
  variables: {B: "2"}         # result: {A: "1", B: "2"} (deep)
```

**Key takeaways**

- Mappings merge recursively. Lists and scalars are replaced. `null` removes a key.
- `rules`, `script`, `tags`, `needs` and `artifacts:paths` are lists: a child that defines them replaces them entirely.
- Changing a keyword from mapping form to string form (like `image`) drops the parent's nested keys.
- `default` and YAML merge keys do not deep-merge. `include` and `extends` do.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* For a template with `cache: {key: deps, paths: [.npm/], policy: pull-push}` and a job with `cache: {policy: pull}`, write the resolved `cache` and verify it in the Full configuration tab.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend the Python `deep_merge` function to support a list of parents, and test it against three real templates and a job from your pipeline. Compare its output with GitLab's merged YAML from the Lint API.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A job extends a template whose `artifacts` mapping includes `reports: junit: report.xml`. The job adds `artifacts: paths: [coverage/]`. Is the JUnit report still uploaded? What if the job had used a YAML merge key instead?" *Hint:* apply the deep-merge rules to nested mappings, then compare with a shallow merge.

<a id="93-cicd-components-and-catalog"></a>
### 9.3 CI/CD Components and Catalog

Includes and templates share YAML, but they do not define a contract. Users have to read the file to learn which variables to set, nothing is typed or validated, and there is no standard way to find or version shared configuration. **CI/CD components** package a reusable unit of configuration with typed inputs and semantic versions, and the **CI/CD Catalog** makes them discoverable. This subchapter covers how to write, structure, release, publish and test them.

#### spec:inputs

**Why it matters.** Templates are usually configured with CI/CD variables, which have three weaknesses. They are untyped strings. They leak into every job as environment variables, so two included templates that both read `IMAGE` interfere with each other. And they cannot change the *structure* of the configuration: variables are not expanded in job names, and only in a limited set of keywords. A template that should create a job named `api-build` in stage `package` for one caller and `worker-build` in stage `build` for another cannot be written with variables. Inputs solve all three problems.

**What it is.** A configuration file can start with a **header** that declares inputs under `spec:inputs`, separated from the body by `---`. In the body, `$[[ inputs.name ]]` is replaced with the input's value **while GitLab builds the configuration**, before rules are evaluated and before any job runs. Think of the file as a function: the header is its signature, the body is its implementation, and `include` is the function call.

Section 5.3 covered inputs for the main pipeline. Here they parameterize included files, which is their main purpose:

```yaml
# templates/docker-build.yml in the project acme/ci-components
spec:
  inputs:
    job_prefix:
      default: docker
      description: Prefix for job names, so the component can be included more than once
    stage:
      default: build
      description: Stage of the build job
    image_name:
      description: Image name below $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE (required, because it has no default)
    context:
      default: .
      description: Docker build context directory
---
"$[[ inputs.job_prefix ]]-build":                       # inputs also work in job names
  stage: $[[ inputs.stage ]]
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]
  variables:
    DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: /certs
  script:
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY"
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE/$[[ inputs.image_name ]]:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" "$[[ inputs.context ]]"
    - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE/$[[ inputs.image_name ]]:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
```

Callers pass values with `inputs` on the `include` entry. The same file can be included several times with different inputs:

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml in a monorepo
stages: [build, test, package]

include:
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/acme/ci-components/docker-build@2.1.0
    inputs:
      job_prefix: api
      image_name: api
      context: services/api
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/acme/ci-components/docker-build@2.1.0
    inputs:
      job_prefix: worker
      stage: package
      image_name: worker
      context: services/worker
# Result: jobs "api-build" (stage build) and "worker-build" (stage package)
```

`inputs` is not limited to components: `include:local`, `include:project` and `include:remote` entries can pass inputs to any file that has a `spec:inputs` header.

**When values are resolved.**

```text
pipeline creation                                               job execution
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ──────────────────────
fetch includes -> validate inputs -> interpolate $[[ inputs ]]  runner expands $VARIABLES
               -> merge files -> extends/!reference -> rules    in the job's shell
```

| | Inputs `$[[ inputs.x ]]` | Variables `$X` |
|---|---|---|
| Resolved | While the configuration is built | Mostly at runtime, by the runner or the shell |
| Scope | Only the file that declares them | Every job, as environment variables |
| Types | string, number, boolean, array | Strings only |
| Validation | `options`, `regex`, required values | None |
| Usable in job names and any keyword | Yes | No |
| Can be overridden after the pipeline starts | No | Yes, by higher-precedence sources |

**Rules for the header.**

- The header is a separate YAML document: `spec:` first, then `---`, then the body.
- Inputs without a `default` are **required**. A missing required input, or an input that the header does not declare, stops pipeline creation with an error.
- Interpolation only works in the file that declares the input. A file it includes needs its own header and receives values through its own `include:inputs`.
- Interpolation functions (`expand_vars`, `truncate`, `posix_escape`) work as described in section 5.3.

**Key takeaways**

- `spec:inputs` declares a file's parameters in a header above `---`. `$[[ inputs.name ]]` interpolates them while the configuration is built.
- Inputs are scoped to their file, typed and validated, unlike variables.
- Inputs can change structure: job names, stages, `needs`, `rules` and any other keyword.
- Callers pass inputs with `include:inputs`, which works for components and for local, project and remote files.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Convert a local file `ci/lint.yml` that reads a `LINT_IMAGE` variable into a file with a `spec:inputs` header and an `image` input. Include it from `.gitlab-ci.yml` with a custom value.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `job_prefix` input and include the file twice, for `frontend/` and `backend/`. Then deliberately omit a required input and pass an undeclared input, and record both pipeline creation errors.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why can inputs be used in a job name while CI/CD variables cannot?" *Hint:* compare the moment each is resolved with the moment GitLab decides which jobs exist.

#### Input Types and Validation

**Why it matters.** A component used by fifty projects receives fifty different interpretations of its parameters: `production` and `prod`, `3.12` and `python3.12`, `"true"` and `"yes"`. Without validation, these mistakes surface at runtime, deep inside a failing job. Typed, validated inputs reject them at pipeline creation, with a message that names the input.

**Types and validation keywords.**

| Keyword | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `type` | `string` (the default), `number`, `boolean` or `array` |
| `default` | Value used when the caller passes nothing. No default makes the input required |
| `options` | A list of allowed values |
| `regex` | A regular expression that string values must match |
| `description` | Shown in the CI/CD Catalog and to people who read the file |

A complete example, which the following topics reuse as the `python-test` component:

```yaml
# templates/python-test.yml in acme/ci-components
spec:
  inputs:
    job_prefix:
      default: python
    stage:
      default: test
    python_version:
      default: "3.12"
      regex: ^3\.(1[0-3])$                 # 3.10 to 3.13 only
      description: Python minor version used for the job image
    root_dir:
      default: .
      description: Directory containing pyproject.toml
    parallel:
      type: number
      default: 2
      description: Number of parallel test shards
    coverage_required:
      type: boolean
      default: true
    report_level:
      default: short
      options: [short, long, line, no]     # passed to pytest --tb
    rules:
      type: array
      default:                             # an array of mappings
        - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
        - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
---
"$[[ inputs.job_prefix ]]-pytest":
  stage: $[[ inputs.stage ]]
  image: python:$[[ inputs.python_version ]]-slim     # embedded in a string: becomes text
  parallel: $[[ inputs.parallel ]]                    # whole value: stays a number
  rules: $[[ inputs.rules ]]                          # whole value: stays an array
  variables:
    COVERAGE_REQUIRED: "$[[ inputs.coverage_required ]]"   # bridged into a variable as "true"/"false"
  script:
    - cd "$[[ inputs.root_dir ]]"
    - pip install -e ".[test]"
    - |
      pytest --tb=$[[ inputs.report_level ]] --junitxml=report.xml \
        --splits "$CI_NODE_TOTAL" --group "$CI_NODE_INDEX" --cov
    - if [ "$COVERAGE_REQUIRED" = "true" ]; then coverage report --fail-under=80; fi
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: $[[ inputs.root_dir ]]/report.xml
```

**Typed interpolation.** If `$[[ inputs.x ]]` is the **entire** YAML value, the input keeps its type: a number stays a number and an array becomes a real YAML list. If it is embedded in a longer string, the value is converted to text. This is what makes `parallel: $[[ inputs.parallel ]]` and `rules: $[[ inputs.rules ]]` valid.

**What validation catches.** All checks run before the pipeline is created. A failing check creates no pipeline and shows an error that names the input:

| Caller passes | Result |
|---|---|
| `python_version: "2.7"` | Rejected: does not match the regex |
| `report_level: verbose` | Rejected: not one of the allowed options |
| `parallel: "four"` | Rejected: not a number |
| `coverage_required: "yes"` | Rejected: not a boolean |
| `paralel: 4` (typo) | Rejected: unknown input name |
| Nothing for an input without a default | Rejected: required value missing |

**Designing good inputs.**

- Give every optional input a sensible `default`, so the simplest usage is one `include` line.
- Make `stage` an input. Callers' stage lists differ.
- Add a `job_prefix` input (or similar) whenever a component may be included more than once.
- Prefer `options` and `regex` over documentation-only constraints.
- Prefer `boolean` and `number` over strings like `"true"` and `"4"`.
- Keep the number of inputs small. A component with thirty inputs is a configuration language, not a building block.

**Key takeaways**

- Input types are `string`, `number`, `boolean` and `array`. `options` and `regex` restrict values, and no `default` means required.
- A whole-value interpolation keeps the type, while an embedded interpolation becomes a string.
- Validation failures prevent pipeline creation and name the offending input, which is far easier to debug than a failing job.
- Design inputs for the common case: defaults everywhere, `stage` and `job_prefix` as inputs, few parameters overall.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add an `environment` input with `options: [dev, staging, production]` to a deployment file and include it with a valid and an invalid value. Record the error.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `needs` input of type `array` with default `[]` to the `python-test` component and use it as the job's `needs`. Include the component once with the default and once with `needs: [build]`, and verify the job graph in both pipelines.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why validate component parameters with `options` and `regex` in `spec:inputs` instead of checking them at the start of the job script?" *Hint:* compare when each check fails, who sees the error and where, and how much runner time is spent before the failure.

#### Component Project Structure

**Why it matters.** GitLab finds components by convention, not by configuration. A file in the wrong place is simply not a component, and a component that relies on files in its own repository fails in every project that uses it. Knowing the expected layout avoids both problems.

**What it is.** A **component project** is an ordinary GitLab project with a `templates/` directory at its root. Each component is either:

- a single file, `templates/<name>.yml`, or
- a directory, `templates/<name>/template.yml`, which can hold additional files such as a component README.

A project can contain many components (up to 100 in current GitLab versions).

```text
acme/ci-components
├── README.md                      # required for the catalog: documents every component
├── LICENSE.md
├── .gitlab-ci.yml                 # tests and releases the components (see Testing Components)
├── templates/
│   ├── python-test.yml            # component "python-test"
│   ├── secret-scan.yml            # component "secret-scan"
│   └── docker-build/
│       ├── template.yml           # component "docker-build"
│       └── README.md              # documentation only: never included in pipelines
├── tests/
│   └── fixtures/python-app/       # sample project used by the component's own tests
└── images/
    └── python-test/Dockerfile     # tools used by the component, shipped as a container image
```

**Referencing a component.**

```text
$CI_SERVER_FQDN / acme/ci-components / python-test @ 1.4.0
└── instance ────┘ └── project path ─┘ └ component ┘ └ version
```

`$CI_SERVER_FQDN` is a predefined variable containing the instance host name (and port, if any). Using it instead of a hard-coded host keeps the configuration portable, for example after a migration to a new domain.

**Only the YAML travels.** When a project includes a component, GitLab copies the component's YAML into the pipeline. The jobs run in the *consuming* project's checkout, so scripts, configuration files or Dockerfiles stored next to the component do **not** exist there:

```yaml
# Broken: scripts/run-tests.sh exists in acme/ci-components, not in the consuming project
python-pytest:
  script:
    - ./scripts/run-tests.sh
```

```yaml
# Fixed: ship the tooling in an image that is versioned with the component
python-pytest:
  image: $CI_REGISTRY/acme/ci-components/python-test:1.4.0
  script:
    - run-tests                    # installed in the image
```

**Best practices for component content.**

| Do | Avoid | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Make `stage` an input | Hard-coding a stage the caller may not have | A missing stage fails pipeline creation |
| Prefix job names with an input | Fixed, generic names like `test` | Collisions are silently deep-merged with the caller's jobs |
| Define everything at job level | Global `default`, top-level `variables`, `workflow` | Global keywords change every job in the caller's pipeline |
| Use predefined variables (`$CI_PROJECT_DIR`, `$CI_COMMIT_SHA`) | Assuming project-specific variables exist | The component runs in many different projects |
| Ship tools in versioned images | Relying on files in the component repository | Only the YAML is included |
| Document each component in the README | Leaving inputs undocumented | The README is the catalog page |

**Key takeaways**

- Components live in `templates/` as `<name>.yml` or `<name>/template.yml`. The file or directory name is the component name.
- A component is referenced as `<host>/<project path>/<component>@<version>`. Use `$CI_SERVER_FQDN` for the host.
- Only the component's YAML is included. Anything else it needs must come from an image or a download.
- Components should be self-contained: job-level configuration only, an input for the stage, prefixed job names.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a component project with a single-file component `hello` that prints a greeting passed as an input, and include it from another project using a commit SHA as the version.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Convert `hello` into a directory component with its own README. Then make it call a shell script stored in the component project, observe the failure in the consuming project, and fix it by shipping the script in an image built by the component project.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why should a component avoid top-level keywords such as `default` or `variables`?" *Hint:* the component's YAML is merged into someone else's pipeline. Think about which of their jobs those keywords would affect.

#### Versioning and Releasing Components

**Why it matters.** A component is a dependency. Consumers need to know whether an update is safe to take, and maintainers need a way to ship breaking changes without breaking everyone at once. Semantic versioning and the release process give both sides that control.

**Semantic versioning.** Component versions use `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. For CI components, "breaking" means anything that can make an existing caller's pipeline fail or behave differently:

| Change | Version bump |
|---|---|
| Fix a bug in a script without changing behavior otherwise | PATCH (`1.4.0` to `1.4.1`) |
| Add an optional input with a default, add an optional job | MINOR (`1.4.1` to `1.5.0`) |
| Remove or rename an input, add a required input, rename a job, change a default, change the default stage | MAJOR (`1.5.0` to `2.0.0`) |

**Version references.**

| Reference | Resolves to | Moves automatically | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@1.4.2` | That exact release (tag) | No | Production, with a bot to propose upgrades |
| `@1.4` | The latest `1.4.x` release | Patches only | Receive fixes automatically |
| `@1` | The latest `1.x.y` release | Minors and patches | Receive features, but no breaking changes |
| `@~latest` | The latest published release | Everything, including majors | Experiments and demos only |
| `@<commit SHA>` | That commit | No | Maximum control, testing unreleased code |
| `@main` | The branch's current commit | Every merge | Developing the component itself |

Partial versions (`@1`, `@1.4`) and `@~latest` only resolve to releases published in the CI/CD Catalog. If a branch, a tag and a commit SHA share a name, GitLab prefers the SHA, then the tag, then the branch.

**Releasing.** A version is published to the catalog when a release is created by the `release` keyword in a CI/CD job (releases created through the UI or API are not published to the catalog), for a tag that is a valid semantic version such as `1.5.0`:

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml in acme/ci-components (the test jobs are shown in Testing Components)
stages: [test, release]

create-release:
  stage: release
  image: registry.gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli:latest       # provides glab for the release keyword
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/            # semantic version tags only
  script:
    - echo "Releasing components version $CI_COMMIT_TAG"
  release:
    tag_name: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
    description: |
      Components in $CI_PROJECT_PATH, version $CI_COMMIT_TAG.
      See CHANGELOG.md for breaking changes and upgrade notes.
```

```text
Release flow

  MR with change ──> review + component tests ──> merge to main
                                                     │
                       maintainer pushes tag 1.5.0 ──┘
                                                     │
  tag pipeline: tests ──> create-release (release keyword)
                                                     │
                       CI/CD Catalog lists 1.5.0 ────┘
                                                     │
  consumers on @1 or @1.5 pick it up at their next pipeline;
  consumers on @1.4.2 stay put until they bump the version
```

**Managing breaking changes.**

- Before removing an input in the next major version, keep it working in a minor release and print a deprecation warning from the job script.
- Document upgrade steps in the release description or a `CHANGELOG.md`.
- Keep fixing the previous major version for a while (for example, from a `1.x` maintenance branch) so consumers can upgrade on their own schedule.
- Protect version tags (**Settings > Repository > Protected tags**, pattern such as `*.*.*`) so that only maintainers can publish.

**Key takeaways**

- Version components with semantic versioning. Any change that can break a caller's pipeline is a major change.
- Exact versions are stable, `@1` and `@1.4` follow compatible updates, and `@~latest` follows everything.
- Partial versions and `~latest` only work for releases published in the catalog.
- Catalog releases come from the `release` keyword in a tag pipeline, with a semantic version tag.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add the `create-release` job to your component project, push tag `1.0.0`, and verify that the release appears. Include the component with `@1.0.0`, `@1` and `@~latest`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Release `1.1.0` with a new optional input, then `2.0.0` that renames an existing input. Show which of three consuming projects, pinned to `@1.0.0`, `@1` and `@~latest`, break at their next pipeline.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your team maintains a deployment component used by 80 projects, and you need to rename its required `env` input to `environment`. How do you roll this out?" *Hint:* a deprecation period in a minor release, a major release, the version references consumers use, and communication.

#### CI/CD Catalog

**Why it matters.** Shared configuration is only useful if people can find it. Without a catalog, teams rebuild the same Docker build or deployment jobs because they do not know a maintained version already exists. The CI/CD Catalog is the instance-wide index of published components, with documentation, versions and usage information on one page.

**What it is.** The catalog lists every **catalog project** the current user can see. Open it from **Search or go to > Explore > CI/CD Catalog**, or from the **Browse CI/CD Catalog** button in the pipeline editor (section 1.3). Each catalog entry shows:

| Element | Source |
|---|---|
| Name and description | The project's name and description |
| Documentation | The project's `README.md` |
| Components and their inputs | Generated from each component's `spec:inputs` |
| Versions | Releases created by the `release` keyword |
| Usage | How many projects use the components |
| Badges | GitLab-maintained, partner or verified creator components |

**Publishing a project.**

1. Add a project description and a `README.md` that documents each component, its inputs and an example.
2. Place at least one component in `templates/`.
3. As a project Owner, go to **Settings > General > Visibility, project features, permissions** and turn on **CI/CD Catalog project**.
4. Create a release with the `release` keyword in a tag pipeline (previous topic).

A good README section for one component:

````markdown
## python-test

Runs pytest with coverage and JUnit reports, split across parallel jobs.

```yaml
include:
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/acme/ci-components/python-test@1
    inputs:
      python_version: "3.13"
      root_dir: backend
```

| Input | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `python_version` | string | `3.12` | Python minor version, 3.10 to 3.13 |
| `parallel` | number | `2` | Number of test shards |
````

**Visibility and access.** Catalog entries follow project visibility: a private catalog project is listed only for its members, an internal one for every signed-in user. Including a component still requires read access to its project, exactly as with `include:project`.

**Components on GitLab.com and self-managed instances.** GitLab maintains official components in the `components` group on GitLab.com, for example security scanners and OpenTofu. A self-managed instance has its own catalog and cannot include components from GitLab.com directly. To use one, mirror its project into your instance, enable it as a catalog project, and create releases there.

**Adopting a component safely.** A component's jobs run with your project's variables and secrets. Before adopting one:

- Read the component's YAML for the version you plan to use, not just the README.
- Check the maintainer, badges and release history.
- Pin an exact version or a major version, never `~latest` in production.
- Check the Full configuration tab to see exactly which jobs and keywords it adds.

**Key takeaways**

- The CI/CD Catalog indexes published component projects, with README, input tables, versions and usage.
- Publishing needs a description, a README, components in `templates/`, the catalog setting and a `release` keyword release.
- Catalog visibility follows project visibility. Using a component needs read access to its project.
- Treat third-party components like any dependency: review, pin and monitor.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Browse the CI/CD Catalog on your instance or on GitLab.com, pick one component, and list its inputs, latest version and the jobs it creates.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Publish your component project from the previous topics to the catalog, with a README that documents every input. Ask a colleague to add it to their project using only the catalog page.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How would you introduce a curated internal catalog of CI components in a company where every team currently writes its own pipelines?" *Hint:* ownership, documentation, versioning policy, badges or naming for trusted components, and measuring adoption through usage data.

#### Testing Components

**Why it matters.** A broken component release breaks every project that uses it. Component code is YAML that only shows its behavior when GitLab builds a pipeline from it, so the only reliable test is to have GitLab do exactly that, in the component project's own pipeline, before a release is created.

**Testing levels.**

| Level | Question | Technique |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration | Does the component produce valid configuration with typical inputs? | Include it at `$CI_COMMIT_SHA` in the project's own pipeline |
| Structure | Does it create the expected jobs? | Query the Jobs API from a verification job |
| Behavior | Do its jobs succeed on a realistic project? | Run them against fixtures stored in the component project |
| Contract | Are invalid inputs rejected? | Send invalid configurations to the CI Lint API and expect failure |

**Self-testing pipeline.** Because the component project's pipeline runs in the component project, the components' jobs can use test fixtures from its repository:

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml in acme/ci-components
stages: [test, verify, release]

include:
  # Instantiate the component from the commit under test, against a fixture project
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/$CI_PROJECT_PATH/python-test@$CI_COMMIT_SHA
    inputs:
      job_prefix: smoke
      root_dir: tests/fixtures/python-app
      parallel: 2
      rules:
        - when: always                     # run in every pipeline of this project

verify-jobs-created:
  stage: verify
  image: alpine:3.20
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl jq
    # List this pipeline's jobs and check that both shards of the component job exist
    - |
      curl --silent --fail --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $API_READ_TOKEN" \
        "$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/pipelines/$CI_PIPELINE_ID/jobs?per_page=100" > jobs.json
    - jq -e 'map(.name) | index("smoke-pytest 1/2") and index("smoke-pytest 2/2")' jobs.json

reject-invalid-inputs:
  stage: verify
  image: alpine:3.20
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl jq
    # Build a configuration with an invalid python_version and ask CI Lint to validate it
    - |
      cat > invalid.yml <<EOF
      include:
        - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/$CI_PROJECT_PATH/python-test@$CI_COMMIT_SHA
          inputs:
            python_version: "2.7"
      EOF
    - jq --null-input --rawfile content invalid.yml '{content: $content}' > body.json
    - |
      curl --silent --fail --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $API_TOKEN" \
        --header "Content-Type: application/json" --data @body.json \
        "$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/ci/lint" > lint.json
    - jq -e '.valid == false' lint.json    # the test passes only if GitLab rejects the input
    - jq -r '.errors[]' lint.json          # show the rejection message in the log

create-release:
  stage: release                           # runs only after test and verify stages succeed
  image: registry.gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli:latest
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/
  script:
    - echo "Releasing $CI_COMMIT_TAG"
  release:
    tag_name: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
    description: "Release $CI_COMMIT_TAG of $CI_PROJECT_PATH"
```

`API_READ_TOKEN` (scope `read_api`) and `API_TOKEN` (scope `api`, needed by the Lint endpoint) are masked project variables holding project access tokens.

**Testing several input combinations.** Each `include` with different inputs and a different `job_prefix` is another test case in the same pipeline. For combinations that conflict with each other (for example, different `stage` values that need different `stages` lists), put each case in a small file under `tests/` and run it as a child pipeline with `trigger:include:local`. Each child pipeline then builds the component independently.

**Key takeaways**

- Test components by having GitLab build a pipeline from them at `$CI_COMMIT_SHA` in the component project's own pipeline.
- Verify structure through the Jobs API, behavior through fixtures, and contracts through the CI Lint API.
- Run the release job only after all tests pass, so a broken version never reaches the catalog.
- Use separate `job_prefix` values or child pipelines to test several input combinations.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a self-test to your component project that includes the component at `$CI_COMMIT_SHA` with default inputs. Break the component's YAML on a branch and observe the pipeline creation error.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add `verify-jobs-created` and `reject-invalid-inputs` jobs for your own component, plus a second test case with different inputs and a different `job_prefix`. Make the release job run only on semantic version tags after all tests succeed.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How do you test a CI/CD component before releasing it, given that it has no code of its own to unit-test?" *Hint:* GitLab itself is the interpreter. Consider configuration validity, created jobs, job behavior on fixtures and rejected inputs.

<a id="94-built-in-templates"></a>
### 9.4 Built-in Templates

GitLab ships a library of CI templates inside the product. Some are starting points meant to be copied and adapted, others are designed to be included and tuned with variables, most notably the security scanners. This subchapter covers both kinds and the techniques for customizing included templates without forking them.

#### Language and Framework Templates

**Why it matters.** Starting a pipeline from a blank file means rediscovering the same basics for every language: which image, how to cache dependencies, how to run the tests. GitLab's language templates give you a working starting point in seconds. Knowing what kind of template you are looking at, and whether to copy or include it, avoids a common mistake.

**Two kinds of templates.** The template directory (`lib/gitlab/ci/templates/` in the GitLab source code) contains two different kinds of files:

| | Pipeline templates | Job templates |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Root of the directory: `Python.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Nodejs.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Go.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Rust.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Maven.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Android.gitlab-ci.yml` | Subdirectories: `Jobs/`, `Security/`, `Workflows/`, `Verify/` |
| Content | A complete pipeline, often with its own `stages`, `image` and `cache` | Jobs or settings designed to be added to an existing pipeline |
| Intended use | **Copy** into `.gitlab-ci.yml`, then adapt | **Include** with `include:template`, then tune with variables |
| Updates | None after copying: the file is yours | Follow your GitLab version |

Including a pipeline template next to your own configuration usually causes conflicts: its `stages`, `default` settings and generic job names merge with yours. Copy pipeline templates; include job templates.

**Copying a pipeline template.** When you create `.gitlab-ci.yml` in the web editor, or open the pipeline editor in a project without one, a template selector offers the pipeline templates. The templates API returns the same files (section 9.1). Treat the result as a first draft:

| Typical content of a starter template | What to change |
|---|---|
| `image: python:latest` or similar | Pin a specific version, such as `python:3.12-slim` |
| A generic cache for the package manager | Key the cache on the lock file (section 8.2) |
| Example jobs for tests, linting or deployment | Delete what you do not need, rename the rest |
| No `rules` or `workflow` | Add `workflow:rules` to avoid duplicate pipelines (section 4.4) |

**Useful job templates.** Some smaller job templates are worth including directly:

| Template | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Workflows/MergeRequest-Pipelines.gitlab-ci.yml` | `workflow:rules` for merge request pipelines, tags and the default branch |
| `Workflows/Branch-Pipelines.gitlab-ci.yml` | `workflow:rules` for branch pipelines and tags only |
| `Verify/Accessibility.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Verify/Browser-Performance.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Verify/Load-Performance-Testing.gitlab-ci.yml` | Quality checks covered in chapter 10 |
| `Auto-DevOps.gitlab-ci.yml` and `Jobs/Build.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jobs/Deploy.gitlab-ci.yml`, ... | Auto DevOps and its building blocks (section 12.6) |

```yaml
# A small Python project: workflow from a template, jobs written by hand
include:
  - template: Workflows/MergeRequest-Pipelines.gitlab-ci.yml

default:
  image: python:3.12-slim

test:
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest
```

GitLab is moving reusable functionality from templates to CI/CD components. Some templates have already been deprecated and removed in favor of components: the Terraform templates, for example, were replaced by the OpenTofu component. Before building on a template, check whether a maintained component exists in the CI/CD Catalog.

**Key takeaways**

- Root-level templates such as `Python.gitlab-ci.yml` are complete starter pipelines: copy them, do not include them.
- Templates in `Jobs/`, `Security/`, `Workflows/` and `Verify/` are designed for `include:template`.
- Starter templates are first drafts: pin images, fix cache keys, remove unused jobs and add workflow rules.
- Prefer a maintained CI/CD component over a template when one exists.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create `.gitlab-ci.yml` from the starter template for your project's language. List three things you would change before using it in production, and change them.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Fetch the content of the `Nodejs` starter template through the templates API, then include `Workflows/MergeRequest-Pipelines.gitlab-ci.yml` in a project that uses it. Explain from the Full configuration tab which pipelines will now be created.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why do GitLab's language templates work well as a starting point but poorly as an `include`?" *Hint:* what a complete pipeline defines at the top level, and how those keys merge with yours.

#### Security Scanner Templates

**Why it matters.** Security scanning is the most common use of included templates. One `include` line adds a maintained scanner with dozens of language-specific analyzers, and GitLab keeps them updated with each release. Chapter 11 covers what each scanner finds and how to manage the results. This topic covers how the templates plug into your pipeline.

**The main templates.**

| Template | Jobs it adds | Stage | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Jobs/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml` | `semgrep-sast` and other analyzers, chosen by the languages in the repository | `test` | Source code analysis |
| `Jobs/SAST-IaC.gitlab-ci.yml` | `kics-iac-sast` | `test` | Terraform, Kubernetes manifests and other infrastructure code |
| `Jobs/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml` | `secret_detection` | `test` | Credentials committed to the repository |
| `Jobs/Dependency-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml` | One job per supported package manager | `test` | Ultimate: vulnerable dependencies |
| `Jobs/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml` | `container_scanning` | `test` | Scans the image named in `CS_IMAGE` |
| `Security/DAST.gitlab-ci.yml` | `dast` | `dast` | Ultimate: scans a running application |

**How they work.** Each template defines hidden base jobs and visible analyzer jobs. The analyzer jobs:

- run in the `test` stage (DAST in `dast`),
- decide with `rules` whether they apply, for example by checking that relevant files exist and that a `*_DISABLED` variable is not set,
- are configured through CI/CD variables,
- upload a security report artifact that GitLab reads (chapter 11),
- usually set `allow_failure: true`, so a scanner problem does not block the pipeline.

```yaml
stages: [build, test, deploy]       # "test" must exist for the scanner jobs

include:
  - template: Jobs/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml
  - template: Jobs/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml
  - template: Jobs/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml

variables:
  SAST_EXCLUDED_PATHS: "spec, test, tests, tmp, node_modules"   # skip test and vendored code
  CS_IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA                   # image built in the build stage

build-image:
  stage: build
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]
  script:
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY"
    - docker build -t "$CS_IMAGE" .
    - docker push "$CS_IMAGE"
```

**The stage pitfall.** The scanner jobs expect a `test` stage. A pipeline with custom stages such as `[build, verify, deploy]` fails at creation with an error saying that the chosen stage does not exist. Either keep a `test` stage or override `stage` for each scanner job (next topic).

**Component equivalents.** The main scanners are also published as components in the `components` group on GitLab.com. They take inputs instead of variables for common settings and can be pinned to a version:

```yaml
stages: [build, verify, deploy]     # no "test" stage needed: the stage is an input

include:
  - component: gitlab.com/components/sast/sast@~latest                         # pin a version in real projects
    inputs:
      stage: verify
  - component: gitlab.com/components/secret-detection/secret-detection@~latest
    inputs:
      stage: verify
```

**Enforcing scans.** An `include` in `.gitlab-ci.yml` can be removed by anyone who can edit that file. To guarantee that scans run in every project of a group, use security policies (scan execution or pipeline execution policies, section 11.3) instead of relying on each project's includes.

**Key takeaways**

- `Jobs/SAST`, `Jobs/Secret-Detection`, `Jobs/Dependency-Scanning`, `Jobs/Container-Scanning` and `Security/DAST` add maintained scanner jobs with one line each.
- Scanner jobs decide with their own rules whether to run, are configured with variables, and upload security reports.
- They need a `test` stage (DAST a `dast` stage) unless you override their stage.
- Component equivalents add inputs and version pinning. Security policies enforce scans centrally.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add SAST and Secret Detection templates to a project, run a pipeline, and list the jobs that were created and the report artifacts they uploaded.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Change the project's stages to `[build, verify, deploy]` and record the error. Fix it once by overriding the stage of each scanner job and once by switching to the component equivalents with a `stage` input. Compare the two configurations.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A team says they have SAST enabled, but no SAST job ever appears in their Go service's pipeline. How would you investigate?" *Hint:* the analyzer jobs' own rules, the files they look for, `*_DISABLED` variables, `workflow:rules`, and the Full configuration tab.

#### Customizing Included Templates

**Why it matters.** Templates are generic, and your project is not. You may need a scanner to start immediately instead of waiting for the build stage, run on a specific runner, ignore a vendored directory, or block the pipeline on findings. Copying the template to change two lines means losing every future update. GitLab's merge rules let you change exactly what you need while keeping the rest of the template current.

**Techniques, from least to most invasive.**

| Technique | Example | Keeps template updates |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Set documented variables | `SAST_EXCLUDED_PATHS`, `SAST_EXCLUDED_ANALYZERS`, `CS_IMAGE` | Yes |
| 2. Redefine the job to override some keys | `semgrep-sast: {needs: [], tags: [small]}` | Yes, except for the keys you override |
| 3. Disable a job | `SAST_DISABLED: "true"`, or include the template conditionally | Yes |
| 4. Replace the job's `rules` | Your own rule list | No: the template's rules are lost |
| 5. Copy the template into your repository | `ci/sast.yml` | No: you own it from now on |

**Overriding job keys.** Redefining a job with the same name deep-merges your keys into the template's job (section 9.1, Include Merge Behavior):

```yaml
include:
  - template: Jobs/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml
  - template: Jobs/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml

semgrep-sast:
  needs: []                        # start immediately instead of waiting for earlier stages
  tags: [docker, small]            # run on cheaper runners
  variables:
    SAST_EXCLUDED_PATHS: "docs, vendor"   # job-level: applies to this analyzer only
  artifacts:
    expire_in: 2 weeks             # merged into the template's artifacts: the report is kept

secret_detection:
  allow_failure: false             # the template allows failure. Make a failing scan block the pipeline
```

To confirm that the merge did what you intended, open the Full configuration tab and search for the job name. You see the template's keys and your overrides combined.

**Overriding rules.** `rules` is a list, so redefining it replaces the template's rules completely, including the checks for `SAST_DISABLED` and for relevant files. A job could then run in projects where the analyzer does not apply. Using `!reference` to the same job does not help either: after the merge, the job's `rules` are your new list, so the reference would point to itself. Prefer one of these approaches:

```yaml
# Option A: control the whole template with include:rules, and leave job rules untouched
include:
  - template: Jobs/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml
    rules:
      - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
      - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

```yaml
# Option B: keep scanning everywhere, but control the job through its documented variable
semgrep-sast:
  variables:
    SAST_DISABLED: $SKIP_SAST      # a project or pipeline variable; "true" disables the job
```

If you must replace the rules, copy them from the template source for **your** GitLab version and add your conditions in front, then review them after every GitLab upgrade.

**Extending a template's hidden jobs.** Templates define hidden base jobs that their analyzer jobs extend, such as `.sast-analyzer` in the SAST template. You can create additional jobs from them, for example to scan a second directory with different settings. Their names are internal details and can change between GitLab versions, so check the template source before relying on them.

**Upgrades.** Because `include:template` follows the GitLab version, review your overrides when you upgrade:

- Read the release notes for changes to the templates you use.
- Test the next version with the `.latest` template variant on a branch before a major upgrade.
- Re-check the Full configuration tab of an important project after each upgrade.
- If you need full control over timing, switch to the equivalent component and pin its version.

**Key takeaways**

- Customize templates with variables first, then by redefining jobs with only the keys you need to change.
- Redefined jobs are deep-merged into the template's jobs, so the rest of the template stays current.
- Replacing `rules` discards the template's own conditions. Control inclusion with `include:rules` or documented `*_DISABLED` variables instead.
- Copying a template is a last resort: it stops all future updates.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Include the SAST template and make `semgrep-sast` start immediately with `needs: []` and run on a runner tagged `small`. Verify the merged job in the Full configuration tab.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Make the SAST and Secret Detection templates run only in merge request and default branch pipelines, without changing any job's `rules`. Then make `secret_detection` block the pipeline when it fails, and check that the template's report artifact is still uploaded.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A teammate overrode `rules` on an included scanner job to add one condition, and now the scanner runs (and fails) in repositories where it does not apply. Explain why and propose a better solution." *Hint:* lists in a deep merge, what the template's rules were checking, and alternatives such as `include:rules` and documented variables.

---

<a id="10-testing-and-code-quality"></a>
## 10. Testing and Code Quality

A pipeline that only prints "Job succeeded" or "Job failed" makes reviewers dig through thousands of log lines to find out what broke. GitLab can read the machine-readable output of test runners, coverage tools, linters and performance tools, and show the results in the merge request where decisions are made: which tests failed for the first time, which changed lines are not covered, which new lint issues a change introduces, and whether a page got slower. This chapter covers the report types behind those views, how to produce them from common tools, and how to turn them into gates such as approval rules.

<a id="101-test-reporting"></a>
### 10.1 Test Reporting

Test reporting turns raw test runner output into structured results that GitLab can compare between branches, show in merge requests and track over time. This subchapter covers the JUnit report format, the merge request test summary, failure history on the default branch, and how to find and manage flaky tests.

#### JUnit Test Reports

**Why it matters.** When a test job fails, the log tells you that *something* failed, but finding the failing assertion in 5,000 lines of output is slow, and comparing the result with the target branch is impossible by eye. Test runners in almost every language can write their results as a JUnit XML file. GitLab reads that file and turns it into a list of test cases with status, duration and failure message, which is what makes every other feature in this subchapter possible.

**What it is.** JUnit XML is a de facto standard that started in the Java JUnit project and is now produced by pytest, Jest, Go tools, RSpec, PHPUnit, .NET loggers and many others. You declare the file with `artifacts:reports:junit`. The runner uploads it as a special report artifact and GitLab parses it.

A JUnit file is a tree of suites and cases:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<testsuites>
  <!-- One suite per test file, class or package, depending on the tool -->
  <testsuite name="tests.test_cart" tests="3" failures="1" errors="0" skipped="1" time="0.042">
    <!-- No child element: the test passed -->
    <testcase classname="tests.test_cart" name="test_add_item" file="tests/test_cart.py" time="0.010"/>

    <!-- <failure>: an assertion did not hold -->
    <testcase classname="tests.test_cart" name="test_total_with_discount" file="tests/test_cart.py" time="0.021">
      <failure message="AssertionError: assert 90 == 85">tests/test_cart.py:27: AssertionError</failure>
      <!-- Attachment syntax: GitLab links this file in the test details -->
      <system-out>[[ATTACHMENT|screenshots/test_total_with_discount.png]]</system-out>
    </testcase>
```
