```text
 3. Compromised or shared build machine         ───► Least-privilege runner design
 4. Tampered artifact between build and deploy  ───► Signing (Sigstore) and provenance (SLSA)
```

#### Protected Branches and Tags

**Why it matters.** In GitLab, *who can push to a ref* largely decides *who can run code with production secrets*: protected CI/CD variables, protected runners and protected environments are only available to pipelines on protected refs. If any developer can push to `main` or create a `v*` tag, any developer can modify `.gitlab-ci.yml` on that ref and print the production credentials. Protected branches and tags (introduced in sections 1.2, 3.1 and 5.2) are therefore a security boundary, not only a workflow convenience.

**What it is.** A protected branch or tag rule restricts who can push, merge, force push, create or delete matching refs. Pipelines on protected refs receive protected resources:

```text
                          protected ref (main, release/*, v*)    unprotected ref (feature/*)
 Protected variables      available                              not available
 Protected runners        can pick up jobs                       cannot
 Protected environments   deploy allowed (if user is allowed)    deploy blocked
 Who controls the code    Maintainers via reviewed merges        any developer with push access
```

**A hardened configuration.**

| Setting | Recommended value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Allowed to push and merge on `main` | Push: No one. Merge: Maintainers | All changes go through merge requests and their approvals |
| Allowed to force push | Off | Prevents rewriting history to hide or replace commits |
| Code owner approval (Premium) | On for `main` | Changes to `.gitlab-ci.yml`, deployment scripts and infra require their owners' approval |
| Protected tags `v*` | Allowed to create: Maintainers (or a release bot) | Tag pipelines publish releases with signing and registry credentials |
| Group-level protected branches (Premium) | Protect `main` for all projects | New projects are protected from day one |

Pair the branch rules with `CODEOWNERS` entries for pipeline files, so that a change to CI configuration needs approval from the platform or security team:

```text
# .gitlab/CODEOWNERS
[CI/CD] @acme/platform-team
/.gitlab-ci.yml
/ci/
/deploy/
```

**Setting it through the API.** Useful for enforcing the same rules across many projects:

```bash
# Protect main: no direct pushes (0), merges by Maintainers (40), no force push, code owner approval
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/protected_branches" \
  --data "name=main&push_access_level=0&merge_access_level=40&allow_force_push=false&code_owner_approval_required=true"

# Protect release tags: only Maintainers (40) can create v* tags
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/protected_tags" \
  --data "name=v*&create_access_level=40"
```

**Push rules (Premium).** **Settings > Repository > Push rules** add server-side checks on every push: reject unsigned commits, require commit author emails from your domain, check that the author is a GitLab user, prevent files matching secret patterns (`id_rsa`, `*.pem`), and limit file size. Rejecting unsigned commits on protected branches makes it harder to impersonate another developer in the history.

**Common gaps.**

- A wildcard such as `release/*` protects existing and future branches, but `release-*` is a different pattern. Check that your naming conventions match the rules.
- Protecting a branch does not protect a tag with the same name. Protect tags separately.
- Developers who can merge can still change `.gitlab-ci.yml` through a merge request. Approvals and code owners are what make that change reviewed.

**Key takeaways**

- Protected refs are the gate to protected variables, runners and environments. Whoever can push to them can effectively use production secrets.
- Disallow direct pushes and force pushes on `main`, protect release tag patterns, and require code owner approval for pipeline files.
- Use group-level protection and push rules (Premium) to make secure defaults automatic.
- Protected branches and protected tags are separate rules. Configure both.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Protect `main` so that nobody can push directly and only Maintainers can merge. Try a direct push as a Developer and as a Maintainer, and read the error messages.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `CODEOWNERS` section requiring `@platform-team` approval for `.gitlab-ci.yml` and enable code owner approval on `main`. Open an MR that changes the pipeline and confirm the required approval appears.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A Developer can't see the production deploy key in project settings. Can they still get it? How?" *Hint:* who can push to which refs, what a pipeline on that ref can read, `.gitlab-ci.yml` changes, and masked versus protected variables.

#### CI_JOB_TOKEN Scope and Allowlists

**Why it matters.** Every job gets a `CI_JOB_TOKEN` that can call the GitLab API and Git as the user who triggered the pipeline (section 1.2). Without limits, a compromised job in a low-value project, for example a malicious test dependency, could use that token to clone private repositories, download packages or read artifacts from *every* project the user can access. Scoping the token limits the blast radius to the projects that really need each other.

**What it is.** The job token is short-lived (valid only while the job runs) and its permissions are the intersection of three things:

```text
   what the triggering user can access
 ∩ what the target project's job token allowlist permits (which source projects/groups)
 ∩ which API endpoints accept job tokens (and, optionally, fine-grained permissions)
 = what CI_JOB_TOKEN can actually do
```

**The inbound allowlist.** Each project controls which *other* projects' job tokens may access it, under **Settings > CI/CD > Job token permissions**. With "Limit access to this project" enabled (the default for new projects), only the listed projects and groups can use their job tokens against it. A job token always works against its own project.

```text
 payments-lib (target)                                   allowlist
 "Limit access to this project": ON                      - group: acme/payments
                                                         - project: acme/platform/release-tools

 acme/payments/checkout  ── CI_JOB_TOKEN ──►  pull package from payments-lib     ✓ allowed (group listed)
 acme/marketing/website  ── CI_JOB_TOKEN ──►  clone payments-lib                 ✗ 403 (not listed)
```

**Managing the allowlist through the API.**

```bash
# Ensure the inbound scope is enforced for payments-lib (project 200)
curl --request PATCH --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/200/job_token_scope" --data "enabled=true"

# Allow every project in group 42 (acme/payments)
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/200/job_token_scope/groups_allowlist" --data "target_group_id=42"

# Allow one specific project (release tooling, project 315)
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/200/job_token_scope/allowlist" --data "target_project_id=315"
```

**Building the allowlist without breaking pipelines.** The project's **job token authentication log** lists which projects have accessed it with job tokens. Before enforcing the scope on an existing project, review the log and add each legitimate caller. Recent GitLab versions can populate the allowlist from the log automatically.

**Fine-grained permissions.** Recent versions let you restrict an allowlist entry to specific resources (for example read packages, read deployments, read or write environments) instead of everything the user can do. Grant only what the calling project needs.

**Using the job token correctly.**

```yaml
use-shared-package:
  script:
    # Authenticate to another project's package registry with the job token, not a personal token
    - pip install --index-url "https://gitlab-ci-token:${CI_JOB_TOKEN}@${CI_SERVER_HOST}/api/v4/projects/200/packages/pypi/simple" payments-lib
```

- Prefer `CI_JOB_TOKEN` over personal or project access tokens stored as variables. It expires with the job and is not tied to a long-lived secret.
- Pushing to a repository with the job token is off by default and must be enabled per project. Leave it off unless a job really needs to push.
- The token cannot do everything a user can do. Only endpoints that document job token support accept it.

**Key takeaways**

- `CI_JOB_TOKEN` acts as the triggering user, limited to the job's lifetime and to projects whose inbound allowlist includes the caller.
- Keep "Limit access to this project" enabled, and allowlist specific projects or groups using the authentication log as evidence.
- Use fine-grained permissions where available, and keep repository push access with the job token disabled unless required.
- Replace long-lived access tokens in variables with the job token wherever an endpoint supports it.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* In project B, try to clone private project A using `CI_JOB_TOKEN` and observe the 403. Add B to A's allowlist and run the job again.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* For a project used by several others, read its job token authentication log, build the allowlist from it, enable enforcement, and verify that an unlisted project is blocked while listed ones keep working.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A popular internal library's CI job was compromised through a malicious dependency. Which GitLab settings determine what the attacker could reach with `CI_JOB_TOKEN`?" *Hint:* the triggering user's memberships, inbound allowlists of other projects, endpoint support, job token push access, and the token's lifetime.

#### Least-Privilege Runner Design

**Why it matters.** A runner executes whatever a job's script says. On a shared runner, the job from an unreviewed feature branch runs on the same machine, with the same network access and possibly the same cached credentials, as the production deployment job. If one job can escape its container, persist on the host, or use the host's cloud identity, it can tamper with other projects' builds or reach production. Runner design decides how much damage a single malicious job can do.

**Principles.**

| Principle | Concrete control |
|---|---|
| Separate trust levels | Different runners for untrusted work (MR and feature branch jobs) and trusted work (protected branch deploys) |
| No shared state between jobs | Ephemeral executors: a fresh VM or container per job, no persistent host volumes |
| No privileged containers | Avoid `privileged = true` and Docker socket mounts. Build images with rootless tools (BuildKit rootless, Kaniko alternatives, Buildah) |
| No ambient credentials | Do not attach cloud IAM roles to runner hosts. Use per-job OIDC tokens (`id_tokens`, section 5.4) scoped by project and ref |
| Restrict what runs | Allowed images, services and pull policies on the runner |
| Restrict the network | Runners for untrusted jobs cannot reach production networks or internal admin endpoints |

**Separating trust levels.** Register a deploy runner as **protected** (it only runs jobs on protected branches and tags), **locked** to its project or group, and **tagged** so that only jobs that ask for it are routed there:

```bash
# Create a protected, project-locked runner that does not run untagged jobs (returns a runner auth token)
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/user/runners" \
  --data "runner_type=project_type&project_id=12345&description=prod-deployer" \
  --data "access_level=ref_protected&locked=true&run_untagged=false&tag_list=prod-deploy"
```

```yaml
deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  tags: [prod-deploy]                         # only the protected runner has this tag
  environment: production
  script: ./deploy.sh
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

A job on a feature branch that adds `tags: [prod-deploy]` stays pending forever: the runner is protected and refuses it.

**Hardening the Docker executor.**

```toml
# /etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml (excerpt)
concurrent = 4

[[runners]]
  name = "untrusted-docker"
  executor = "docker"
  [runners.docker]
    image = "alpine:3.20"
    privileged = false                                   # no access to host devices or kernel capabilities
    cap_drop = ["NET_RAW"]                               # drop capabilities jobs do not need
    security_opt = ["no-new-privileges"]                 # setuid binaries cannot escalate privileges
    allowed_images = ["registry.example.com/ci/*:*", "docker.io/library/*:*"]   # only approved image sources
    allowed_services = ["registry.example.com/ci/*:*", "docker.io/library/postgres:*"]
    allowed_pull_policies = ["always"]                   # never reuse a locally cached, possibly tampered image
    volumes = ["/cache"]                                 # no host paths such as /var/run/docker.sock
    disable_cache = false
    network_mode = "ci-isolated"                         # a Docker network without routes to internal services
```

**Ephemeral runners.** With the Docker Autoscaler or instance executors (chapter 6), each VM can be limited to a single job (`max_use_count = 1`), so nothing a job leaves behind (a modified binary, a background process, a stolen cache) survives to the next one. On Kubernetes, run untrusted jobs in a dedicated namespace with Pod Security Admission set to `restricted`, network policies, and no service account token mounted.

**Shared runners on GitLab.com.** GitLab-hosted runners already give each job a fresh, isolated VM. The risk shifts to what *your* jobs can reach: avoid long-lived cloud keys in variables and use OIDC federation with conditions on project path and ref.

**Key takeaways**

- A runner is only as trustworthy as the least trusted job it runs. Separate runners for untrusted branches and trusted deployments.
- Register deploy runners as protected, locked and tagged. Feature branch jobs cannot use them.
- Avoid privileged mode, Docker socket mounts and host volumes. Restrict images, services and pull policies.
- Prefer ephemeral, single-use execution environments and per-job OIDC credentials over ambient host credentials.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Register a protected runner with a unique tag and show that a job using that tag runs on `main` but stays pending on a feature branch.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure a Docker runner with `allowed_images`, `allowed_pull_policies` and no privileged mode. Write jobs that try to use a disallowed image, mount the Docker socket, and run `docker build`, and record which fail and why. Then build the image with a rootless builder instead.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your company uses one pool of self-managed shell-executor runners for all projects, including deployments. What risks do you see, and how would you redesign it?" *Hint:* persistence between jobs, shared file systems and credentials, untrusted MR code, protected runners, ephemeral executors and OIDC.

#### Securing Pipelines from Forks

**Why it matters.** Open source and inner source projects accept merge requests from forks. The person who opens a fork MR controls *all* of its content, including `.gitlab-ci.yml`, build scripts, test files and dependency manifests. If that code runs with the parent project's secrets or on its runners, the contributor can steal credentials or abuse infrastructure with a single MR.

**What it is.** GitLab runs fork MR pipelines **in the fork project by default**:

```text
 contributor/fork (fork)                             acme/app (parent)
 ───────────────────────                             ─────────────────
 MR from fork:feature → acme/app:main

 Default:  pipeline runs in the FORK
           - fork's CI/CD variables (none of the parent's)
           - fork's runners (or GitLab.com shared runners, billed to the fork's namespace)
           - parent sees results in the MR, but its secrets are never exposed

 Optional: a parent member with Developer+ clicks "Run pipeline" in the parent
           - runs the FORK'S CODE and the FORK'S .gitlab-ci.yml in the PARENT project
           - with the parent's non-protected variables and the parent's runners
           - GitLab shows a warning: review the changes first
```

Running in the parent is useful when tests need the parent's infrastructure, but it is equivalent to executing untrusted code with your project's credentials. Protected variables remain unavailable (the MR ref is not protected), which is why deploy and release secrets must always be protected variables.

**Controls.**

| Control | How |
|---|---|
| Review before running in the parent | Inspect `.gitlab-ci.yml`, scripts, dependency changes and test files in the diff before clicking **Run pipeline** |
| Disable running fork pipelines in the parent | Project setting allowing fork pipelines to run in the parent project (API: `ci_allow_fork_pipelines_to_run_in_parent_project`). Turn it off if you never need it |
| Keep secrets protected | Only protected variables for credentials. Unprotected variables are readable by fork pipelines run in the parent |
| Exclude sensitive jobs | Rules that never run deploy or publish jobs for fork MRs |
| Isolate runners | Run fork MR jobs on a dedicated, unprivileged runner pool with no network access to internal systems |
| Restrict pipeline variables | Limit who can pass variables when running pipelines (minimum role setting for pipeline variables) |

**Excluding sensitive jobs for fork MRs.** In an MR pipeline from a fork that runs in the parent, `CI_PROJECT_ID` is the parent and `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_PROJECT_ID` is the fork:

```yaml
.not-from-fork:
  rules:
    # Fork MR running in the parent: the source project differs from the current project
    - if: $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_PROJECT_ID && $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_PROJECT_ID != $CI_PROJECT_ID
      when: never
    - when: on_success

integration-tests-with-sandbox-creds:
  extends: .not-from-fork                     # never runs for fork MRs, even if a maintainer starts it
  script: ./run-integration-tests.sh
```

This rule protects against a maintainer accidentally running jobs that use sensitive, non-protected variables. It does not protect against a malicious `.gitlab-ci.yml` in the fork, because the fork's version of the file is the one that runs. Only review and the protected/unprotected boundary protect against that.

**Public project settings.** For public projects, also check **Settings > CI/CD > General pipelines**: whether job logs and artifacts are visible to non-members (**Project-based pipeline visibility**), and that masked variables never appear in logs that anyone can read.

**Key takeaways**

- Fork MR pipelines run in the fork by default, without the parent's variables or runners. That is the safe default.
- Running a fork MR pipeline in the parent executes untrusted code and CI configuration with the parent's non-protected variables and runners. Review first, or disable the option.
- Store every credential as a protected variable so that MR pipelines, including fork MRs, can never read it.
- Use rules on `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_PROJECT_ID` and dedicated runners to reduce the impact of mistakes.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Fork a test project, open an MR to the parent, and check in which project the pipeline runs and whether a parent variable is visible to it.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* As a parent maintainer, run the fork MR's pipeline in the parent project with an unprotected and a protected variable defined. Verify which one the job can print, then add the `.not-from-fork` rule to a sensitive job and confirm it is skipped.
> 3. **Interview question:** "An open source project wants to run its expensive GPU integration tests on contributions from forks. How would you allow that safely?" *Hint:* maintainer review before running, isolated runners without credentials, protected variables, and what the contributor controls in the MR.

#### Artifact Signing with Sigstore

**Why it matters.** Between build and deployment, an artifact passes through registries, caches and mirrors. If an attacker replaces `app:1.4.0` in a registry with a backdoored image, the deploy job pulls it without noticing, because a tag name proves nothing about content. A signature binds an artifact's exact digest to an identity, so deployers can verify "this image was built by the `acme/app` pipeline on `main`" before running it.

**What it is.** **Sigstore** is an open source signing ecosystem that removes the hardest part of signing: managing private keys. Its tool **cosign** supports *keyless* signing:

```text
 1. GitLab job requests an OIDC ID token (id_tokens, aud: sigstore)
        └─ token contains claims: project path, ref, pipeline, CI config path...
 2. cosign sends the token to Fulcio (Sigstore CA)
        └─ Fulcio issues a short-lived (10 min) certificate whose identity is the job's CI config URI
 3. cosign signs the artifact digest with an ephemeral key, discards the key
 4. Signature + certificate are recorded in Rekor (public transparency log)
        └─ and the signature is stored next to the image in the registry

 Verification: check the signature, the certificate chain, the Rekor entry,
               and that the identity matches the expected project, ref and issuer
```

Nothing long-lived needs protecting: the identity is the pipeline itself, attested by GitLab's OIDC issuer.

**Signing a container image.** Keyless signing with the public Sigstore instance works on GitLab.com:

```yaml
build-and-sign:
  stage: build
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]
  variables:
    IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA
    COSIGN_YES: "true"                         # do not prompt to confirm upload to the transparency log
  id_tokens:
    SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN:                         # cosign reads this variable automatically
      aud: sigstore
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache cosign
    - docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" -p "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" "$CI_REGISTRY"
  script:
    - docker build --pull -t "$IMAGE" .
    - docker push "$IMAGE"
    # Sign the immutable digest, never the mutable tag
    - IMAGE_DIGEST="$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$IMAGE")"
    - cosign sign "$IMAGE_DIGEST" --annotations "com.gitlab.ci.pipeline.url=$CI_PIPELINE_URL"
    - echo "IMAGE_DIGEST=$IMAGE_DIGEST" >> build.env
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dotenv: build.env
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

**Verifying before deployment.** Verification must check *who* signed, not only that *someone* did:

```yaml
verify-and-deploy:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:3.20
  needs: [build-and-sign]                      # receives IMAGE_DIGEST from the dotenv report
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache cosign
  script:
    # The identity is the CI config URI: <server>/<project path>//<config path>@<ref>
    - >
      cosign verify "$IMAGE_DIGEST"
      --certificate-identity "https://gitlab.com/acme/app//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/main"
      --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://gitlab.com"
    - ./deploy.sh "$IMAGE_DIGEST"              # deploy by digest, the exact bytes that were verified
```

In Kubernetes, an admission controller such as the Sigstore policy-controller or Kyverno can enforce the same check for every pod, so unsigned images cannot run even if someone bypasses the pipeline.

**Signing other artifacts.** `cosign sign-blob` signs files such as release tarballs or SBOMs and writes a bundle to publish next to them:

```bash
cosign sign-blob dist/app-1.4.0.tar.gz --bundle dist/app-1.4.0.tar.gz.sigstore.json
cosign verify-blob dist/app-1.4.0.tar.gz --bundle dist/app-1.4.0.tar.gz.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity "https://gitlab.com/acme/app//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/tags/v1.4.0" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://gitlab.com"
```

**Caveats.**

| Topic | Detail |
|---|---|
| Self-managed GitLab | The public Fulcio instance trusts GitLab.com's issuer, not yours. Run a private Sigstore stack, or use key-based signing (`cosign generate-key-pair`, key in a KMS or protected variable) |
| Privacy | Rekor is public. Keyless signing in a private project publishes its path, ref and pipeline URLs in the log. Use a private Sigstore instance or key-based signing without the transparency log if that is unacceptable |
| What a signature proves | Who built the artifact, not that it is safe. A signed backdoor is still a backdoor if the source or pipeline was compromised. Pair signing with protected refs and provenance |

**Key takeaways**

- Signing binds an artifact digest to an identity. Verification before deployment detects tampering in registries and caches.
- Keyless signing uses a GitLab OIDC token (`id_tokens` with `aud: sigstore`), a short-lived Fulcio certificate and the Rekor transparency log. No private key to manage.
- Always sign and deploy by digest, and verify the exact certificate identity and issuer, not just any valid signature.
- On self-managed GitLab or for private metadata, use a private Sigstore instance or key-based signing.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* On GitLab.com, sign an image with keyless cosign in a pipeline and verify it locally with `cosign verify`, using the correct certificate identity for your project and branch.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a verification step to the deploy job, then push a different image to the same tag manually and show that verification by the tag's digest fails. Explain why deploying by tag would have missed it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is `cosign verify` with only `--certificate-oidc-issuer https://gitlab.com` not enough to trust an image?" *Hint:* who else can obtain a certificate from that issuer, and which claims (project, ref, config path) the identity must pin.

#### SLSA Provenance and Attestation

**Why it matters.** A signature says *who* produced an artifact. Consumers and auditors increasingly ask *how*: from which source commit, by which build system, with which parameters and dependencies? If a release binary cannot be traced to a reviewed commit and a trusted pipeline, nobody can tell whether it contains code that never went through review, which is what happened in several major supply chain attacks such as SolarWinds. **Provenance** is the verifiable record of how an artifact was built.

**What it is.** **SLSA** (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, pronounced "salsa") is a framework that defines increasing levels of build integrity:

| SLSA build level | Requirement | Protects against |
|---|---|---|
| Build L0 | None | Nothing |
| Build L1 | Provenance exists, describing how the artifact was built | Mistakes, unknown build origins |
| Build L2 | Builds run on a hosted build platform that generates and **signs** the provenance | Tampering after the build, forged provenance by individuals |
| Build L3 | Hardened build platform: builds are isolated from each other, and signing material is unreachable by the build's own steps | A compromised build step forging provenance, cross-build contamination |

Provenance is expressed as an **in-toto attestation**: a statement with a *subject* (the artifact's name and digest) and a *predicate* (the SLSA provenance describing the build).

**Generating provenance with GitLab Runner.** The runner can produce provenance for a job's artifacts. Set `RUNNER_GENERATE_ARTIFACTS_METADATA`:

```yaml
build-release:
  stage: build
  image: golang:1.23
  variables:
    RUNNER_GENERATE_ARTIFACTS_METADATA: "true"   # runner writes SLSA provenance for the artifacts
  script:
    - CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o dist/app ./cmd/app
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - dist/app                                  # provenance covers these files
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
```

The runner uploads an extra file, `artifacts-metadata.json` (named after `artifacts:name`), alongside the artifacts. Simplified:

```json
{
  "_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v1",
  "subject": [
    { "name": "dist/app", "digest": { "sha256": "9f2c1e...a41b" } }
  ],
  "predicateType": "https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1",
  "predicate": {
    "buildDefinition": {
      "buildType": "https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner/...",
      "externalParameters": {
        "source": "https://gitlab.com/acme/app",
        "entryPoint": "build-release"
      },
      "internalParameters": { "name": "saas-linux-small-amd64", "executor": "docker+machine" },
      "resolvedDependencies": [
        { "uri": "https://gitlab.com/acme/app", "digest": { "sha256": "<commit sha>" } }
      ]
    },
    "runDetails": {
      "builder": { "id": "https://gitlab.com/acme/app/-/runners/12270859" },
      "metadata": {
        "invocationID": "8148375512",
        "startedOn": "2026-10-15T08:01:12Z",
        "finishedOn": "2026-10-15T08:03:40Z"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The file on its own is unsigned, which corresponds to **SLSA Build L1**. To reach L2, the provenance must be signed by the build platform, so that a consumer can verify it was not edited after the fact.

**Signing the attestation.** cosign can sign the provenance as an in-toto attestation for the binary, using the same keyless identity as in the previous topic, and write a bundle to publish next to the release:

```yaml
attest-release:
  stage: release
  image: alpine:3.20
  needs: [build-release]                        # provides dist/app and artifacts-metadata.json
  id_tokens:
    SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: sigstore
  variables:
    COSIGN_YES: "true"
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache cosign jq
    # cosign builds the in-toto statement itself; pass only the SLSA predicate
    - jq '.predicate' artifacts-metadata.json > provenance-predicate.json
    - >
      cosign attest-blob dist/app
      --type slsaprovenance1
      --predicate provenance-predicate.json
      --bundle dist/app.provenance.sigstore.json
  artifacts:
    paths: [dist/app.provenance.sigstore.json]  # publish with the release (section 8.4)
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
```

For container images the equivalent is `cosign attest <image digest> --type slsaprovenance1 --predicate ...`, which stores the attestation in the registry next to the image.

Consumers verify the attestation's signature and identity, then check its content, for example that `externalParameters.source` is the expected repository and that the commit in `resolvedDependencies` is a reviewed commit on a protected ref:

```bash
cosign verify-blob-attestation dist/app \
  --bundle dist/app.provenance.sigstore.json \
  --type slsaprovenance1 \
  --certificate-identity "https://gitlab.com/acme/app//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/tags/v1.4.0" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://gitlab.com"
```

Recent GitLab versions are adding built-in attestation and verification support (including through the `glab` CLI and CI/CD components). Check the documentation for your version before building your own tooling.

**Getting closer to Build L3 with GitLab.**

- Generate provenance on the platform side (the runner), not with a script that the build itself controls.
- Run release builds on ephemeral, isolated runners (previous topics), so one build cannot influence another.
- Keep signing identities out of reach of the build steps where possible, for example by signing in a separate job, on a protected runner, that only consumes the build's output digest.
- Build only from protected tags or branches, with reviewed changes, so that the provenance points to code that went through review.

**Key takeaways**

- Provenance records how an artifact was built: source, commit, builder, entry point and parameters. SLSA defines build levels for how trustworthy that record is.
- `RUNNER_GENERATE_ARTIFACTS_METADATA: "true"` makes GitLab Runner produce SLSA v1 provenance for job artifacts (Build L1).
- Sign the provenance (for example `cosign attest`) and attach it to the artifact to approach Build L2. Verify both the signature and the content.
- Higher levels depend on isolated, ephemeral builds and signing that the build steps cannot tamper with.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Enable `RUNNER_GENERATE_ARTIFACTS_METADATA` in a build job, download `artifacts-metadata.json`, and check that the subject's SHA-256 matches `sha256sum` of the artifact.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Attach a signed SLSA provenance attestation to an image with `cosign attest`, then write a verification script that fails unless the provenance's source repository and commit match the expected values.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Explain the difference between signing an artifact and providing SLSA provenance for it. Which supply chain attacks does each one stop?" *Hint:* identity versus build process, registry tampering versus a compromised build step, and what happens when the source itself was malicious.

---

<a id="12-deployment-and-environments"></a>
## 12. Deployment and Environments

A pipeline that builds and tests code but cannot get that code to users safely only does half the job. This chapter covers the delivery half: how GitLab models the places you deploy to as **environments**, how it gives every merge request a temporary deployment, which strategies limit the damage of a bad release, how to deploy to common targets such as Kubernetes, the major clouds and plain servers, how to manage infrastructure itself through Git, and what Auto DevOps automates for you. Knowing these mechanisms is what lets a team deploy many times a day without making each deployment an event.

> **Tiers at a glance.** Environments, deployments, review apps, `auto_stop_in`, rollbacks, feature flags, GitLab Pages, the GitLab agent for Kubernetes, GitLab-managed Terraform state and Auto DevOps are available on **all tiers**. Protected environments, deployment approvals, the cross-project environments dashboard, Pages parallel deployments and agent impersonation for CI jobs require **Premium**. Each topic notes its tier.

<a id="121-environments"></a>
### 12.1 Environments

An environment is a named place your code runs, such as `staging` or `production`, and every deployment to it is recorded. This subchapter covers how jobs declare environments, the difference between fixed and generated environments, how tiers and URLs describe them, and how to control who may deploy to them and who must approve first.

Without environments, a pipeline is only a list of scripts. GitLab cannot tell you what is running in production, which commit it came from or who deployed it. With environments, every deployment job leaves a record:

```text
  pipeline #812 (commit a1b2c3)                       GitLab records
  ┌───────┐   ┌──────┐   ┌──────────────────┐          ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ build │──►│ test │──►│ deploy-prod      │────────► │ Environment "production"                  │
  └───────┘   └──────┘   │ environment:     │          │   Deployment #57  a1b2c3  success  alice  │
                         │   production     │          │   Deployment #56  9f8e7d  success  bob    │
                         └──────────────────┘          │   Deployment #55  4c5d6e  failed   alice  │
                                                       └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                                          ▲ history, rollback, protection, approvals
```

#### environment Keyword

**Why it matters.** "What version is running in staging right now?" should never need a Slack thread. The `environment` keyword tells GitLab that a job deploys somewhere. GitLab then tracks each run of that job as a **deployment**: which commit, which pipeline, who started it and whether it succeeded. Every other feature in this chapter (rollbacks, protection, approvals, review apps, dashboards) builds on that record.

**What it is.** `environment` is a job keyword. Its short form is just a name:

```yaml
deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh staging
  environment: staging                  # short form: only the name
```

The long form accepts more settings:

```yaml
deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh production
  environment:
    name: production                    # required; creates the environment on first use
    url: https://shop.example.com       # "Open" button in the UI and the MR widget
    deployment_tier: production         # explicit tier (next topics)
    action: start                       # default: this job creates a deployment
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

| Sub-keyword | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `name` | Environment name. Letters, digits, spaces and `- _ / $ { }`. Cannot start or end with `/` |
| `url` | Public address of the deployed app |
| `deployment_tier` | `production`, `staging`, `testing`, `development` or `other` |
| `action` | What the job does to the environment (table below) |
| `on_stop` | Job that tears the environment down (section 12.2) |
| `auto_stop_in` | Stop the environment automatically after a period (section 12.2) |
| `kubernetes` | Link the environment to a GitLab agent and namespace (section 12.4) |

**`environment:action`.** Not every job that touches an environment deploys to it. A database backup, a smoke test or a `terraform plan` needs the environment's protection and scoped variables, but should not appear as a new deployment. `action` expresses this:

| Action | Creates a deployment | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `start` (default) | Yes | The actual deploy |
| `prepare` | No | Work before deploying: build with environment-scoped secrets, run `terraform plan` |
| `verify` | No | Smoke tests or checks after deploying |
| `access` | No | Jobs that only need the environment's variables or protection, such as a backup |
| `stop` | No (stops the environment) | Tear down the environment (section 12.2) |

```yaml
smoke-test-production:
  stage: verify
  script: ./smoke-test.sh "$CI_ENVIRONMENT_URL"   # URL comes from the environment
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://shop.example.com
    action: verify                                # gets production variables, no new deployment record
```

**Predefined variables.** Inside a job with an environment, GitLab sets:

| Variable | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME` | `review/feature-login` | The name after variable expansion |
| `CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG` | `review-feature-lo-x7k2pa` | Lowercase, DNS-safe, at most 24 characters. May get a short random suffix to stay unique. Use it in hostnames and Kubernetes names |
| `CI_ENVIRONMENT_URL` | `https://...` | Only if `url` is set |
| `CI_ENVIRONMENT_TIER` | `development` | The deployment tier |
| `CI_ENVIRONMENT_ACTION` | `start` | The job's action |

**Environment-scoped variables.** A variable can be limited to one environment or a wildcard such as `review/*` (section 5.2). Only jobs whose `environment:name` matches the scope receive it. This is the main reason to give even non-deploying jobs an `environment` with `action: access` or `prepare`.

**The deployment lifecycle.** The environment record is created the first time a pipeline contains a job that uses it. Each `start` job creates a deployment that follows the job's state:

```text
created ──► running ──► success
   │            └─────► failed / canceled
   └──► blocked (waiting for approval, 12.1) ──► running ...
   └──► skipped (job did not run)
```

The environment's "last deployment" is the most recent **successful** one. A failed deployment does not change what GitLab reports as running.

**Key takeaways**

- `environment` turns a job into a tracked deployment. That record is the basis for history, rollback, protection and approvals.
- Use the long form for `url`, `deployment_tier`, `action`, `on_stop` and `auto_stop_in`.
- `action: prepare`, `verify` and `access` give a job the environment's variables and protection without creating a deployment.
- `CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG` is the DNS-safe name to use in hostnames and resource names.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add `environment: staging` to a deploy job that only runs `echo`. Run the pipeline and open **Operate > Environments**. Find the deployment, its commit and the user who triggered it.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `smoke-test` job with `action: verify` and a backup job with `action: access` to the same environment. Confirm that neither creates a new entry in the deployment history, and that both can read a variable scoped to that environment.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why would you attach an environment to a job that does not deploy anything?" *Hint:* environment-scoped variables, protected environment access rules, and keeping the deployment history accurate.

#### Static vs Dynamic Environments

**Why it matters.** A team has a few long-lived environments that always exist (staging, production) and many short-lived ones that come and go with branches (one per merge request). Hardcoding a job per branch is impossible. Dynamic environments let one job definition create a new environment for every branch.

**What it is.**

| | Static environment | Dynamic environment |
|---|---|---|
| Name | Fixed string: `staging`, `production` | Contains variables: `review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` |
| Lifetime | Long-lived, rarely stopped | Created per branch or MR, stopped when no longer needed |
| Count | A handful per project | Potentially hundreds |
| URL | Fixed | Usually derived from the slug, or reported by the deploy job |
| Typical use | Shared staging, production | Review apps (section 12.2), per-developer sandboxes |

```yaml
deploy-review:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh "$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG"
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG                       # one environment per branch
    url: https://$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG.review.example.com   # hostname built from the DNS-safe slug
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
```

**Which variables can appear in the name.** The name is computed when the pipeline is created, so it can only use predefined variables, project/group variables and variables defined in the YAML or passed to the pipeline. It **cannot** use variables created in the job's `script` or by a `dotenv` report, because those do not exist yet.

**Environment folders.** A `/` in the name groups environments into folders in the UI. All `review/*` environments collapse into one "review" row, which keeps the environments list readable even with 200 open merge requests:

```text
Operate > Environments
  ▸ review (37)                 ← folder: review/feature-login, review/fix-cart, ...
    staging       a1b2c3  2 h ago
    production    9f8e7d  1 d ago
```

The folder prefix also works as a wildcard scope for variables (`review/*`) and protected environments.

**Dynamic URLs.** Some platforms assign a random URL only after deploying (serverless functions, preview hosts). The deploy job writes the URL to a `dotenv` report, and `environment:url` references that variable (section 5.3):

```yaml
deploy-preview:
  script:
    - URL=$(./deploy-preview.sh)                   # the platform prints the generated URL
    - echo "DYNAMIC_ENVIRONMENT_URL=$URL" >> deploy.env
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dotenv: deploy.env                           # GitLab reads it when the job finishes
  environment:
    name: preview/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: $DYNAMIC_ENVIRONMENT_URL                  # filled in from the dotenv report
```

**Key takeaways**

- Static environments have fixed names and live long. Dynamic environments put variables in the name and are created per branch or MR.
- Environment names are resolved at pipeline creation. Variables from `script` or `dotenv` cannot be used in the name, but `dotenv` can provide the URL.
- A `/` in the name creates a UI folder and a natural wildcard for variables and protection.
- Build hostnames from `CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG`, not from the raw branch name.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a dynamic environment `review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` with an `echo` deploy job. Push three branches and look at the folder in **Operate > Environments**.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a deploy job that generates a random URL in its script, passes it through a `dotenv` report, and sets it as `environment:url`. Check that the "Open" button in the environment page uses that URL.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A developer wants the environment name to include the version number computed in the build job's script. Why does that not work, and what would you suggest?" *Hint:* when the name is evaluated, and whether the version could come from a tag or pipeline variable instead.

#### Environment Tiers and URLs

**Why it matters.** Names are free text. One team calls production `prod`, another `live`, a third `eu-production`. GitLab needs a fixed vocabulary to know which environments matter most: for group-level protection rules, for DORA metrics such as deployment frequency, and for showing the right environment in merge requests. **Deployment tiers** provide it. URLs connect the environment record to the running application.

**Tiers.** Every environment has exactly one of five tiers. If you do not set `deployment_tier`, GitLab guesses from the name:

| Tier | Names GitLab maps to it automatically (examples) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `production` | `production`, `prod`, `live` | Serves real users |
| `staging` | `staging`, `stage`, `pre`, `demo`, `model` | Last check before production |
| `testing` | `test`, `qa`, `qc` | Automated or manual testing |
| `development` | `dev`, `review`, `trunk` | Developer and review environments |
| `other` | Anything else | Unclassified |

Set the tier explicitly whenever the name is ambiguous:

```yaml
deploy-eu:
  script: ./deploy.sh eu-central
  environment:
    name: eu-central               # GitLab would guess "other"
    deployment_tier: production    # it really serves customers
```

**What tiers drive.**

| Feature | How the tier is used |
|---|---|
| Group-level protected environments (Premium) | Protect every `production`-tier environment in all projects of a group (next topic) |
| DORA metrics and CI/CD analytics | Deployment frequency, lead time and change failure rate count deployments to `production` tier |
| `CI_ENVIRONMENT_TIER` | Scripts can branch on the tier instead of parsing names |

**URLs.** `environment:url` adds an **Open** button on the environment page and a **View app** link in the merge request widget. It can use variables, so dynamic environments get per-branch links.

**Route maps.** For static sites and documentation, a route map links changed source files to their public pages. Reviewers then see "View on review/..." next to each changed file in the merge request. The map is a YAML file at `.gitlab/route-map.yml`:

```yaml
# .gitlab/route-map.yml
- source: /content\/(.+?)\.md/      # regex on the source path (delimited by /)
  public: '\1.html'                  # public path, using capture groups
- source: 'index.md'                 # exact path (quoted string)
  public: 'index.html'
```

**Key takeaways**

- The five tiers are `production`, `staging`, `testing`, `development` and `other`. GitLab infers the tier from common names.
- Set `deployment_tier` explicitly for names like `eu-central` or `customer-a`, or group-level protection and DORA metrics will miss them.
- `environment:url` powers the Open button and the MR's "View app" link. Route maps link individual changed files to their deployed pages.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create environments named `prod`, `qa` and `blue` with `echo` jobs. Check which tier each received, then fix `blue` with `deployment_tier`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a route map to a small static site with Markdown pages deployed as a review app. Open a merge request that changes one page and use the per-file link to view it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your DORA dashboard shows zero production deployments although the team deploys daily. What is the likely cause?" *Hint:* how GitLab decides which environments are production.

#### Protected Environments

**Why it matters.** Protected branches stop just anyone from changing `main`, but a deploy job on an unprotected branch can still deploy to production unless something stops it. A Developer could add a job with `environment: production` to a feature branch, or retry an old deploy job. Protected environments (Premium) move the decision of *who may deploy* from the pipeline YAML, which anyone with push access can edit, into project or group settings that only Maintainers control.

**What it is.** A protected environment has a list of who is **allowed to deploy**: roles, specific users or groups. When a job targets that environment, GitLab checks the person who triggered the job. If that person is not allowed, the job fails with an access error and the deployment never runs. The check applies to the first run and to every retry or manual play.

```text
deploy-prod job created by Dana (Developer)
        │
        ▼
 Is "production" protected? ──no──► run
        │ yes
        ▼
 Is Dana in "allowed to deploy"? ──no──► job fails: "You do not have permission to deploy"
        │ yes
        ▼
 Approval rules? (next topic) ──none──► run
```

**Configuring.** In **Settings > CI/CD > Protected environments**, choose the environment (names and wildcards such as `review/*` work) and the deployers. The same through the API:

```shell
# Protect "production": Maintainers (access level 40) and the "sre" group (ID 77) may deploy
curl --request POST \
  --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
        "name": "production",
        "deploy_access_levels": [
          { "access_level": 40 },
          { "group_id": 77 }
        ]
      }' \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/protected_environments"
```

**Group-level protection.** Large organizations protect environments by **tier** across every project in a group (**Group > Settings > CI/CD > Protected environments**). One rule then covers every `production`-tier environment in hundreds of projects, and project Maintainers cannot weaken it. This is why setting `deployment_tier` correctly matters.

**Combining it with the rest.** A protected environment is one layer:

| Layer | What it stops | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Protected branch or tag | Unreviewed code reaching the deploy ref | Repository settings |
| Protected variables (section 5.2) | Secrets reaching pipelines on unprotected refs | CI/CD variables |
| Environment-scoped variables | Production credentials reaching non-production jobs | CI/CD variables |
| Protected environment | Unauthorized people starting a production deployment | CI/CD settings |
| Deployment approvals | A single person deploying without a second look | CI/CD settings |

A common setup: production credentials are both **protected** and **scoped to `production`**, the `production` environment is protected for the release team, and the deploy job runs only on `main`.

**Things to know.**

- Protection checks the person who triggered the job. A scheduled pipeline runs as the schedule owner, so that person must be allowed to deploy.
- Users and groups listed as deployers must be members of the project, or the group must be invited to it.
- Jobs that use the environment with `action: prepare`, `verify` or `access` are subject to the same protection.

**Key takeaways**

- Protected environments (Premium) restrict who can run jobs that target an environment, independently of who can edit `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
- Allow deployers by role, user or group. Wildcards protect whole folders.
- Group-level rules protect a tier across all projects. They rely on correct `deployment_tier` values.
- Combine with protected branches, protected and environment-scoped variables, and approvals for defense in depth.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Protect a `production` environment so that only Maintainers can deploy. Trigger the deploy job as a Developer and read the failure message.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Protect `production` with the API, then use `GET /projects/:id/protected_environments` to list the rule. Add a group as an additional deployer and verify that a member of that group with the Developer role can now deploy.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A Developer cannot edit protected branches but can push a feature branch. List every way they could still reach production credentials or deploy, and how you would close each gap." *Hint:* YAML changes on a feature branch, unprotected variables, environment scopes, and who triggers retries.

#### Deployment Approvals

**Why it matters.** Some changes need a second person: a regulated release, a database migration, a Friday-evening hotfix. Asking for approval in chat leaves no record and is easy to skip. Deployment approvals (Premium) make GitLab hold the deployment until the right people approve it in GitLab, and store who approved, when and why.

**What it is.** Approval rules belong to a protected environment. Each rule names an approver (a role, a user or a group) and how many approvals are required. When a job targets the environment, its deployment goes into the **blocked** state and waits until all rules are satisfied.

```text
pipeline ──► deploy-prod  [waiting for approval]
                 │
   Rule "QA"    needs 1 of group qa         [approved] by Ana (10:02)
   Rule "SRE"   needs 1 of group sre        [approved] by Bo  (10:15)  "Load test OK"
                 │
                 ▼
             deployment proceeds    (a rejection by any approver blocks it for good)
```

**Configuring.** When protecting the environment, add approval rules in the UI or the API:

```shell
curl --request POST \
  --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
        "name": "production",
        "deploy_access_levels": [ { "group_id": 77 } ],
        "approval_rules": [
          { "group_id": 81, "required_approvals": 1 },
          { "access_level": 40, "required_approvals": 1 }
        ]
      }' \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/protected_environments"
```

The first rule requires one approval from the QA group (ID 81), the second one approval from any Maintainer. Both must be satisfied.

**Approving.** Approvers open the environment, find the blocked deployment and choose **Approve** or **Reject**, optionally with a comment. Automation can do the same through the Deployments API:

```shell
# Approve deployment 4711 with a comment
curl --request POST \
  --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  --data "status=approved" \
  --data "comment=Load test passed, change ticket CHG-2231" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/deployments/4711/approval"
```

**Rules of thumb.**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Can the person who triggered the pipeline approve? | No, by default. The project setting **Allow pipeline triggerer to approve deployment** changes this. |
| Does a rejection count? | One rejection blocks the deployment. Run a new pipeline after fixing the problem. |
| Do approvals carry over to a retried job? | No. A new deployment needs new approvals. |
| Is the job still manual after approval? | If the job is also `when: manual`, someone allowed to deploy still has to start it. Use `when: manual` only if you want an extra "go" moment after approval. |
| Where is the audit trail? | On the deployment's approval details and in audit events. |

**Approvals versus manual jobs.** `when: manual` asks *anyone who can run the job* to click play. Approvals ask *specific people* to sign off, require a count, record a decision and comment, and cannot be bypassed by editing the YAML. Use manual jobs for convenience gates and approvals for control.

**Key takeaways**

- Deployment approvals (Premium) attach approval rules to a protected environment. The deployment stays blocked until every rule is satisfied.
- Rules can require approvals from roles, users or groups, with a count per rule.
- Approve or reject in the UI or with `POST /deployments/:id/approval`. Each decision is recorded with its comment.
- By default, the person who triggered the pipeline cannot approve their own deployment.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add an approval rule requiring one Maintainer approval to a protected `production` environment. Run a deploy and approve it from the environment page with a comment.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure two rules (QA group and SRE group). Write a small script that lists blocked deployments with `GET /projects/:id/deployments?status=blocked` and approves one through the API. Then reject a different deployment and observe the job.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Compare `when: manual` on a production job with deployment approvals. When is a manual job enough?" *Hint:* who can click it, whether the YAML can be changed to remove it, and what an auditor wants to see.

#### Environment Dashboard

**Why it matters.** An on-call engineer at 3 a.m. needs to answer "what changed, where and when" quickly. The environment pages answer it for one project; the environments dashboard answers it across many.

**What it is.** GitLab has three levels of environment views:

| View | Where | Tier | Shows |
|---|---|---|---|
| Environments list | **Operate > Environments** in a project | All | Every environment with its last deployment, commit, deployer, URL, and buttons to open, stop, roll back or re-deploy |
| Environment details | Click an environment | All | Full deployment history, approvals, Kubernetes resources when linked to an agent (section 12.4), stop and rollback controls |
| Environments dashboard | **Your work > Environments** | Premium | Your chosen projects side by side, each with its environments' latest deployment and pipeline status |

```text
Environments dashboard
┌────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
│ shop/web               │ shop/api               │ shop/payments          │
│  production  ● success │  production  ● success │  production  ● failed  │
│   a1b2c3  alice  12m   │   77aa01  bob   3h     │   c0ffee  dana  5m     │
│  staging     ● running │  staging     ● success │  staging     ● success │
└────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘
```

**Reading deployments with the API.** The data behind these views is available for scripts, status pages and chat bots:

```shell
# Last successful production deployment: commit, user and finish time
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/deployments?environment=production&status=success&order_by=finished_at&sort=desc&per_page=1" \
  | jq '.[0] | {sha, ref, user: .user.username, finished_at}'

# All environments that are still running (not stopped)
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/environments?states=available" \
  | jq -r '.[] | "\(.name)\t\(.tier)\t\(.external_url)"'
```

**Deployments in merge requests and commits.** A merge request shows which environments its changes were deployed to, with links. A commit can be checked in the environment's history to see whether, when and where it was deployed. This is often the fastest way to answer "is my fix live yet?".

**Key takeaways**

- The project environments list and details pages are available on all tiers and offer history, stop, rollback and re-deploy.
- The cross-project environments dashboard (Premium) shows many projects' environments at once.
- The Environments and Deployments APIs expose the same data for scripts and status tooling.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* After several deployments, use the environment details page to find which commit is in production and who deployed it. Then find the same data with the Deployments API.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a script that prints, for a list of project IDs, the commit SHA and age of the last successful `production` deployment, and flags any project whose last production deployment failed.
> 3. **Interview question:** "During an incident you suspect a deployment caused it, but several services deployed in the last hour. How would you use GitLab to narrow it down quickly?" *Hint:* cross-project views, deployment timestamps, and the commits each deployment contained.

<a id="122-review-apps"></a>
### 12.2 Review Apps

A review app is a temporary, per-merge-request deployment of the application, so reviewers can click through a change instead of imagining it from a diff. This subchapter shows how to build review apps from dynamic environments, how to tear them down reliably, and how to keep forgotten ones from piling up and costing money.

```text
 MR !41 "New checkout"  ──► review/new-checkout   https://review-new-checkout.review.example.com
 MR !42 "Fix cart"      ──► review/fix-cart       https://review-fix-cart.review.example.com
 main                   ──► staging ──► production

 MR merged or branch deleted  ──► on_stop job tears down review/<branch>
 nobody pushes for 3 days     ──► auto_stop_in stops it anyway
```

#### Configuring Review Apps

**Why it matters.** Screenshots in a merge request show what the author chose to show. A product manager, designer or QA engineer who can open the actual running change finds problems a code reviewer will not: a broken layout on mobile, a confusing flow, a slow page. Catching them before merge is much cheaper than after release. Review apps also give automated tests such as DAST, accessibility and performance testing (chapters 10 and 11) a realistic target per merge request.

**What it is.** A review app is not a separate feature. It is the combination of:

1. A **dynamic environment** named after the branch (section 12.1).
2. A **deploy job** that runs in merge request pipelines and deploys to a unique hostname or namespace.
3. A **stop job** that removes the deployment (next topic).
4. Optionally, `auto_stop_in` for automatic expiry.

GitLab then shows a **View app** button in the merge request widget.

**A complete example** for a container image deployed to Kubernetes with Helm:

```yaml
stages: [build, deploy]

variables:
  IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA

build:
  stage: build
  image: docker:27.3
  services: [docker:27.3-dind]
  script:
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin "$CI_REGISTRY"
    - docker build -t "$IMAGE" .
    - docker push "$IMAGE"

deploy-review:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine/k8s:1.31.2                 # contains kubectl and helm
  script:
    - kubectl config use-context acme/infra:review-agent   # GitLab agent context (section 12.4)
    # One release and one namespace per review app; the slug already starts with "review-"
    - >
      helm upgrade --install "$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG" ./chart
      --namespace "$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG" --create-namespace
      --set image.tag="$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
      --set ingress.host="$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG.review.example.com"
      --wait --timeout 5m
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: https://$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG.review.example.com
    on_stop: stop-review                   # next topic
    auto_stop_in: 3 days                   # topic after next
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"

stop-review:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine/k8s:1.31.2
  variables:
    GIT_STRATEGY: none                     # the branch may already be deleted
  script:
    - kubectl config use-context acme/infra:review-agent
    - helm uninstall "$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG" --namespace "$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG" --ignore-not-found
    - kubectl delete namespace "$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG" --ignore-not-found
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    action: stop
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
      when: manual                         # runs on demand or when GitLab stops the environment
```

**Design decisions for review apps.**

| Decision | Options | Advice |
|---|---|---|
| Isolation | Namespace per app, shared namespace with prefixed names, separate VM | A namespace per review app makes cleanup a single `delete namespace` |
| Routing | Wildcard DNS `*.review.example.com` plus an ingress controller | One wildcard DNS record and certificate, then hostnames are free |
| Data | Shared review database, a database per app, seeded fixtures | Seeded per-app data avoids reviewers stepping on each other |
| Secrets | Variables scoped to `review/*` | Never give review apps production credentials |
| Who triggers | Every MR, or only labeled MRs | Gate on a label for expensive apps: `if: $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_LABELS =~ /review-app/` |
| Hostname length | DNS labels are limited to 63 characters | Use `CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG` (24 characters), not the branch name |

**Review apps without Kubernetes.** The same pattern works for any target that can host many instances: a static site uploaded to `s3://bucket/$CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG/`, a Docker Compose project per slug on a shared VM, a preview deployment on a hosting platform with a `dotenv` URL, or GitLab Pages parallel deployments (section 12.4).

**Key takeaways**

- A review app is a dynamic environment plus a deploy job in MR pipelines plus a stop job. GitLab adds a **View app** link to the merge request.
- Name environments `review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` and build hostnames and namespaces from `CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG`.
- Isolate each review app (namespace, prefix, path) so it can be removed in one step, and scope only non-production secrets to `review/*`.
- Gate expensive review apps on a label or manual trigger.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Deploy a static site as a review app to a path or bucket prefix named after `CI_ENVIRONMENT_SLUG`. Open a merge request and use the **View app** button.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Make review apps opt-in: deploy only when the merge request has the `review-app` label. Add the label to an existing MR and confirm that a new pipeline creates the app.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your review apps share one staging database, and QA keeps reporting flaky results. How would you redesign the data layer?" *Hint:* per-app databases or schemas, seeded fixtures, and the cost and time of each approach.

#### environment:on_stop

**Why it matters.** Starting a review app is easy. Remembering to delete it is not. Every forgotten review app keeps pods, databases and load balancers running. `on_stop` links a deploy job to the job that undoes it, so GitLab can run the teardown for you at the right moment.

**What it is.** `environment:on_stop: <job name>` on the deploy job names a **stop job**. The stop job targets the same environment with `environment:action: stop`. GitLab runs the stop job when:

- Someone clicks **Stop** on the environment (in the environments list or the MR widget).
- The branch is deleted, for example when a merge request is merged with "Delete source branch".
- The environment reaches its `auto_stop_in` time (next topic).
- The stop environment API is called.

When the stop job succeeds, the environment moves to **stopped**.

```text
deploy-review  ──(environment: review/x, on_stop: stop-review)──► environment "review/x" available
                                                                         │
       branch deleted / Stop clicked / auto_stop_in / API ───────────────┤
                                                                         ▼
stop-review    ──(environment: review/x, action: stop)───────────────► environment "review/x" stopped
```

**Requirements that trip people up.**

| Requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| Stop job uses the **same environment name** | GitLab matches the two jobs by environment |
| Stop job has `action: stop` | Otherwise it is just another deployment |
| Stop job is in the **same pipeline**, in the same stage as the deploy job or a later one, with compatible `rules` | GitLab looks for the stop job in the pipeline of the last deployment. If `rules` excluded it, there is nothing to run |
| Stop job is `when: manual` | It must not run immediately after the deploy |
| `GIT_STRATEGY: none` (or `GIT_DEPTH` with a checkout of a still-existing ref) | When the branch has been deleted, cloning it would fail |
| Teardown does not need repository files | With `GIT_STRATEGY: none` there is no checkout; use an image that has the tools, or fetch scripts from elsewhere |

**Using `needs` with stop jobs.** If the stop job is in the same stage, it does not need `needs`. If you use `needs` elsewhere, make sure the stop job does not depend on jobs that might not exist in that pipeline; a stop job blocked by missing dependencies cannot run.

**Handling stop failures.** If the stop job fails, the environment stays **available** and the resources keep running. Make teardown idempotent (`--ignore-not-found`, `|| true` only for "already gone" cases) so retries succeed. An environment can also be force-stopped in the UI or API without running a job, which marks it stopped but leaves any resources behind.

```shell
# Stop an environment through the API (runs its on_stop job)
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/environments/88/stop"

# Force: mark it stopped without running the stop job (resources are NOT removed)
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  --data "force=true" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/environments/88/stop"
```

**Beyond review apps.** Any temporary environment benefits from `on_stop`: a load-test cluster, a per-branch database, a demo for a customer.

**Key takeaways**

- `on_stop` names the stop job. The stop job uses the same environment name, `action: stop` and usually `when: manual`.
- GitLab runs it on **Stop**, branch deletion, `auto_stop_in` expiry and the stop API.
- Keep the stop job in the same pipeline with compatible `rules`, and use `GIT_STRATEGY: none` because the branch may be gone.
- Make teardown idempotent. A failed stop job leaves the environment and its resources running.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add an `on_stop` job to a review app that deletes its files or namespace. Merge the MR with "Delete source branch" enabled and confirm that the stop job ran and the environment is stopped.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Break the setup on purpose: give the stop job different `rules` from the deploy job. Observe what happens when you click **Stop**, then fix it. Also make the teardown idempotent and run it twice.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why does the stop job usually set `GIT_STRATEGY: none`, and what does that imply for how the teardown script is written?" *Hint:* the state of the branch when the stop job runs, and where the teardown logic must live.

#### auto_stop_in

**Why it matters.** Merge requests get abandoned. Branches stay open for weeks while nobody looks at the review app. `on_stop` only helps if something triggers it. `auto_stop_in` provides that trigger based on time, so an idle review app expires on its own.

**What it is.** `environment:auto_stop_in` sets how long after the last deployment the environment should be stopped. GitLab periodically checks for expired environments and stops them, running the `on_stop` job if one is defined.

```yaml
deploy-review:
  script: ./deploy-review.sh
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    on_stop: stop-review
    auto_stop_in: 2 days            # natural language durations: "1 hour", "1 week", "30 minutes"
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
```

**How the timer behaves.**

| Event | Effect on the timer |
|---|---|
| A new deployment to the environment | The timer restarts from that deployment |
| A user clicks **Prevent auto stopping** (pin) on the environment | The environment is kept until unpinned or stopped manually |
| `auto_stop_in: never` | Disables automatic stopping for that environment |
| The timer expires | GitLab stops the environment and runs `on_stop` if configured |

The check runs as a background task, so an environment may be stopped somewhat after its exact expiry time.

**Choosing a duration.**

| Environment type | Typical `auto_stop_in` |
|---|---|
| Review app with significant cost (cluster resources, databases) | `1 day` to `3 days` |
| Cheap static review app | `1 week` |
| Load test or ephemeral demo | `2 hours` |
| Staging, production | Do not set it (they should never expire) |

**Restarting a stopped review app.** Re-run the deploy job of the latest pipeline, or push a new commit. The environment becomes available again and the timer starts over.

**Key takeaways**

- `auto_stop_in` stops an environment a set time after its last deployment, and runs its `on_stop` job.
- Each new deployment resets the timer. Pin an environment in the UI to keep it, or use `never`.
- Use short durations for costly review apps and never set it on long-lived environments.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Set `auto_stop_in: 30 minutes` on a review app and observe the "Auto stop in" time on the environment page. Wait for it to expire and check that the stop job ran.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Pin one review app with **Prevent auto stopping**, push a new commit to another, and compare the stop times of both. Then read the `auto_stop_at` field of each environment through the Environments API.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your cloud bill doubled because of review apps even though `on_stop` is configured everywhere. What would you check?" *Hint:* abandoned but undeleted branches, failed stop jobs, and resources created outside the namespace the stop job deletes.

#### Cleaning Up Stale Environments

**Why it matters.** Even with `on_stop` and `auto_stop_in`, environments accumulate. Projects that existed before you added auto-stop, stop jobs that failed, branches renamed by force pushes: after a year a project can have thousands of stopped and forgotten environments. They slow down the UI, confuse dashboards and, when a stop job failed, still hold real resources.

**What it is.** Cleanup has two levels: **stopping** environments (and their resources) and **deleting** stopped environment records. GitLab provides API endpoints for both.

| Goal | API | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Stop environments with no activity since a date | `POST /projects/:id/environments/stop_stale` with `before` | Runs their `on_stop` jobs. Protected environments are skipped |
| Delete stopped review apps older than a date | `DELETE /projects/:id/environments/review_apps` with `before`, `limit`, `dry_run` | Only affects environments in the `review/` folder. `dry_run` is `true` by default |
| Delete one environment | `DELETE /projects/:id/environments/:environment_id` | The environment must be stopped first |

**A scheduled cleanup pipeline.** Run it from a pipeline schedule (section 3.5) with a project access token that has the `api` scope, stored as a masked variable:

```yaml
cleanup-environments:
  image: alpine:3.20
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule" && $SCHEDULE_TYPE == "env-cleanup"
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl jq coreutils
  script:
    - API="$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID"
    - CUTOFF=$(date -u -d '14 days ago' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)   # GNU date from coreutils
    # 1. Stop environments that have not been updated for 14 days (runs their on_stop jobs)
    - >
      curl --fail --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $CLEANUP_TOKEN"
      "$API/environments/stop_stale?before=$CUTOFF"
    # 2. Preview which stopped review apps would be deleted
    - >
      curl --fail --silent --request DELETE --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $CLEANUP_TOKEN"
      "$API/environments/review_apps?before=$CUTOFF&dry_run=true"
      | jq -r '.scheduled_entries[].name'
    # 3. Delete them for real
    - >
      curl --fail --request DELETE --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $CLEANUP_TOKEN"
      "$API/environments/review_apps?before=$CUTOFF&dry_run=false&limit=100"
```

**Do not forget the resources outside GitLab.** Deleting an environment record removes nothing in your cloud. A complete cleanup also covers:

- Kubernetes namespaces with a `review-` prefix whose environment no longer exists. A periodic job can list namespaces with a label such as `app.gitlab.com/env` and delete orphans.
- Container images tagged per branch in the registry (section 7.4).
- DNS records, buckets, databases or certificates created per review app.
- `stop-review` jobs that failed. Search for failed jobs named `stop-review` and retry them after fixing the cause.

**Key takeaways**

- Stopping and deleting are different steps. Only stopped environments can be deleted.
- `stop_stale` stops inactive environments and runs their `on_stop` jobs. `DELETE environments/review_apps` bulk-deletes old stopped review apps, with `dry_run` on by default.
- Schedule a cleanup job with a scoped access token.
- Clean up the resources outside GitLab too: namespaces, images, DNS, databases.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Call `DELETE /projects/:id/environments/review_apps` with `dry_run=true` on a project with several review apps and read the response.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Build the scheduled cleanup job above, then add a step that deletes Kubernetes namespaces labeled as review apps whose environment is no longer available.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Design a lifecycle policy for review apps in a monorepo with 300 open merge requests and a fixed cloud budget." *Hint:* opt-in creation, short `auto_stop_in`, resource quotas per namespace, scheduled cleanup, and reporting on cost per environment.

<a id="123-deployment-strategies"></a>
### 12.3 Deployment Strategies

Every deployment is a bet that the new version works. Deployment strategies limit how much you lose when the bet goes wrong: they expose a new version to a small share of traffic first, keep the old version ready to take over, or separate shipping code from turning it on. This subchapter covers the common strategies, how to express them in GitLab pipelines, and how to roll back and guard against unsafe deployments.

| Strategy | Exposure of the new version | Rollback speed | Extra cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recreate (stop old, start new) | 100% at once, with downtime | Slow (redeploy) | None | Internal tools, batch jobs |
| Rolling / incremental | Grows in steps (10% → 100%) | Medium | Little | Most stateless services |
| Canary | Small share, then a decision | Fast (remove canary) | Small | Risky changes on high-traffic services |
| Blue-green | 0% then 100% by switching traffic | Instant (switch back) | Double capacity during switch | Releases that need instant rollback |
| Feature flags | Per feature, per user group | Instant (toggle) | Code complexity | Separating deploy from release |

#### Incremental Rollouts

**Why it matters.** Deploying a new version to all servers at once means every user meets a bug at the same moment. Rolling the version out in steps (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) means that if errors spike at 10%, 90% of users never notice, and you stop the rollout.

**What it is.** An incremental rollout replaces old instances with new ones in several steps, with a check between steps. In GitLab you model each step as a job: either **manual** (a person decides to continue) or **timed** (`when: delayed` continues automatically after a pause, unless someone cancels). The jobs all deploy to the same environment and share a `resource_group` (section 4.5) so two steps never run at once.
