└── templates/                       │                          │
    ├── deployment.yaml              └──── helm upgrade --install ────┘
    └── ingress.yaml                         + --set image.tag=$CI_COMMIT_SHA
```

**Deploying a chart from a pipeline.**

```yaml
.helm-deploy:
  image: alpine/k8s:1.31.2
  script:
    - kubectl config use-context "$KUBE_CONTEXT"          # agent context, environment-scoped variable
    - >
      helm upgrade --install shop ./chart
      --namespace "$K8S_NAMESPACE" --create-namespace
      --values "chart/values-$CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME.yaml"
      --set image.repository="$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE"
      --set image.tag="$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
      --atomic --wait --timeout 10m
      --history-max 10
  resource_group: $CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME

helm-lint:
  stage: test
  image: alpine/k8s:1.31.2
  script:
    - helm lint ./chart --values chart/values-production.yaml
    - helm template shop ./chart --values chart/values-production.yaml > rendered.yaml
    - kubeconform -strict -summary rendered.yaml            # validate against Kubernetes schemas

deploy-staging:
  extends: .helm-deploy
  stage: deploy
  environment: { name: staging, url: "https://staging.shop.example.com" }
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

deploy-production:
  extends: .helm-deploy
  stage: production
  environment: { name: production, url: "https://shop.example.com" }
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual
```

**Important flags.**

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `upgrade --install` | Install if the release does not exist, upgrade if it does. Idempotent |
| `--atomic` | Wait for readiness and roll back automatically if the upgrade fails (implies `--wait`). Renamed `--rollback-on-failure` in Helm 4 |
| `--wait --timeout` | Job fails if resources are not ready in time, so the deployment record is honest |
| `--history-max` | Limit stored release revisions (each is a Secret in the namespace) |
| `--values` / `--set` | Environment values file plus per-pipeline overrides such as the image tag |

**Publishing charts.** When several services or teams share a chart, publish it as a versioned package instead of copying it. GitLab's package registry supports Helm repositories, and the container registry accepts charts as OCI artifacts:

```yaml
publish-chart:
  stage: release
  image: alpine/k8s:1.31.2
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/
  script:
    - VERSION="${CI_COMMIT_TAG#v}"
    - helm package ./chart --version "$VERSION" --app-version "$VERSION"
    # Option A: GitLab Helm repository (package registry), channel "stable"
    - >
      curl --fail --request POST
      --user "gitlab-ci-token:$CI_JOB_TOKEN"
      --form "chart=@shop-$VERSION.tgz"
      "$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/packages/helm/api/stable/charts"
    # Option B: OCI artifact in the container registry
    - echo "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | helm registry login "$CI_REGISTRY" -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin
    - helm push "shop-$VERSION.tgz" "oci://$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE/charts"
```

Consumers add the repository with `helm repo add --username <user> --password <token> acme "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/<id>/packages/helm/stable"`, or install directly from `oci://registry.example.com/acme/shop/charts/shop --version 1.4.0`.

**Helm and GitOps.** Instead of running `helm upgrade` from CI, a Flux `HelmRelease` can install the chart from the GitLab registry and reconcile it continuously. The pipeline then only publishes the chart and updates the `HelmRelease` version in the fleet repository (previous topics).

**Key takeaways**

- Helm templates manifests into a chart, uses values files per environment and tracks release history.
- Deploy with `helm upgrade --install --atomic --wait --timeout`, setting the image tag to the commit SHA.
- Lint and render charts in CI (`helm lint`, `helm template`, schema validation) before deploying.
- Publish shared charts to the GitLab Helm repository or as OCI artifacts in the container registry.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a chart with `helm create`, add `values-staging.yaml` and `values-production.yaml`, and deploy the staging release from a pipeline through the GitLab agent.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Deploy a version whose readiness probe always fails with `--atomic`. Observe the automatic rollback in `helm history`, and check what GitLab records for the deployment.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your team has a chart copied into 40 service repositories, and each copy has drifted. How would you consolidate?" *Hint:* a versioned shared chart in the registry, per-service values, a migration plan, and how to roll out chart upgrades safely.

#### Infrastructure Plan Review in Merge Requests

**Why it matters.** Reviewing a `.tf` diff tells you what the author changed in the code. It does not tell you what will happen to real infrastructure. A one-line change to a resource's `name` can force a **replacement** that destroys and recreates a production database. The plan shows the actual effect, so it must be in front of the reviewer before the merge.

**What it is.** Three layers of plan visibility in a merge request:

| Layer | What the reviewer sees | How |
|---|---|---|
| Terraform report widget | "Reported Resource Changes: 2 to add, 1 to change, 1 to delete", with a link to the full job log | `artifacts:reports:terraform` with the JSON summary (previous topic) |
| Plan as an MR comment | The full human-readable plan in a collapsible block | A job that posts `tofu show` output with the Notes API |
| Policy checks | Pass or fail on organization rules (no public buckets, no deletions of protected resources) | IaC scanning (chapter 11), OPA/Conftest on `tofu show -json` |

**Posting the plan as a comment.** Update a single comment instead of adding a new one on every push. A hidden HTML marker identifies it:

```yaml
plan-comment:
  stage: build
  image: alpine:3.20
  needs: [plan]
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl jq
  script:
    - cd "$TF_ROOT"                           # plan.txt comes from the plan job's artifacts
    - MARKER="<!-- tofu-plan:$TF_STATE_NAME -->"
    # Build the comment body: marker, summary, full plan in a collapsible block
    - |
      {
        echo "$MARKER"
        echo "### OpenTofu plan for \`$TF_STATE_NAME\`"
        echo
        grep -E '^Plan:|^No changes' plan.txt || true
        echo
        echo '<details><summary>Full plan</summary>'
        echo
        echo '```diff'
        head -c 60000 plan.txt              # MR notes have a size limit
        echo '```'
        echo '</details>'
      } > body.md
    - API="$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/merge_requests/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID/notes"
    # Find our previous comment, if any
    - >
      NOTE_ID=$(curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $PLAN_BOT_TOKEN" "$API?per_page=100"
      | jq --arg m "$MARKER" '[.[] | select(.body | startswith($m))][0].id // empty')
    - |
      if [ -n "$NOTE_ID" ]; then
        curl --fail --silent --request PUT --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $PLAN_BOT_TOKEN" \
          --data-urlencode "body@body.md" "$API/$NOTE_ID" > /dev/null
      else
        curl --fail --silent --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $PLAN_BOT_TOKEN" \
          --data-urlencode "body@body.md" "$API" > /dev/null
      fi
```

`PLAN_BOT_TOKEN` is a project access token with the `api` scope and the Reporter role, stored as a masked variable. The job only reads `plan.txt` from the `plan` job's artifacts, so it needs no OpenTofu binary or cloud credentials, and the comment shows exactly the plan that the widget summarizes.

**Apply after merge versus apply before merge.**

| | Apply after merge (common) | Apply before merge |
|---|---|---|
| Flow | MR shows the plan; after merge, `main` plans again and a person runs the manual apply | The MR's own plan is applied from the MR, then the MR is merged |
| `main` reflects reality | Yes, once applied | Only if the merge follows a successful apply |
| Risk | The plan on `main` can differ from the MR plan if other MRs merged in between, so review it again before applying | Several open MRs can apply conflicting changes out of order |
| GitLab support | Native: protected environment on the apply job | Needs merge checks, locking and discipline |

For apply-after-merge, keep the window small: merged results pipelines or merge trains (section 3.1) make the MR plan run against the latest `main`, so it matches what `main` will plan.

**Approvals for infrastructure.** Combine plan visibility with ownership rules:

```text
# CODEOWNERS
/infra/production/   @acme/platform-team      # platform team must approve production changes
/infra/network/      @acme/network-team
```

With CODEOWNERS approval required on the protected branch and the apply job behind a protected environment (with deployment approvals for production), an infrastructure change needs a reviewed plan, an owner's approval and an authorized person to apply it.

**Key takeaways**

- Reviewers need the plan, not just the code diff: replacements and deletions are only visible in the plan.
- The `terraform` report gives a summary widget. Posting the full plan as one updated MR comment gives the details.
- Add policy checks (IaC scanning, OPA) on the plan for rules that should never depend on a reviewer noticing.
- With apply after merge, re-check the plan on `main` before applying, and use merged results pipelines to keep the MR plan current.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add the `terraform` report to your plan job and open a merge request that adds one resource and changes another. Read the widget and follow its link to the full plan.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Implement the plan comment job with a project access token. Push twice to the same merge request and confirm that the comment is updated, not duplicated. Then add a Conftest check that fails the pipeline if the plan deletes any resource of type `aws_db_instance`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A reviewer approved an MR whose plan showed one change, yet the apply on `main` destroyed a resource. How could that happen, and how do you prevent it?" *Hint:* other merges between plan and apply, stale plans, and what the apply job should show or check before running.

<a id="126-auto-devops"></a>
### 12.6 Auto DevOps

Auto DevOps is GitLab's ready-made pipeline: it detects the project's language, builds a container image, runs security scanners, creates review apps and deploys to Kubernetes, all without a `.gitlab-ci.yml`. This subchapter explains what it does, which stages it runs, how to customize it without giving up its defaults, how Auto Deploy works, and when it is the right choice.

#### Auto DevOps Overview

**Why it matters.** A team with a dozen small services may not want to write and maintain a dozen pipelines. Auto DevOps gives every project a complete, opinionated CI/CD pipeline from build to production, based on GitLab's best-practice templates. It is also a useful reference: reading its templates shows how GitLab itself recommends wiring builds, scans and deployments.

**What it is.** Auto DevOps is a large CI/CD template, `Auto-DevOps.gitlab-ci.yml`, that GitLab uses as the pipeline of a project when:

1. Auto DevOps is enabled for the project, its group or the instance, **and**
2. The project has **no** `.gitlab-ci.yml` (or a custom CI configuration path).

The template includes job templates for each stage (`Jobs/Build.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jobs/Deploy.gitlab-ci.yml`, the security scanner templates and others). Each job has `rules` that check variables and repository contents, so only the relevant jobs run.

```text
            ┌───────── always (if detected) ─────────┐  ┌─────── needs Kubernetes or AWS ───────┐
 push ──►   build ──► test ──► scanners ──────────────►  review app (branches) ──► DAST
                                (SAST, secrets,          staging / canary / production (default branch)
                                 dependencies,           incremental rollout, browser performance
                                 containers)
```

**Enabling it.**

| Level | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Project | Settings > CI/CD > Auto DevOps > **Default to Auto DevOps pipeline** | Also choose the deployment strategy here (Auto Deploy topic) |
| Group | Group > Settings > CI/CD > Auto DevOps | Applies to all projects in the group that do not override it |
| Instance | Admin > Settings > CI/CD | When enabled instance-wide, GitLab disables it in a project after the first failed Auto DevOps pipeline, so it does not keep failing |

**What it needs.**

| Feature | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Build | Runners that can build images: Docker-in-Docker with privileged mode, or a supported alternative |
| Build detection | A `Dockerfile`, or a language Cloud Native Buildpacks can detect (Node.js, Python, Go, Java, Ruby, PHP, .NET...) |
| Review apps and deploys to Kubernetes | A cluster connected with the GitLab agent, `KUBE_CONTEXT` set to the agent context, `KUBE_INGRESS_BASE_DOMAIN` set to a wildcard domain, and an ingress controller |
| Deploys to AWS | `AUTO_DEVOPS_PLATFORM_TARGET` set to `ECS`, `FARGATE` or `EC2`, plus AWS settings (Auto Deploy topic) |

```yaml
# Minimal project or group CI/CD variables for a Kubernetes target (set in Settings > CI/CD > Variables)
KUBE_CONTEXT: acme/infra:auto-devops-agent        # agent context, as in section 12.4
KUBE_INGRESS_BASE_DOMAIN: apps.example.com        # *.apps.example.com points at the ingress controller
```

Without a deploy target, Auto DevOps still builds, tests and scans, which is useful on its own.

**Key takeaways**

- Auto DevOps is a GitLab-maintained template pipeline that runs when enabled and the project has no `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
- It detects the build method (Dockerfile or Cloud Native Buildpacks) and enables jobs based on repository contents and variables.
- Deployment features need a Kubernetes cluster through the agent (`KUBE_CONTEXT`, `KUBE_INGRESS_BASE_DOMAIN`) or an AWS target.
- Enabled instance-wide, it disables itself in a project after the first failure.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Enable Auto DevOps on a small project with a `Dockerfile` and no `.gitlab-ci.yml`. List the jobs it created and find the image it pushed to the container registry.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Open the `Auto-DevOps.gitlab-ci.yml` template in the GitLab source, and trace which `rules` decide whether the `review` and `production` jobs are added. Note which variables control them.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why does GitLab ignore Auto DevOps as soon as a project adds a `.gitlab-ci.yml`, and what does that imply for teams that want to extend it?" *Hint:* precedence of explicit configuration, and including the template from your own file.

#### Auto DevOps Stages

**Why it matters.** Using Auto DevOps well means knowing what each stage does and what it expects, so you know which parts to keep, tune or replace. Some stages have been deprecated over the years as GitLab moved functionality elsewhere, and older tutorials still mention them.

**What it is.** The main stages and the jobs they create:

| Stage (feature) | Job(s) | What it does | Runs when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Auto Build | `build` | Builds an image with the `Dockerfile` or Cloud Native Buildpacks, pushes it to the container registry tagged with the commit SHA | Always |
| Auto Test | `test` | Runs tests detected by Herokuish buildpacks | Only with Herokuish-based builds; not supported with Cloud Native Buildpacks (the default). Most projects add their own test jobs |
| Auto Code Quality | `code_quality` | Code Climate based analysis | Deprecated since GitLab 17.3 (section 10.3); run your own linters with a Code Quality report instead |
| Auto SAST | `semgrep-sast` and others | Static analysis (section 11.1) | Matching source files exist |
| Auto Secret Detection | `secret_detection` | Credentials in code (section 11.1) | Always |
| Auto Dependency Scanning | dependency scanning jobs | Vulnerable dependencies | Supported lockfiles exist |
| Auto Container Scanning | `container_scanning` | Vulnerabilities in the built image | After build |
| Auto Review Apps | `review`, `stop_review` | Deploys every branch except the default to `review/<branch>` | Kubernetes configured |
| Auto DAST | `dast`, `dast_environment_deploy` | Dynamic scan against the review app or a dedicated DAST environment | Ultimate, review apps or DAST environment available |
| Auto Deploy | `staging`, `canary`, `production`, `production_manual`, `rollout <n>%` | Deploys the default branch (next topics) | Kubernetes or AWS configured |
| Auto Browser Performance | `browser_performance` | sitespeed.io against the deployed URL (chapter 10) | After deploy, Premium for the MR widget |

Each stage can be switched off with a `*_DISABLED` variable:

```yaml
# Project CI/CD variables (or variables: in a .gitlab-ci.yml that includes the template)
TEST_DISABLED: "true"                   # we run our own tests
CODE_QUALITY_DISABLED: "true"
BROWSER_PERFORMANCE_DISABLED: "true"
REVIEW_DISABLED: "true"                 # no review apps for this project
DAST_DISABLED: "true"
```

**Build details.** Auto Build prefers a `Dockerfile` when one exists. Otherwise it uses Cloud Native Buildpacks, with the builder image set by `AUTO_DEVOPS_BUILD_IMAGE_CNB_BUILDER`. Useful variables:

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `DOCKERFILE_PATH` | Use a Dockerfile in another location |
| `AUTO_DEVOPS_BUILD_IMAGE_EXTRA_ARGS` | Extra `docker build` arguments, such as `--build-arg` |
| `AUTO_DEVOPS_BUILD_IMAGE_FORWARDED_CI_VARIABLES` | CI variables to pass into the build as build args |
| `AUTO_DEVOPS_BUILD_IMAGE_CNB_BUILDER` | Buildpacks builder image |

**Key takeaways**

- Auto DevOps chains build, (optional) test, security scanners, review apps, DAST, deploy and performance testing.
- Every stage has `rules`. Most can be disabled with a `*_DISABLED` variable.
- Auto Build uses the `Dockerfile` if present, otherwise Cloud Native Buildpacks.
- Auto Test and Auto Code Quality are legacy. Plan to provide your own test and lint jobs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run Auto DevOps on a project without a `Dockerfile` and identify which buildpack was used from the `build` job log. Then add a `Dockerfile` and compare.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Disable the stages you do not need with `*_DISABLED` variables, and confirm in the next pipeline which jobs remain. Explain why the security jobs still appear.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Auto DevOps reports no test results for your Node.js service, yet the pipeline is green. Why, and what would you change?" *Hint:* which build method is in use and how Auto Test depends on it.

#### Customizing Auto DevOps

**Why it matters.** Few projects fit any default exactly. You may need a different test command, an extra job, a custom Helm chart or a secret passed to the app. Rewriting the whole pipeline throws away everything Auto DevOps does well. Customization lets you keep the template and change only what differs.

**What it is.** There are four levels of customization, from lightest to heaviest:

| Level | How | Keeps upstream updates |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Variables | Project or group CI/CD variables (`*_DISABLED`, `STAGING_ENABLED`, `HELM_UPGRADE_EXTRA_ARGS`...) | Yes |
| 2. Include and override | `.gitlab-ci.yml` that includes `Auto-DevOps.gitlab-ci.yml` and redefines or adds jobs | Mostly (overridden jobs are yours) |
| 3. Pick job templates | Include only `Jobs/Build.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jobs/Deploy.gitlab-ci.yml` and others you want | Yes, per template |
| 4. Custom chart or values | `chart/` directory in the repository, `AUTO_DEVOPS_CHART`, or `.gitlab/auto-deploy-values.yaml` | Deploy logic yes, chart is yours |

**Level 2: include and override.** Once you add a `.gitlab-ci.yml`, Auto DevOps no longer runs by itself, so include the template explicitly. Jobs with the same name are merged with your definition:

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
include:
  - template: Auto-DevOps.gitlab-ci.yml

variables:
  STAGING_ENABLED: "1"                    # staging, then manual production
  TEST_DISABLED: "true"                   # replaced by our own job below

unit-tests:                               # new job in the template's "test" stage
  stage: test
  image: node:22-alpine
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm test -- --reporter=junit --reporter-options output=junit.xml
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml

production_manual:                        # override part of a template job
  rules:                                  # simplified: copy the template's other conditions too
    - if: $CI_DEPLOY_FREEZE
      when: never                         # no production deploys during freezes
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual
```

Overriding `rules` replaces the template's rules for that job entirely, so copy any conditions you still need (look them up in the template).

**Level 3: pick individual templates.**

```yaml
include:
  - template: Jobs/Build.gitlab-ci.yml           # Auto Build only
  - template: Jobs/Deploy.gitlab-ci.yml          # review, staging, production jobs
  - template: Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml

# Every stage a template job uses must exist, even if that job's rules exclude it
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy
  - review
  - dast
  - staging
  - canary
  - production
  - incremental rollout 10%
  - incremental rollout 25%
  - incremental rollout 50%
  - incremental rollout 100%
  - performance
  - cleanup
```

**Application configuration and secrets.** Auto Deploy passes every CI/CD variable prefixed with `K8S_SECRET_` into a Kubernetes Secret that the application receives as environment variables, with the prefix removed. Scope them per environment:

```text
CI/CD variable                         scope         →  in the pod
K8S_SECRET_DATABASE_URL = postgres://… production    →  DATABASE_URL=postgres://…
K8S_SECRET_FEATURE_X     = "on"        review/*      →  FEATURE_X=on
```

**Level 4: deployment chart and values.** Auto Deploy uses the `auto-deploy-app` Helm chart. Adjust it with a values file, or replace it:

```yaml
# .gitlab/auto-deploy-values.yaml (picked up automatically, or set HELM_UPGRADE_VALUES_FILE)
replicaCount: 3
livenessProbe:
  path: /healthz
readinessProbe:
  path: /ready
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
  limits:   { memory: 512Mi }
```

Put a complete chart in a `chart/` directory to use your own chart instead, or point `AUTO_DEVOPS_CHART` and `AUTO_DEVOPS_CHART_REPOSITORY` at a published chart. `HELM_UPGRADE_EXTRA_ARGS` adds flags to the `helm upgrade` call.

**Key takeaways**

- Prefer variables, then include-and-override, then individual job templates, then a custom chart. Each step takes on more maintenance.
- A `.gitlab-ci.yml` turns off implicit Auto DevOps, so include `Auto-DevOps.gitlab-ci.yml` explicitly to extend it.
- Overriding a template job's `rules` replaces all of them.
- `K8S_SECRET_*` variables become environment variables in the deployed pods. `.gitlab/auto-deploy-values.yaml` or a `chart/` directory customize the deployment.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a `.gitlab-ci.yml` that includes `Auto-DevOps.gitlab-ci.yml`, disables Auto Test and adds your own test job with a JUnit report.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `K8S_SECRET_` variable scoped to `production`, deploy, and confirm with `kubectl exec ... env` through the agent that the pod received it without the prefix. Then add `.gitlab/auto-deploy-values.yaml` with custom probes and check the rendered Deployment.
> 3. **Interview question:** "You override the `production` job's `rules` to add a condition, and now production deploys run on feature branches. What happened?" *Hint:* how job merging treats arrays like `rules`.

#### Auto Deploy

**Why it matters.** Auto Deploy is the part of Auto DevOps that delivers the built image to environments. It packs many of this chapter's techniques (review apps, staging, canaries, incremental rollouts, stop jobs) into a few variables. Understanding it lets you use it confidently or copy its patterns into your own pipelines.

**What it is.** Auto Deploy jobs run the `auto-deploy-image` tool, which runs `helm upgrade` with the `auto-deploy-app` chart (or your chart) using the agent context in `KUBE_CONTEXT`. What it deploys depends on the branch and the chosen strategy:

```text
feature branch ──► review  (review/<branch>, auto-stops, stop_review on branch deletion)

default branch, strategy:
  "Continuous deployment to production"           ──► production
  "...using timed incremental rollout"            ──► timed rollout 10% ─► 25% ─► 50% ─► 100% (5 min apart)
  "Automatic deployment to staging, manual to production"
                                                  ──► staging ──► production_manual (or rollout n% manual)
  + CANARY_ENABLED                                ──► canary (manual) before production
```

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `STAGING_ENABLED` | Deploy the default branch to `staging` automatically, production becomes manual |
| `CANARY_ENABLED` | Add a manual `canary` job that deploys to the production environment with a canary track |
| `INCREMENTAL_ROLLOUT_MODE` | `manual` or `timed`: production in steps of 10/25/50/100% |
| `REVIEW_DISABLED`, `PRODUCTION_REPLICAS`, `REPLICAS` | Turn off review apps; replica counts per environment |
| `KUBE_NAMESPACE` | Override the default namespace (by default derived from project name, project ID and environment) |
| `ROLLOUT_RESOURCE_TYPE` | `deployment` (default) or `statefulset` |
| `AUTO_DEPLOY_IMAGE_VERSION` | Pin the deploy tool version |

**Databases and migrations.** For non-production convenience, Auto Deploy can provision a PostgreSQL database per environment with `POSTGRES_ENABLED: "true"`. For production, use a managed database and pass its URL in a `K8S_SECRET_DATABASE_URL` variable. Migrations run as part of the deployment when `DB_MIGRATE` is set to a command:

```yaml
variables:
  DB_MIGRATE: "bin/rails db:migrate"      # runs in the new image before the app is upgraded
  DB_INITIALIZE: "bin/rails db:setup"     # runs only on the first deployment of an environment
```

Migrations still need to be backward compatible with the running version (expand and contract, section 12.3), especially with canaries and incremental rollouts, where old and new versions run side by side.

**Deploying to AWS instead of Kubernetes.** `AUTO_DEVOPS_PLATFORM_TARGET` switches Auto Deploy to AWS:

| Target | Required settings (examples) | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `ECS` / `FARGATE` | `CI_AWS_ECS_CLUSTER`, `CI_AWS_ECS_SERVICE`, `CI_AWS_ECS_TASK_DEFINITION` | Registers a task definition with the new image and updates the service |
| `EC2` | `CI_AWS_CF_CREATE_STACK_FILE`, `CI_AWS_EC2_DEPLOYMENT_FILE`, S3 push settings | CloudFormation stack plus CodeDeploy |

These targets authenticate with AWS variables in the project. Check whether your GitLab version supports OIDC for them; otherwise keep the credentials protected, environment-scoped and narrowly permissioned.

**What you get in GitLab.** Auto Deploy jobs declare environments with URLs, `on_stop` and `auto_stop_in` for review apps, so everything from sections 12.1 and 12.2 works: environment history, rollbacks, protected environments and approvals on `production`, and deploy freezes through your own rule overrides.

**Key takeaways**

- Auto Deploy deploys branches to review apps and the default branch to production, optionally through staging, canary and incremental rollout steps.
- Choose the strategy in the Auto DevOps settings or with `STAGING_ENABLED`, `CANARY_ENABLED` and `INCREMENTAL_ROLLOUT_MODE`.
- `DB_MIGRATE` and `DB_INITIALIZE` run database commands during deployment. Use the bundled PostgreSQL only outside production.
- `AUTO_DEVOPS_PLATFORM_TARGET` deploys to ECS, Fargate or EC2 instead of Kubernetes.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* With a cluster connected through the agent, enable Auto DevOps on a sample app, open a merge request and use the review app. Merge it and watch the review app stop and production deploy.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Switch to "Automatic deployment to staging, manual deployment to production" with `INCREMENTAL_ROLLOUT_MODE: manual` and `CANARY_ENABLED`. Run the canary, then the rollout steps, and inspect the pods of each track in the environment's Kubernetes overview.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Auto Deploy runs `DB_MIGRATE` before upgrading the app. During a 10% rollout, what can go wrong with a migration that renames a column?" *Hint:* which application versions run against the migrated schema, and for how long.

#### When to Use Auto DevOps

**Why it matters.** Auto DevOps saves a lot of work in some situations and adds friction in others. Choosing it, or choosing to move away from it, is an architectural decision about how much control a team needs over its delivery process.

**Comparison.**

| Criterion | Auto DevOps | Custom pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| Time to first deployment | Minutes, if a cluster is ready | Hours to days |
| Fit for standard web services in containers | Good | Good |
| Unusual builds (monorepos, mobile apps, native binaries, multi-image) | Poor | Full control |
| Security scanning | Included and maintained by GitLab | You include templates or components yourself |
| Deployment target | Kubernetes (auto-deploy chart) or AWS ECS/EC2 | Anything |
| Understanding and debugging | Large template, many variables, behavior defined upstream | Your own, readable YAML |
| Upgrades | Template changes with GitLab versions, sometimes unexpectedly | Changes only when you change it |
| Consistency across many projects | Very high by default | Needs shared components or templates (chapter 9) |

**Good fits.**

- Many small, similar containerized services, where consistency matters more than per-project tuning.
- Prototypes, internal tools and teams new to CI/CD that want a working pipeline with security scanning from day one.
- Learning: reading the generated jobs is a practical guide to GitLab CI/CD patterns.

**Poor fits.**

- Projects with non-standard builds, monorepos with selective builds, or targets other than Kubernetes and AWS.
- Regulated environments that require every pipeline step to be explicitly reviewed and pinned.
- Teams that have already overridden most jobs: at that point the template adds indirection without value.

**A common path.** Many organizations use Auto DevOps to start, then move to **shared CI/CD components** maintained by a platform team (chapter 9): the same consistency, but with explicit inputs, versioning, and only the pieces each project needs. The Auto DevOps job templates (`Jobs/Build.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jobs/Deploy.gitlab-ci.yml`) are a reasonable intermediate step.

```text
Auto DevOps (implicit) ──► include Auto-DevOps + overrides ──► individual Jobs/* templates ──► own components
   zero config               small deviations                  pick what you need             full control, versioned
```

**Key takeaways**

- Auto DevOps fits fleets of standard containerized services and teams that want a full pipeline immediately.
- It fits poorly with unusual builds, non-Kubernetes targets, strict audit requirements and heavily customized projects.
- Migrate gradually: include and override, then individual job templates, then your own versioned CI/CD components.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* List three projects you know (or invent) and decide for each whether Auto DevOps fits, with one reason per project.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Take a project running Auto DevOps and replace it with an explicit `.gitlab-ci.yml` that uses `Jobs/Build.gitlab-ci.yml`, a scanner component and your own deploy job. Compare the job lists before and after to make sure nothing important was dropped.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your company has 150 microservices on Auto DevOps and a GitLab upgrade changed a template default that broke deployments. How do you prevent that in the future without losing consistency?" *Hint:* pinning (`AUTO_DEPLOY_IMAGE_VERSION`), versioned CI/CD components, and testing template changes on a canary group of projects.

## 13. Pipeline Optimization

A pipeline that works is only the beginning: if it takes forty minutes, developers stop waiting for it, batch their changes and merge on hope. If it burns through the compute quota by the middle of the month, it stops running at all. This chapter covers how to find where a pipeline spends its time, how to cut that time and its cost without weakening what the pipeline checks, and how to keep a monorepo pipeline fast when one repository holds many services.

> **Tiers at a glance.** Everything in this chapter works on **all tiers**: `GIT_DEPTH`, `GIT_STRATEGY`, `workflow:auto_cancel`, `rules:changes`, parent-child pipelines, `include:local` with wildcards and inputs, the Usage Quotas page and CI/CD analytics. Compute quotas apply to GitLab-hosted runners on GitLab.com, and their size depends on the tier (section 1.2). Setting compute quotas for instance runners on a self-managed instance requires **Premium**, as do merge trains and required code owner approval, which this chapter mentions in passing.

<a id="131-speed-and-efficiency"></a>
### 13.1 Speed and Efficiency

This subchapter is about making the developer's wait shorter: measuring where the time goes, cutting the cost of fetching code and images, and designing the pipeline so that a broken change fails in the first minute, not the last.

A job's duration is more than its script. Every job pays a fixed setup cost before the first command runs, and on ephemeral runners it pays that cost again every time:

```text
 job created
    │
    ▼
 ┌────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐
 │ queued │─►│ prepare executor │─►│ get sources │─►│ restore cache │─►│ download artifacts │─►│ step_script │─►│ save cache, upload │
 └────────┘  │ (image pull)     │  │ (git)       │  │               │  │                    │  │ after_script│  │ artifacts          │
             └──────────────────┘  └─────────────┘  └───────────────┘  └────────────────────┘  └─────────────┘  └────────────────────┘
  runner      13.1 images          13.1 GIT_*,      8.2 caching        8.1, 3.2 needs           the actual work   8.1, 8.2
  capacity                          13.3 sparse
```

#### Analyzing Pipeline Duration

**Why it matters.** "The pipeline is slow" is a feeling, not a diagnosis. A pipeline can be slow because jobs wait for a free runner, because each job spends two minutes pulling a 3 GB image, because stages force fast jobs to wait for slow ones, or because one test suite really takes twenty minutes. Each cause has a different fix, and fixing the wrong one wastes effort. Worse, speeding up a job that is not on the **critical path** saves compute minutes but not one second of the developer's wait.

**Three numbers, three meanings.** GitLab reports duration in several ways, and they answer different questions:

| Measure | What it counts | Where to see it | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pipeline duration | Time during which at least one job was running | Pipeline page header, Pipelines API `duration` | How long developers wait for feedback |
| Queued duration | Time jobs spent waiting for a runner | Pipeline header, job sidebar, API `queued_duration` | Whether runner capacity is the bottleneck |
| Total job time | Sum of all job durations | Sum of job `duration` values | What you pay in compute minutes and runner capacity |

Six jobs of five minutes each, all running in parallel, give a pipeline duration of five minutes but a total job time of thirty. Both numbers matter, but for different audiences: developers care about the first, whoever pays the runner bill cares about the third.

**The critical path.** The pipeline cannot finish before its longest chain of dependent jobs. That chain is the critical path, and only shortening it shortens the pipeline:

```text
             0   2   4   6   8   10  12 min
             |   |   |   |   |   |   |
lint         ████                          2 min
build        ██████                        3 min
unit               ████████                4 min  (needs: build)
e2e                ████████████████        8 min  (needs: build)   <- critical path: build + e2e = 11 min
docs         ██                            1 min

Pipeline duration: 11 min        Total job time: 2 + 3 + 4 + 8 + 1 = 18 min
```

Halving `unit` saves 2 compute minutes and zero minutes of waiting. Splitting `e2e` into two parallel halves of 4 minutes (section 4.5) cuts the pipeline to 7 minutes, because `build + unit` and `build + e2e` are now both 7 minutes long. The critical path has moved, and the next optimization must target whichever chain is now the longest.

**Where to look in the UI.**

| View | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Pipeline page header | Total duration and queued time of the pipeline |
| Pipeline graph, **Group jobs by: Job dependencies** with **Show dependencies** | The `needs` graph: follow the arrows to find the critical path (section 3.2) |
| Job page sidebar | The job's duration, queued time and runner |
| Job log | Collapsible sections (`prepare_executor`, `get_sources`, `restore_cache`, `download_artifacts`, `step_script`, `archive_cache`, `upload_artifacts_on_success`). Each section header shows how long it took |
| Job log with `FF_TIMESTAMPS: "true"` | A timestamp on every log line, useful for spotting slow commands inside `script` |
| **Analyze > CI/CD analytics** | Duration and success trends across many pipelines (section 14.2) |

```yaml
variables:
  FF_TIMESTAMPS: "true"        # runner feature flag: prefix every log line with a timestamp
```

**Measuring with the API.** For a precise picture, pull the job data and draw a timeline. The script below uses only the Python standard library:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# pipeline_timeline.py: print a text timeline of one pipeline's jobs
# Usage: GITLAB_TOKEN=glpat-... python3 pipeline_timeline.py <project_id> <pipeline_id>
import json
import os
import sys
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime

API = os.environ.get("GITLAB_API", "https://gitlab.com/api/v4")
project_id, pipeline_id = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
SCALE = 15  # seconds per character in the timeline

def get(path):
    req = urllib.request.Request(API + path, headers={"PRIVATE-TOKEN": os.environ["GITLAB_TOKEN"]})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
        return json.load(resp)

def ts(value):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00"))  # API returns ISO 8601 in UTC

pipeline = get(f"/projects/{project_id}/pipelines/{pipeline_id}")
# Trigger (bridge) jobs are listed by /bridges, not /jobs, so they are not shown here
jobs = get(f"/projects/{project_id}/pipelines/{pipeline_id}/jobs?per_page=100")
jobs = [j for j in jobs if j["started_at"] and j["finished_at"]]   # skip jobs that never ran
start = min(ts(j["started_at"]) for j in jobs)

print(f"{'job':<24}{'queued':>8}{'run':>8}  timeline (1 char = {SCALE} s)")
for job in sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j["started_at"]):
    offset = (ts(job["started_at"]) - start).total_seconds()
    bar = " " * int(offset // SCALE) + "#" * max(1, int(job["duration"] // SCALE))
    queued = job["queued_duration"] or 0                           # can be null for old jobs
    print(f"{job['name']:<24}{queued:>7.0f}s{job['duration']:>7.0f}s  {bar}")

print(f"\nPipeline duration: {pipeline['duration'] / 60:.1f} min, "
      f"queued: {(pipeline['queued_duration'] or 0) / 60:.1f} min, "
      f"total job time: {sum(j['duration'] for j in jobs) / 60:.1f} min")
```

```text
job                       queued     run  timeline (1 char = 15 s)
lint                          4s    118s  #######
build                         3s    181s  ############
unit                         52s    243s              ################
e2e                          49s    482s              ################################
docs                          5s     61s  ####

Pipeline duration: 11.2 min, queued: 1.1 min, total job time: 18.1 min
```

The 50 seconds of queueing on `unit` and `e2e` are a hint in themselves: when `build` finished, there was no free runner for the next jobs.

**From symptom to fix.** Once you know which phase is slow, the fix usually follows:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Where to look |
|---|---|---|
| High queued time | Too few runners or low `concurrent`/`limit` | Sections 6.3, 6.4, 13.2 |
| Long `prepare_executor` ("Pulling docker image") | Large image, cold pulls, distant registry | Optimizing Image Size and Pull Time (this subchapter) |
| Long `get_sources` | Deep clone, large repository, submodules, LFS | `GIT_DEPTH`, `GIT_STRATEGY`, section 13.3 |
| Long `restore_cache` / `archive_cache` | Oversized caches, slow cache storage | Section 8.2 |
| Long `download_artifacts` | Jobs download artifacts they do not use | `dependencies`, `needs:artifacts` (sections 8.1, 3.2) |
| Fast jobs wait for slow ones in earlier stages | Stage barriers | `needs` (section 3.2) |
| Long `step_script` | The work itself | Parallel jobs and test splitting (4.5), runner sizing (13.2), tool caches (8.2) |

**Key takeaways**

- Distinguish pipeline duration (developer wait), queued duration (runner capacity) and total job time (cost).
- Only the critical path determines pipeline duration. Find it with the dependency view, then shorten it. It moves after every improvement.
- Job log sections and `FF_TIMESTAMPS` show which phase of a job is slow. Each phase has its own fix.
- Measure before and after every change, ideally over several pipelines, because single runs vary.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open your slowest recent pipeline. Write down its duration, its queued time and the sum of its job durations. Which job ends last, and which jobs does it depend on?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Run `pipeline_timeline.py` on the same pipeline, then extend it to print the time each job spent in `get_sources` and `prepare_executor` by downloading the job trace (`GET /projects/:id/jobs/:job_id/trace`) and parsing the `section_start` and `section_end` markers.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your team spent a sprint making the unit tests 60% faster, but developers say the pipeline feels just as slow. What happened?" *Hint:* critical path, queueing, and what the developer actually waits for.

#### GIT_DEPTH and Shallow Clones

**Why it matters.** Before running anything, each job fetches the repository. A ten-year-old repository can have hundreds of thousands of commits, and downloading all of that history in every job costs time and network traffic, while most jobs only need the files of one commit. A **shallow clone** fetches only the most recent commits, which can turn a two-minute checkout into a few seconds.

**What it is.** `GIT_DEPTH` sets how many commits the runner fetches, counting back from the commit being built. It maps to `git fetch --depth`:

```text
Full history (GIT_DEPTH: 0)         Shallow (GIT_DEPTH: 3)

  A ─ B ─ C ─ ... ─ X ─ Y ─ Z           X ─ Y ─ Z
  └────── 120,000 commits ──┘           └── 3 ──┘   older history is simply absent
```

You can set the depth in two places:

| Where | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Settings > CI/CD > General pipelines > Git shallow clone** | Project default. New projects use **20**. `0` means a full clone. The maximum is 1000 |
| `GIT_DEPTH` variable (global or per job) | Overrides the project setting |

```yaml
variables:
  GIT_DEPTH: 10                  # most jobs: just the latest commits

semantic-release:
  variables:
    GIT_DEPTH: 0                 # this job reads the full history and all tags
  script:
    - npx semantic-release
```

**What breaks with shallow clones.** Shallow clones are fast because history is missing, and some tools need that history:

| Tool or command | Why it fails or misbehaves | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `git describe`, version tools (setuptools-scm, GitVersion, semantic-release) | The latest tag is older than the fetched commits | `GIT_DEPTH: 0` for that job |
| `git diff origin/main...HEAD` | The merge base is not in the fetched history, and `origin/main` may not exist at all (next paragraph) | Fetch the target branch with enough depth |
| SonarQube blame, `git log`-based changelogs | History or authorship is incomplete | Full or deeper clone for that job only |
| Retried jobs and long queues with very low depth | The branch moved more than `GIT_DEPTH` commits, and the job's commit is no longer reachable from the fetched tip | Keep the depth comfortably above the number of pushes that can happen while a job waits |

**Only the pipeline's ref is fetched.** The runner does not fetch every branch. It fetches the refspecs configured for the project, which by default cover just the ref the pipeline runs for. A job on `feature/login` therefore has no `origin/main`. When a job needs to compare against the target branch, fetch it explicitly:

```yaml
changed-files-check:
  variables:
    GIT_DEPTH: 50
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
  script:
    # Fetch the target branch with the same depth so that a merge base is likely to exist
    - git fetch --depth=50 origin "$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME"
    # Three dots: diff from the merge base, which is what the merge request changes
    - git diff --name-only "origin/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME...HEAD"
```

If the merge base is still outside both shallow histories, `git diff` fails with `no merge base`. Deepen the fetch (`git fetch --deepen=200`) or, for small repositories, use `git fetch --unshallow`.

**Related settings.** `GIT_FETCH_EXTRA_FLAGS` adds flags to the runner's `git fetch`. Its default is `--prune --quiet`, and setting it **replaces** that default, so repeat those flags if you want to keep them. Submodules have their own depth setting, `GIT_SUBMODULE_DEPTH` (see the next topic).

**Key takeaways**

- `GIT_DEPTH` controls how many commits each job fetches. New projects default to 20, and `0` means full history.
- Use a small global depth and raise it only for jobs that need history: versioning, changelogs, blame-based analysis.
- The runner fetches only the pipeline's ref. Fetch the target branch yourself before diffing against it.
- A depth that is too low makes queued or retried jobs fail when their commit falls outside the fetched history.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run the same job with `GIT_DEPTH: 0` and `GIT_DEPTH: 1` on a repository with long history. Compare the duration of the "Getting source from Git repository" section and the output of `git rev-list --count HEAD`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write an MR-only job that lists the files changed in the merge request using `git diff` against the target branch, with `GIT_DEPTH: 10`. Make it work on a branch whose merge base is 40 commits behind the tip of `main`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A release job using `git describe --tags` works on a developer's laptop but prints a commit hash instead of a version in CI. Why?" *Hint:* what a shallow clone contains, and whether the tag's commit is in it.

#### GIT_STRATEGY Options

**Why it matters.** Shallow clones reduce how much history is fetched. `GIT_STRATEGY` decides whether the runner fetches anything at all, and whether it can reuse a checkout left by an earlier job. A deploy job that only uses artifacts does not need the source code, and a persistent runner that already has a checkout should not throw it away and download everything again.

**What it is.** `GIT_STRATEGY` is a CI/CD variable with these values:

| Value | What the runner does | Speed | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `clone` | Removes the build directory and fetches the repository from scratch | Slowest, always clean | You suspect a corrupted or polluted working copy |
| `fetch` | Reuses an existing checkout if there is one: fetches new commits, then cleans with `git clean` | Fast on persistent runners | Default for most jobs |
| `none` | No Git operations. The build directory may contain leftovers from earlier jobs | Fastest | Jobs that need only artifacts, caches or external tools |
| `empty` | Like `none`, but empties the build directory first (recent runner versions) | Fastest, clean | Like `none` when leftovers could interfere |

The project default is set in **Settings > CI/CD > General pipelines > Git strategy** (new projects use `fetch`). The variable overrides it per pipeline or per job.

**`fetch` depends on the executor.** It only helps when the build directory survives between jobs:

| Executor | Does the checkout persist? | Effect of `fetch` |
|---|---|---|
| Shell, SSH, VirtualBox (persistent hosts) | Yes | Large saving: only new commits are downloaded |
| Docker | Yes, in a volume per runner, project and concurrency slot (unless the runner disables it) | Large saving on long-lived Docker hosts |
| Kubernetes, Docker Autoscaler, Instance with fresh VMs, GitLab-hosted runners | No: each job starts on an empty pod or VM | Behaves like `clone`. Reduce the cost with `GIT_DEPTH` instead |

After a `fetch`, the runner runs `git clean` with `GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS` (default `-ffdx`: remove untracked and ignored files, including nested repositories). Narrow the flags to keep useful leftovers, for example `-ffdx -e node_modules/` to keep installed dependencies on a persistent shell runner.

**Skipping Git entirely.** Jobs that only deploy or publish what an earlier job built do not need the repository:

```yaml
build:
  stage: build
  script: make dist
  artifacts:
    paths: [dist/]

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  variables:
    GIT_STRATEGY: none           # no clone: artifacts are still downloaded
  needs: [build]
  script:
    - ./dist/deploy --env production   # comes from the artifact, not from the repository
  environment: production
```

With `none` or `empty`, artifacts and caches are still restored, and predefined variables such as `CI_COMMIT_SHA` are still set. Only the working copy is missing, so any script that calls `git` or reads repository files fails.

**Related variables.**

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GIT_CHECKOUT: "false"` | Fetch, but do not check out files (useful when a job only runs `git` commands, or performs its own sparse checkout) |
| `GIT_SUBMODULE_STRATEGY` | `none` (default), `normal` (top-level submodules) or `recursive` |
| `GIT_SUBMODULE_DEPTH` | Shallow depth for submodules |
| `GIT_SUBMODULE_PATHS` | Only these submodules, for example `libs/a :(exclude)libs/b` |
| `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE: 1` | Do not download Git LFS file contents during checkout. Pull them later with `git lfs pull --include=...` only where needed |
| `GIT_CLONE_PATH` | Custom build directory (the runner must allow it with `custom_build_dir`) |

```yaml
lint:
  variables:
    GIT_SUBMODULE_STRATEGY: none       # linting the main repo does not need vendored submodules
    GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE: "1"           # nor the 2 GB of design assets stored in LFS
  script: make lint

integration-tests:
  variables:
    GIT_SUBMODULE_STRATEGY: recursive
    GIT_SUBMODULE_DEPTH: 1             # submodules at their pinned commit, without their history
  script: make integration-test
```

**Key takeaways**

- `fetch` reuses an existing checkout and is the right default, but only helps where build directories persist. On ephemeral runners it acts like `clone`.
- `none` and `empty` skip Git entirely. Use them for jobs that work only with artifacts.
- `GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS` controls what `fetch` removes. Narrow it carefully to keep dependency folders on persistent runners.
- Submodules and LFS can cost more than the main repository. Fetch them only in jobs that need them.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add `GIT_STRATEGY: none` to a job that only reads artifacts and compare its log with the default: which section disappears, and how much time is saved?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* On a self-managed Docker or shell runner, run the same job three times with `clone` and three times with `fetch`. Explain the difference in the "Getting source" section, then repeat on a GitLab-hosted runner and explain why the difference vanishes.
> 3. **Interview question:** "After switching a shell runner to `GIT_STRATEGY: fetch` with `GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS: none`, tests start passing locally but failing in CI at random. What could be happening?" *Hint:* files left by previous jobs, possibly from other branches.

#### Fail-Fast Pipeline Design

**Why it matters.** A pipeline's most valuable output is a failure, delivered as early as possible. If a missing semicolon is reported after 25 minutes of integration tests, the developer has already switched context, and the runners spent 25 minutes on a change that was never going to pass. Fail-fast design orders and connects jobs so that the cheapest checks most likely to fail run first, and so that a failure stops work that no longer matters.

**The principle.** Order checks by how much each one costs and how likely it is to fail:

```text
Seconds           Minutes                     Tens of minutes
┌────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ lint       │    │ unit tests          │     │ integration / e2e tests      │
│ format     │──► │ build               │ ──► │ performance, DAST            │
│ type check │    │ fast security scans │     │ deploy to review/staging     │
└────────────┘    └─────────────────────┘     └──────────────────────────────┘
 cheap, catch      moderate cost              expensive: run only when the
 most mistakes                                cheaper checks have passed
```

**Techniques.**

| Technique | How | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Cheap checks first | Lint and format jobs with `needs: []` | Results within a minute, in parallel with everything else |
| Gate expensive jobs | `needs: [lint, unit]` on e2e jobs | E2E never starts for a change that fails lint |
| Stop on first failure | `workflow:auto_cancel:on_job_failure: all` (section 4.4) | One failure cancels the rest of the pipeline |
| Fail fast inside a job | `pytest -x` or `--maxfail=N`, `jest --bail`, `go test -failfast` | The job stops at the first failing test |
| Tight timeouts | Short `timeout` on jobs that normally take 2 minutes (section 4.3) | A hung job fails in 10 minutes, not 60 |
| Previously failed tests first | `pytest --failed-first` with `.pytest_cache` cached | Re-running a broken MR shows the known failure immediately |
| Tests for changed code first | GitLab's Fail Fast testing template for RSpec (`Verify/FailFast.gitlab-ci.yml`, Premium), or tools such as `jest --changedSince` | Likely failures surface before the full suite |

```yaml
workflow:
  auto_cancel:
    on_job_failure: all            # any failure cancels the remaining jobs (section 4.4)

stages: [check, test, e2e]

lint:
  stage: check
  needs: []                        # starts immediately, does not wait for anything
  timeout: 5m                      # normally takes 40 seconds
  script: npm run lint

typecheck:
  stage: check
  needs: []
  timeout: 5m
  script: npx tsc --noEmit

unit:
  stage: test
  needs: []                        # independent of lint: runs in parallel
  script: npx jest --bail          # stop at the first failing test file
  cache:
    key: jest-$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    paths: [.jest-cache/]

e2e:
  stage: e2e
  needs: [lint, typecheck, unit]   # expensive: only after all cheap checks pass
  script: npx playwright test --max-failures=5   # stop after five failing tests
```

**Choose what "fail" should cancel.** `on_job_failure: all` is right for merge request pipelines, where any failure blocks the merge anyway. On the default branch, you may prefer to see every failure at once, because several people fix them in parallel. Use `workflow:rules:auto_cancel` to apply it only to MR pipelines:

```yaml
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
      auto_cancel:
        on_job_failure: all        # MRs: stop at the first failure
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      auto_cancel:
        on_job_failure: none       # main: run everything and report every failure
```

**Trade-offs.** Fail-fast can hide information: if lint fails and cancels the unit tests, the developer fixes lint, pushes, and only then discovers a failing test. When the cheap checks are very fast, running them in parallel with the unit tests (instead of gating the unit tests on them) gives fast feedback without hiding failures. Reserve gating for genuinely expensive jobs. Jobs with `allow_failure: true` do not count as failures and never trigger cancellation.

**Key takeaways**

- Order work from cheap and failure-prone to expensive and stable, and start cheap checks immediately with `needs: []`.
- Gate expensive jobs with `needs` on the cheap checks, so a broken change never reaches them.
- `on_job_failure: all` cancels the rest of the pipeline on the first failure. Scope it with `workflow:rules` if some branches need a full failure report.
- Test runners have their own fail-fast flags, and short timeouts stop hung jobs early.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Take a stage-based pipeline and add `needs: []` to lint and format jobs. Measure how many seconds after the push the first failure is now reported when you push a formatting error.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure `on_job_failure: all` for MR pipelines only. Push a commit that breaks lint and one that breaks a unit test, and record which jobs run, which are canceled and how many compute minutes each pipeline used.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A team gated all tests behind lint and complains that developers now need three pushes to find all problems. How would you redesign the pipeline?" *Hint:* which checks are cheap enough to run in parallel, and which are expensive enough to justify a gate.

#### Optimizing Image Size and Pull Time

**Why it matters.** The `prepare_executor` phase, where the runner pulls the job image and service images, often takes longer than the script itself. On ephemeral runners, such as GitLab-hosted runners, autoscaled VMs or fresh Kubernetes nodes, every pull is cold: a 2 GB image is downloaded and unpacked in every job. Ten jobs per pipeline, a hundred pipelines a day, and image pulls become a large share of both the wait and the bill.

**What determines pull time.**

```text
pull time  ≈  bytes not already on the host  /  bandwidth to the registry  +  unpack time
                     │                                  │
     smaller images, shared base layers,      registry close to the runners,
     pull_policy if-not-present               Dependency Proxy, no rate limiting
```

| Lever | How | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Smaller base | `-slim` or `-alpine` variants instead of full images | 7.1 |
| Fewer layers to download | One purpose-built image per job type instead of one huge toolbox | 7.1 |
| Shared base layers | Build all CI images `FROM` the same base: its layers are pulled once per host | This topic |
| Multi-stage builds | Download and compile tools in a builder stage, copy only the binaries | This topic |
| Clean in the same layer | `apt-get install ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in a single `RUN` | 7.1 |
| Reuse local copies | `pull_policy: if-not-present` on persistent runners for images pinned by tag or digest | 7.1 |
| Nearby, cached registry | Dependency Proxy for Docker Hub images, or the project's container registry | 7.4 |

**Find the fat.** Measure the image before optimizing it:

```bash
# Size of each local image
docker image ls --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}  {{.Size}}'

# Size of each layer and the instruction that created it, newest first
docker history --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' registry.example.com/platform/ci-tools:1.3

# Interactive explorer: wasted space per layer, files added and removed
dive registry.example.com/platform/ci-tools:1.3
```

In the job log, the "Preparing the docker executor" section shows how long the pull took and whether the image was already present ("Using locally found image" versus "Pulling docker image").

**Multi-stage CI images.** Tools are often downloaded with `curl`, unpacked with `tar` or compiled with a toolchain that the jobs themselves never use. A multi-stage build leaves all of that behind:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: download tools. curl and tar stay in this stage only.
FROM alpine:3.20 AS tools
ARG KUBECTL_VERSION=v1.31.1
ARG HELM_VERSION=v3.16.2
RUN apk add --no-cache curl tar \
 && curl -fsSLo /kubectl "https://dl.k8s.io/release/${KUBECTL_VERSION}/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl" \
 && chmod +x /kubectl \
 && curl -fsSL "https://get.helm.sh/helm-${HELM_VERSION}-linux-amd64.tar.gz" | tar -xz -C / linux-amd64/helm

# Stage 2: the image jobs pull. Only runtime needs and the two binaries.
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache bash git ca-certificates
COPY --from=tools /kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl
COPY --from=tools /linux-amd64/helm /usr/local/bin/helm
```

**Pull through the Dependency Proxy.** Pulling public images straight from Docker Hub is subject to its rate limits and to the speed of the internet link. The group's Dependency Proxy caches them inside GitLab. The runner authenticates to it automatically:

```yaml
default:
  # Pulled from the group's Dependency Proxy cache instead of Docker Hub
  image: ${CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_GROUP_IMAGE_PREFIX}/node:22-alpine
  services:
    - name: ${CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_GROUP_IMAGE_PREFIX}/postgres:16-alpine
      alias: db
```

**Kubernetes specifics.** On the Kubernetes executor, images are pulled by the node's container runtime, so the node's image cache matters. Set the runner's `pull_policy` to `if-not-present` for pinned images, keep CI nodes long-lived enough for their cache to pay off, and remember that a node scaled up for a burst of jobs starts with an empty cache. Pulls also count against `poll_timeout` (section 6.2).

**Key takeaways**

- Image pull time is part of every job's duration, and it is paid in full on ephemeral runners.
- Measure with `docker history` or `dive` and with the `prepare_executor` section before optimizing.
- Use slim bases, multi-stage builds, shared base layers and one image per job type to keep images small.
- Pull through the Dependency Proxy or a nearby registry, and reuse local copies with `if-not-present` where the runner persists.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use `docker history` on the largest image your pipeline uses and identify the three biggest layers. Which Dockerfile instructions created them?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Rewrite a CI image that downloads tools with `curl` into a multi-stage build. Compare the compressed size in the container registry and the pull time in the job log before and after, on a GitLab-hosted runner.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Pipelines on your Kubernetes runners are fast in the afternoon but slow every morning. Image pulls account for most of the difference. What is going on, and what would you do?" *Hint:* overnight scale-down, empty node image caches, and pre-pulling or keeping a minimum node pool.

<a id="132-cost-and-resource-management"></a>
### 13.2 Cost and Resource Management

Speed is one side of optimization and cost is the other. This subchapter covers how GitLab meters CI usage, how to choose machine sizes that are both fast and economical, how to give jobs the CPU and memory they need without wasting a cluster, and how to stop paying for pipelines whose results nobody uses.

#### Compute Minutes and Quotas

**Why it matters.** On GitLab.com, jobs on GitLab-hosted runners consume **compute minutes** from a monthly quota. When the quota runs out, those jobs stop running, and the whole team is blocked until the next month or until someone buys more. Understanding how minutes are counted is the basis for every cost decision in this subchapter.

**What it is.** Compute usage is metered per job:

```text
compute minutes  =  job duration (minutes)  x  cost factor of the runner
```

| Element | Details |
|---|---|
| Who consumes | Jobs on GitLab-hosted (instance) runners. Jobs on your own project or group runners consume nothing |
| Whose quota | The **top-level namespace** (top-level group or personal namespace). All projects under it share one quota |
| Monthly quota | Depends on the tier: 400 (Free), 10,000 (Premium), 50,000 (Ultimate) on GitLab.com at the time of writing (section 1.2) |
| Cost factor | Grows with machine size: 1 for small Linux, up to 12 for 2xlarge (section 6.1). Some programs, such as GitLab for Open Source, get reduced factors |
| Reset | The monthly quota resets on the first of each month. Unused minutes do not roll over |
| Additional minutes | Can be purchased. They are used only after the monthly quota is exhausted and are not reset monthly |

**A worked example.** A Premium group with 20 developers:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Pipelines per developer per working day | 12 |
| Working days per month | 22 |
| Jobs per pipeline | 6 on small (factor 1), averaging 4 minutes; 1 on large (factor 3), 6 minutes |
| Compute minutes per pipeline | 6 x 4 x 1 + 1 x 6 x 3 = 24 + 18 = **42** |
| Monthly usage | 20 x 12 x 22 x 42 = **221,760** |
| Included quota | 10,000 |

The included quota covers less than 5% of the usage. The options are to buy minutes, to add self-managed runners for the bulk of the work (section 6.4), or to cut the minutes per pipeline with the techniques in this chapter. Usually it is a mix of all three.

**What happens when the quota runs out.** GitLab notifies namespace owners by email and with in-app banners as the quota runs low. Once it is exhausted, new jobs that need instance runners fail with the reason `ci_quota_exceeded`, and running jobs may be stopped. Jobs on project and group runners are not affected, which is why many teams keep at least one self-managed runner as a fallback for critical pipelines.

**Monitoring usage.** **Settings > Usage Quotas > Pipelines** on the top-level group shows the current month's usage, a monthly history and a per-project breakdown. The same data is available through GraphQL, which is useful for chargeback reports or alerts:

```bash
# Monthly compute usage of a group and its projects
curl --silent --request POST "https://gitlab.com/api/graphql" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"query": "query { ciMinutesUsage(namespaceId: \"gid://gitlab/Group/1234\") { nodes { month minutes sharedRunnersDuration projects { nodes { name minutes } } } } }"}' \
  | jq '.data.ciMinutesUsage.nodes[] | {month, minutes, projects: [.projects.nodes[] | {name, minutes}]}'
```

`minutes` is the compute usage after the cost factor. `sharedRunnersDuration` is the raw runtime in seconds. A big gap between the two points at expensive machine types.

**Self-managed instances.** Self-managed GitLab has no included quota, because the runners are your own. Administrators can still set a compute quota for instance runners per namespace (**Admin > Settings > CI/CD > Continuous Integration and Deployment > Compute quota**, Premium), and set each instance runner's cost factor for public and private projects. This is the usual way to share one central runner fleet fairly between departments.

**Levers to reduce consumption.**

| Lever | Typical saving | Topic |
|---|---|---|
| Cancel redundant pipelines and avoid duplicates | 10% to 40% in active repositories | Reducing Redundant Pipeline Runs |
| Run only jobs affected by a change | Large in monorepos | 13.3 |
| Right-size machines | Can lower both time and cost | Runner Sizing and Machine Types |
| Shorter setup (images, clones, caches) | Seconds to minutes per job | 13.1, 8.2 |
| Move steady heavy load to own runners | Removes it from the quota entirely | 6.4 |

**Key takeaways**

- Compute minutes are job duration times the runner's cost factor, counted only on GitLab-hosted runners.
- The quota belongs to the top-level namespace and resets monthly. Purchased minutes are consumed after it runs out.
- Exhausted quotas make instance-runner jobs fail with `ci_quota_exceeded`. Own runners keep working.
- Track usage per project in Usage Quotas or through GraphQL, and act before the end of the month.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open **Usage Quotas > Pipelines** for your top-level group (or personal namespace). Identify the three projects with the highest usage this month and their most frequent pipeline sources.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a scheduled job that queries `ciMinutesUsage` and fails (or sends a message) when the current month's usage exceeds a pro-rated budget, for example 50% of the quota before the 10th of the month.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Halfway through the month, your group's compute quota is 90% used. What do you do today, this week and this quarter?" *Hint:* immediate fallback runners or purchased minutes, then the biggest consumers, then structural changes.

#### Runner Sizing and Machine Types

**Why it matters.** Machine size is the one cost decision that can make a pipeline both faster and cheaper. A bigger runner costs more per minute, but if the job uses the extra cores it finishes in proportionally fewer minutes. A wrong choice in either direction wastes money: a large runner for a single-threaded lint job, or a small runner for a parallel test suite that would finish four times faster on a bigger one.

**The break-even rule.** On GitLab-hosted runners, the cost of a job is `duration x cost factor`. Moving a job from size A to size B saves money only if it speeds up more than the cost factor grows:

```text
cheaper on B   ⇔   duration_B / duration_A   <   factor_A / factor_B

small (1) → medium (2):   must finish in less than 1/2 of the time
medium (2) → large (3):   must finish in less than 2/3 of the time
large (3) → xlarge (6):   must finish in less than 1/2 of the time
```

Whether a job speeds up depends on what limits it:

| Job type | Bound by | Benefits from more cores? |
|---|---|---|
| Lint, format, small scripts | Single thread, startup time | Rarely |
| Compilation (C/C++, Rust, Go, Java) | CPU, parallel | Yes, if the build tool runs in parallel |
| Test suites with parallel workers | CPU and memory | Yes, up to the number of workers |
| Docker image builds | CPU, network, disk | Partly |
| Deploys, API calls, waiting on external systems | Network or remote services | No |
| Large in-memory workloads (bundlers, JVM builds, ML) | Memory | Yes, through the extra memory rather than the cores |

**Measure, do not guess.** Run the same job on every size with a matrix:

```yaml
size-benchmark:
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - SIZE: [small, medium, large, xlarge]
  tags: ["saas-linux-${SIZE}-amd64"]          # matrix variable selects the machine
  image: node:22
  script:
    - echo "CPUs visible to the job: $(nproc)"
    - npm ci
    - npx jest --maxWorkers="$(nproc)"         # make the test runner use every core
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "web"         # only when started manually from the UI
```

A typical result for a CPU-heavy suite:

| Size | Cost factor | Duration | Compute minutes | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| small | 1 | 20 min | 20 | Slow |
| medium | 2 | 11 min | 22 | Faster, slightly more expensive |
| large | 3 | 6 min | 18 | **Fastest per minute spent: choose this** |
| xlarge | 6 | 5 min | 30 | Diminishing returns: the suite cannot use 16 cores |

**Make the tool use the machine.** A bigger runner helps only if the tool runs in parallel. Many tools need to be told:

| Tool | Parallelism setting |
|---|---|
| `make` | `make -j"$(nproc)"` |
| pytest (with pytest-xdist) | `pytest -n auto` |
| Jest | `--maxWorkers=N` |
| Gradle | `--parallel`, `org.gradle.workers.max` |
| Maven | `-T 1C` (one thread per core) |
| Cargo | Parallel by default. `-j N` to cap |

Inside containers, the number of CPUs a tool detects can be wrong. `nproc` and Node's `os.cpus()` report the CPUs the process may be scheduled on, not a CPU limit enforced by quota. On a Kubernetes node with 32 cores and a job limit of 2 CPUs, the tool may start 32 workers and spend its time throttled (next topic). Pass explicit worker counts in that case.

**Self-managed fleets.** The same reasoning applies to your own runners, with more choices:

| Option | When it fits |
|---|---|
| Separate runners per size, selected by tags (`ci-small`, `ci-large`) | Mixed workloads: lint on cheap machines, builds on big ones |
| Spot or preemptible instances | `interruptible` jobs that can tolerate being stopped. Not for deploys |
| arm64 instances | Often cheaper per core. Requires arm64-compatible images |
| Larger instances running several concurrent jobs | Shared caches and images on the host, fewer cold starts |

**Key takeaways**

- A bigger runner is cheaper per job when the job's speed-up exceeds the cost factor increase.
- Benchmark each heavy job on several sizes with `parallel:matrix` and tags, and choose by compute minutes and duration together.
- More cores help only if the tool runs in parallel. Configure worker counts explicitly, especially inside containers.
- Keep light jobs on small runners: most lint and deploy jobs gain nothing from size.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run your slowest test job on `small` and `large` GitLab-hosted runners. Calculate the compute minutes of each and decide which size it should use.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Use the `size-benchmark` matrix for your test suite. Plot duration and compute minutes per size, find the size with the lowest compute minutes, and explain where the speed-up stops.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Moving the build from `medium` to `xlarge` made it only 10% faster. What would you check before concluding the build cannot benefit from more cores?" *Hint:* the build tool's parallelism setting, detected CPU count, memory limits, and network-bound steps such as dependency downloads.

#### Job Resource Requests and Limits

**Why it matters.** On self-managed runners, many jobs share the same hosts. Without limits, one job's memory-hungry build can starve the neighbors or crash the node. With limits set too low, jobs are killed or throttled. With requests set too high, a cluster sized for 50 parallel jobs runs 10. Requests and limits decide how densely jobs are packed and how they behave under pressure.

**Requests versus limits.** Both concepts come from Kubernetes, and the Docker executor has equivalent settings:

| | Request | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | What the job is guaranteed, and what the scheduler reserves | The most the job may use |
| CPU | Determines how many jobs fit on a node | Usage above it is **throttled**: the job runs slower |
| Memory | Determines how many jobs fit on a node | Usage above it gets the process **killed** (OOMKilled, exit code 137) |
| Set too low | Overcommitted nodes, noisy neighbors | Throttled or killed jobs |
| Set too high | Wasted capacity, pods stuck in `Pending` | Little protection for neighbors |

```text
Node: 8 CPU, 32 GiB         requests: 2 CPU / 4 GiB per job
┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
│  job A   │  job B   │  job C   │  job D   │   4 jobs fit by CPU (8 / 2)
│ 2 CPU    │ 2 CPU    │ 2 CPU    │ 2 CPU    │   memory is only half used (16 of 32 GiB)
│ 4 GiB    │ 4 GiB    │ 4 GiB    │ 4 GiB    │   → requests do not match the node shape
└──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘
```

**Kubernetes executor.** The runner's `config.toml` sets defaults and the maximum that jobs may request (section 6.2). Jobs override them with variables:

```yaml
webpack-build:
  image: node:22
  variables:
    KUBERNETES_CPU_REQUEST: "2"                 # reserved: the scheduler places the pod where 2 CPUs are free
    KUBERNETES_CPU_LIMIT: "4"                   # may burst to 4 CPUs, throttled above
    KUBERNETES_MEMORY_REQUEST: "4Gi"
    KUBERNETES_MEMORY_LIMIT: "6Gi"              # above this the build container is OOM-killed
    KUBERNETES_EPHEMERAL_STORAGE_REQUEST: "10Gi"  # node_modules and build output need disk too
    NODE_OPTIONS: "--max-old-space-size=5120"   # keep Node's heap below the container limit
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npx webpack --mode production
```

| Variable family | Applies to | Capped by (config.toml) |
|---|---|---|
| `KUBERNETES_CPU_*`, `KUBERNETES_MEMORY_*` | Build container | `cpu_limit_overwrite_max_allowed`, `memory_request_overwrite_max_allowed`, ... |
| `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_CPU_*`, `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_MEMORY_*` | Service containers | `service_*_overwrite_max_allowed` |
| `KUBERNETES_HELPER_CPU_*`, `KUBERNETES_HELPER_MEMORY_*` | Helper container (Git, cache, artifacts) | `helper_*_overwrite_max_allowed` |
| `KUBERNETES_EPHEMERAL_STORAGE_*` | Local disk of the build container | `ephemeral_storage_*_overwrite_max_allowed` |

If a job asks for more than the maximum, or the maximum is not configured, the override is refused. Remember that the pod's total is the sum of the build, helper and service containers.

**Docker executor.** Limits live only in the runner's `config.toml`. Jobs cannot change them from `.gitlab-ci.yml`, so offer different sizes as different runners with different tags:

```toml
[[runners]]
  name = "docker-large"                  # registered with the tag "ci-large"
  executor = "docker"
  [runners.docker]
    image = "alpine:3.20"
    cpus = "4"                           # build container may use at most 4 CPUs
    memory = "8g"                        # hard limit: exceeding it kills the process (exit 137)
    memory_swap = "8g"                   # same as memory: no swap, so jobs fail instead of crawling
    shm_size = 536870912                 # 512 MiB /dev/shm for headless browsers (Docker default: 64 MiB)
    service_cpus = "1"                   # limits for each service container
    service_memory = "2g"
```

**Reading the symptoms.**

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `exit code 137`, `OOMKilled` in `kubectl describe pod` | Memory limit too low | Raise the limit, or cap the tool's memory (`-Xmx`, `--max-old-space-size`) |
| Job much slower on the cluster than on a laptop | CPU throttling: more threads than the CPU limit | Raise the limit or set worker counts to match it |
| Pod `Pending` until `poll_timeout` | No node has room for the requests | Lower requests, add larger nodes, or check autoscaling (section 6.4) |
| Pod evicted for disk pressure | Ephemeral storage not requested | Set `KUBERNETES_EPHEMERAL_STORAGE_REQUEST` |
| Chrome or Playwright crashes in Docker | `/dev/shm` too small | Raise `shm_size` or use `--disable-dev-shm-usage` |

Size requests from measurements, not guesses: `kubectl top pod` during a job, or container metrics in Prometheus (section 6.4), over several typical runs. A common starting point is a request near the job's typical usage and a memory limit 25% to 50% above its peak.

**Key takeaways**

- Requests decide placement and density. Limits decide what happens under pressure: CPU is throttled, memory is killed.
- On Kubernetes, jobs set resources with `KUBERNETES_*` variables up to the runner's `*_overwrite_max_allowed` values. Build, helper and service containers are sized separately.
- On Docker, limits are per runner in `config.toml`. Expose sizes as tagged runners.
- Keep tool settings (heap sizes, worker counts) consistent with container limits.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run a job that allocates more memory than its limit (for example `python -c "x = bytearray(3 * 1024**3)"` with a 2Gi limit) and find the evidence of the OOM kill in the job log and, on Kubernetes, in `kubectl describe pod`.
