> 2. *(Intermediate)* Measure the CPU and memory usage of your three heaviest jobs with `kubectl top pod` across five runs each. Propose requests and limits for each, and calculate how many of each job fit on your node type.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your CI cluster has plenty of free CPU according to the dashboards, but jobs sit in `Pending`. What could cause this?" *Hint:* requests versus actual usage, memory or ephemeral storage requests, node selectors and taints.

#### Reducing Redundant Pipeline Runs

**Why it matters.** The cheapest pipeline is the one that never runs. In active repositories, a large share of pipelines produce results nobody looks at: a branch pipeline and an MR pipeline for the same commit, five pipelines for five quick pushes where only the last one matters, a full test run for a typo in a README, or a nightly schedule that tests the same commit every night for a week. Removing these saves compute minutes and frees runners for the pipelines that matter.

**Sources of redundancy and their fixes.**

| Redundancy | Fix | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Branch and MR pipeline for the same push | `workflow:rules` that pick one pipeline type | 4.4 |
| Older pipelines still running after a new push | Auto-cancel plus `interruptible: true` | 4.3, 4.4 |
| Full pipeline for documentation-only changes | `rules:changes` on code jobs | 4.1 |
| Expensive jobs on draft merge requests | Make them manual for drafts | This topic |
| Pushes that need no CI at all | `[skip ci]` in the commit message or `git push -o ci.skip` | This topic |
| Release tag pipeline rebuilding what `main` already built | Promote the tested artifact or image instead of rebuilding | This topic |
| Schedules testing an unchanged commit | Skip early when nothing changed | This topic |

**A lean MR pipeline.** The configuration below combines the main techniques. It creates one pipeline per push, cancels outdated work, skips code jobs for documentation changes and makes the end-to-end tests manual while the MR is a draft:

```yaml
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"          # MR pipelines for MRs
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never                                               # no duplicate branch pipeline
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH                                     # branches without an MR
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
  auto_cancel:
    on_new_commit: interruptible                                # cancel outdated interruptible jobs

default:
  interruptible: true                                           # safe default; deploy jobs opt out

.code-changes: &code-changes
  - src/**/*
  - package.json
  - package-lock.json
  - .gitlab-ci.yml

unit:
  script: npm test
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
      changes: *code-changes                                    # docs-only MRs skip this job
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

e2e:
  script: npx playwright test
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event" && $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TITLE =~ /^(\[Draft\]|\(Draft\)|Draft:)/
      when: manual                                              # drafts: run on demand only
      allow_failure: true                                       # do not block the pipeline status
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
      changes: *code-changes
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

**Skipping CI on purpose.** For pushes that need no pipeline, such as a WIP backup or a bulk branch cleanup, there are two ways to skip CI:

```bash
git commit -m "Update team contacts [skip ci]"     # [ci skip] also works
git push -o ci.skip                                # push option: no commit message change needed
```

If the project requires a successful pipeline before merging, enable **Settings > Merge requests > Skipped pipelines are considered successful**, or skipped MRs cannot be merged.

**Build once, promote many times.** A common hidden duplicate: `main` builds and tests an image, then a release tag on the same commit builds it again. Instead, the tag pipeline can retag the image that `main` already produced:

```yaml
release-image:
  image:
    name: gcr.io/go-containerregistry/crane:debug      # debug variant includes a shell
    entrypoint: [""]                                   # clear the crane entrypoint (section 7.1)
  variables:
    GIT_STRATEGY: none                                  # nothing from the repository is needed
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
  script:
    - crane auth login "$CI_REGISTRY" -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" -p "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD"
    # The image built and tested on main for this exact commit gets the release tag: no rebuild
    - crane tag "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" "$CI_COMMIT_TAG"
```

This saves the build minutes, and it also guarantees that the released image is the one that was tested.

**Scheduled pipelines.** A nightly schedule that runs a two-hour suite against an unchanged commit wastes two hours. A first job can compare the commit with the one tested by the previous scheduled pipeline and stop early. Also review the schedule list regularly: schedules created for one-off experiments tend to stay active indefinitely.

**Key takeaways**

- One pipeline per push: use `workflow:rules` to avoid branch and MR duplicates, and auto-cancel with `interruptible` to stop outdated work.
- Use `rules:changes` so documentation and unrelated changes skip expensive jobs, and make heavy jobs manual on draft MRs.
- `[skip ci]` and `-o ci.skip` skip pipelines intentionally. Allow skipped pipelines to count as successful if merges require a pipeline.
- Build artifacts and images once and promote them, instead of rebuilding the same commit for tags or environments.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Count the pipelines created in your project in the last week by source (**Build > Pipelines**, filter by source or use the API). How many were canceled, skipped or duplicates of the same commit?
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Apply the lean MR pipeline configuration to a project. Push a documentation-only change, a draft MR and three quick consecutive commits, and compare the compute minutes used with the original configuration.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is `rules:changes` alone not enough to skip a pipeline for documentation-only changes on a brand-new branch?" *Hint:* what `changes` is compared against when no previous push exists, and `compare_to`.

<a id="133-monorepo-strategies"></a>
### 13.3 Monorepo Strategies

A monorepo keeps many services and libraries in one repository. That makes atomic cross-service changes easy, but a naive pipeline builds and tests everything on every commit. This subchapter covers how to run only what a change affects, how to give each service its own pipeline, how to share configuration without chaos, and how to fetch only the part of a huge repository that a job needs.

```text
monorepo/                                   change to services/api/handler.py
├── libs/common/      ◄── used by api, worker
├── services/api/     ◄── changed                 ─► run: api pipeline
├── services/web/                                 ─► skip: web
├── services/worker/                              ─► skip: worker (unless libs/common changed)
└── docs/                                         ─► skip: docs
```

#### Path-Based Job Triggering

**Why it matters.** In a monorepo with ten services, a change to one service's handler should not rebuild and retest the other nine. Path-based triggering adds jobs to the pipeline only when files they depend on changed. It is the simplest and most common monorepo optimization, and it often cuts pipeline cost by an order of magnitude.

**What it is.** `rules:changes` (section 4.1) matches when at least one changed file matches at least one pattern. In a monorepo, each service's jobs list the paths that affect that service: its own folder, the shared libraries it uses and the CI configuration that defines it.

```yaml
# Hidden job templates: one rule set per service, reused by all of that service's jobs
.api-rules:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
      changes:
        - services/api/**/*
        - libs/common/**/*                  # shared library: its consumers must be retested
        - ci/templates/python.yml           # the template that defines these jobs
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      changes:                              # main: only if this push changed the service
        - services/api/**/*
        - libs/common/**/*

.web-rules:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
      changes:
        - services/web/**/*
        - ci/templates/node.yml
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH     # main: always run, as a safety net

api-test:
  extends: .api-rules
  image: python:3.12-slim
  script:
    - cd services/api
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest

web-test:
  extends: .web-rules
  image: node:22-alpine
  script:
    - cd services/web
    - npm ci
    - npm test
```

**What "changed" means on each pipeline type.** The comparison base is the main source of surprises:

| Pipeline | Compared against | Consequence in a monorepo |
|---|---|---|
| Merge request | The MR's target branch | Exactly the files the MR changes. The ideal case |
| Push to an existing branch | The branch's previous tip | Only the latest push, not the whole branch: a job can be skipped although an earlier push in the same branch changed its files |
| New branch, tag, schedule, API, manual run | No base: `changes` is **always true** | Everything runs |
| With `compare_to: refs/heads/main` | `main` | Branch pipelines behave like MR pipelines |

**Two policies for the default branch.** `compare_to: refs/heads/main` is useless on `main` itself, because comparing `main` with `main` finds no changes. The example above shows the two sensible choices:

1. **Run everything on `main`** (as `.web-rules` does). Simple and safe: the default branch is fully tested after every merge, which catches anything the path rules missed. Costs more.
2. **Run only changed services on `main`** (as `.api-rules` does), using plain `changes`, which compares with the previous push. Cheaper, but a dependency missing from the path list is never caught by a full run. Pair it with a scheduled full pipeline, for example nightly.

**The dependency problem.** Path rules are only as correct as the dependencies they encode. If `services/worker` starts importing `libs/common` and nobody updates `.worker-rules`, a breaking change in the library passes CI and fails in production. Mitigations:

| Approach | How it keeps rules correct |
|---|---|
| Include shared paths generously | Over-triggering costs minutes. Under-triggering costs incidents |
| Full pipeline on the default branch or nightly | Catches missed dependencies within hours |
| Generate rules from the build graph | Tools such as Nx (`nx affected`), Turborepo (`turbo run test --filter=...[origin/main]`), Bazel or Pants know the real dependencies. Use them in a generated child pipeline (section 3.3) |
| Code owners on `ci/` and rule templates | Changes to trigger rules get reviewed by the platform team |

**Key takeaways**

- `rules:changes` with per-service path lists runs only the affected services' jobs. Put shared libraries and CI files in every dependent list.
- MR pipelines compare with the target branch, push pipelines with the previous push, and new branches, tags and schedules match everything.
- Decide deliberately what the default branch runs: everything, or changed services plus a regular full run.
- Hand-written path lists drift from real dependencies. Keep a safety net, or derive the lists from a build tool's dependency graph.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* In a repository with two folders, `frontend/` and `backend/`, create one test job per folder with `rules:changes`. Open MRs that change only one folder, both folders, and only `README.md`, and record which jobs run each time.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add a `libs/shared/` folder used by both services. Update the rules so that a library change runs both test jobs, and add a nightly schedule that runs every job regardless of changes.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your monorepo uses path-based rules, and a library change broke a service in production although CI was green. How did that happen, and how would you prevent it structurally?" *Hint:* the rules encode a dependency graph by hand. Where can the real graph come from?

#### Per-Service Child Pipelines

**Why it matters.** Path rules on individual jobs work until the root `.gitlab-ci.yml` holds 150 jobs for 15 services. Then every job name must be unique across the repository, every team edits the same file, all services share one stage list, and the pipeline graph is unreadable. Giving each service its own **child pipeline** (section 3.3) isolates its jobs, its stages and its status, while the parent decides which children to start.

**What it is.** The parent pipeline contains one trigger job per service. Each trigger job uses `rules:changes` to decide whether the service is affected, and starts a child pipeline from a configuration file:

```text
parent pipeline
├── api      (trigger, changes: services/api/**, libs/common/**)  ─►  child: build ─► test ─► package
├── web      (trigger, changes: services/web/**)                  ─►  not created
└── worker   (trigger, changes: services/worker/**, libs/common/**) ─► child: build ─► test ─► package
```

When the services are built the same way, one child template with **inputs** (section 9.3) serves them all. Inputs are interpolated when the child configuration is loaded, so they can be used anywhere in the file, including job names and `changes` paths:

```yaml
# ci/service-pipeline.yml: child pipeline template shared by all Python services
spec:
  inputs:
    service:
      description: Folder name under services/
    python_version:
      default: "3.12"
---
stages: [build, test, package]

default:
  image: python:$[[ inputs.python_version ]]-slim
  interruptible: true

build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - cd services/$[[ inputs.service ]]
    - pip wheel --wheel-dir dist .
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - services/$[[ inputs.service ]]/dist/   # block style: brackets in a [flow] list would break YAML

test:
  stage: test
  needs: [build]
  script:
    - cd services/$[[ inputs.service ]]
    - pip install dist/*.whl pytest
    - pytest

package:
  stage: package
  needs: [test]
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH           # images only from main
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]
  script:
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE/$[[ inputs.service ]]:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" services/$[[ inputs.service ]]
```

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml (parent)
stages: [services]

.service-trigger:
  stage: services
  trigger:
    strategy: depend                    # the parent's status reflects the child's (section 3.3)

api:
  extends: .service-trigger
  trigger:
    include:
      - local: ci/service-pipeline.yml
        inputs:
          service: api
  rules:
    - changes: [services/api/**/*, libs/common/**/*, ci/service-pipeline.yml]

worker:
  extends: .service-trigger
  trigger:
    include:
      - local: ci/service-pipeline.yml
        inputs:
          service: worker
          python_version: "3.11"        # this service has not migrated yet
  rules:
    - changes: [services/worker/**/*, libs/common/**/*, ci/service-pipeline.yml]

web:
  extends: .service-trigger
  trigger:
    include: services/web/.gitlab-ci.yml   # a service with its own, hand-written child pipeline
  rules:
    - changes: [services/web/**/*]
```

`extends` deep-merges the `trigger` hash, so each job ends up with both `strategy: depend` from the template and its own `include`. The examples assume `workflow:rules` already prevent duplicate pipelines (section 4.4), which is why the trigger rules can use bare `changes`.

**Comparing the approaches.**

| | Path rules in one pipeline | Per-service child pipelines | Dynamically generated children |
|---|---|---|---|
| Job naming | Must be unique across the repository | Unique per child only | Generated |
| Stages | One shared list | Each child has its own | Generated |
| Pipeline view | One large graph | One collapsible box per service | One collapsible box per service |
| Cross-service `needs` | Possible | Not between sibling children | Not between sibling children |
| Overhead | Lowest | One extra pipeline and trigger job per service | Plus a generator job |
| Best for | A few services | Many services with separate owners | Many services where the set of affected ones comes from a build tool (section 3.3) |

**Things to watch.**

- **Variables.** By default, a child receives the trigger job's YAML variables but not pipeline variables (for example from a manual run). Use `trigger:forward:pipeline_variables: true` if children need them.
- **Artifacts across services.** A child job can download artifacts from the parent with `needs:pipeline:job` (section 3.3), but not from a sibling child. Build shared outputs in the parent.
- **Depth limits.** Children can trigger their own children, but nesting is limited (section 3.3). One level of per-service children is usually enough.
- **Merge request status.** With `strategy: depend`, the MR shows a failure when any affected service fails, without anyone opening the child pipelines.

**Key takeaways**

- One trigger job per service, each with `rules:changes`, starts only the child pipelines that a change affects.
- A child template with `spec:inputs` lets many similar services share one definition. Inputs are interpolated anywhere in the file.
- Children isolate job names, stages and status. Use `strategy: depend` so failures reach the parent and the MR.
- Siblings cannot `needs` each other. Produce shared artifacts in the parent.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Convert a two-service repository from path rules on jobs to two trigger jobs, each starting a child pipeline from the service's own `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Verify that changing one service starts only one child.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Replace the per-service files with a single `ci/service-pipeline.yml` template using `spec:inputs`. Add an input that controls whether the `package` job runs, and use it to disable packaging for one service.
> 3. **Interview question:** "When would you choose dynamically generated child pipelines over static per-service trigger jobs in a monorepo?" *Hint:* number of services, how often services are added, and where the knowledge of what is affected actually lives.

#### Shared Configuration in Monorepos

**Why it matters.** In a monorepo, one CI configuration serves many teams. If every service copies the same twenty lines of setup, a fix to that setup means twenty edits and twenty chances to miss one. If everything sits in one shared file, every team blocks on every other team's review. A good structure keeps common behavior in one place and lets each team own its service's specifics.

**A layout that scales.**

```text
.
├── .gitlab-ci.yml                  # entry point: workflow, stages, includes only
├── .gitlab/CODEOWNERS
├── ci/
│   ├── defaults.yml                # default:, global variables, workflow:rules
│   ├── templates/
│   │   ├── python.yml              # .python-test, .python-build (hidden jobs)
│   │   └── node.yml                # .node-test, .node-build
│   └── service-pipeline.yml        # child template (previous topic)
└── services/
    ├── api/.gitlab-ci.yml          # owned by the api team: extends the templates
    ├── web/.gitlab-ci.yml
    └── worker/.gitlab-ci.yml
```

The root file only wires things together. `include:local` accepts wildcards, so adding a service does not require editing it:

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
include:
  - local: ci/defaults.yml
  - local: ci/templates/*.yml           # every template file
  - local: services/*/.gitlab-ci.yml    # every service contributes its own jobs

stages: [build, test, package, deploy]
```

```yaml
# ci/templates/python.yml
.python-test:
  image: python:3.12-slim
  variables:
    PIP_CACHE_DIR: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pip
  cache:
    key: pip-$SERVICE                   # one cache per service: no cross-service thrashing
    paths: [.cache/pip]
  script:
    - cd "services/$SERVICE"
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest --junitxml=report.xml
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: services/$SERVICE/report.xml
```

```yaml
# services/api/.gitlab-ci.yml (owned by the api team)
.api-rules:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
      changes: [services/api/**/*, libs/common/**/*, ci/templates/python.yml]
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

api-test:                               # prefixed with the service: names are global
  extends: [.python-test, .api-rules]
  variables:
    SERVICE: api
```

**Rules that keep it sane.** Everything included into one pipeline shares one namespace, so conventions matter:

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| Prefix job and hidden-job names with the service (`api-test`, `.api-rules`) | Two includes defining the same key are merged, and the later one silently wins (section 9.1) |
| Define `stages`, `workflow` and `default` only in root-level files | They are global. A service file that redefines them affects every service |
| Use variables or inputs for service differences, not copies | One template, many services |
| Give each service its own cache key | Shared keys make services overwrite each other's caches |
| Protect `ci/` with code owners | Template changes affect every team |

```text
# .gitlab/CODEOWNERS (the last matching pattern wins)
/ci/                              @platform-team
/services/api/                    @api-team
/services/api/.gitlab-ci.yml      @api-team @platform-team
```

With required code owner approval (Premium), the platform team must approve every template change, and both teams review changes to a service's CI file.

**Where shared configuration should live.**

| Location | Versioning | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `ci/` in the monorepo, included with `include:local` | Same commit as the code | Monorepo-specific conventions that change with the code |
| `include:local` with `inputs` | Same commit | Parameterized templates without copying |
| CI/CD components from a separate project (section 9.3) | Released versions | Organization-wide building blocks shared with other repositories |

Templates in the same repository change atomically with the code that uses them, which is one of the main advantages of a monorepo. Use components for what genuinely needs to be shared beyond it.

**Key takeaways**

- Keep the root `.gitlab-ci.yml` small: global settings plus wildcard includes of templates and per-service files.
- Templates hold common behavior, and service files extend them with variables or inputs. No copying.
- All included files share one namespace: prefix names, keep global keywords in root files, and use per-service cache keys.
- Protect shared CI files with code owners, and use versioned components only for configuration shared outside the monorepo.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Move the jobs of two services from the root `.gitlab-ci.yml` into `services/<name>/.gitlab-ci.yml` files and include them with a wildcard. Confirm in the pipeline editor's **Full configuration** tab that the merged result is unchanged.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a `.node-test` template used by two services, with per-service cache keys. Then define a job with the same name in both service files and observe what the merged configuration contains.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Ten teams share one monorepo pipeline. How do you let each team change its own CI configuration freely while preventing one team from breaking everyone else's pipeline?" *Hint:* file ownership, namespacing, global keywords, and where validation happens before merge.

#### Sparse and Partial Clones

**Why it matters.** Large monorepos can reach tens of gigabytes, with millions of files and years of history. Even a shallow clone downloads every file of the current commit, so a job that tests one small service still transfers and writes the entire tree, and fifty parallel jobs do it fifty times. Git can fetch less: **partial clones** skip file contents until they are needed, and **sparse checkouts** write only selected folders to disk.

**Three ways to fetch less.**

| Technique | Git option | What is skipped | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shallow clone | `--depth N` | Old history (commits, trees and blobs) | Tools that need history break (13.1) |
| Partial clone | `--filter=blob:none` | File contents (blobs) not needed for the checkout. Fetched on demand later | Later operations that need old blobs contact the server |
| Sparse checkout | `git sparse-checkout set <dirs>` | Files outside the chosen folders in the working tree | Jobs cannot see files outside those folders |

```text
                       history          file contents         working tree
full clone             all commits      all blobs             all files
shallow (depth 1)      1 commit         blobs of 1 commit     all files
partial (blob:none)    all commits      only checked-out      all files
partial + sparse       all commits      only sparse folders   only sparse folders   ◄ smallest for monorepos
```

The combination of partial clone and sparse checkout fits monorepo jobs best: the job gets full history (so `git log` and `git diff` work) but downloads only the contents of the folders it uses.

**Doing it in a job.** The runner's standard Git step does not set up sparse checkouts, so the usual approach is to skip it with `GIT_STRATEGY: none` and clone manually. `CI_REPOSITORY_URL` already contains the job token, so no extra credentials are needed:

```yaml
api-test:
  image: python:3.12                      # full image: includes git (slim does not)
  variables:
    GIT_STRATEGY: none                    # skip the runner's full checkout
  script:
    # Partial clone: commits and trees, but no file contents yet; no checkout yet either
    - git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout "$CI_REPOSITORY_URL" repo
    - cd repo
    # Cone mode: these folders plus all files at the repository root
    - git sparse-checkout set --cone services/api libs/common
    # MR and merged results commits may not be on a branch, so fetch the exact commit
    - git fetch --filter=blob:none origin "$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
    - git checkout --detach "$CI_COMMIT_SHA"     # downloads blobs for the sparse folders only
    - cd services/api
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest
```

Make sure the shared paths in `sparse-checkout set` match the paths in the job's `rules:changes`. They describe the same dependency, and when they drift apart, a job either misses files it needs or runs for changes it cannot see.

**Native clone on recent runners.** Recent GitLab Runner versions can run a real `git clone` instead of `git init` plus `git fetch` when the `FF_USE_GIT_NATIVE_CLONE` feature flag is enabled with `GIT_STRATEGY: clone`, and then pass extra flags with `GIT_CLONE_EXTRA_FLAGS` (for example `--filter=blob:none`). This gives a partial clone without a manual script, but no sparse checkout. Check your runner version's documentation before relying on it.

**Interaction with other features.**

| Feature | Effect of sparse or partial clones |
|---|---|
| `rules:changes` | None: GitLab evaluates changes on the server, before any clone |
| Artifacts and caches | Paths are relative to the project directory. With a manual clone into `repo/`, artifact paths must include `repo/` |
| Generators that run `git diff` | Work with partial clones, because commits and trees are present. Only file contents are fetched lazily |
| Git LFS | Combine with `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1` and `git lfs pull --include="services/api/**"` |
| Persistent runners with `fetch` | A manual clone into a fresh folder discards the reuse benefit. Weigh the two on persistent hosts |

**Server side.** Every clone also costs the GitLab server (Gitaly) CPU to compute and compress the data. Many parallel full clones of a large monorepo can slow Git operations for everyone. Partial and shallow clones reduce that load too, and administrators of self-managed instances can enable Gitaly's pack-objects cache, which lets identical concurrent clones share one computation.

**Key takeaways**

- Shallow clones cut history, partial clones (`--filter=blob:none`) cut file contents, and sparse checkouts cut the working tree.
- Partial plus sparse is the best fit for monorepo jobs: full history, but only the folders the job needs.
- Use `GIT_STRATEGY: none` and a manual clone from `CI_REPOSITORY_URL`, and fetch `CI_COMMIT_SHA` explicitly.
- Keep sparse paths aligned with `rules:changes` paths, and adjust artifact paths to the manual clone folder.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* On a large public repository, compare `git clone`, `git clone --depth 1` and `git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse` followed by `git sparse-checkout set <one folder>`. Record time, transferred size (from Git's output) and `du -sh` of the result.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Convert one monorepo test job to a partial, sparse clone using the pattern above. Make it publish a JUnit report as an artifact, and compare its `get_sources` plus clone time with the original job.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Fifty parallel jobs clone the same 8 GB monorepo, and developers report that `git push` becomes slow during pipeline peaks. What is happening, and what would you change on the CI side and on the server side?" *Hint:* Gitaly load from pack generation, partial and sparse clones, fewer jobs that need sources, and the pack-objects cache.

---

<a id="14-monitoring-debugging-and-troubleshooting"></a>
## 14. Monitoring, Debugging and Troubleshooting

Every pipeline eventually fails in a way its author did not foresee. How quickly you recover depends on how well you can see inside it. This chapter covers three levels of visibility. The first is a single failing job: reading its log, tracing it, opening a terminal into it and reproducing it locally. The second is the pipeline's behavior over weeks and months: success rates, durations, DORA metrics and value streams. The third is getting the right signal to the right people at the right moment, through notifications, webhooks and commit statuses.

> **Tiers at a glance.** Job logs, `CI_DEBUG_TRACE`, collapsible sections, interactive web terminals (on your own runners), CI Lint, project-level CI/CD analytics, badges, pipeline emails, Slack and Microsoft Teams integrations, project webhooks and the Commit Status API work on **all tiers**. Group webhooks, group-level value stream analytics with custom value streams, and CI/CD for external repositories (which reports status back to GitHub) require **Premium**. DORA metrics, the Value Streams Dashboard and external status checks require **Ultimate**. Root Cause Analysis requires a **GitLab Duo add-on**. Its packaging has changed several times, so check the current documentation before planning around it.

<a id="141-debugging-pipelines"></a>
### 14.1 Debugging Pipelines

This subchapter is a toolkit for answering one question as quickly as possible: *why did this job fail?* The tools are ordered from cheapest to most invasive. Read the log first, then add tracing, then structure the output, then open a shell inside the job, then reproduce it on your machine. The subchapter ends with a catalog of configuration errors that stop a pipeline before any job runs.

```text
            cheap, always available                                   expensive, invasive
  ┌────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
  │ read the   │─►│ CI_DEBUG_TRACE│─►│ log sections │─►│ web terminal │─►│ run locally  │
  │ job log    │  │ / set -x      │  │ + context    │  │ into the job │  │ (same image) │
  └────────────┘  └───────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘
   failure_reason    every command     find the slow     inspect files,    iterate in
   exit code         and variable      or broken step    env, network      seconds
```

#### Reading Job Logs

**Why it matters.** The job log is the only first-hand record of what happened inside a job. Most failures can be diagnosed from it alone, provided you know where to look. Section 1.3 introduced the structure of a log. This topic is about reading a log *systematically* when it is long, noisy or misleading.

**Start with the failure reason, not the log.** Before scrolling, check *how* the job failed. GitLab classifies every failure, and the class tells you which half of the problem to investigate: your code, or the infrastructure around it. The reason appears in the job header (for example "There has been a timeout failure or the job got stuck") and as `failure_reason` in the Jobs API:

| `failure_reason` | What happened | Where to look |
|---|---|---|
| `script_failure` | A command in `before_script` or `script` exited non-zero | The `step_script` section: your code, tests or scripts |
| `runner_system_failure` | The runner could not prepare or run the job (image pull, disk, Docker daemon, network) | The `prepare_executor` and `get_sources` sections, and the runner host |
| `stuck_or_timeout_failure` | No runner picked the job up in time, or the job exceeded its timeout | Runner tags and availability, `timeout` (sections 4.3, 6.3) |
| `job_execution_timeout` | The job ran longer than its `timeout` | Slow step or hanging process: look at the last lines before the cut |
| `missing_dependency_failure` | Artifacts the job depends on expired or were deleted | `needs`/`dependencies`, `artifacts:expire_in` (section 8.1) |
| `unmet_prerequisites` | Something required before the job could start was missing, such as a Kubernetes environment the job deploys to | Environment and agent configuration (section 12.4) |
| `scheduler_failure` | GitLab could not assign the job to a runner | Instance health, runner registration |
| `api_failure` | The runner and GitLab lost contact while the job ran | Network between runner and GitLab, GitLab availability |

```bash
# List the failed jobs of pipeline 98765, with their failure reason and the stage they belong to
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/pipelines/98765/jobs?scope[]=failed" |
  jq -r '.[] | "\(.stage)\t\(.name)\t\(.failure_reason)\t\(.web_url)"'
```

**Read the exit code.** The last line of a failed script job is `ERROR: Job failed: exit code N`. The number is the exit status of the command that failed, and some values have a fixed meaning:

| Exit code | Usual meaning | Typical cause in CI |
|---|---|---|
| `1` | Generic failure | Failing tests, linter findings, a script's `exit 1` |
| `2` | Misuse of a shell builtin, or a tool's "usage error" | Wrong flags, syntax error in a shell script |
| `126` | Command found but not executable | Missing `chmod +x` on a script committed from Windows |
| `127` | Command not found | Tool not installed in the image, typo, wrong `PATH` |
| `130` | Interrupted (SIGINT) | Rare in CI: an interactive tool waiting for input |
| `137` | Killed (SIGKILL, 128 + 9) | Out of memory (OOM killer or Kubernetes `OOMKilled`), or a forced kill |
| `139` | Segmentation fault (128 + 11) | Native crash, often an image or architecture mismatch |
| `143` | Terminated (SIGTERM, 128 + 15) | Job canceled or timed out while the process was running |

**How the runner decides that a job failed.** With Bash-family shells, the runner executes `before_script` and `script` as one script with `set -eo pipefail`. Two consequences follow:

- The **first** command that exits non-zero stops the job. Lines below it never run, so the error is almost always just above the `ERROR: Job failed` line.
- A failure **anywhere in a pipe** fails the line. `pytest | tee report.txt` fails when `pytest` fails, even though `tee` succeeded.

The reverse is also true: a command that fails *without* a non-zero exit code cannot fail the job. Common examples are a script that ends with `echo "done"` after an ignored error, `|| true` added to "fix" a flaky step, and tools that print errors but always exit 0. `after_script` runs in a separate shell, and by default its failures do not change the job status at all.

**Reading a long log.** For logs of thousands of lines, a few techniques save most of the time:

```text
Job log (simplified, 4,812 lines)

 1  Running with gitlab-runner 19.4.0 (abcdef12)
 2    on k8s-runner-03 Qx81aB2c, system ID: r_9f8e7d6c5b4a
 ...
41  $ npm ci                                                <- step_script begins
 ...
4790  FAIL src/cart/total.test.ts
4791    ● total › applies the discount once
4792      Expected: 90
4793      Received: 81                                      <- first real error, read upward from the end
4805  npm ERR! Lifecycle script `test` failed with error
4806  npm ERR! code 1                                        <- noise caused by the error above
4811  Cleaning up project directory and file based variables
4812  ERROR: Job failed: exit code 1
```

1. **Read from the bottom up.** Find the last `$ command` line, then the *first* error message below it. Later messages are usually consequences ("npm ERR! code 1") rather than causes.
2. **Use the log search.** The job log page has a search box that highlights matches, and every line number is a link (`#L4793`) you can paste into an issue or chat.
3. **Open the raw log.** Very long logs are truncated in the browser. The **Show complete raw** link (`/-/jobs/<id>/raw`) returns the full plain-text log, which you can pipe through `grep`.
4. **Compare with the last green run.** Open the same job in the most recent successful pipeline and compare the image digest, tool versions and the last few commands. "What changed?" is often faster than "what is wrong?".
5. **Enable timestamps** with `FF_TIMESTAMPS: "true"` (section 13.1) when you suspect a hang or a slow step.

```bash
# Fetch the full log of job 554433 and show every line that looks like an error, with its line number
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/jobs/554433/trace" |
  grep -n -i -E "error|fail|fatal|exception|denied|not found" | head -40

# Same thing with the glab CLI, which also streams the log of a running job
glab ci trace 554433
```

**Messages that are not your code.** Some log lines point straight at infrastructure or at a limit:

| Log message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `This job is stuck because you don't have any active runners online or available with any of these tags assigned to them: gpu` | No online runner matches the job's tags (section 6.3) |
| `ERROR: Job failed: execution took longer than 1h0m0s seconds` | Job timeout reached |
| `Job's log exceeded limit of 4194304 bytes.` | The runner's `output_limit` (default 4096 KB) was reached. The job keeps running, but further output is lost |
| `ERROR: Job failed (system failure): ... no space left on device` | Runner host or volume is full |
| `ERROR: Preparation failed: ... pull access denied` / `manifest unknown` | Image name or tag is wrong, or registry credentials are missing (section 7.1) |
| `WARNING: Uploading artifacts ... 413 Request Entity Too Large` | Artifact exceeds the maximum artifact size |
| `[MASKED]` where you expected a value | A masked variable's value was redacted in the log, which is expected (section 5.2) |

**Key takeaways**

- Check `failure_reason` first. It tells you whether to debug your code (`script_failure`) or the infrastructure (`runner_system_failure`, `stuck_or_timeout_failure`).
- The exit code carries meaning: `127` is a missing command, `137` usually means out of memory, `143` a cancellation or timeout.
- Scripts run with `set -eo pipefail`. The first failing command ends the job, and the real error sits just above the final `ERROR` line.
- Commands that swallow errors (`|| true`, tools that always exit 0) produce green jobs that hide real failures.
- For long logs, use the raw log, `grep -n` and a comparison with the last successful run.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Write a job whose script runs `false | tee out.txt` followed by `echo "still here"`. Predict the result, run it, and explain what you see using `pipefail`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a script that lists every failed job across the last 50 pipelines of your default branch and counts them by `failure_reason`. Use the result to decide whether your instability comes mostly from code or from infrastructure.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A job fails with exit code 137 roughly once in ten runs, always in the same test step. What do you suspect, and how do you confirm it?" *Hint:* 128 + 9, memory limits of the executor, parallel test workers, and the runner's or the Kubernetes pod's events.

#### CI_DEBUG_TRACE

**Why it exists.** Sometimes the log does not contain enough information. A variable may have an unexpected value, a `rules`-dependent variable may not be set, a script may branch the wrong way, or the failure may happen inside the runner's own preparation steps, which are normally hidden. Debug tracing makes the runner print *every* command it executes and *every* variable it sets, including the runner's internal setup script.

**What it does.** Setting the predefined variable `CI_DEBUG_TRACE` to `"true"` enables shell tracing (the equivalent of `set -x`) for the whole job script that the runner generates. The log then shows:

- the export of every CI/CD variable available to the job,
- each command, after variable expansion, prefixed by `+`,
- the runner's internal steps, such as the Git fetch commands and cache and artifact handling.

```yaml
unit-tests:
  variables:
    CI_DEBUG_TRACE: "true"           # trace this job only; remove after debugging
  script:
    - ./scripts/run-tests.sh
```

```text
Job log with CI_DEBUG_TRACE (simplified)

++ export CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME=feature/cart
++ export CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE=merge_request_event
++ export DATABASE_URL=postgres://ci:[MASKED]@postgres:5432/test   <- masked part stays hidden
++ export TEST_SHARD=                                              <- empty: the culprit
+ ./scripts/run-tests.sh
+ '[' -z '' ']'
+ echo 'No shard given, running the full suite'
```

**Where to set it.**

| Scope | How | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| One job | `variables:` in that job | You know which job misbehaves |
| One run | Add `CI_DEBUG_TRACE` = `true` in the **Run pipeline** form, or in the variables of a manual job before you start it | Reproduce a failure once without committing anything |
| Whole pipeline | Top-level `variables:` | Rarely: the logs of all jobs become huge |
| Services | `CI_DEBUG_SERVICES: "true"` | Print the logs of `services:` containers (databases, Docker-in-Docker) in the job log |

**Security: treat a debug log as sensitive.** Debug tracing prints the values of all variables. The runner still replaces masked values with `[MASKED]`. Unmasked variables are printed in clear text, and so are values *derived* from secrets, such as a token that was decoded, concatenated or URL-encoded. To limit the damage:

- Enable it only for one job or one run, never as a permanent setting on a shared branch.
- GitLab restricts access to logs produced with debug logging enabled: only users with at least the Developer role can view them. In public projects, check this before you trace.
- When you are done, erase the log (**Erase job log** on the job page, or `POST /projects/:id/jobs/:job_id/erase`) if it may contain anything sensitive.
- Rotate any secret that appeared unmasked.

**Narrower alternatives.** Full tracing is often more than you need. Tracing only your own script keeps the runner's internals and the variable dump out of the log:

```yaml
unit-tests:
  script:
    - set -x                         # trace from here on, in this job only
    - ./scripts/run-tests.sh
    - set +x                         # stop tracing before anything sensitive
    - ./scripts/upload-results.sh
```

For a single value, `echo "TEST_SHARD=${TEST_SHARD:-<unset>}"` is even cheaper. Problems on the runner side (registration, executor, autoscaling) are not visible in job logs at all. For those, raise the runner's own log level (`log_level = "debug"` in `config.toml`, or `gitlab-runner --debug run`) and read the runner's service logs (section 6.3).

**Key takeaways**

- `CI_DEBUG_TRACE: "true"` prints every command and every variable, including the runner's internal setup steps.
- Set it for one job or one run, through job `variables` or the Run pipeline form, and remove it afterwards.
- Masked values stay masked, but unmasked and derived secrets appear in clear text. Erase the log and rotate secrets if needed.
- `set -x` in your own script is a narrower, safer form of tracing. `CI_DEBUG_SERVICES` shows service container logs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Run a job once with `CI_DEBUG_TRACE: "true"` set from the Run pipeline form. Find in its log the Git commands the runner used to fetch the source, and the value of `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* A job uses a PostgreSQL service and fails with "connection refused". Use `CI_DEBUG_SERVICES` to find out whether the database started, how long it took, and whether the job tried to connect too early. Fix it with a readiness loop.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A colleague proposes enabling `CI_DEBUG_TRACE` permanently on all pipelines 'to make debugging easier'. What is your answer?" *Hint:* secrets in logs, who can read logs, log size and storage, and narrower alternatives.

#### Collapsible Log Sections

**Why they exist.** A long log is hard to read because important lines are buried among routine ones. Package installs, downloads and verbose test output push the one interesting line out of sight. Sections let you fold the routine parts away and name the steps, and each section header shows how long that step took. The runner already does this for its own phases (`prepare_executor`, `get_sources`, `step_script` and so on, see section 13.1). Custom sections apply the same idea to your script.

**How they work.** A section is delimited by two special lines that the job log viewer recognizes. The ANSI escape sequences (`\e[0K`, an "erase line" code, and `\r`) hide the markers themselves, so only the header text remains visible:

```text
\e[0Ksection_start:<unix timestamp>:<section name>[collapsed=true]\r\e[0K<header text>
... lines inside the section ...
\e[0Ksection_end:<unix timestamp>:<section name>\r\e[0K
```

- The **section name** may contain only letters, numbers, `_`, `.` and `-`, and must be the same in the start and end markers.
- The **timestamps** are Unix seconds. GitLab subtracts them to display the duration next to the header.
- `[collapsed=true]` is optional. Without it, the section is expanded by default.

```yaml
build:
  script:
    - echo -e "\e[0Ksection_start:$(date +%s):deps[collapsed=true]\r\e[0KInstall dependencies"
    - npm ci
    - echo -e "\e[0Ksection_end:$(date +%s):deps\r\e[0K"
    - npm run build                  # stays visible: this is the part people care about
```

**Reusable helpers.** Writing escape sequences by hand is error-prone. Put two small functions in a script that every job sources. This version uses `printf` with octal escapes, so it works in `sh` (for example on Alpine images) as well as in `bash`, where `echo -e` is not portable:

```bash
# ci/log.sh: source it in before_script, then call section_start / section_end
section_start() {   # usage: section_start <name> "<header>" [collapsed]
  _collapsed=""
  [ "${3:-}" = "collapsed" ] && _collapsed="[collapsed=true]"
  printf '\033[0Ksection_start:%s:%s%s\r\033[0K\033[1;36m%s\033[0m\n' \
    "$(date +%s)" "$1" "$_collapsed" "$2"          # \033[1;36m: bold cyan header
}

section_end() {     # usage: section_end <name>
  printf '\033[0Ksection_end:%s:%s\r\033[0K\n' "$(date +%s)" "$1"
}
```

```yaml
default:
  before_script:
    - . ci/log.sh                    # "." (source) keeps the functions in the job's shell

integration-tests:
  script:
    - section_start db "Start database and apply migrations" collapsed
    - ./scripts/db-up.sh
    - section_end db
    - section_start tests "Integration tests"
    - pytest tests/integration
    - section_end tests
```

The rendered log then reads like a table of contents:

```text
> Start database and apply migrations                                     00:42
v Integration tests                                                       03:17
    ============================= test session starts =============================
    ...
```

**Automatic per-command sections.** The runner feature flag `FF_SCRIPT_SECTIONS: "true"` wraps every line of `script` in its own section, with its duration. It requires no script changes, and is useful when you want to see which command is slow without editing anything.

```yaml
variables:
  FF_SCRIPT_SECTIONS: "true"         # one collapsible, timed section per script line
```

**PowerShell.** On Windows runners, use the PowerShell escape character:

```powershell
Write-Host "`e[0Ksection_start:$([DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeSeconds()):restore[collapsed=true]`r`e[0KRestore NuGet packages"
dotnet restore
Write-Host "`e[0Ksection_end:$([DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeSeconds()):restore`r`e[0K"
```

**Sections are machine-readable too.** The markers remain in the raw log, so you can parse them to measure step durations across many jobs. This is how the timeline script in section 13.1 could be extended to break each job down by phase.

**Key takeaways**

- Sections are delimited by `section_start` and `section_end` markers with Unix timestamps, hidden by ANSI escape codes.
- Use `[collapsed=true]` for routine steps, so that the important output is visible when the log opens.
- Keep the escape sequences in a sourced helper script. Prefer `printf` over `echo -e` for portability.
- `FF_SCRIPT_SECTIONS` gives a timed section for every script line, with no script changes.
- Section markers in the raw log allow automated per-step timing.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add a collapsed "Install dependencies" section and an expanded "Run tests" section to one of your jobs. Check that the durations shown in the UI match your expectations.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create `ci/log.sh` with the helpers above, include it in a shared template (section 9.1), and use it in three jobs. Then write a script that downloads one job's raw log and prints each section's name and duration from the markers.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your test job's log is 30,000 lines and developers say they 'never find the failure'. How would you restructure the output without losing information?" *Hint:* sections, collapsing, quieter tool flags, test reports (section 10.1) and artifacts for the full output.

#### Interactive Web Terminals

**Why they exist.** Some failures cannot be understood from the outside. A file may be missing from a path you thought it was in, DNS may resolve differently inside the job, or a tool may behave differently in the runner's environment than on your machine. In these cases you want what you would do on any broken server: open a shell and look around. An interactive web terminal opens a shell *inside the running job's environment*, directly from the job page.

**How it works.**

```text
 Browser (job page, "Debug")
     │  WebSocket over HTTPS
     ▼
 GitLab (Workhorse proxies the terminal connection)
     │  WebSocket to advertise_address
     ▼
 Runner session server (:8093) ───► job container / pod  (same image, files, variables)
```

The runner opens a small **session server** that GitLab connects to. GitLab proxies your browser's connection to it, and the runner attaches a shell to the job's container.

**Requirements.**

| Requirement | Details |
|---|---|
| Runner you control | GitLab-hosted runners on GitLab.com do not offer web terminals. You need your own runner |
| Supported executor | Docker and Kubernetes (and the Shell executor on Unix-like systems). Not SSH, VirtualBox or Parallels |
| `[session_server]` in `config.toml` | `listen_address`, plus an `advertise_address` that the GitLab server can reach (section 6.3) |
| Network path | GitLab must reach the runner on the session port, and any reverse proxy in front of GitLab must allow WebSocket upgrades |
| Permissions | Only users allowed to run and update the job can open its terminal |

```toml
# config.toml (runner)
[session_server]
  listen_address = "[::]:8093"                        # where the runner listens
  advertise_address = "runner-01.example.com:8093"    # what GitLab connects to
  session_timeout = 1800                              # seconds a session may stay open
```

**Using it.** While a job is running, the job page shows a **Debug** button that opens the terminal. Jobs often finish (or fail) too quickly to catch, so give yourself time. Add an opt-in pause that only applies when you ask for it:

```yaml
integration-tests:
  script:
    - |
      if ! ./scripts/run-integration-tests.sh; then
        if [ "${DEBUG_PAUSE:-}" = "true" ]; then           # set in the Run pipeline form
          echo "Tests failed, waiting 15 minutes for a debug session"
          sleep 900
        fi
        exit 1                                            # still fail the job afterwards
      fi
```

Start a pipeline with `DEBUG_PAUSE=true`, wait for the failure message, click **Debug**, and inspect the environment: `env | sort`, `ls -la`, `cat` the config files, `curl` the service, rerun the failing command with extra flags. When a terminal session is attached, the runner keeps the job's environment available until you close the session or `session_timeout` expires.

**Security.** A web terminal is a shell with all of the job's variables, including protected and masked secrets, and with the job's network access. Treat access to it like SSH access to a deployment host. Restrict who can run jobs on runners that expose a session server, and do not expose the session port to the internet.

**When you cannot use it.** On GitLab-hosted runners, the closest alternatives are richer diagnostics in `after_script`, artifacts with the full output (`artifacts:when: always`), or reproducing the job locally with the same image (next topic).

**Key takeaways**

- A web terminal is a shell inside the running job, opened from the job page with **Debug**.
- It needs your own runner, a supported executor (Docker, Kubernetes, Shell) and a reachable `[session_server]`.
- Keep a failing job alive on purpose with an opt-in `sleep` gated by a variable such as `DEBUG_PAUSE`.
- The terminal has the job's secrets and network access. Control who can use it, and keep the session port private.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* On a self-managed runner, configure `[session_server]`, run a job that sleeps for five minutes, open its terminal and print the job's working directory and the image's OS release (`cat /etc/os-release`).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add the `DEBUG_PAUSE` pattern to a template so that every job can be paused on failure. Make sure the pause never applies to pipelines on protected branches.
> 3. **Interview question:** "The Debug button appears, but the terminal never connects and eventually shows a connection error. Where do you look?" *Hint:* `advertise_address`, firewalls between GitLab and the runner, the WebSocket configuration of the reverse proxy, and TLS.

#### Running Pipelines Locally

**Why it matters.** The push-wait-read cycle is slow: every attempt costs a commit, a pipeline and a few minutes. When you are fixing a script or a build step, you want to iterate in seconds. Running the job, or at least its commands, on your own machine shortens that loop dramatically.

**What "locally" can mean.** A GitLab pipeline has two layers that can be reproduced separately:

| Layer | What it covers | How to reproduce it locally |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration | Which jobs exist, includes, `extends`, `rules`, `needs` | CI Lint, pipeline editor, Lint API (section 1.3), `gitlab-ci-local --preview` |
| Execution | What a job's script does in its image | `docker run` with the job's image, `gitlab-ci-local`, or plain scripts |

**What does not work: `gitlab-runner exec`.** Older guides suggest `gitlab-runner exec docker <job>`. This command is deprecated. It never supported includes, artifacts passed between jobs, `needs` or most of modern GitLab CI, so do not build a workflow around it.

**Option 1: run the job's commands in the job's image.** This is the most faithful option and needs nothing beyond Docker. Use the same image (ideally the same digest) and the same working directory, and set the variables the script relies on:

```bash
# Reproduce the "unit-tests" job by hand in its image
docker run --rm -it \
  --volume "$PWD":/builds/shop/api \
  --workdir /builds/shop/api \
  --env CI=true \
  --env CI_PROJECT_DIR=/builds/shop/api \
  --env CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME="$(git branch --show-current)" \
  --env CI_COMMIT_SHA="$(git rev-parse HEAD)" \
  python:3.12-slim bash
# Inside the container: paste the job's before_script and script lines one by one
```

The differences that remain are the user ID, mounted volumes, services and network, and secrets. Each of them can be the real cause of a CI-only failure, so check them deliberately when a job passes locally but fails in CI.

**Option 2: `gitlab-ci-local`.** This open-source tool (not maintained by GitLab) reads your `.gitlab-ci.yml`, resolves includes, `extends`, `needs` and artifacts, and runs jobs in Docker containers on your machine:

```bash
npm install --global gitlab-ci-local      # also available through Homebrew

gitlab-ci-local --list                    # jobs, stages, when and needs, as the tool understands them
gitlab-ci-local --preview                 # fully merged configuration (includes and extends resolved)
gitlab-ci-local unit-tests                # run one job in its image
gitlab-ci-local --needs e2e               # run "e2e" and every job it needs, in order
gitlab-ci-local --variable DEPLOY_ENV=staging deploy-staging   # override a variable for this run
```

Things to keep in mind:

- Jobs without an `image` run directly in your shell, not in a container. Set a `default:image` to avoid surprises.
- Secrets are not available. Provide test values through the tool's variables file (see its documentation), and never commit real secrets to it.
- Remote includes from private projects need a token, and `rules` that depend on merge request or pipeline-source variables may evaluate differently than on the server.

**Option 3: design jobs so that they run anywhere.** The most durable fix is structural. Keep the YAML thin and put the logic into scripts or `make` targets that run unchanged on a laptop and in CI:

```yaml
# Thin job: the YAML only chooses the environment; the logic lives in the repository
unit-tests:
  image: python:3.12-slim
  script:
    - make test                      # the same command developers run locally
```

```makefile
# Makefile
test:
	pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
	pytest --junitxml=report.xml
```

**Comparison.**

| Approach | Fidelity | Effort | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| CI Lint / pipeline editor | Configuration only | None | "Why does this job not appear?" |
| `docker run` with the job's image | High for one job | Low | Script and tooling failures |
| `gitlab-ci-local` | Medium to high, multi-job | Low to medium | Iterating on multi-job flows, `needs` and artifacts |
| Thin YAML + `make` targets | High, permanent | One-time refactoring | Preventing CI-only bugs in the first place |
| Web terminal in the real job | Exact | Needs a self-managed runner | Environment-specific failures |

**Key takeaways**

- Separate configuration problems (use Lint and the pipeline editor) from execution problems (run the job in its image).
- `docker run` with the job's image, working directory and key variables reproduces most script failures in seconds.
- `gitlab-ci-local` simulates multi-job pipelines locally. It is third-party software, and secrets and some `rules` behave differently.
- `gitlab-runner exec` is deprecated and incomplete. Do not rely on it.
- Thin YAML that calls scripts or `make` targets makes every job reproducible by design.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Pick a job from one of your pipelines and reproduce it with `docker run` using the same image. List every difference you had to work around (variables, services, files).
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Install `gitlab-ci-local`, run `--preview` on a project that uses includes and `extends`, and compare the output with the pipeline editor's **Full configuration** tab. Then run a two-job chain with `--needs` and check that artifacts are passed.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A job passes on every developer's laptop but fails in CI with a permissions error when writing to a directory. What differences between the two environments would you check first?" *Hint:* the user ID inside the container, file ownership of the cloned sources, read-only paths, and the image tag versus the local image.

#### AI-Assisted Root Cause Analysis

**Why it exists.** Many CI failures are repetitive: a dependency conflict, a missing environment variable, an out-of-memory kill, a breaking change in a tool's new release. Recognizing them is easy for someone who has seen them before and slow for someone who has not. Large language models have seen a great many such logs, so they can often explain an unfamiliar error quickly and point to a likely fix.

**GitLab Duo Root Cause Analysis.** On a failed job's page, GitLab offers a **Troubleshoot** action (also available as `/troubleshoot` in GitLab Duo Chat when you are viewing the job). It sends the relevant part of the job log to GitLab Duo, which returns:

- a plain-language explanation of what failed,
- the likely root cause,
- one or more suggested fixes, often with a code or configuration change.

```text
 Failed job page ──"Troubleshoot"──► GitLab Duo
                                        │ input: truncated job log (mostly the end),
                                        │        plus job context
                                        ▼
                               Explanation + likely cause + suggested fix
                                        │
                                        ▼
                     You verify, apply in a branch, rerun the pipeline
```

**Availability.** Root Cause Analysis requires a GitLab Duo add-on, and on self-managed instances an administrator must turn GitLab Duo on. Groups and projects can also turn it off. Packaging has changed between releases, and newer releases add agent-based flows that can propose a fix as a merge request. Check the current documentation for your version and tier.

**Using it well.** The model sees mostly the *log*. It does not see your infrastructure, your runner configuration or code that is not in the log. Its answer is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis:

| Do | Avoid |
|---|---|
| Check the cited log lines yourself before acting | Applying a suggested fix you do not understand |
| Ask follow-up questions in Duo Chat ("why would this pass locally?") | Treating "add `|| true`" or "increase the timeout" as a fix |
| Verify the fix in a branch pipeline | Pasting logs into public AI tools: logs can contain internal hostnames and unmasked values |
| Use it to learn unfamiliar tools' error formats | Relying on it for infrastructure failures that are invisible in the log |

**Make failures easier to analyze, for people and for AI.** Both work better when the log ends with clear context. A small `after_script` that prints diagnostics only on failure helps every reader:

```yaml
default:
  after_script:
    - |
      if [ "$CI_JOB_STATUS" = "failed" ]; then             # set by the runner in after_script
        echo "---------- diagnostic context ----------"
        echo "image:  $CI_JOB_IMAGE"
        echo "runner: $CI_RUNNER_DESCRIPTION"
        df -h . | tail -1                                  # disk space left in the build dir
        (free -m 2>/dev/null || cat /proc/meminfo | head -3) # memory, whichever tool exists
        git log -1 --format='commit: %h %s'
      fi
```

**A tool-independent triage script.** Whether you then read the result yourself or hand it to an assistant, extracting the essentials of every failed job in a pipeline saves time:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# failed_excerpts.py: print failure reason and the error excerpt of every failed job in a pipeline
# Usage: GITLAB_TOKEN=glpat-... python3 failed_excerpts.py <project_id> <pipeline_id>
import json
import os
import re
import sys
import urllib.request

API = os.environ.get("GITLAB_API", "https://gitlab.com/api/v4")
project_id, pipeline_id = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
ERROR = re.compile(r"error|fail|fatal|exception|denied|not found|killed", re.IGNORECASE)
ANSI = re.compile(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*[A-Za-z]")              # strip color codes and section markers

def get(path, raw=False):
    req = urllib.request.Request(API + path, headers={"PRIVATE-TOKEN": os.environ["GITLAB_TOKEN"]})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
        body = resp.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        return body if raw else json.loads(body)

jobs = get(f"/projects/{project_id}/pipelines/{pipeline_id}/jobs?scope[]=failed&per_page=100")
for job in jobs:
    lines = ANSI.sub("", get(f"/projects/{project_id}/jobs/{job['id']}/trace", raw=True)).splitlines()
    tail = lines[-200:]                                   # the cause is almost always near the end
    hits = [l for l in tail if ERROR.search(l)][:15]
    print(f"=== {job['stage']} / {job['name']}  ({job['failure_reason']})  {job['web_url']}")
    print("\n".join(hits or tail[-15:]))                  # fall back to the last lines
    print()
```

**Key takeaways**

- GitLab Duo Root Cause Analysis (**Troubleshoot** on a failed job) explains failures and suggests fixes from the job log. It requires a Duo add-on, and availability varies by version.
- The model sees mostly the log, so its answer is a hypothesis: verify the cited lines and test the fix in a branch.
- Reject "fixes" that hide failures (`|| true`, longer timeouts) unless you understand why they are correct.
- Failure-only diagnostics in `after_script` and short, clear error output make logs easier to analyze for both people and AI.
- Logs can contain sensitive data. Use only AI tools approved for your organization's code and logs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Break a job on purpose (a missing dependency, a wrong command name). If you have GitLab Duo, use **Troubleshoot** and judge whether the explanation and fix are correct. If not, use `failed_excerpts.py` and diagnose it yourself.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Add the diagnostic `after_script` to a shared template. Then cause an out-of-memory failure (for example, a test that allocates a large array) and check whether the diagnostics make the cause obvious.
> 3. **Interview question:** "An AI assistant suggests fixing a flaky integration test by adding `retry: 2` to the job. When is that acceptable, and when is it harmful?" *Hint:* infrastructure flakiness versus real race conditions, `retry:when`, and how retries hide failure trends.

#### Common Configuration Errors

**Why it matters.** Configuration errors are a different kind of failure: no job runs at all, or the wrong jobs run. GitLab reports them as a pipeline with the `yaml invalid` label, an error banner in the pipeline editor, or sometimes as a pipeline that silently does not appear. Knowing the usual messages turns a confusing banner into a one-line fix.

**A method for any configuration error.**

```text
 Error banner / no pipeline
        │
        ├─ 1. Read the message: it names the job and the key ("jobs:build:script ...")
        ├─ 2. Pipeline editor ► Validate (or CI Lint with "simulate") for the right branch
        ├─ 3. Full configuration tab: inspect the merged YAML after includes, extends, !reference
        └─ 4. Bisect: comment out includes or jobs until the error disappears
```

Step 3 matters most when includes are involved, because the error refers to the *merged* configuration, which may not look like any single file you wrote. The Lint API returns the merged result too:

```bash
# Validate the configuration stored on a branch and print the merged YAML GitLab actually sees
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/ci/lint?ref=feature/cart&dry_run=true" |
  jq -r '.valid, .errors[], .merged_yaml'
```

**Errors that block the pipeline.** The messages below are typical. Exact wording varies slightly between versions.

| Error message (abridged) | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `(<unknown>): did not find expected key while parsing a block mapping at line 7 column 3` | YAML syntax: wrong indentation, tabs, an unclosed quote | Fix indentation at or above the reported line, and use spaces only |
| `jobs:build config contains unknown keys: scirpt` | Typo in a keyword | Correct the keyword |
| `jobs:build:script config should be a string or a nested array of strings up to 10 levels deep` | A script line was parsed as a map, usually because of `: ` inside an unquoted line | Quote the whole line: `- 'echo "status: ok"'` |
| `deploy job: chosen stage deploy does not exist; available stages are .pre, build, test, .post` | `stage:` names a stage missing from `stages:` | Add the stage, or fix its name |
| `'unit' job needs 'build' job, but 'build' does not exist in the pipeline...` | The needed job is absent: a typo, or excluded by its `rules` | Fix the name, align the `rules`, or use `needs: [{ job: build, optional: true }]` |
| `jobs:test config key may not be used with rules: only` | `rules` mixed with `only`/`except` (or job-level `when`) in one job | Use `rules` alone (section 4.2) |
| `test: unknown key in extends (.base-job)` | `extends` points to a job that does not exist after merging | Fix the name, or check that the include defining it is loaded |
| `test: circular dependency detected in extends` | Two templates extend each other | Break the cycle |
| `Local file ci/build.yml does not exist!` | Wrong path in `include:local`, or the file is missing on this branch | Fix the path. Local includes are resolved on the pipeline's commit |
| `Project platform/ci-templates not found or access denied!` | Wrong path, or the user running the pipeline cannot read that project | Fix the path, or grant access (also check the scheduled pipeline owner's access) |
| `jobs config should contain at least one visible job` | Every job is hidden (starts with `.`), or only templates were included | Add a visible job, or fix the include |
| `Maximum of 150 nested includes are allowed!` | Include chain or fan-out too large | Flatten the includes, or use components (section 9.3) |
| `variables config should be a hash of key value pairs...` | A variable value has the wrong type, for example an unquoted `true`, `yes` or a list | Quote the value: `ENABLE_X: "true"` |

**Errors that are not reported.** The most confusing problems produce a *valid* configuration that does the wrong thing:

| Symptom | Common cause | Where it is covered |
|---|---|---|
| No pipeline at all after a push | `workflow:rules` excluded it. **Run pipeline** shows "Pipeline filtered out by workflow rules." | Section 4.4 |
| Pipeline not created, "The rules configuration prevented any jobs from being added to the pipeline." | Every job's `rules` evaluated to "do not add" | Section 4.1 |
| Job missing from the pipeline | First-match semantics in `rules`, or a comparison against an unset variable | Section 4.1 |
| Two pipelines per push (branch + MR) | Missing `workflow:rules` for MR pipelines | Section 4.4 |
| Job runs on every push despite `rules:changes` | New branches and some pipeline sources have no "before" commit to compare with | Section 4.1, `compare_to` |
| Value has unexpected content | YAML typing: `0755` is read as the octal number 493, `1.10` as `1.1` | Section 2.1 |
| A password containing `$` is cut off | Variable expansion inside the value | `$$` or `expand: false` (section 5.1) |

**Prevention.** Lint configuration changes in merge requests, and run `glab ci lint` or the Lint API in a pre-commit hook or in the template project's own pipeline (section 1.3). Keep shared templates versioned (`include:ref` or component versions), so that a broken template does not break every consumer at once.

**Key takeaways**

- Error messages name the job and the key at fault. Read them literally before guessing.
- Errors refer to the merged configuration: inspect it in the pipeline editor's **Full configuration** tab or in the Lint API's `merged_yaml`.
- Most blocking errors are typos, YAML structure problems, missing stages, unresolvable `needs` and `extends`, and include paths or access.
- The hardest problems are valid configurations that behave wrongly: `workflow:rules`, `rules` order, `rules:changes` and YAML typing.
- Lint in merge requests and version shared templates, so that errors are caught before they reach a pipeline.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Introduce each of these errors in a test project one at a time and record the exact message: a keyword typo, a missing stage, a `needs` on a nonexistent job, an unquoted `echo "a: b"` script line.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a project that includes a template from another project, then remove your access to that project. Run a scheduled pipeline and a manual pipeline as different users, and explain the results.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Developers say 'the pipeline doesn't start any more' after a template change, but CI Lint on their `.gitlab-ci.yml` says it is valid. How do you investigate?" *Hint:* which ref Lint validated against, `workflow:rules` in the template, simulated pipeline creation, and the merged configuration.

<a id="142-observability-and-metrics"></a>
### 14.2 Observability and Metrics

Debugging explains one failure. Observability shows trends: whether the pipeline is getting slower, whether the default branch is red more often than last quarter, whether changes take days or hours to reach production. This subchapter covers GitLab's built-in analytics for pipelines, delivery performance (DORA) and the flow of work (value streams), and the badges that put a project's health on its front page. Runner-level metrics with Prometheus are covered in section 6.4.

```text
 Level                 Question                                   GitLab feature
 ───────────────────── ────────────────────────────────────────── ──────────────────────────
 Runner fleet          Do we have enough capacity?                 Runner Prometheus metrics (6.4)
 Pipeline              Is CI fast and reliable?                    CI/CD analytics, API
 Delivery              How fast and safely do we ship?             DORA metrics
 Whole process         Where does work wait, idea to production?   Value stream analytics
 At a glance           Is this project healthy right now?          Badges
```

#### CI/CD Analytics

**Why it matters.** A pipeline that slowly degrades never produces an incident. Five extra seconds per week, one more flaky test per month, and after a year the pipeline takes twice as long and fails one run in five. Developers adapt by retrying, waiting and batching changes, and the cost is invisible until someone measures it.

**What GitLab provides.** In a project, **Analyze > CI/CD analytics** shows pipeline statistics over a chosen period: the number of pipelines by status, success and failure rates, and duration trends, with filters such as branch and pipeline source. The page has been redesigned in recent releases, so the exact charts and labels depend on your version. At group level, the same menu shows release statistics (Premium) and, on Ultimate, DORA metrics (next topic). Related views elsewhere:

| View | Shows | Section |
|---|---|---|
| **Analyze > CI/CD analytics** | Pipeline counts, success rate, durations over time | This topic |
| **Analyze > Repository analytics** | Code coverage history per job | 10.2 |
| **Build > Pipelines**, **Tests** tab | Test failures per pipeline, recently failed tests | 10.1 |
| **Usage quotas** | Compute minutes per project | 13.2 |
| Runner metrics in Prometheus | Queue, concurrency, failures per runner | 6.4 |

**Metrics worth tracking.** The built-in charts cover the basics. These are the metrics that most often reveal real problems:

| Metric | Why it matters | Healthy direction |
|---|---|---|
| Default-branch success rate | A red default branch blocks everyone who branches from it | High and stable |
| Time the default branch stays red | How quickly breakage is noticed and fixed | Short (minutes to hours) |
| Median and 95th-percentile duration | The median is the usual wait. The p95 is the wait that drives people to context-switch | Flat or falling |
| Queued duration | Runner capacity (section 13.1) | Near zero |
| Retry rate per job | Flakiness: jobs that pass only on retry | Low, and trending down |

**Measuring it yourself.** For metrics the UI does not show, such as the time the default branch stays red, query the data directly. The GraphQL API returns pipeline durations in bulk, which the REST list endpoint does not:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# ci_health.py: success rate, duration percentiles and "time red" for one branch
# Usage: GITLAB_TOKEN=glpat-... python3 ci_health.py shop/api main 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z
import json
import os
import statistics
import sys
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime

URL = os.environ.get("GITLAB_GRAPHQL", "https://gitlab.com/api/graphql")
project, ref, since = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
QUERY = """
query($project: ID!, $ref: String!, $since: Time!, $after: String) {
  project(fullPath: $project) {
    pipelines(ref: $ref, updatedAfter: $since, first: 100, after: $after) {
      nodes { status duration createdAt finishedAt }
      pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }
    }
  }
}"""

def fetch_all():
    after, nodes = None, []
    while True:
        payload = json.dumps({"query": QUERY, "variables":
                              {"project": project, "ref": ref, "since": since, "after": after}}).encode()
        req = urllib.request.Request(URL, data=payload, headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['GITLAB_TOKEN']}", "Content-Type": "application/json"})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
            page = json.load(resp)["data"]["project"]["pipelines"]
        nodes += page["nodes"]
        if not page["pageInfo"]["hasNextPage"]:
            return nodes
        after = page["pageInfo"]["endCursor"]

def ts(value):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00"))

done = [p for p in fetch_all() if p["status"] in ("SUCCESS", "FAILED") and p["finishedAt"]]
done.sort(key=lambda p: p["finishedAt"])                       # chronological order
durations = sorted(p["duration"] for p in done if p["duration"])

# "Time red": from the first failed pipeline to the next successful one
red_seconds, red_since = 0.0, None
for p in done:
    if p["status"] == "FAILED" and red_since is None:
        red_since = ts(p["finishedAt"])
    elif p["status"] == "SUCCESS" and red_since is not None:
        red_seconds += (ts(p["finishedAt"]) - red_since).total_seconds()
        red_since = None

success = sum(p["status"] == "SUCCESS" for p in done)
print(f"pipelines: {len(done)}, success rate: {success / len(done):.0%}")
```
