```python
print(f"duration p50: {statistics.median(durations) / 60:.1f} min, "
      f"p95: {durations[int(len(durations) * 0.95) - 1] / 60:.1f} min")
print(f"{ref} was red for {red_seconds / 3600:.1f} hours in total")
```

```text
pipelines: 412, success rate: 87%
duration p50: 11.4 min, p95: 23.9 min
main was red for 31.5 hours in total
```

Run a script like this as a scheduled pipeline (section 3.5) and store the output as an artifact, or push the numbers to your monitoring system to get a trend line.

**Key takeaways**

- **Analyze > CI/CD analytics** shows pipeline counts, success rates and durations. Labels vary by version, and group-level views add release statistics and DORA.
- Track default-branch success rate, time red, median and p95 duration, queued time and retry rate.
- p95 duration is the wait that makes developers context-switch, so watch it alongside the median.
- Use the GraphQL API for bulk pipeline data (durations included), and schedule the analysis to get trends.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open **Analyze > CI/CD analytics** for a project you work on and write down its success rate and typical duration for the last month. Compare the default branch with all branches.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Run `ci_health.py` for your default branch, then extend it to count, per job name, how often a job failed and then passed on retry, using job data from the REST API. Name the three flakiest jobs.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your manager wants one number for 'CI health' on a dashboard. Which would you choose, and what would it hide?" *Hint:* success rate versus time red versus p95 duration, and why any single metric can be gamed.

#### DORA Metrics

**Why they exist.** "Are we getting better at delivering software?" needs an answer that does not depend on opinion. The DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) program found four metrics that, measured together, distinguish high-performing teams. Two measure **throughput** and two measure **stability**, so a team cannot improve one side by sacrificing the other without it showing (section 1.1).

**How GitLab calculates them.** GitLab computes all four from data it already has, mainly deployments to production-tier environments and incidents:

| Metric | GitLab's definition | Data it needs |
|---|---|---|
| Deployment frequency | Number of successful deployments to production-tier environments per day | Jobs with `environment:` and `deployment_tier: production` (section 12.1) |
| Lead time for changes | Median time from a merge request being merged to its code running in production | MR merges, followed by production deployments |
| Time to restore service | Median time incidents stayed open in the period | Incidents (issues of type incident) |
| Change failure rate | Incidents divided by production deployments in the period | Incidents and deployments |

Recent DORA reports rename "time to restore service" to "failed deployment recovery time", and GitLab's labels may follow. The meaning is the same.

```text
 merge ──────────── lead time for changes ────────────► deployed to production ──┐
                                                                                 │ deployment frequency
                                                                                 ▼ counts these events
                        incident opened ── time to restore ──► incident closed
                        └── change failure rate = incidents / deployments ──┘
```

**Feeding the metrics correctly.** DORA dashboards are only as good as the events behind them:

```yaml
deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./scripts/deploy.sh production
  environment:
    name: prod-eu                    # any name works...
    deployment_tier: production      # ...but only the tier makes it count for DORA
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

```bash
# Deployments done outside GitLab CI (for example by a legacy tool) can be recorded through the API
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/deployments" \
  --data "environment=production" --data "sha=$DEPLOYED_SHA" \
  --data "ref=main" --data "tag=false" --data "status=success"

# Open an incident when production breaks: time to restore runs until it is closed
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/issues" \
  --data "title=Checkout returns 500 after deploy" --data "issue_type=incident"
```

Incidents can also be created automatically from alerts (GitLab's alert integrations or an external monitoring tool calling the API), which removes the human delay from time to restore.

**Reading the metrics.** On Ultimate, DORA charts are available under **Analyze > CI/CD analytics** in projects and groups, and in the **Value Streams Dashboard**, which compares periods and groups and can classify projects into DORA performance levels. The DORA API returns the raw numbers:

```bash
# Monthly median lead time for changes (seconds) for one project
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/dora/metrics?metric=lead_time_for_changes&interval=monthly&start_date=2026-04-01&end_date=2026-09-30" |
  jq -r '.[] | "\(.date)  \((.value // 0) / 3600 | floor) h"'

# Group-wide deployment frequency; other metrics: deployment_frequency, time_to_restore_service, change_failure_rate
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups/42/dora/metrics?metric=deployment_frequency&interval=monthly&environment_tiers[]=production"
```

**Common pitfalls.**

| Problem | Effect | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Production environment without `deployment_tier: production` (for example `live`, `eu-central`) | Deployments not counted | Set the tier explicitly |
| Review apps or staging accidentally tiered as production | Deployment frequency inflated, lead time distorted | Audit tiers of all environments |
| Incidents tracked outside GitLab | Time to restore and change failure rate stay empty or near zero | Create incidents in GitLab, via alerts or the API |
| Direct pushes to the default branch, without MRs | Lead time misses those changes | Protect the branch, require MRs |
| Targets attached to individual metrics | People optimize the number, not the outcome (smaller, meaningless deployments; incidents not filed) | Look at all four together, as trends, at team level |

**Key takeaways**

- DORA measures throughput (deployment frequency, lead time) and stability (time to restore, change failure rate). Read all four together.
- GitLab counts deployments to environments with `deployment_tier: production`, and uses incidents for the stability metrics.
- Record deployments made outside GitLab CI with the Deployments API, and create incidents through alerts or the Issues API.
- DORA dashboards and the DORA API require Ultimate. Use them for team-level trends, not individual targets.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* List every environment in one of your projects with its deployment tier. Identify any that are misclassified for DORA purposes.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Simulate a month of activity in a test project: ten production deployments through CI, two incidents opened and closed through the API. Query all four metrics with the DORA API and check that they match your manual calculation.
> 3. **Interview question:** "After introducing feature flags, your deployment frequency doubled but change failure rate also rose. How would you interpret this, and what would you look at next?" *Hint:* smaller batches, what counts as an incident, flag-related failures, and time to restore.

#### Value Stream Analytics

**Why it exists.** DORA's lead time starts at merge. For most teams, the larger delays come *before* that point: an issue waits weeks to be planned, a merge request waits days for review, a fix waits for the next release window. Value stream analytics (VSA) measures the time work spends in each step from idea to production, so you can see where it waits.

**The model.** A value stream is a sequence of **stages**. Each stage is defined by a start event and an end event, and GitLab measures, for every issue or merge request, the time between the two. The default value stream has six stages:

```text
 Issue ───► Plan ───► Code ───► Test ───► Review ───► Staging
   │          │         │         │          │           │
 issue     added to   first     MR's last   MR created  MR merged
 created   board or   commit    pipeline    → MR        → first deployed
 → added   milestone  mention   started →   merged      to production
 to board/ → first    → MR      finished
 milestone commit     created
           mention
```

| Stage | Start event | End event | What a long stage means |
|---|---|---|---|
| Issue | Issue created | Issue added to a board or milestone | Triage backlog |
| Plan | Issue added to a board or milestone | Issue first mentioned in a commit | Work waits before anyone starts it |
| Code | Issue first mentioned in a commit | Merge request created | Long-running branches |
| Test | MR's last pipeline started | MR's last pipeline finished | Slow CI (chapter 13) |
| Review | Merge request created | Merge request merged | Review bottleneck, slow approvals |
| Staging | Merge request merged | MR first deployed to production | Infrequent deployments, manual gates |

Above the stages, VSA shows summary metrics such as lead time (issue created to closed), cycle time (first commit to issue closed), new issues and deploys. Ultimate adds deployment frequency here as well.

**Linking matters.** Stages are calculated from links between objects, so the data is only complete when work is connected. Use closing patterns (`Closes #42`) in merge request descriptions or commit messages, mention issues in commits, and deploy through environments. An MR that is not linked to an issue contributes to Review and Staging, but not to Plan or Code.

**Custom value streams.** On Premium and above, you can create value streams at group level with your own stages. Start and end events include issue and MR creation, closing and merging, label added or removed, first commit time, last pipeline start and finish, and first deployment to production. For example:

| Custom stage | Start event | End event | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Waiting for review | Label `workflow::ready-for-review` added | Label `workflow::ready-for-review` removed | Measure review queue time precisely |
| CI feedback | Merge request created | MR's last pipeline finished | First feedback a developer gets |
| Release wait | Merge request merged | MR first deployed to production | Time code sits on main before shipping |

Label-based stages are the most flexible: if your workflow uses scoped labels for states, VSA can measure the time spent in each state.

**Reading VSA responsibly.** Each stage shows the median time and the list of items, sortable by duration. Look at the slowest items, not only at the median: a handful of items that waited three weeks usually tell you more than the median does. As with DORA, use the data to find bottlenecks in the process, not to rank people.

**Key takeaways**

- VSA measures time from idea to production as a chain of stages, each defined by a start and an end event.
- The default stages (Issue, Plan, Code, Test, Review, Staging) need linked work: closing patterns, commit mentions and environment deployments.
- The Test stage reflects CI duration, and the Staging stage reflects deployment frequency and release gates.
- Custom value streams (Premium) with label-based stages model your team's actual workflow.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Open **Analyze > Value stream analytics** for a project and find its slowest stage. Open the three slowest items in that stage and describe why each one waited.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Design a custom value stream for a team that uses the scoped labels `workflow::in-progress`, `workflow::review` and `workflow::done`. Define the start and end events of each stage.
> 3. **Interview question:** "DORA lead time for changes is under a day, yet customers wait months for requested features. How can both be true, and which tool shows the gap?" *Hint:* lead time starts at merge, and the Issue and Plan stages of VSA.

#### Pipeline and Coverage Badges

**Why they exist.** A badge is a tiny image, usually at the top of a README, that shows a project's status at a glance: whether the default branch is passing, how much code is covered by tests, what the latest release is. It costs nothing to maintain, and it makes a broken default branch visible to everyone who opens the project.

**Built-in badges.** GitLab generates three badges as SVG images:

| Badge | Image URL | Options |
|---|---|---|
| Pipeline status | `https://<host>/<project>/badges/<ref>/pipeline.svg` | `ignore_skipped=true` shows the last non-skipped status, `key_text` and `key_width` change the label |
| Coverage | `https://<host>/<project>/badges/<ref>/coverage.svg` | `job=<name>` picks one job's coverage, `min_good`, `min_acceptable` and `min_medium` set the color thresholds (defaults 95, 90, 75) |
| Latest release | `https://<host>/<project>/-/badges/release.svg` | `order_by=release_at` instead of creation date |

The coverage badge shows the value extracted by the `coverage` keyword (section 10.2). Without `job=`, it shows the average across all jobs that report coverage.

```markdown
<!-- README.md -->
[![pipeline status](https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/badges/main/pipeline.svg)](https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/-/commits/main)
[![coverage report](https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/badges/main/coverage.svg?job=unit-tests&min_good=85&min_acceptable=75)](https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/-/commits/main)
[![latest release](https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/-/badges/release.svg)](https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/-/releases)
```

**Project and group badges.** Instead of editing every README, add badges under **Settings > General > Badges**. They appear in the project header. Group badges appear on every project in the group, and placeholders make one definition work everywhere:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Name | `pipeline` |
| Link | `https://gitlab.example.com/%{project_path}/-/commits/%{default_branch}` |
| Badge image URL | `https://gitlab.example.com/%{project_path}/badges/%{default_branch}/pipeline.svg` |

Other placeholders include `%{project_id}`, `%{project_name}`, `%{commit_sha}` and `%{latest_tag}`. Badges can also be managed through the API (`POST /projects/:id/badges` with `link_url` and `image_url`, or `/groups/:id/badges`).

**Custom badges from a job.** For any other metric, such as lint score, bundle size or dependency freshness, generate an SVG in a job, store it as an artifact, and reference the latest artifact by URL:

```yaml
lint-badge:
  stage: test
  image: python:3.12-slim
  script:
    - pip install anybadge pylint
    # Extract the score from "Your code has been rated at 8.73/10"
    - score=$(pylint src --exit-zero | sed -n 's/^Your code has been rated at \([-0-9.]*\)\/.*/\1/p')
    - anybadge --label=pylint --value="$score" --file=pylint.svg 4=red 6=orange 8=yellow 10=green
  artifacts:
    paths: [pylint.svg]              # the latest artifacts of a ref are kept by default
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

```markdown
![pylint](https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/-/jobs/artifacts/main/raw/pylint.svg?job=lint-badge)
```

**Visibility.** Badge URLs follow the project's visibility. For a private or internal project, the image loads only for signed-in users with access. A badge copied into an external site, such as a public mirror's README, shows a broken image.

**Key takeaways**

- GitLab serves pipeline, coverage and latest-release badges as SVGs under `/badges/<ref>/...` and `/-/badges/release.svg`.
- Use `job=` and the `min_*` thresholds to make the coverage badge show the right job with meaningful colors.
- Group badges with placeholders such as `%{project_path}` and `%{default_branch}` give every project the same badges with one definition.
- Custom metrics become badges through an SVG artifact and the `/-/jobs/artifacts/<ref>/raw/<path>?job=<name>` URL.
- Badges of private projects do not render for anonymous viewers.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Add pipeline and coverage badges to a project's README, with the coverage badge pointing at one specific job and custom color thresholds.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Define a group-level pipeline badge with placeholders, and check that it renders correctly in three projects with different default branch names.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your README's pipeline badge says 'passed', but the last commit on main has a failed pipeline. What could explain it?" *Hint:* which ref the badge points to, skipped and canceled pipelines, `ignore_skipped`, and image caching by the browser or a proxy.

<a id="143-notifications-and-integrations"></a>
### 14.3 Notifications and Integrations

A failure that nobody notices is worse than one that is noticed late. This subchapter covers how GitLab tells people and systems what happened: email, chat integrations, webhooks for your own automation, and commit statuses that connect GitLab with external CI systems and other Git hosts. The common goal is the right event, to the right audience, with as little noise as possible.

| Mechanism | Audience | Direction | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Email notifications | People | GitLab → inbox | "Your pipeline failed" |
| Slack / Microsoft Teams | Teams | GitLab → channel | "main is broken", deployment announcements |
| Webhooks | Systems | GitLab → your HTTP service | Custom automation, dashboards, ticketing |
| Commit Status API | Systems | External system → GitLab | External CI or checks shown in the pipeline |
| External status checks | Systems | GitLab ↔ external service | Merge request approval by an external tool |

#### Pipeline Email Notifications

**Why it matters.** Email is the default channel: it reaches everyone without setup. It is also the easiest one to ruin with noise. A developer who receives fifty pipeline emails a day filters them all away, including the one that matters.

**Two independent mechanisms.**

1. **Personal notifications.** Each user receives pipeline emails based on their own notification settings (**User settings > Notifications**, per group or project):

| Event | Who receives it | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Failed pipeline | The user who triggered the pipeline | On |
| Fixed pipeline | The user who triggered the pipeline, when a pipeline succeeds after a failure | On |
| Successful pipeline | The user who triggered the pipeline | Off: enable it with the **Custom** notification level |

"The user who triggered the pipeline" is the pusher, the person who clicked **Run pipeline**, or the **owner of a schedule** for scheduled pipelines. Nightly failures therefore go to whoever owns the schedule, which is a common reason why nobody notices them. Assign schedule ownership to someone who acts on the results (section 3.5).

2. **The Pipeline status emails integration.** Under **Settings > Integrations > Pipeline status emails**, a project sends pipeline results to a fixed list of addresses, such as a team mailing list, regardless of who triggered the pipeline:

| Setting | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Recipients | Comma-separated addresses (for example a team distribution list) |
| Notify only broken pipelines | Skip successful pipelines |
| Branches for which notifications are sent | All, default, protected, or default and protected branches |

```bash
# Configure the integration through the API: only broken pipelines on default and protected branches
curl --request PUT --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/integrations/pipelines-email" \
  --data "recipients=team-checkout@example.com" \
  --data "notify_only_broken_pipelines=true" \
  --data "branches_to_be_notified=default_and_protected"
```

**Filtering on the receiving side.** GitLab emails carry headers you can filter on, such as `X-GitLab-Project`, `X-GitLab-Project-Path`, `X-GitLab-Pipeline-Id` and `X-GitLab-NotificationReason`. A Sieve rule (supported by many mail servers) can sort CI mail into its own folder:

```sieve
require ["fileinto"];
# Pipeline emails from the checkout service go to their own folder
if allof (exists "X-GitLab-Pipeline-Id",
          header :is "X-GitLab-Project-Path" "shop/checkout") {
  fileinto "CI/checkout";
}
```

**Reducing noise.**

- Keep "Failed pipeline" and "Fixed pipeline" on, and "Successful pipeline" off.
- Send team-wide email only for broken pipelines on default and protected branches. Feature-branch failures belong to their author.
- Avoid noise sources: duplicate pipelines (section 4.4) and flaky jobs both produce emails nobody needs.

**Key takeaways**

- Personal notifications go to the user who triggered the pipeline: the pusher, the person who ran it, or the schedule owner.
- Failed and fixed pipeline emails are on by default. Successful pipeline emails need the Custom notification level.
- The Pipeline status emails integration sends results to fixed recipients, filtered to broken pipelines and selected branches.
- Use `X-GitLab-*` headers to filter mail, and remove noise at the source (duplicates, flakiness).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Set your notification level for one project to **Custom** with only Failed and Fixed pipeline enabled. Break and fix a pipeline, and check which emails arrive.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Configure Pipeline status emails for a team address, limited to broken pipelines on the default branch. Then create a scheduled pipeline owned by a bot or service account and work out who is notified when it fails.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A nightly security scan has been failing for three weeks and nobody noticed. What went wrong, and how do you prevent it from happening again?" *Hint:* schedule ownership, who receives failure emails, team-level notifications and chat alerts.

#### Slack and Microsoft Teams Integrations

**Why they exist.** Teams coordinate in chat. A failed deployment posted in the team channel is seen within minutes, discussed in a thread and fixed, while an email to one person may sit unread. Chat integrations also make events visible to people who did not trigger them, which is what you want for the default branch and production.

**Slack.** The recommended integration is the **GitLab for Slack app**. It sends notifications to channels and adds slash commands. On GitLab.com you install it from the project's **Settings > Integrations**. On self-managed instances, an administrator must set it up first. The older **Slack notifications** integration, based on Slack incoming webhooks, is deprecated in favor of the app.

**Microsoft Teams.** The **Microsoft Teams notifications** integration posts to a channel through an incoming webhook URL that you create in Teams. Microsoft is retiring the older Office 365 connectors, so create the webhook with the Teams **Workflows** app and follow GitLab's documentation for the current steps.

**What to configure.** Both integrations offer similar options:

| Option | Recommended setting |
|---|---|
| Trigger events | Pipeline and deployment events, and whatever else the channel's audience needs. Avoid push events in busy projects |
| Notify only broken pipelines | On, for team channels |
| Branches for which notifications are sent | Default branch, or default and protected branches |
| Channel per event (Slack) | Separate channels for deployments and failures, so one does not drown out the other |

```bash
# Microsoft Teams: notify a channel about broken pipelines on default and protected branches only
curl --request PUT --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/integrations/microsoft-teams" \
  --data-urlencode "webhook=$TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL" \
  --data "pipeline_events=true" \
  --data "push_events=false" \
  --data "notify_only_broken_pipelines=true" \
  --data "branches_to_be_notified=default_and_protected"
```

**ChatOps with Slack slash commands.** The GitLab for Slack app adds `/gitlab` commands, so that people can act without leaving the chat:

```text
/gitlab shop/api issue show 42                  # show an issue in the channel
/gitlab shop/api deploy staging to production   # run the manual production job of the latest staging deployment
/gitlab shop/api run smoke-test                 # ChatOps: run a CI job whose output is posted back
```

ChatOps commands run CI jobs with the permissions of the GitLab user linked to the Slack account, so protected branch and environment rules still apply.

**Custom messages from a job.** Integrations send generic event messages. For a tailored message, such as a deployment announcement with the version and changelog link, post to a webhook from a job. This works with any chat tool that accepts webhooks:

```yaml
announce-deploy:
  stage: .post
  image:
    name: curlimages/curl:8.10.1
    entrypoint: [""]                 # the image's entrypoint is curl itself; reset it for the runner
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG             # only for release pipelines
  script:
    - |
      curl --fail --silent --show-error -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
        --data "{\"text\": \"Deployed ${CI_PROJECT_PATH} ${CI_COMMIT_TAG} to production: ${CI_PIPELINE_URL}\"}" \
        "$SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL"         # masked, protected variable (section 5.2)
```

Build the JSON with `jq` if the message contains free text, such as a commit title, so that quotes and newlines are escaped correctly.

**Key takeaways**

- Use the GitLab for Slack app (the webhook-based Slack integration is deprecated) and the Microsoft Teams notifications integration (with a Workflows webhook).
- Limit team channels to broken pipelines on default and protected branches, and to deployments.
- Slack slash commands enable ChatOps, which respects the linked user's permissions.
- For tailored messages, post to a chat webhook from a job, with the webhook URL in a masked, protected variable.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Connect a test project to a Slack or Teams channel and enable pipeline events for broken pipelines on the default branch only. Break the default branch and check the message.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a job that runs only when a production deployment fails (`when: on_failure` in its rules) and posts a message to a chat webhook containing the environment, the failed job name and a link to the pipeline. Use `jq` to build the payload.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your deployment channel receives so many notifications that people muted it. How would you redesign the notification setup?" *Hint:* events per channel, broken-only, branch filters, deployments versus pipelines, and actionable messages.

#### Pipeline Webhooks

**Why they exist.** Built-in integrations cover common tools. Everything else needs a hook: opening a ticket in your service desk when production deployment fails, updating an internal dashboard, triggering a job in another CI system, collecting pipeline data for analytics. Webhooks let GitLab call *your* HTTP endpoint whenever an event happens, so you do not have to poll the API.

**What is sent.** Under **Settings > Webhooks** you choose a URL, a secret token and the trigger events. For CI/CD, the relevant triggers are:

| Trigger | `X-Gitlab-Event` header | `object_kind` | Fires when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pipeline events | `Pipeline Hook` | `pipeline` | A pipeline's status changes (created, running, success, failed, canceled...) |
| Job events | `Job Hook` | `build` | A job's status changes |
| Deployment events | `Deployment Hook` | `deployment` | A deployment starts, succeeds, fails or is canceled |
| Release events | `Release Hook` | `release` | A release is created, updated or deleted |

A pipeline event payload (abridged) looks like this:

```json
{
  "object_kind": "pipeline",
  "object_attributes": {
    "id": 98765,
    "ref": "main",
    "tag": false,
    "sha": "1a2b3c4d5e6f...",
    "source": "push",
    "status": "failed",
    "duration": 412,
    "queued_duration": 9,
    "url": "https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/-/pipelines/98765"
  },
  "user": { "username": "alice", "name": "Alice Example" },
  "project": { "path_with_namespace": "shop/api", "default_branch": "main" },
  "commit": { "title": "Apply discount once", "url": "https://gitlab.example.com/shop/api/-/commit/1a2b3c4d" },
  "builds": [
    { "name": "unit-tests", "stage": "test", "status": "failed", "failure_reason": "script_failure" },
    { "name": "build", "stage": "build", "status": "success" }
  ]
}
```

**Receiving webhooks safely.** A webhook receiver is a public endpoint that triggers actions, so treat it like any other API:

1. **Verify the secret token.** GitLab sends it in the `X-Gitlab-Token` header. Compare it in constant time and reject mismatches.
2. **Respond quickly.** GitLab waits only a few seconds (10 by default) for a response. Acknowledge immediately and do the work asynchronously.
3. **Expect duplicates and many events.** One pipeline produces several events (pending, running, then a final status), and deliveries can be retried. Filter on the status you care about, and use the `X-Gitlab-Event-UUID` header (and `Idempotency-Key` in recent versions) to ignore repeats.
4. **Filter in the receiver.** Branch filters in the webhook settings apply to push events only. For pipelines, check `ref`, `source` (child pipelines have `source: parent_pipeline`) and `status` yourself.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# hook_receiver.py: react to failed pipelines on the default branch
# Usage: GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=... python3 hook_receiver.py
import hmac
import json
import os
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

SECRET = os.environ["GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET"]
seen = set()                                              # event UUIDs already handled (in memory)

def handle(event):
    attrs, project = event["object_attributes"], event["project"]
    if attrs["status"] != "failed" or attrs["ref"] != project["default_branch"]:
        return                                            # only a red default branch matters here
    if attrs.get("source") == "parent_pipeline":
        return                                            # the parent pipeline reports it already
    failed = [b["name"] for b in event.get("builds", []) if b["status"] == "failed"]
    # Replace print with a call to your ticketing or paging system
    print(f"{project['path_with_namespace']}: {attrs['ref']} is red, "
          f"failed jobs: {', '.join(failed)} ({attrs['url']})")

class Hook(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        token = self.headers.get("X-Gitlab-Token", "")
        if not hmac.compare_digest(token, SECRET):        # constant-time comparison
            self.send_response(401)
            self.end_headers()
            return
        body = self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"]))
        self.send_response(200)                           # acknowledge first...
        self.end_headers()
        uuid = self.headers.get("X-Gitlab-Event-UUID")
        if self.headers.get("X-Gitlab-Event") == "Pipeline Hook" and uuid not in seen:
            seen.add(uuid)
            threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(json.loads(body),)).start()   # ...then work

HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), Hook).serve_forever()
```

```bash
# Register the webhook for pipeline events only
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/hooks" \
  --data "url=https://hooks.example.com/gitlab" \
  --data "token=$GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET" \
  --data "pipeline_events=true" \
  --data "push_events=false"
```

**Operating webhooks.**

- **Recent events.** Each webhook's edit page lists recent deliveries, with request, response and status code, and can resend them. It is the first place to look when "the hook didn't fire".
- **Test.** The **Test** button sends a sample event of the chosen type, which is useful while building a receiver.
- **Automatic disabling.** Webhooks that keep failing are disabled temporarily, and permanently after many consecutive failures. Monitor your receiver and re-enable the hook after fixing it.
- **Scope.** Project webhooks are available on all tiers. Group webhooks (Premium) receive events from every project in the group, which suits central tooling. Instance-wide system hooks are an administrator feature and do not include pipeline events.

**Key takeaways**

- Pipeline, job, deployment and release events can be delivered to any HTTP endpoint as JSON, identified by the `X-Gitlab-Event` header.
- Verify `X-Gitlab-Token` in constant time, respond within seconds, and process events asynchronously.
- Expect several events per pipeline and possible repeats. Filter by status, ref and source, and deduplicate with the event UUID.
- Use **Recent events** to debug deliveries. Repeatedly failing webhooks are disabled automatically.
- Group webhooks (Premium) centralize automation across many projects.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Point a project webhook with pipeline events at a request inspection service you control (or the receiver above, exposed through a tunnel). Run a pipeline and count how many events it produces.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Extend `hook_receiver.py` to compute, per project, the time from a default-branch pipeline failing to the next successful one, using only webhook events. Persist state so that a restart does not lose it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "You built a webhook receiver that creates a ticket for every failed production deployment, but sometimes two tickets are created for the same failure. Why, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* retries, multiple event types, idempotency keys, and acknowledging before processing.

#### External Commit Status Reporting

**Why it exists.** Not every check runs in GitLab CI. A legacy Jenkins job, a performance lab, a third-party scanner or a hardware test rig may validate the same commit. Their results belong next to GitLab's own jobs, in the pipeline and the merge request, and must be able to block a merge. In the other direction, when GitLab CI builds code hosted elsewhere (for example on GitHub), its results must show up on that platform. Commit statuses connect the two.

**Options.**

| Mechanism | Direction | Attaches to | Can block merging | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Commit Status API | External system → GitLab | A commit (appears as a job in the pipeline) | Yes, through "Pipelines must succeed" | All |
| External status checks | GitLab → external service → GitLab | A merge request | Yes, with "Status checks must succeed" | Ultimate |
| CI/CD for external repositories + GitHub integration | GitLab CI → GitHub | A GitHub commit or pull request | Yes, through GitHub branch protection | Premium |
| Calling another platform's status API from a job | GitLab CI → anywhere | Whatever that platform supports | Depends on that platform | All |

**The Commit Status API.** An external system posts a state for a commit SHA. GitLab shows each status as a job in an **external** stage of that commit's pipeline. If no pipeline exists for the SHA, GitLab creates one:

```text
Pipeline #98765  (push, main)
     build              test                 external
 ┌────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────┐
 │ (v) build  │──►│ (v) unit     │   │ (>) perf/load-test      │  <- posted by the perf lab,
 └────────────┘   └──────────────┘   │ (v) jenkins/integration │     links to its own UI
                                     └─────────────────────────┘
```

```bash
# Called by the external system: report that the load test started, then its result
API="https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/statuses/$SHA"

curl --fail --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" "$API" \
  --data-urlencode "state=running" \
  --data-urlencode "name=perf/load-test" \
  --data-urlencode "ref=feature/cart" \
  --data-urlencode "target_url=https://perf.example.com/runs/881" \
  --data-urlencode "description=Load test started"

# ... later ...
curl --fail --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" "$API" \
  --data-urlencode "state=failed" \
  --data-urlencode "name=perf/load-test" \
  --data-urlencode "ref=feature/cart" \
  --data-urlencode "target_url=https://perf.example.com/runs/881" \
  --data-urlencode "description=p95 latency 640 ms exceeds budget of 400 ms"
```

The key fields are:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state` | `pending`, `running`, `success`, `failed`, `canceled` or `skipped` |
| `name` (or `context`) | Identifies the check. Posting again with the same name updates that status |
| `ref` | The branch or tag. It determines which pipeline the status joins |
| `pipeline_id` | Attach to a specific pipeline when one SHA has several |
| `target_url`, `description` | Link to and summary of the external result, shown in GitLab |
| `coverage` | Optional coverage value, as for GitLab jobs |

Two details often cause errors. First, states must follow a valid sequence: a status that is already `success` cannot go back to `running`, and the API rejects such a transition. Use a new `name` for a rerun, or post the final state directly. Second, the token's user must have at least the Developer role in the project. Use a project access token with the `api` scope for each external system, so that every status can be traced to its source.

Jenkins is the most common example: the GitLab plugin for Jenkins uses this API to report stage results back to GitLab, so the merge request shows Jenkins results alongside GitLab CI jobs.

**External status checks (Ultimate).** These work at the merge request level instead of the commit level. GitLab sends merge request data to a configured external service whenever the MR changes. The service evaluates it (for example a compliance or change-management system) and responds through the API:

```bash
# Called by the external service after evaluating merge request !128
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/12345/merge_requests/128/status_check_responses" \
  --data "sha=$MR_HEAD_SHA" \
  --data "external_status_check_id=7" \
  --data "status=passed"         # or failed
```

**Reporting GitLab results to other platforms.** When the code lives on GitHub, **CI/CD for external repositories** (Premium) mirrors the repository into GitLab and runs pipelines there, and the **GitHub integration** posts pipeline statuses back to GitHub commits and pull requests. For other platforms, or for finer control, a job can call the platform's status API directly:

```yaml
.report-github:
  stage: .post
  image:
    name: curlimages/curl:8.10.1
    entrypoint: [""]
  script:
    - |
      curl --fail --silent -X POST \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
        -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
        "https://api.github.com/repos/acme/shop-api/statuses/$CI_COMMIT_SHA" \
        -d "{\"state\": \"$GH_STATE\", \"context\": \"gitlab-ci\", \"target_url\": \"$CI_PIPELINE_URL\"}"

report-success:
  extends: .report-github
  variables:
    GH_STATE: success
  rules:
    - when: on_success               # every job in earlier stages passed

report-failure:
  extends: .report-github
  variables:
    GH_STATE: failure
  rules:
    - when: on_failure               # at least one job in an earlier stage failed
```

GitLab has no predefined variable that holds the overall pipeline status during the run, so the pattern uses two jobs in `.post` and lets `when: on_success` and `when: on_failure` choose which one runs. The built-in GitHub integration does this for you.

**Key takeaways**

- The Commit Status API lets any external system add a check to a commit. It appears as a job in the `external` stage and counts for "Pipelines must succeed".
- Identify each check with a stable `name`, attach it to the right `ref` (or `pipeline_id`), and respect valid state transitions.
- Give each external system its own project access token with the `api` scope.
- External status checks (Ultimate) gate merge requests through an external service's pass or fail response.
- For code hosted on GitHub, CI/CD for external repositories with the GitHub integration (Premium) reports GitLab pipeline results back automatically.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Use the Commit Status API to post `running` and then `success` for a check named `manual/review` on the latest commit of a branch. Find it in the pipeline graph and in the merge request.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Enable "Pipelines must succeed" on a project, then post a `failed` external status to an MR's head commit. Confirm that merging is blocked, and work out how the external system can unblock it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your company runs GitLab CI and a separate hardware-in-the-loop test lab. How would you make the lab's results block merge requests, and what would happen when the lab is offline?" *Hint:* commit status versus external status checks, `pending` states, timeouts, and who can override a blocked merge.

---

<a id="15-administration-automation-and-migration"></a>
## 15. Administration, Automation and Migration

The earlier chapters looked at GitLab CI/CD from inside one project. This chapter takes the view of the people who run it for many projects at once: administrators who set instance-wide defaults and limits, platform teams who give hundreds of teams shared building blocks and enforce standards, and engineers who automate GitLab through its APIs, its CLI and Terraform. It ends with moving existing pipelines from Jenkins, GitHub Actions, CircleCI and Azure DevOps to GitLab without stopping delivery along the way.

> **Tiers at a glance.** Instance settings, plan limits, object storage and instance-level variables are available on **all tiers**, but only to administrators of a self-managed instance. GitLab Dedicated exposes some of them through its own console, and GitLab.com exposes none. CI/CD components, the CI/CD Catalog, the REST and GraphQL APIs, `glab`, the Terraform provider and external CI configuration files also work on **all tiers**. The instance template repository, custom project templates, compliance frameworks, protected environment approvals, compute quotas for instance runners on self-managed, and CI/CD for external repositories require **Premium**. Pipeline execution policies and scan execution policies require **Ultimate**.

<a id="151-instance-level-cicd-administration"></a>
### 15.1 Instance-Level CI/CD Administration

On a self-managed instance, one administrator decision affects every project. This subchapter covers the settings that control CI/CD defaults, the limits that protect the instance from runaway pipelines, where artifacts and job logs are physically stored, how long logs live, and how to offer teams ready-made templates. Every topic here requires administrator access (**Admin area**) on a self-managed instance.

```text
 Admin area (instance)            Top-level group            Project
 ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────┐
 │ defaults             │ ──────► │ may override   │ ──────► │ may override       │
 │ (artifact expiry,    │         │ some defaults  │         │ some defaults      │
 │  Auto DevOps, ...)   │         └────────────────┘         └────────────────────┘
 │                      │
 │ ceilings and limits  │ ──────► apply everywhere; only an administrator can raise them
 │ (artifact size, jobs │
 │  per pipeline, ...)  │
 └──────────────────────┘
```

#### Instance CI/CD Settings

**Why it matters.** A self-managed GitLab instance may host thousands of projects. Configuring each one by hand is not realistic, so most CI/CD behavior starts from instance-wide defaults. Think of them as a building code: the city sets minimum rules once, and each owner can furnish their own house within them. Some instance settings are only **defaults** that groups or projects can override. Others are **ceilings** that only an administrator can change. Before you change one, know which kind it is.

**Where to find them.** Most settings are in **Admin area > Settings > CI/CD**, under *Continuous Integration and Deployment*. All of them can also be read and changed through the Application settings API (`/application/settings`), which is what you should use to keep the configuration reviewable and repeatable.

| Setting (UI) | API attribute | Default | Effect | Kind |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Default to Auto DevOps pipeline for all projects | `auto_devops_enabled` | On | Projects without a `.gitlab-ci.yml` run Auto DevOps (section 12.6) | Default |
| Enable instance runners for new projects | `shared_runners_enabled` | On | New projects can use instance runners | Default |
| Maximum artifacts size (MB) | `max_artifacts_size` | 100 | Largest artifact archive a job can upload | Ceiling (administrators can set it per group or project) |
| Default artifacts expiration | `default_artifacts_expire_in` | 30 days | Applies to jobs that do not set `artifacts:expire_in` | Default |
| Keep the latest artifacts for all jobs in the latest successful pipelines | `keep_latest_artifact` | On | Artifacts of the latest successful pipeline per ref never expire | Default (projects can turn it off) |
| Archive jobs | `archive_builds_in_human_readable` | Not set | Jobs older than this can no longer be retried or run | Instance-wide |
| Default CI/CD configuration file | `default_ci_config_path` | `.gitlab-ci.yml` | Path used by new projects | Default |
| Maximum includes | `ci_max_includes` | 150 | Number of `include` entries a pipeline can resolve | Ceiling |
| Protect CI/CD variables by default | `protected_ci_variables` | Off | New variables are created as protected | Default |
| Instance runner compute quota (Premium) | `shared_runners_minutes` | 0 (unlimited) | Compute minutes per namespace per month on instance runners | Ceiling (overridable per namespace) |

The exact list changes between releases. Read the CI/CD settings page of your version's documentation before an upgrade, because new settings sometimes come with a new default.

**Reading and changing settings through the API.** Store the desired values in a repository and apply them from a pipeline or a script, so that every change is reviewed and recorded:

```bash
# Read the current CI/CD-related settings (requires an administrator token)
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/application/settings" |
  jq '{auto_devops_enabled, shared_runners_enabled, max_artifacts_size,
       default_artifacts_expire_in, keep_latest_artifact,
       archive_builds_in_human_readable, ci_max_includes}'

# Change them: shorter default expiry, larger artifacts, Auto DevOps off by default
curl --silent --request PUT --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/application/settings" \
  --data "default_artifacts_expire_in=7 days" \
  --data "max_artifacts_size=250" \
  --data "auto_devops_enabled=false" \
  --data "archive_builds_in_human_readable=1 year"   # jobs older than a year become read-only
```

**Instance-level CI/CD variables.** Variables defined in **Admin area > Settings > CI/CD > Variables** (or through `/admin/ci/variables`) are available to every job on the instance. They have the lowest precedence of all stored variables: group and project variables with the same key override them (section 5.1).

```bash
# Corporate HTTP proxy, available to every job on the instance
curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/admin/ci/variables" \
  --data "key=HTTPS_PROXY" \
  --data "value=http://proxy.corp.example.com:3128" \
  --data "protected=false"           # also needed on feature branches
```

Instance variables are a good place for infrastructure facts that every job needs: proxy settings, the hostname of an internal registry or package mirror, a certificate bundle. They are a poor place for secrets. Any user who can edit a `.gitlab-ci.yml` on the instance can print a variable that reaches their job, so an instance-wide secret is effectively shared with every developer. Keep secrets at the narrowest scope possible, and preferably in an external secrets manager (section 5.4).

**Key takeaways**

- Instance settings are either **defaults** (groups and projects can override them) or **ceilings** (only an administrator can raise them). Know which kind a setting is before you change it.
- Manage settings through the Application settings API from version control, not through clicks in the Admin area.
- Shorter default artifact expiry and "Archive jobs" are the simplest instance-wide levers on storage and database growth.
- Instance variables have the lowest precedence and reach every job. Use them for shared infrastructure facts, never for secrets.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* On a test instance, find the default artifact expiration and the maximum artifact size in the Admin area, then read the same values through the API with `curl` and `jq`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Write a small script that stores the desired CI/CD application settings in a JSON file, compares them with the live values, and prints the differences before applying them. Run it from a scheduled pipeline in an "instance-config" project.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A team asks you to add their deployment token as an instance-level CI/CD variable because 'every project needs it'. What do you answer?" *Hint:* who can read variables in a job, precedence, group variables, and an external secrets manager with OIDC.

#### Pipeline and Job Limits

**Why it matters.** A shared instance has to be protected from mistakes. A typo in a `parallel:matrix` can create thousands of jobs, a trigger loop can spawn downstream pipelines endlessly, and a test that prints a stack trace in a loop can produce a log of several gigabytes. Limits work like circuit breakers: they stop one project from exhausting resources that everyone else depends on. As an administrator, you need to know which limits exist, where they are configured, and what users see when they hit one.

**Categories of limits.**

| Category | Examples | Where it is configured |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration size | Maximum YAML size and nesting depth, maximum number of includes | Application settings |
| Pipeline shape | Jobs per pipeline (`ci_pipeline_size`), jobs listed in `needs` (`ci_needs_size_limit`, default 50), pipelines in one parent-child or multi-project hierarchy (`pipeline_hierarchy_size`, default 1000), jobs created by one `parallel` or `parallel:matrix` (200) | Plan limits (the 200 job limit for `parallel` is fixed) |
| Activity | Jobs in active pipelines (`ci_active_jobs`), pipeline schedules per project (`ci_pipeline_schedules`), pipeline subscriptions (`ci_project_subscriptions`), pipeline creation rate per project, user and commit | Plan limits, **Admin area > Settings > Network** |
| Data size | Job log size (`ci_jobs_trace_size_limit`, default 100 MB), artifact size (overall and per report type), `dotenv` report size and number of variables | Plan limits, application settings |
| Time | Project job timeout (default 60 minutes), the runner's `maximum_timeout` | Project settings, runner settings (section 6.3) |
| Runner side | `concurrent`, `limit`, `output_limit` (log size the runner sends) | Runner `config.toml` (section 6.3) |

**Plan limits.** Many CI limits are stored per *plan*. GitLab.com has several plans (Free, Premium, Ultimate). A self-managed instance normally has only one, called `default`, so changing `default` changes the limit for the whole instance. On self-managed, a value of `0` usually means "no limit".

```bash
# Inspect the CI limits of the default plan
curl --silent --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/application/plan_limits?plan_name=default" |
  jq '{ci_pipeline_size, ci_active_jobs, ci_needs_size_limit,
       ci_pipeline_schedules, ci_project_subscriptions, pipeline_hierarchy_size}'

# Cap pipelines at 2,000 jobs and active jobs at 5,000 per project
curl --silent --request PUT --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/application/plan_limits" \
  --data "plan_name=default" \
  --data "ci_pipeline_size=2000" \
  --data "ci_active_jobs=5000"
```

Some limits are not exposed through the API and are changed from the Rails console on a GitLab node:

```ruby
# sudo gitlab-rails console
limits = Plan.default.actual_limits

limits.update!(ci_jobs_trace_size_limit: 200)  # maximum job log size, in MB
limits.update!(dotenv_variables: 50,           # variables a dotenv report may define
               dotenv_size: 10.kilobytes)      # maximum size of the dotenv file
```

**What users see.** When a limit is reached, GitLab refuses to create the pipeline or the job, or truncates the data, and it says why. Common symptoms:

| Symptom | Limit involved | Usual fix (before raising the limit) |
|---|---|---|
| Pipeline not created, error about too many jobs | `ci_pipeline_size` | Split into parent-child pipelines (section 3.3) |
| Pipeline not created, error about too many active jobs | `ci_active_jobs` | Auto-cancel redundant pipelines, mark jobs `interruptible` (section 4.4) |
| YAML error: a job needs too many jobs | `ci_needs_size_limit` | Use stages or an aggregation job instead of a very long `needs` list |
| YAML error: too many includes, or the configuration is too large | `ci_max_includes`, YAML size | Merge small includes, use components with inputs |
| Downstream pipeline not created | `pipeline_hierarchy_size`, downstream rate limit | Look for trigger loops; reduce fan-out |
| Log ends with a "log exceeded limit" message | Runner `output_limit` or `ci_jobs_trace_size_limit` | Reduce verbosity; save the full output as an artifact |
| `dotenv` variables missing in later jobs | `dotenv_variables`, `dotenv_size` | Pass fewer values, or use a JSON artifact |

**A sound policy.** A limit hit is a symptom. Before raising one, ask whether the pipeline should be designed differently. Raise a limit when the need is legitimate (a large monorepo, a test matrix that really needs 300 combinations), and document why. Keep a record of changed limits next to the application settings in version control, because limits are easy to forget during an upgrade or a migration to a new instance.

**Key takeaways**

- Limits protect a shared instance from runaway pipelines: too many jobs, trigger loops, huge logs and artifacts.
- Most CI limits are **plan limits**. On self-managed, the `default` plan applies to the whole instance, and you change it through the Plan limits API or the Rails console.
- Runner-side limits (`output_limit`, `concurrent`, `maximum_timeout`) are configured separately, on the runner.
- Treat a limit hit as a design problem first, and raise limits deliberately and with a written reason.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Read the `default` plan limits of a test instance through the API and write down the values of `ci_pipeline_size`, `ci_needs_size_limit` and `ci_pipeline_schedules`.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Set `ci_pipeline_size` to 10 on a test instance, then push a pipeline with 12 jobs. Read the error, restore the limit, and rewrite the pipeline as a parent with two child pipelines that stay under the limit.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Users complain that pipelines 'sometimes don't start' after a busy release day. How do you find out which limit, if any, is responsible?" *Hint:* the error shown on the pipeline page, `ci_active_jobs`, the pipeline creation rate limit, and the instance logs.

#### Artifact and Log Object Storage

**Why it matters.** Artifacts and job logs are the fastest-growing data in most GitLab instances. By default they are written to the local disk of the GitLab node. That works for a single small server and fails as soon as the instance grows: disks fill up, backups become slow, and with several web and Sidekiq nodes every node needs access to the same files. **Object storage** (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, or an S3-compatible system such as MinIO) solves all three problems. It scales without resizing disks, it is cheaper per gigabyte, and every node can reach it.

**What GitLab stores, and where.**

| Data | Default local path (Linux package) | Object type in the configuration |
|---|---|---|
| Job artifacts, including archived job logs | `/var/opt/gitlab/gitlab-rails/shared/artifacts` | `artifacts` |
| Live job log chunks (default mode) | `/var/opt/gitlab/gitlab-ci/builds` | Not used unless incremental logging is enabled |
| Package registry files | `/var/opt/gitlab/gitlab-rails/shared/packages` | `packages` |
| Terraform state | `/var/opt/gitlab/gitlab-rails/shared/terraform_state` | `terraform_state` |
| Secure files | `/var/opt/gitlab/gitlab-rails/shared/ci_secure_files` | `ci_secure_files` |
| LFS objects, uploads, merge request diffs, Pages, dependency proxy | Various paths under `shared/` | `lfs`, `uploads`, `external_diffs`, `pages`, `dependency_proxy` |

The runner's distributed cache is separate: it is configured on the runner, not in GitLab (section 8.2).

**How a job log travels.** Understanding the path of a log explains most storage questions:

```text
 Runner                       GitLab (Rails / Sidekiq)                       Storage
 ┌───────────┐  PATCH chunks  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
 │ job runs, │ ─────────────► │ 1. live log is appended           │ ──► local disk (builds dir)
 │ streams   │                │    (or kept in Redis and object   │     or Redis + object storage
 │ output    │                │     storage with incremental      │     (incremental logging)
 └───────────┘                │     logging)                      │
                              │ 2. job finishes: Sidekiq archives │
                              │    the log as a "trace" artifact  │ ──► artifacts storage
                              └───────────────────────────────────┘     (local or object storage)
```

Once a job finishes, its log is stored like an artifact. Moving artifacts to object storage therefore moves archived logs as well. Live logs are different: in the default mode they are written to a local directory, which every Rails node must share. **Incremental logging** keeps live chunks in Redis and object storage instead, removing the need for shared storage in a multi-node installation. It is enabled with the `ci_enable_live_trace` feature flag and requires object storage.

**Configuring object storage (Linux package).** The *consolidated* form in `/etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb` defines the connection once and one bucket per object type. Use a separate bucket for each type:

```ruby
# /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb
gitlab_rails['object_store']['enabled'] = true
gitlab_rails['object_store']['proxy_download'] = false        # clients download directly with pre-signed URLs
gitlab_rails['object_store']['connection'] = {
  'provider' => 'AWS',
  'region' => 'eu-central-1',
  'use_iam_profile' => true                                   # instance role instead of static keys
}
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['artifacts']['bucket']       = 'acme-gitlab-artifacts'
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['packages']['bucket']        = 'acme-gitlab-packages'
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['terraform_state']['bucket'] = 'acme-gitlab-terraform-state'
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['ci_secure_files']['bucket'] = 'acme-gitlab-secure-files'
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['lfs']['bucket']             = 'acme-gitlab-lfs'
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['uploads']['bucket']         = 'acme-gitlab-uploads'
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['external_diffs']['bucket']  = 'acme-gitlab-mr-diffs'
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['dependency_proxy']['bucket'] = 'acme-gitlab-dependency-proxy'
gitlab_rails['object_store']['objects']['pages']['bucket']           = 'acme-gitlab-pages'
```

Apply it with `sudo gitlab-ctl reconfigure`. On Helm chart installations, the equivalent settings live under `global.appConfig.object_store` and per-type `global.appConfig.<type>.bucket`.

**Moving existing data.** Changing the configuration affects only new files. Existing files stay on disk until you migrate them:

```bash
# Move existing artifacts (including archived job logs) to object storage
sudo gitlab-rake gitlab:artifacts:migrate

# Other CI-related data
sudo gitlab-rake gitlab:packages:migrate
sudo gitlab-rake gitlab:terraform_states:migrate
sudo gitlab-rake gitlab:ci_secure_files:migrate

# Check that nothing is left behind before deleting local files
sudo find /var/opt/gitlab/gitlab-rails/shared/artifacts -type f | grep -v tmp | wc -l
```

**Operational points.**

- **`proxy_download`.** With `false`, users and runners download directly from the bucket using pre-signed URLs, which keeps load off GitLab. Set it to `true` when clients cannot reach the bucket directly, for example from an isolated network.
- **Do not let bucket lifecycle rules delete GitLab data.** GitLab's database keeps a record of every file. If a lifecycle rule deletes objects, the records stay and downloads fail. Expire data through GitLab (`expire_in`, pipeline cleanup) so that the database and the bucket stay consistent. Lifecycle rules are safe for storage *classes* (moving old objects to cheaper tiers) only if GitLab can still read them without a restore step.
- **Backups.** The GitLab backup does not include object storage. Back the buckets up separately, for example with versioning and cross-region replication.
- **Least privilege.** Prefer instance roles or workload identity over static access keys, and grant GitLab access only to its own buckets.

**Key takeaways**

- Object storage is the standard for artifacts, logs and packages beyond a single small server: it scales, costs less, and every node can reach it.
- Archived job logs are stored as artifacts, so they follow the `artifacts` object storage configuration. Live logs need incremental logging to leave local disk.
- Use the consolidated configuration with one bucket per object type, then migrate existing data with the `gitlab:*:migrate` Rake tasks.
- Delete data through GitLab, not through bucket lifecycle rules, and back up buckets separately.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* On a test instance with MinIO, configure the consolidated object storage for artifacts only. Run a job that uploads an artifact and find the object in the bucket.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Migrate existing artifacts with `gitlab:artifacts:migrate`. Verify that old artifacts and old job logs can still be downloaded and viewed, and measure how much local disk space was freed.
> 3. **Interview question:** "To save money, someone added a lifecycle rule that deletes objects older than 90 days from the artifacts bucket. What problems will users see, and what would you do instead?" *Hint:* database records pointing to missing files, `keep_latest_artifact`, archived logs, `expire_in` and pipeline cleanup.

#### Job Log Retention

**Why it matters.** Unlike artifacts, job logs have **no expiration by default**. An instance running a few thousand jobs a day accumulates terabytes of logs over the years. Logs also carry risk: a secret printed by mistake stays readable for as long as the log exists. On the other hand, some organizations must keep build and deployment logs for a fixed time as audit evidence. A retention policy reconciles these needs: keep what you must, delete what you can.

**What does *not* delete logs.**

- `artifacts:expire_in` and the default artifact expiration remove artifacts, not the job log.
- The **Archive jobs** setting makes old jobs read-only (they can no longer be retried), but keeps their logs.
- Deleting objects from the bucket directly breaks the database references (see the previous topic).

**What does delete logs.**

| Mechanism | Scope | Removes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Erase job** (UI or `POST /projects/:id/jobs/:job_id/erase`) | One job | Log and artifacts of that job | For leaked secrets; requires Maintainer |
| **Delete pipeline** (UI or `DELETE /projects/:id/pipelines/:pipeline_id`) | One pipeline | The pipeline, its jobs, logs and artifacts | Requires Owner |
| **Automatic pipeline cleanup** (project setting on recent versions, API attribute `ci_delete_pipelines_in_seconds`) | One project | Pipelines older than the configured age, with everything attached | The easiest durable policy. Check whether your version has it |
| Script over the Pipelines API | Any set of projects | Pipelines older than a cutoff | Works on every version. Shown below |

**Designing a policy.** Decide retention per *class* of project rather than per project:

| Class | Example | Suggested retention | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regulated production services | Payments, health data | As required by the regulation (often 1 to 7 years), for deployment pipelines at least | Audit evidence |
| Ordinary services | Most product teams | 6 to 12 months | Enough to investigate regressions |
| Experiments, sandboxes | Training projects | 30 to 90 days | No long-term value |

For audit evidence, a full job log is often not the best record anyway. Release evidence (section 8.4), deployment records in environments (section 12.1) and audit events (section 11.3) are smaller, structured and easier to show an auditor.

**Example: a retention job over the API.** This script deletes pipelines older than a cutoff in every project of a group, except projects marked as regulated. It runs as a scheduled pipeline in an administration project:

```python
# prune_pipelines.py: delete pipelines older than RETENTION_DAYS in a group
# Usage: GITLAB_TOKEN=glpat-... python3 prune_pipelines.py acme 180 [--dry-run]
import datetime
import os
import sys

import gitlab

group_path, days = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
dry_run = "--dry-run" in sys.argv
cutoff = (datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)
          - datetime.timedelta(days=days)).isoformat()

gl = gitlab.Gitlab("https://gitlab.example.com", private_token=os.environ["GITLAB_TOKEN"])
group = gl.groups.get(group_path)

for ref in group.projects.list(include_subgroups=True, archived=False, iterator=True):
    project = gl.projects.get(ref.id)
    if "retention:regulated" in project.topics:          # opt-out for audited projects
        continue
    old = project.pipelines.list(updated_before=cutoff, iterator=True)
    for pipeline in old:
        print(f"{project.path_with_namespace} #{pipeline.id} {pipeline.updated_at}")
        if not dry_run:
            pipeline.delete()                             # removes jobs, logs and artifacts
```

Run it with `--dry-run` first and review the output. Deletion is irreversible.

**Handling a leaked secret.** When a secret appears in a log, retention policy is too slow. Erase the job immediately, rotate the secret, and check whether other jobs printed it too, for example with the log search technique from section 14.1.

**Key takeaways**

- Job logs never expire by default. Artifact expiration and "Archive jobs" do not remove them.
- Delete logs through GitLab (erase job, delete pipeline, automatic pipeline cleanup, API scripts) so that the database and storage stay consistent.
- Define retention per class of project, balancing audit requirements, risk and storage cost.
- For audit purposes, structured evidence (releases, deployments, audit events) is usually better than raw logs.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Erase the log of one job through the API and confirm in the UI that the log and the artifacts are gone but the job entry remains.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Run the retention script with `--dry-run` against a test group, add a project topic to exclude one project, and schedule the script to run weekly with a project access token.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your security team wants all job logs deleted after 30 days, and your compliance team wants deployment logs kept for five years. How do you satisfy both?" *Hint:* classes of projects, separate deployment projects or pipelines, structured evidence instead of raw logs.

#### Instance Template Repository

**Why it matters.** When a developer creates a new file in the GitLab web editor and chooses **Apply a template**, GitLab offers built-in templates for `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Dockerfile`, `.gitignore` and `LICENSE` files. Those are generic. Most organizations want to offer *their own* starting points: a `.gitlab-ci.yml` that already includes the company's components, a `Dockerfile` based on the approved base image. The **instance template repository** (Premium, self-managed) adds these organization templates to the same dropdown.

**How it works.** An administrator selects a project in **Admin area > Settings > Templates**. Files in specific top-level directories of that project's default branch appear in the template dropdowns across the instance:

```text
platform/file-templates  (project selected as the instance template repository)
├── gitlab-ci/
│   ├── node-service.yml          -> appears under ".gitlab-ci.yml" templates as "node-service"
│   └── java-library.yml
├── Dockerfile/
│   └── python-api.dockerfile     -> appears under "Dockerfile" templates
├── gitignore/
│   └── acme-java.gitignore
└── LICENSE/
    └── acme-proprietary.txt
```

A template in `gitlab-ci/` should be short and point to centrally maintained configuration, not contain it:

```yaml
# gitlab-ci/node-service.yml
# Starting point for Node.js services. Do not copy jobs into this file:
# update the pipeline template instead, so every service benefits.
include:
  - project: platform/pipeline-templates
    ref: v3.2.0                       # pin a released version (section 15.2)
    file: templates/node-service.yml
    inputs:
      node_version: "22"
      deploy: true
```

**The key limitation: templates are copied, not linked.** Applying a template copies its contents into the project once. Later changes to the template do not reach projects that already used it. That is why the template above only contains an `include`: the copied part stays trivial, and the real logic lives where it can be updated centrally.

**Related features compared.**

| Feature | What it provides | Updates propagate? | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| Built-in templates (`include:template`) | GitLab's own CI templates, included by reference (section 9.4) | Yes, with GitLab upgrades | All |
| Instance template repository | Organization file templates in the web editor dropdowns | No, copied once | Premium |
| Custom project templates (instance or group) | Whole projects to start new repositories from | No, copied once | Premium |
| `include:project` and CI/CD components | Shared configuration referenced at run time (sections 9.1, 9.3) | Yes, according to the pinned version | All |

The usual pattern combines them: a custom project template or file template gives a new project the right skeleton, and that skeleton references centrally versioned configuration.

**Key takeaways**

- The instance template repository adds organization-specific `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Dockerfile`, `.gitignore` and `LICENSE` templates to the web editor (Premium, self-managed).
- Files go into the `gitlab-ci/`, `Dockerfile/`, `gitignore/` and `LICENSE/` directories of the selected project.
- Templates are copied once. Keep CI templates down to an `include` of centrally maintained configuration.
- These templates are not available through `include:template`, which only serves GitLab's built-in templates.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. *(Beginner)* Create a template project with one file in `gitlab-ci/`, select it as the instance template repository, and apply the template in a new project through the web editor.
> 2. *(Intermediate)* Create a custom project template for a Node.js service that includes a README, a `Dockerfile` and a `.gitlab-ci.yml` with a pinned `include:project`. Create two projects from it and change the central pipeline template. Confirm that both projects pick up the change on their next pipeline.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why is a 300-line `.gitlab-ci.yml` template in the instance template repository a maintenance problem two years later?" *Hint:* copying versus referencing, drift, and how many copies you would have to fix for one security change.

<a id="152-governance-at-scale"></a>
### 15.2 Governance at Scale

With five projects, every team can write its own pipeline. With five hundred, that freedom becomes a cost: the same Docker build is solved forty different ways, a security fix has to be applied in hundreds of places, and nobody can say which projects actually run the mandatory scans. This subchapter covers how a platform team turns pipeline configuration into a product, through shared component libraries, standardized pipeline templates and a centrally run runner fleet, and how it enforces the parts that are not optional. The guiding principle is to make the right way the easy way, and to enforce only what must be enforced.

```text
                 Governance model: pave the road, then guard the edges

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ENFORCE (cannot be removed by projects)                                   │
  │   pipeline execution policies, scan execution policies, approval policies │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ STANDARDIZE (default path, easy to adopt, possible to extend)             │
  │   golden pipeline templates  ──uses──►  component library                 │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ PROVIDE (shared infrastructure)                                           │
  │   instance and group runners, registries, secrets, object storage         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Organization-Wide Component Libraries

**Why it matters.** Section 9.3 explained how to write a single CI/CD component. At organization scale, the challenge is not writing components but *running a library of them*: deciding who owns each one, how versions are released and retired, how teams find them, and how the platform team knows who depends on what. A component library works like an internal standard library for pipelines. It is only useful if people trust it, and they trust it only if it is maintained like a product.

**Structure the library.** A common layout is one group for all components, with one project per domain. Each project can contain several related components and is published to the CI/CD Catalog:

```text
platform/ci-components                         (group, owned by the platform team)
├── build          components: node-build, java-build, go-build, container-image
├── test           components: junit-merge, coverage-gate, e2e-playwright
├── security       components: dependency-audit, sbom, image-sign
├── deploy         components: helm-deploy, k8s-rollout, release-notes
└── catalog-docs   handbook: how to use, contribute, and request components
```

Grouping components by domain, rather than one project per component, keeps the number of projects manageable while still letting each domain release independently. Each project follows the structure from section 9.3: a `templates/` directory, a README with examples for every input, and a pipeline that tests the components and releases them.

**Make ownership and contribution explicit.**

| Concern | Recommended practice |
|---|---|
| Ownership | One owning team per component project, recorded in `CODEOWNERS` and in the README |
| Contributions | Inner source: any team can open a merge request, and the owners review it |
| Versioning | Strict semantic versioning. Renaming or removing an input, or changing a default in a way that changes behavior, is a **major** release |
| Changelog | Every release lists changes and migration steps. The release description appears in the Catalog |
| Deprecation | Announce deprecated inputs or components in the changelog and in job output, support the previous major version for a fixed period (for example 6 months), then archive |
| Quality | Every component has tests that run it in a real pipeline before release (section 9.3) |
| Support | A channel or issue tracker where users report problems, with an agreed response time |

**Choose a version policy for consumers.** How consumers reference a component decides how changes reach them:

```yaml
include:
  # Pinned exact version: nothing changes until someone bumps it (with Renovate or a merge request)
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/platform/ci-components/build/node-build@2.4.1
    inputs:
      node_version: "22"

  # Major version only: receives minor and patch releases automatically
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/platform/ci-components/security/sbom@1

  # Latest release: convenient in experiments, risky in production pipelines
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/platform/ci-components/test/junit-merge@~latest
```

| Reference | Updates arrive | Good for | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@2.4.1` | Only when bumped | Regulated or critical pipelines | Projects fall behind, including on security fixes |
| `@2.4` or `@2` | Automatically, within the minor or major version | Most projects, *if* the library follows semver strictly | A bad release reaches everyone at once |
| `@~latest` | Every release, including majors | Sandboxes, component testing | Breaking changes arrive without warning |
| `@<commit SHA>` | Never | Reproducing an old pipeline exactly | No updates at all |

A practical policy for most organizations is "pin the major version, and the library guarantees semver". Teams with stricter needs pin exact versions and let a bot such as Renovate open merge requests for new releases.

**Self-managed instances and GitLab.com components.** A self-managed Catalog only lists components hosted on that instance. To use a component published on GitLab.com (for example `components/sast`), mirror its project into your instance, then reference the mirrored path. Mirroring also gives you a chance to review what you run.

**Measure adoption.** The Catalog shows how many projects used each component recently. To see exactly which project uses which version, ask GitLab for the resolved includes of each project. The CI Lint API returns the list of included files, components included:

```python
# component_usage.py: which projects in a group include which components, at which version
# Usage: GITLAB_TOKEN=glpat-... python3 component_usage.py acme platform/ci-components
import collections
import os
import sys

import gitlab

group_path, library = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
gl = gitlab.Gitlab("https://gitlab.example.com", private_token=os.environ["GITLAB_TOKEN"])
usage = collections.defaultdict(list)

for ref in gl.groups.get(group_path).projects.list(include_subgroups=True, archived=False, iterator=True):
    project = gl.projects.get(ref.id)
    try:
        lint = project.ci_lint.get()                    # lints the default branch configuration
    except gitlab.GitlabError:
        continue                                        # no pipeline configuration or no access
    for inc in getattr(lint, "includes", []) or []:
        if inc.get("type") == "component" and library in inc.get("location", ""):
            usage[inc["location"]].append(project.path_with_namespace)

for location, projects in sorted(usage.items()):
```
